statement:
You're not going to understand everything right away. Please ask your questions on our class message board! When you ask questions, other students benefit when they read and participate in the conversation. Instructors can also teach better when you ask questions, since it shows your thought process.

Below is the AoPS advice on how to ask a good question:

Most often, we ask others questions to get answers. But at AoPS, we won't just tell you what the next step is or what you need to do in order to get a perfect score. Instead, we'll help you understand the material and ask questions that help you develop your own critical thinking skills. This will allow you to solve the problem on your own.

Some students may find this frustrating because the homework is due that day, and they just want to be told what to do. Please understand that you will not learn as much this way, and we will not just give you the answer or solution.

**Moderate Level Question-Asking: Be Specific**

Statements like "Please help" or "I'm stuck" are very hard to answer. After all, there aren't any details there! These statements will generally get a response of "What do you need help with?" or "What are you stuck on?" or "What don't you understand?"

In order to get help, think carefully about what you're are stuck on and try to tell us about it in your question. Some examples are: "I don't understand what the question means when it says ____." "Can someone explain how (some property) applies to this problem?"

**Expert Level Question-Asking: Providing Background**

In addition to asking specific questions, great questions include some background. If we know about what you have already tried or how you're thinking about the problem, it will help us give better, more relevant tips. Expert-level questions look like this:

"I tried (some approach), but now I'm stuck. Can someone give me a hint?" "It seems like we can use (some property) on this problem. I can tell how it applies ____ but I'm stuck on how it works with ____. Any tips?"

Knowing what you are having trouble with is an important skill to develop. To help us assist you in the best way, try to figure out specifically what is stopping you from moving forward. Try to make your question as specific as possible. We are here to help you, but we need some information to directly respond to your inquiry.

**Getting Started**

Regarding homework questions, AoPS has a general policy that students should get the discussion started. If you tell us you have no idea how to start, we will prompt you to come up with an idea to get the ball rolling. It doesn't even have to be a good idea, but looking at a problem and coming up with ideas is an important problem-solving skill that we want you to practice. After you get in the habit of coming up with ideas, then you can sort out the good ones. __source__

Select the **three** statements that agree with the handbook's viewpoint on asking questions, as applied to a physics class.

Whoever answers the question should tell you the answer to the problem you're trying to solve.

Asking questions can be part of the process of solving a problem.

'"How do I get started on this problem?" is an expert level question

Questions should communicate what specific part of a problem you are stuck on.

It's often helpful to start your question about a problem by saying what laws of physics you think are relevant.

If you're stuck, it's the instructor's responsibility to tell you the first step on a problem to get you going.

statement:
On hot days you can sometimes see __mirages__.

PhysicsStuff.com

The reflection of people walking can make it look like there's a puddle of water on the ground, but there isn't.

A mirage happens when the air just above the ground is much warmer than the air higher up.

PhysicsStuff.com

Under these conditions, light will bend down and then up again, creating the mirage.

Madhav University

The diagram suggests there is a layer of hot air, then a layer of cold air, as if these layers were cleanly separated from each other. In fact, there's a gradient, with the temperature getting continuously cooler the further we go from the ground. A better diagram would show many different layers, or a gradient of color from red to blue indicating temperature.

Remember from class that light takes the path of least time between its starting and end points.

What does this imply about the speed of light through air?

Choose one.

The speed of light is always equal to $$c$$ by definition, so it doesn't imply anything.

The speed of light is faster in hot air than in cold air.

The speed of light is faster in cold air than in hot air.

The speed of light is slower in air than in a vacuum, but the same regardless of the air temperature.

Nothing; the light is pulled down by gravity, not the temperature of the air.

name: We will use __normalized scientific notation__ for both large and small numbers. In this…
desc: We will use __normalized scientific notation__ for both large and small numbers. In this notation, any number can be represented by a number (called the "coefficient") greater than $$1.0$$ and less than $$10,$$ multiplied by ten to some power. For example, here are some numbers…
statement:
We will use __normalized scientific notation__ for both large and small numbers. In this notation, any number can be represented by a number (called the "coefficient") greater than $$1.0$$ and less than $$10,$$ multiplied by ten to some power. For example, here are some numbers written in both the ordinary decimal notation and in normalized scientific notation.

The word "normalized" in "normalized scientific notation" means that the coefficient is greater than or equal to $$1$$ and less than $$10.$$ For example, $$42.1 \times 10^5$$ is in scientific notation, but not normalized scientific notation. In normalized scientific notation, we'd write $$4.21 \times 10^6$$ instead.

$$\begin{tabular}{ r | r } \text{decimal notation} & \text{normalized scientific notation} \\ \hline 350 & $$3.50 \times 10^2\,\,\;$$ \\ 10{,}005 & $$1.0005 \times 10^4\,\,\;$$ \\ 14.3 & $$1.43 \times 10^1\,\,\;$$ \\ 578{,}240.92 & $$5.7824092 \times 10^5\,\,\;$$\\ 0.00037 & $$3.7 \times 10^{-4}$$ \end{tabular}$$

If you would like a tutorial on scientific notation, there is one available on the class homepage.

We also want to report the results of our calculations to an appropriate number of __significant figures__.

For example, if a problem says that something travels $$2.2 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$0.91 \;\mathrm{s},$$ it's reasonable to give the object's speed as $$2.4 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ but the precise calculation giving $$\dfrac{2.2 \;\mathrm{m}}{0.91 \;\mathrm{s}} = 2.417582\ldots \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ has digits that aren't meaningful, since the original measurements are not known to that level of detail.

In a lab report or scientific document, adding the extra digits could confuse the reader by making them think your data was far more precise than it really was. As a guideline, give your calculations to the same number of digits as used in the data.

--------------------

The speed of sound is usually faster in solids than in air. It's especially fast in beryllium, a rare metal that is exceptionally stiff and light. Beryllium is sometimes used when weight is extremely important, for example in satellites. A sample of beryllium looks like this:

By Alchemist-hp = Alchemist-hp (pse-mendelejew.de) - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=4283181

Suppose a student wants to find the speed of sound $$v$$ through a sample of beryllium. Using a micrometer (a device for precise distance measurements) and electronic timing equipment, they measure that sound travels $$1.08 \times 10^{-1} \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$8.51 \times 10^{-6} \;\mathrm{s}.$$ What speed of sound do they compute?

Give your answer in normalized scientific notation and to an appropriate number of significant figures.

statement:
In this problem, you'll practice __estimation__ and __unit conversions__. These are both essential skills that we'll use throughout the course.

--------

Estimate the average speed at which human hair grows in miles per hour.

There is no one answer to this question - different hairs grow at different rates, and grow unsteadily. Still, there is a range which is approximately correct. To be marked correct on this question you should be within one An __order of magnitude__ is a factor of ten, so your answer can be ten times as fast as ours, or ten times as slow, or anywhere between those limits. of our estimate.

In physics, when we estimate, we don't just guess our final answer. Instead, we start with something we know and work from there. Try to estimate the speed that hair grows based on some life experience you have, and use whatever units are most convenient. Then convert your units to miles per hour.

Here are a few conversion factors that could help:

$$\begin{aligned} 2.54 \;\mathrm{cm} & = 1 \;\mathrm{in} \\ 12 \;\mathrm{in} & = 1 \;\mathrm{ft} \\ 5280 \;\mathrm{ft} & = 1 \;\mathrm{mi} \\ \end{aligned}$$

You may also want to use conversion factors related to hours, days, months, or years.

Enter your answer using normalized scientific notation, meaning that the coefficient should be greater than or equal to one and less than ten.

statement:
In this problem, you'll practice the notation and interpretation of speed and velocity.

-------------------------

Below is a sketch of an __Atwood machine__, an 18th century invention intended to measure the strength of gravity. The device consists of a pulley (a circular ring that can easily spin, but otherwise can't move around left/right or up/down), a rope that goes over the pulley, and weights on either side of the rope. The box $$H$$ is heavier than the box $$L.$$

The weights are initially held with $$L$$ down low and $$H$$ up high, then released. $$H$$ will start falling downward, and it will pull on the rope as it falls, which pulls $$L$$ upward.

To help you visualize this motion, look at this gif:

"Low Friction Atwood Machine", mittechtv, YouTube

(In this gif one of the weights has some slight side-to-side wobble, which you should ignore. Model the motion as purely in the up/down direction.)

Let the velocity of the heavier box be $$v_{y;H}$$ and the lighter box $$v_{y;L}.$$ The speeds are $$v_H$$ and $$v_L.$$ We define the upward direction to be positive, so upward motion is a positive velocity.

One second after the boxes are released, we measure the velocities $$v_{y;H}$$ and $$v_{y;L}.$$ (The boxes don't hit the ground or reach the pulley in this one second.)

Which statements below are true? Select two.

You do not need to find the values of $$v_{y;H}$$ or $$v_{y;L},$$ or make any quantitative measurements, to answer this question.

Note that statements (a) and (b) are about velocities. (c) through (e) are about speeds.

$$v_{y;L} = - v_{y;H}$$

$$v_{y;L} = v_{y;H}$$

$$v_H > v_L$$

$$v_H < v_L$$

$$v_H = v_L$$

Ayesha McGowan is a professional road racing cyclist.

Jeff Clark, https://www.liv-cycling.com/global/campaigns/representation-matters-ayesha-mcgowan/23833

In 2021, McGowan competed in a multi-day race near Avignon, France. The race took her into the western portion of the Alps mountain range. As you would expect, she rode relatively slowly when climbing steep mountains and very fast when coming down.

McGowan's bike has a computer that records its speed. After her rides, McGowan shares data on her speed versus time, along with some other data, publicly on the internet. Below is a plot of some of Ayesha's data during one day of the race. Time is indicated along the top. The total time was close to four hours.

How far did McGowan ride this day?

Your answer should be accurate to within $$20 \;\mathrm{mi}.$$

We haven't worked on a problem like this yet, but you can still do it! Start by finding McGowan's average speed as closely as you can based on the graph.

Take a look at the following dot diagram. The dots were made $$1 \;\mathrm{s}$$ apart, and the scale is $$1:1,$$ so the dots' distance apart on your computer monitor is their distance apart in real life.

The dots should display the correct distance apart on most computers. However, if your browser is not set to a $$100\%$$ zoom, or for various other reasons, it's possible the dots will not display correctly for you. The distance between the last two dots should be about $$3.9 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$ If it is not, you can multiply all your distances by a scaling factor to answer this question. For example, if you measure that distance to be $$3.0 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ you can multiply all your measurements by $$\dfrac{3.9 \;\mathrm{cm}}{3.0 \;\mathrm{cm}} = 1.3$$

**a)**

Did the object modeled by this dot diagram have positive or negative velocity? How do you know? If it's impossible to tell, explain why.

statement:
In August 2022, a woman in Vancouver rented a car for three days. When she returned it, the rental company billed her more than $$\$9{,}000.$$ The company said its rate was $$\dfrac{\$0.25}{\mathrm{km}}$$ and that she had driven $$36{,}482\;\mathrm{km}$$ during the rental.

Show that this bill cannot describe a real trip by finding the average speed the car would need to cover $$36{,}482\;\mathrm{km}$$ in three days, and converting that speed into everyday units. What most likely happened?

Useful facts: there are $$24\;\mathrm{h}$$ in a day, $$5\;\mathrm{km}\approx 3\;\mathrm{mi},$$ and Earth's circumference is about $$40{,}000\;\mathrm{km}.$$

desc: You want to measure a cyclist's speed from a video. The video plays at $$20$$ frames per second. By comparing the bicycle to a known length — its __wheelbase__ of $$0.977\;\mathrm{m}$$ — you can turn pixel measurements in the video into real distances. In the video, the…
statement:
You want to measure a cyclist's speed from a video. The video plays at $$20$$ frames per second. By comparing the bicycle to a known length — its __wheelbase__ of $$0.977\;\mathrm{m}$$ — you can turn pixel measurements in the video into real distances.

In the video, the wheelbase measures $$65$$ pixels. Between frame $$18$$ and frame $$20,$$ the bicycle's front wheel advances $$47$$ pixels along the road.

__(a)__ How far, in meters, did the bicycle move between frame 18 and frame 20?

__(b)__ How much time elapsed between those two frames?

__(c)__ What was the cyclist's average speed over this interval?

__(d)__ Suppose the $$47$$-pixel measurement could be off by as much as $$2$$ pixels. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the distance, and write the speed in the form (value) $$\pm$$ (uncertainty).

statement:
A skater rides back and forth on a curved ramp. We describe her location with a coordinate $$x$$ measured __along the track__ from the left edge. The simulation marks the track with evenly spaced dashes — $$4$$ dashes per meter — numbered starting from the left edge.

__(a)__ In the picture above, the skater is at dash $$10.$$ What is her coordinate $$x$$ (her distance from the left edge, measured along the track)?

__(b)__ Explain the difference between the skater's __position__ and her __coordinate__.

__(c)__ Now suppose we move the origin so that $$x=0$$ is at the lowest point of the ramp instead of the left edge, giving a new coordinate $$x'$$ (shown below). For each of the following, state whether it changes: her position, her coordinate, her speed, and her displacement between two instants.

__(d)__ Her average velocity between two instants is $$v_x=\dfrac{x_2-x_1}{t_2-t_1}=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}.$$ If she is moving to the left (toward smaller $$x$$), what is the sign of $$v_x$$? How are her speed $$v$$ and her velocity $$v_x$$ related?

label: MCH01
name: The Speed of Light — In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rapidly spinning toothed…
desc: In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rapidly spinning toothed wheel (a __cog__) and a distant mirror. Light passes through a gap between two teeth, travels to a mirror $$8.0\;\mathrm{km}$$ away, and reflects straight back toward the wheel. If the wheel…
statement:
In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rapidly spinning toothed wheel (a __cog__) and a distant mirror. Light passes through a gap between two teeth, travels to a mirror $$8.0\;\mathrm{km}$$ away, and reflects straight back toward the wheel.

If the wheel turns slowly, the light returns through the same gap and is seen. Fizeau sped the wheel up until, at $$13.7$$ revolutions per second, the returning light was just blocked: while the light made its round trip, the wheel turned just far enough for the next __tooth__ to move into the gap's place.

The wheel has $$720$$ teeth (and $$720$$ gaps between them). Find Fizeau's value for the speed of light, $$c.$$

Hint: with $$720$$ teeth and $$720$$ gaps there are $$1440$$ equal segments around the wheel. Being blocked by the next tooth means the wheel rotated by exactly one of these segments during the light's round trip.

label: MCH01
name: Bending Light — Light travels more slowly through glass than through empty space. In a typical glass it…
desc: Light travels more slowly through glass than through empty space. In a typical glass it moves at about $$0.7c,$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light in vacuum (about $$3\times10^8\;\mathrm{m/s}$$). Consider a beam of light that goes from a point $$A$$ in vacuum to a point $$B$$…
statement:
Light travels more slowly through glass than through empty space. In a typical glass it moves at about $$0.7c,$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light in vacuum (about $$3\times10^8\;\mathrm{m/s}$$).

Consider a beam of light that goes from a point $$A$$ in vacuum to a point $$B$$ inside a glass block. It could follow many different paths; physicists model light as taking the __path of least time__. The figure below shows $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and two possible paths: a straight dashed path and a bent solid path.

__(a)__ The straight-line path from $$A$$ to $$B$$ is the shortest in distance. Give a reason it might __not__ be the path of least time.

__(b)__ Use __extreme cases__ to build intuition: predict the kind of path light takes (i) if the glass slowed light a billion-fold, and (ii) if the glass slowed light by only a tiny amount (say $$0.00001\%$$).

__(c)__ Using the least-time idea, explain why light __bends__ (refracts) as it crosses from vacuum into glass.

__(d)__ A lens is a piece of glass shaped so that __every__ path from $$A$$ to $$B$$ takes the same amount of time, as in the figure below. Explain what this does to the light.

label: MCH01
name: Distant Galaxies — Astronomers find that essentially every distant galaxy is moving __away__ from us, and…
desc: Astronomers find that essentially every distant galaxy is moving __away__ from us, and that a galaxy's recession speed $$v$$ is proportional to its distance $$D$$ from us: $$v=H_0\,D,$$ where $$H_0$$ is a constant (the __Hubble constant__). The graph below shows this pattern —…
statement:
Astronomers find that essentially every distant galaxy is moving __away__ from us, and that a galaxy's recession speed $$v$$ is proportional to its distance $$D$$ from us: $$v=H_0\,D,$$ where $$H_0$$ is a constant (the __Hubble constant__). The graph below shows this pattern — each point is a galaxy, and galaxies that are farther away recede faster.

To interpret this law, work a toy model with simple numbers. Take $$H_0=0.5\;\dfrac{\mathrm{m/s}}{\mathrm{m}}$$ (half a meter per second, per meter), and assume each object has always moved at a constant speed.

__(a)__ An object is $$D=3\;\mathrm{m}$$ away. Find its speed $$v,$$ and how long ago it was at our location.

__(b)__ Repeat for an object $$D=4\;\mathrm{m}$$ away.

__(c)__ Now take a general distance $$D.$$ Show that the time since the object was at our location is the same for __every__ object, and express that time using $$H_0.$$

__(d)__ What is the physical meaning of $$\dfrac{1}{H_0},$$ and what surprising conclusion does this simple model suggest about the past of the universe?

statement:
This problem asks you to think qualitatively about acceleration and free fall. You'll visualize acceleration using a free falling stick.

-------------------------------

There is a challenge that many people find surprising: hold a dollar bill vertically and invite a friend to put two fingers on either side of it, near the bottom, ready to grab the dollar bill.

Chegg, https://www.chegg.com/homework-help/questions-and-answers/classic-trick-person-1-hangs-dollar-bill-hand-dangles-fingers-person-2-person-1-releases-b-q31489919

Ask your friend to try to catch the dollar after you drop it, but without moving their hand down. (This is pretty fun - try it yourself with a friend of family member!)

Free fall acceleration is high enough that almost no one can react quickly enough to catch the dollar.

Suppose you want to modify this idea to measure your friend's reaction time. Instead of dropping a dollar, you'll drop a stick that's long enough that your friend will be able to catch it.

You know $$g,$$ the local free fall acceleration, so you can calculate how the stick will fall. You put marks on the stick labeled with times in such a way that when your friend grabs it, their fingers are at a mark corresponding to their reaction time.

For example, if your friend's reaction time is $$0.25 \;\mathrm{s},$$ then when they catch the stick, their fingers will be on top of a mark on the stick labeled $$``0.25 \;\mathrm{s}".$$ Your markings will correspond to reaction times of $$0.05 \;\mathrm{s}, 0.10 \;\mathrm{s}, 0.15 \;\mathrm{s}$$ etc. starting at the bottom of the stick and increasing up to the top.

Which of the following shows the correct spacing between the marks on the stick?

statement:
On their wedding day, a couple jumped off a cliff into water below. (As a celebration, not out of despair.)

Zvonimir Barisin

There's another photo taken just before they hit the water. In this question, we'll try to figure out what that photo looks like. (That photo is included in the solution.) This gives us more qualitative practice with free fall acceleration.

-----------------------------------

To model the jump of bride and groom off a cliff, we make some simplifications: - assume they both are falling vertically from the same height, but the bride started falling a moment before the groom - ignore air drag - ignore that they are holding hands - model each person as a point at their __center of mass__. This is intuively the center spot of a person. When standing, it's roughly few inches behind the belly button

Then we can define a few terms related to the gap between bride and groom:

__separation:__ how far beneath the groom the bride is __speed gap__: the difference in speed between the bride and groom __acceleration gap__: the difference in magnitude of acceleration between the bride and groom __time gap__: the time between the bride reaching a certain height and the groom reaching that same height

As the couple fell and before they hit the water, these quantities may have changed. **Categorize each according to whether it increased, stayed the same, or decreased.** Categories can hold multiple quantities, and categories are allowed to be empty. Every quantity needs to go in one category.

Reflecting on your answers, try to guess what the photo taken just before they hit the water looks like.

----------------------------

Suppose you are watching a video of an object undergoing constant acceleration. The video is playing back in slow motion, but you didn't know that. You can make accurate distance measurements, but all of your time measurements are wrong because the video is playing back at $$\dfrac12$$ speed, but you thought it was playing at normal speed.

Suppose the real magnitude of acceleration of the object being filmed was $$a.$$ What magnitude of acceleration will you find after making and analyzing your measurements?

You should put a number in the box below. For example, if the magnitude of acceleration you find is ten times the real magnitude of acceleration the object had, you should put $$10$$ in the box.

Part A. In this multi-part problem, you'll build a model to understand the relative importance between fast reaction time and safe speed when driving. The first part guides you on how to get a model ready for analysis, and the second part asks the question we're interested in about driving.

The difficulty of the problem set is starting to increase around here, so expect to think longer and make some false starts on the later problems. The harder you work on a problem, the better it feels to finally solve it. Remember that after you've given a problem some thought, the message boards are there for discussion.

--------

A car is moving at velocity $$v_{x0}$$ along the positive $$x$$ direction. The driver needs to stop suddenly.

Then: 1) The car will continue at its original velocity $$v_{x0}$$ for a short time $$t_r$$ until the driver hits the brakes. $$t_r$$ is the driver's reaction time. 2) The car will get slower and slower as the driver presses the brakes. The acceleration is $$a_x.$$ Eventually the car stops.

During the second phase, constant acceleration is a fairly good model for most cars.

Note that $$v_{x0} >0$$ and $$a_x < 0$$ due to the directions of motion and acceleration.

Below is a plot of $$v_x,$$ over time in this model, beginning at the moment the driver sees a problem and ending shortly after the car stops.

Find the distance $$\Delta x$$ the car moves before stopping in terms of $$v_{x0}, t_r,$$ and $$a_x.$$

Part B. Young people generally have somewhat faster reaction times than elderly people.

Suppose that an elderly driver drives at $$v_{x0; \mathrm{elderly}} = 25 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (about $$56 \;\mathrm{mph})$$ and the distance they need to come to a complete stop is $$\Delta x = 60 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

A cocky young driver thinks their faster reaction time allows them to drive safely at a higher speed. Assume the reaction times are $$t_{r;\mathrm{elderly}} = 0.6 \;\mathrm{s}$$ for the elderly driver and $$t_{r;\mathrm{young}} = 0.4 \;\mathrm{s}$$ for the young driver, and that $$a_x$$ is the same for each driver.

The young driver needs to stop in the same distance, $$\Delta x = 60 \;\mathrm{m},$$ as the elderly driver. What is the maximum possible initial speed $$v_{x0;\mathrm{young}}$$ for the young driver such that they can still stop within a distance $$\Delta x?$$

Use the model you developed in the previous question to answer this one. Your answer should be accurate to within $$0.5 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

This is one of the later problems on the set, and it's a multi-step problem that is probably going to take you little time, plus at least a sheet full of scratch work. It's okay to make false starts on problems like these, and a great idea to discuss them in the homework forum after you've worked on them a bit. Our homeworks will generally start with short problems you might be able to do in one step and build towards more complex problems like this one.

You won't be able to take a couple of numbers from the problem, put them in a single equation, and get the answer. Instead, first work on making a __plan__ for how you'll solve the problem. For example, ask yourself whether there is some quantity you could calculate which isn't the answer, but would be helpful in finding the answer.

The acceleration $$a_x$$ is something like that, so you could break the problem down into: 1) Use the given information to find $$a_x$$ 2) Use $$a_x$$ to figure out $$v_{x0;\mathrm{young}}$$ You may need to break those steps down further as well to figure out how you're going to find $$a_x$$ and what you're going to do with it once you have it.

statement:
Part A. In this multi-part problem, you'll practice several stages of conducting an experiment, including understanding what the experiment is for, building a model of what happens in the experiment, deciding what data to collect, deciding how to analyze that data, and drawing conclusions from the experiment.

-----------------------------------

An __Atwood machine__ is a rope with weights on either end. The rope hangs over a pulley. The weights usually have different mass, and the more massive weight accelerates towards the ground while the less massive weight accelerates upward.

"Low Friction Atwood Machine", mittechtv, YouTube

You can assume the weights move with constant acceleration and that they are released from rest.

We can use an Atwood machine to measure $$g,$$ assuming we have a model of the acceleration of the machine that includes $$g.$$ Later, we will build such a model, but we'll ignore complications like the weight of the string or friction in the pulley.

A different experiment to measure $$g$$ is simply to drop an object and time how long it takes to fall. There are several differences between this free fall experiment and an experiment using the Atwood machine.

Most of these differences make the Atwood experiment more accurate than the free fall experiment, but one does not. **Select the one difference that makes the Atwood machine __less__ accurate than a similar free fall experiment.**

You can assume that in both experiments, the times are being taken by a single person with a stopwatch.

There is friction in the pulley of the Atwood machine, but negligible friction in free fall (because air drag is very small). Assume our models do not account for friction.

The Atwood machine has a much lower acceleration than free fall.

We can take data with many different sets of weights in the Atwood machine. This gives different accelerations. In free fall, all weights have the same acceleration.

In the Atwood machine, we can release the lighter weight from ground level and find the time for the heavier weight to reach the ground. This makes the starting and ending points we're timing right next to each other, rather than far apart as for free fall.

Part B. Before we try an experiment with the Atwood machine, we should understand how we expect it to behave. A good way to start building our intuition for it is to think about extreme cases, or special cases. These are special values of the weights such that the behavior of the Atwood machine is easier to understand.

There are two extreme / special cases we should check: equal masses and very uneven masses.

We can call the mass of the heavier box $$m_H$$ and the mass of the lighter box $$m_L.$$ Then the equal masses special case is $$m_H = m_L.$$ The very uneven masses extreme case is $$m_H \gg m_L.$$ You can imagine that the heavier box has the mass of an entire mountain (but somehow still fits in the same size box) and the lighter box has the mass of a single flea.

What should the magnitude of acceleration of the Atwood machine be in each case?

Part C. Now we'll try to select a model for the acceleration of the Atwood machine.

In the Atwood machine, if we double $$m_H$$ and also double $$m_L,$$ it's as if we simply had two copies of the Atwood machine right next to each other, with the masses lightly touching. The two copies would each run with the same acceleration as each other, so doubling each mass in this way doesn't affect the acceleration.

Extending this argument, it's only the ratio of masses, $$\dfrac{m_L}{m_H},$$ that affects the acceleration. We can call this ratio $$r.$$

$$r$$ is always between zero and one, since by definition the denominator is bigger than the numerator.

Part F. In this optional discussion problem, you conduct the experiment at home, share your results, and discuss your and other experiments with your classmates.

---------

If you would like to do some hands on experimentation, build your own Atwood machine at home. You are welcome to buy a pulley, but you could also run some string over any smooth rod with low friction. If you can wrap a portion of a broom handle in Teflon tape, that may make a low-friction surface to support your rope. You could also try making your own pulley using instructions you find online.

A stack of coins makes a convenient way to adjust the masses in your Atwood machine.

If you collect data, find accelerations, plot them, and find $$g,$$ share how you made your Atwood machine and your plot to the class forum. You can also see what other students did and compare results and techniques.

If you are having trouble finding suitable materials, you could also take data using a simulated Atwood machine, such as this one: (http://physics.bu.edu/~duffy/HTML5/Atwoods_machine.html)

name: The Shanghai Tower Elevator — Shanghai Tower is a skyscraper $$632\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall. Its high-speed…
desc: Shanghai Tower is a skyscraper $$632\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall. Its high-speed elevator has a display that shows your current height, so a rider can collect data during the trip. Watching the display, you see the elevator rise $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ in the first $$5.2\;\mathrm{s}$$ of the…
statement:
Shanghai Tower is a skyscraper $$632\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall. Its high-speed elevator has a display that shows your current height, so a rider can collect data during the trip. Watching the display, you see the elevator rise $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ in the first $$5.2\;\mathrm{s}$$ of the ride.

__(a)__ Assume the elevator's height is proportional to time, so that $$\dfrac{10\;\mathrm{m}}{5.2\;\mathrm{s}}=\dfrac{630\;\mathrm{m}}{t}.$$ Under that assumption, how long should it take the elevator to rise the full $$630\;\mathrm{m}$$ to the top?

__(b)__ In reality the elevator reaches the top in just $$55\;\mathrm{s}.$$ What was wrong with the assumption in part (a)?

__(c)__ The figure below is a __motion diagram__ for the ride: a dot marks the elevator's position at equal time intervals, and an arrow points from each dot to the next. The arrows show the direction of motion. What does the __length__ of each arrow represent?

__(d)__ Velocity is the rate of change of position. Using $$y$$ as a vertical coordinate, the average velocity is $$v_{y;\mathrm{avg}}=\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta t}.$$ When an object's velocity is changing, the object has __acceleration__ — the rate of change of velocity. By analogy with the velocity formula, write a formula for the average acceleration $$a_{y;\mathrm{avg}}.$$

__(e)__ Near the top, the elevator slows down before stopping. In everyday speech people call this "deceleration." In physics, is the elevator accelerating while it slows down?

__(f)__ The elevator is at rest both at the start and at the end of the $$55\;\mathrm{s}$$ ride. Compute the average acceleration over the __entire__ ride. The elevator clearly did accelerate during the trip — how can your answer be consistent with that?

label: MCH02
name: Reading the Elevator's Velocity Graph — The graph below shows the velocity $$v_y$$ of the Shanghai Tower…
desc: The graph below shows the velocity $$v_y$$ of the Shanghai Tower elevator during its $$55\;\mathrm{s}$$ trip up the building (the positive direction is up). The velocity rises steadily from $$0$$ to $$18\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ during the first $$20\;\mathrm{s},$$ stays at…
statement:
The graph below shows the velocity $$v_y$$ of the Shanghai Tower elevator during its $$55\;\mathrm{s}$$ trip up the building (the positive direction is up). The velocity rises steadily from $$0$$ to $$18\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ during the first $$20\;\mathrm{s},$$ stays at $$18\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ until $$35\;\mathrm{s},$$ and then falls steadily back to $$0$$ at $$55\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Recall that the average acceleration is $$a_{y;\mathrm{avg}}=\dfrac{\Delta v_y}{\Delta t}.$$

__(a)__ According to the graph, at what times is the elevator moving upward? What would the graph look like during a portion of a trip where the elevator moves downward?

__(b)__ Acceleration has the units of velocity divided by the units of time. What are the units of acceleration, and what are they called?

__(c)__ Find the average acceleration of the elevator between $$35\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$55\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Then interpret $$\Delta v_y,$$ $$\Delta t,$$ and $$a_{y;\mathrm{avg}}$$ as features of the graph.

__(d)__ What is the acceleration between $$20\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$35\;\mathrm{s}?$$

__(e)__ An object's acceleration is positive. Is its __speed__ increasing or decreasing? (Careful — the question asks about speed, not velocity.) Use a velocity versus time graph to justify your answer.

__(f)__ An elevator has __negative__ acceleration and __increasing__ speed. Describe in detail what the elevator is doing.

label: MCH02
name: A Faster Elevator and a Trip to Andromeda — The Shanghai Tower elevator climbs $$H=630\;\mathrm{m}$$ in…
desc: The Shanghai Tower elevator climbs $$H=630\;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$55\;\mathrm{s}.$$ It speeds up with acceleration of magnitude $$a_0=0.9\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ cruises at constant velocity for a while, then slows down with the same magnitude of acceleration. Imagine redesigning the…
statement:
The Shanghai Tower elevator climbs $$H=630\;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$55\;\mathrm{s}.$$ It speeds up with acceleration of magnitude $$a_0=0.9\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ cruises at constant velocity for a while, then slows down with the same magnitude of acceleration. Imagine redesigning the ride to get rid of the constant-speed section: the elevator accelerates at $$a_0$$ for the first half of the trip and decelerates at $$a_0$$ for the second half, so its velocity versus time graph is an upside-down V. Call the maximum speed $$v_{\rm max}$$ and the total trip time $$t_{\rm tot}.$$

__(a)__ During the first half, the speed climbs steadily from $$0$$ to $$v_{\rm max}.$$ What is the average speed for the whole trip, in terms of $$v_{\rm max}?$$ Use it to write the height as $$H=v_{\rm avg}\,t_{\rm tot}.$$

__(b)__ The acceleration $$a_0$$ is the slope of the first half of the velocity graph, which rises by $$v_{\rm max}$$ over a time $$\dfrac{t_{\rm tot}}{2}.$$ Use this to express $$v_{\rm max}$$ in terms of $$a_0$$ and $$t_{\rm tot}.$$

__(c)__ Combine parts (a) and (b) to find $$t_{\rm tot}$$ in terms of $$H$$ and $$a_0.$$ Then evaluate it for the Shanghai Tower. How much time does eliminating the cruise section actually save, compared with the real $$55\;\mathrm{s}$$ ride?

__(d)__ Now imagine a super skyscraper __nine times__ as tall, with the same $$a_0.$$ Without plugging all the numbers back in, use the __proportionality__ $$t_{\rm tot}\propto\sqrt{H}$$ to find the trip time. Then explain intuitively why nine times the height takes only three times the time.

__(e)__ Finally, take the same speed-up-then-slow-down trip to the Andromeda galaxy, a distance of $$2.4\times10^{22}\;\mathrm{m},$$ with the same $$a_0=0.9\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Use the proportionality again to find the trip time in years. Light takes more than $$2{,}500{,}000$$ years to reach Andromeda, and nothing travels faster than light. What does that tell you about our constant-acceleration model?

label: MCH02

statement:
NASA's Space Power Facility in Ohio is a chamber $$37\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall from which nearly all the air can be pumped out, used for testing space equipment. For a TV show, NASA dropped a bowling ball and a feather side by side from the top of the chamber — once with the air still in the room, and once after pumping the air out.

__(a)__ With air in the room (shown above), which object hits the floor first, and why?

__(b)__ With the air removed (shown above, in slow motion), the result changes. What happens, and what general principle about falling objects does it demonstrate?

__(c)__ Three hypotheses for how objects move while falling: (1) they fall at a constant speed — "the speed of gravity"; (2) they fall with constant acceleration; (3) they fall with bigger and bigger acceleration over time. Use everyday experience to rule out hypothesis (1). (Hint: think about an apple falling on your head from $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ versus from $$100\;\mathrm{m}.$$)

__(d)__ The standard model of free fall is that all objects accelerate toward Earth with the same constant acceleration, whose magnitude is called $$g.$$ Roughly what is the value of $$g,$$ and is it exactly the same everywhere on Earth?

label: MCH02
name: A Scale in an Elevator — A person stands on a bathroom scale while riding an elevator and films the scale's…
desc: A person stands on a bathroom scale while riding an elevator and films the scale's display. Before the elevator moves, the scale reads about $$124\;\mathrm{lbs}.$$ For roughly the first $$2.5\;\mathrm{s}$$ of the ride the reading climbs to about $$130\;\mathrm{lbs},$$ then it…
statement:
A person stands on a bathroom scale while riding an elevator and films the scale's display. Before the elevator moves, the scale reads about $$124\;\mathrm{lbs}.$$ For roughly the first $$2.5\;\mathrm{s}$$ of the ride the reading climbs to about $$130\;\mathrm{lbs},$$ then it returns to $$124\;\mathrm{lbs}$$ for most of the trip, and for the final $$2.5\;\mathrm{s}$$ it dips below normal before the elevator stops. The whole ride lasts about $$14\;\mathrm{s}.$$

Useful background: you can feel acceleration, but not velocity. When something accelerates you with magnitude $$a,$$ it feels exactly as if there were extra gravity of strength $$a$$ pulling you in the direction __opposite__ the acceleration — this is the __equivalence principle__, which Einstein used in inventing general relativity. So a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at $$a$$ reads heavier than normal by the fraction $$\dfrac{a}{g}.$$ Take $$g\approx10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ Was the elevator going up or down? Explain using the scale readings.

__(b)__ Estimate the magnitude of the elevator's acceleration from the change in the scale reading.

__(c)__ The graph below models the elevator's acceleration $$a_y$$ over time: $$+0.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ from $$0$$ to $$2.5\;\mathrm{s},$$ zero from $$2.5\;\mathrm{s}$$ to $$11.5\;\mathrm{s},$$ and $$-0.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ from $$11.5\;\mathrm{s}$$ to $$14\;\mathrm{s}.$$ The change in velocity over any interval is the __signed area__ between the acceleration curve and the horizontal axis (area below the axis counts as negative). Use this to find the elevator's cruising speed $$v_{\rm max}$$ during the middle of the ride.

__(d)__ Sketch the resulting velocity versus time graph. The elevator's displacement is the signed area between the __velocity__ curve and the horizontal axis. Use it to estimate how far the elevator rose during the whole ride.

__(e)__ A floor of a building is typically about $$4.3\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall. If the rider got on at the first floor, what floor did they most likely get off on?

label: MCH02
name: Measuring g with a Popping Balloon — Here is an experiment to test whether free fall is constant acceleration…
desc: Here is an experiment to test whether free fall is constant acceleration — and to measure that acceleration. A weight hangs from a balloon in a stand. When the balloon is popped, the bang starts a timer on a smartphone, and at that same moment the weight begins to fall. When the…
statement:
Here is an experiment to test whether free fall is constant acceleration — and to measure that acceleration. A weight hangs from a balloon in a stand. When the balloon is popped, the bang starts a timer on a smartphone, and at that same moment the weight begins to fall. When the weight lands on a metal plate, the second bang stops the timer. The drop height $$h$$ is measured with a ruler, and the experiment is repeated for several heights.

The heights $$h$$ (the __independent variable__, set by the experimenters) and fall times $$t_{\rm fall}$$ (the __dependent variable__, measured) were: $$\begin{array}{c|c} h\;(\mathrm{m}) & t_{\rm fall}\;(\mathrm{s}) \\ \hline 0.70 & 0.38 \\ 0.95 & 0.43 \\ 1.20 & 0.49 \\ 1.45 & 0.54 \\ 1.70 & 0.58 \\ 1.95 & 0.63 \\ 2.20 & 0.66 \\ 2.45 & 0.70 \end{array}$$

__(a)__ Suppose free fall has constant acceleration of magnitude $$g.$$ Then a velocity versus time graph for the falling weight is a straight line starting at zero with slope $$-g$$ (taking up as positive), so the average speed during the fall is half the final speed. Show that this hypothesis predicts $$h=\tfrac12 g\,t_{\rm fall}^2,$$ or equivalently $$t_{\rm fall}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}.$$

__(b)__ One way to test the hypothesis is to plot $$t_{\rm fall}$$ against $$h$$ and draw a straight line through the points. When the experimenters did this, the line passed close to the points, but it crossed the vertical axis at $$(0,\,0.26\;\mathrm{s}),$$ and the points started below the line, drifted above it in the middle, and dropped below again at the end. Explain why both observations show that a straight line is the wrong model here.

__(c)__ Since the hypothesis says $$t_{\rm fall}\propto\sqrt{h},$$ a better idea is to plot $$t_{\rm fall}$$ against $$\sqrt{h}$$ instead. (The square roots of the heights are $$0.84,$$ $$0.98,$$ $$1.10,$$ $$1.20,$$ $$1.30,$$ $$1.40,$$ $$1.48,$$ $$1.57$$ in units of $$\sqrt{\mathrm{m}}.$$) The result is shown below. What should this plot look like if the constant-acceleration hypothesis is right, and does it?

__(d)__ The best-fit line through the data passes through the origin with slope $$c=0.445\;\dfrac{\mathrm{s}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{m}}}.$$ According to the model in part (a), what should the slope of this line be in terms of $$g?$$ Use the measured slope to find $$g.$$

desc: Football player Josh Imatorbhebhe's famous vertical jump was caught on video with a running timer. The first frame in which his feet have left the ground reads $$1.41\;\mathrm{s},$$ and the first frame in which he touches down again reads $$2.31\;\mathrm{s}.$$ While he is in the…
statement:
Football player Josh Imatorbhebhe's famous vertical jump was caught on video with a running timer. The first frame in which his feet have left the ground reads $$1.41\;\mathrm{s},$$ and the first frame in which he touches down again reads $$2.31\;\mathrm{s}.$$ While he is in the air, he is in free fall with acceleration of magnitude $$g=9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ downward. An object falling from rest for a time $$t$$ drops a distance $$h=\tfrac12 g t^2.$$

__(a)__ While Imatorbhebhe is rising, what is his acceleration (sign and magnitude)? What is his acceleration at the very top of the jump, where he is momentarily stationary?

__(b)__ Explain why the time he spends going up equals the time he spends coming down, and use that to find his fall time $$t_{\rm fall}$$ from the timer readings.

__(c)__ How high did he rise after leaving the ground?

__(d)__ The frame timing could be off by a frame or so, so $$t_{\rm fall}$$ might reasonably be $$0.44\;\mathrm{s}$$ or $$0.46\;\mathrm{s}$$ instead of $$0.45\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Recompute the height with those times and use the results to attach an uncertainty to your answer, writing it as (value) $$\pm$$ (uncertainty).

__(e)__ The officially measured vertical jump was $$47.1$$ inches, which is $$1.196\;\mathrm{m}$$ — well outside your uncertainty range. The physics and the timing are fine. Look at the takeoff photo: his toes are still pointed at the ground but his heels are high. Resolve the discrepancy.

label: MCH02
name: Olympic Divers — Olympic high divers step off a platform $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the water. A second…
desc: Olympic high divers step off a platform $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the water. A second event uses a springboard only $$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the water, but springboard divers bounce a considerable height upward before falling. Treat the divers as being in free fall once in the…
statement:
Olympic high divers step off a platform $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the water. A second event uses a springboard only $$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the water, but springboard divers bounce a considerable height upward before falling. Treat the divers as being in free fall once in the air, with $$g\approx10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ In free fall from rest, the fall time from a height $$h$$ is $$t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}},$$ and the speed grows by $$g$$ every second ($$v=g\,t$$).

__(a)__ Estimate how fast a high diver is going when they enter the water after stepping off the $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ platform. (First find the time of the fall, then the speed.)

__(b)__ Give at least two reasons this estimate might be somewhat inaccurate for a real dive.

__(c)__ A springboard diver jumps to a height $$h$$ __above the springboard__, so they rise for a time $$t_{\rm rise}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$$ and then fall a total distance $$h+3\;\mathrm{m}$$ to the water. (The rise formula is the same as the fall formula: either way, the speed runs steadily between zero and a maximum with acceleration $$g.$$) Write an equation for the jump height $$h$$ that gives the springboard diver the same total air time as the $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ platform dive, and verify that $$h\approx1.2\;\mathrm{m}$$ solves it.

statement:
Part A. unsupported_type: DynamicGraph

Part B. This part of the problem lets you practice algebra skills in physical modeling.

-------------------------------

Because the horizontal component of velocity is constant in projectile motion, an equation for the horizontal position over time of some small piece of water shot out of the fountain is $$x = x_0 + v_{x0}t.$$

And an equation for the vertical position over time is $$y = y_0 + v_{y0} t - \dfrac12 g t^2.$$

The initial positions $$x_0$$ and $$y_0$$ only depend on our choice of origin, so they don't model any useful information about the speed of the water. We can also choose the time $$t = 0$$ to be when the water is moving horizontally, so $$v_{y0} = 0.$$ That lets us simplify to $$\begin{aligned}x & = v_{x0} t \\ y & = y_0 - \dfrac12 g t^2 \end{aligned}$$

Find $$y$$ as a function of $$x.$$

Then, assuming $$g = 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and using your answer from part (A), find $$v_{x0},$$ the horizontal speed of the water.

You should be accurate to within $$1 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Give your answer to the nearest $$ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

This problem is qualitative, and explores an application of projectile motion. The challenge is in figuring out what all the different pieces of the problem mean, not in doing a complicated calculation.

------------------

In principle, we can find square roots of numbers by dropping objects. The time it takes an object to fall from height $$h$$ to the ground obeys $$t \propto \sqrt{h}.$$ To calculate $$\sqrt{7},$$ for example, we drop two objects, one from $$7$$ times as high as the other, and time both their falls. The ratio of those times would be $$\sqrt{7}.$$

Accurate timing is difficult, so let's explore another square root calculator.

The markings on the ground are supposed to be set up so that the ball hits the square root of the number it was released from. For example, if the ball is released from marking $$9,$$ it should hit marking $$3$$ on the ground.

statement:
In the ancient Greek poem __The Odyssey__, the hero Odysseus has to shoot an arrow through a series of twelve axes set up in a row. (There are holes in the axes for an arrow to go through.)

In 2019, the TV show __MythBusters Jr.__ replicated the feat.

Below is a side view of the axes, plus the path the arrow must follow in a dotted parabola. The arrow must stay in a narrow vertical zone to travel through all the axes.

Model the arrow as a

The arrow has some length to it, so it may be surprising that we can model it as a point. To make this work, we extend the horizontal region the arrow travels through past the end of the axes by the length of an arrow. This has already been accounted for; you don't need to adjust the model to include the arrow length.

. To travel through all 12 axes, the arrow needs to stay within a region $$4.0 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ high while traveling a horizontal distance $$3.9 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

These parameters should let you find a minimum speed of the arrow.

A longbow like Odysseus's might have been able to shoot an arrow $$300 \;\mathrm{m}$$ when shot at an angle of $$45^\circ.$$

Would Odysseus's longbow shoot the arrow fast enough to get through the axes? Justify your answer quantitatively. You may ignore air resistance on the arrow.

label: MCH03
name: A Ball Dropped from a Moving Ship — A ship glides through the water at constant velocity. A sailor hanging…
desc: A ship glides through the water at constant velocity. A sailor hanging onto the top of the mast holds a ball out and releases it — without throwing it forward or backward at all. Ignore air drag throughout this problem. __(a)__ As the ball falls, does the mast pull ahead of the…
statement:
A ship glides through the water at constant velocity. A sailor hanging onto the top of the mast holds a ball out and releases it — without throwing it forward or backward at all. Ignore air drag throughout this problem.

__(a)__ As the ball falls, does the mast pull ahead of the ball, does the ball pull ahead of the mast, or does the ball fall right alongside the mast the whole way down? Explain your answer.

__(b)__ Describe the path of the falling ball as seen by the sailor, and as seen by a camera fixed to the shore. Each observer measures motion from their own perspective, called their __reference frame__ — and both descriptions are valid.

__(c)__ Now imagine a trampoline bolted to the bed of a truck driving down a straight road at constant velocity. Can you bounce on the trampoline normally, or does the truck slide out from under you while you are in the air? What could the driver do to put you in big trouble mid-bounce? (Reference frames moving at constant velocity are called __inertial reference frames__; the fact that the laws of physics are the same in every inertial reference frame is called the __principle of relativity__.)

__(d)__ Now let's measure how fast the ship is moving. The film clip is in slow motion, so we cannot simply time it with a stopwatch. Instead, first derive a formula: an object dropped from rest in free fall speeds up steadily, so after a time $$t$$ its speed is $$g\cdot t,$$ and its __average__ speed during the fall is $$\dfrac12 gt.$$ Use this to find the distance $$d$$ the object falls in time $$t.$$

__(e)__ Use the sailor as a scale: he is probably $$1.7$$ to $$1.8\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall, and since his legs are bent in the clip, it is about $$1.5\;\mathrm{m}$$ from his shoes to his head. The ball falls about three sailor-lengths along the mast, so the drop height is about $$d\approx 5\;\mathrm{m}.$$ How long does the ball take to fall? Use $$g\approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(f)__ While the ball falls, the ship advances a bit more than one sailor-length, about $$\Delta x\approx 2\;\mathrm{m}.$$ How fast is the ship going?

__(g)__ In the shore camera's reference frame, classify the ball's __horizontal__ motion and its __vertical__ motion: is each one no motion, constant velocity, or constant acceleration?

label: MCH03
name: Frogs, Dolphins, and Two Falling Balls — An object hurled through the air with no significant influence from…
desc: An object hurled through the air with no significant influence from anything except gravity is called a __projectile__. While in the air, every projectile has the same acceleration: $$a_y = -g$$ vertically and $$a_x = 0$$ horizontally. These three quick questions are about what…
statement:
An object hurled through the air with no significant influence from anything except gravity is called a __projectile__. While in the air, every projectile has the same acceleration: $$a_y = -g$$ vertically and $$a_x = 0$$ horizontally. These three quick questions are about what that means.

__(a)__ Which has greater acceleration while in the air — a leaping dolphin or a jumping frog? (Ignore air drag.)

__(b)__ Three projectiles are launched from ground level and follow the trajectories shown below; their maximum heights and horizontal ranges all differ. Air resistance can be ignored. Which one is in the air for the longest time? Does the horizontal distance each projectile covers matter to your answer?

__(c)__ A ball is dropped straight down off the end of a table. At the same moment, a second ball is launched perfectly horizontally from exactly the same height. Which ball hits the ground first?

desc: In the town of Glacier View, Alaska, the sky doesn't get dark on the 4th of July, so there are no fireworks. Instead, the town launches old junked cars horizontally off a cliff $$90\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall. (This really happens!) How fast would a car have to be going at the cliff…
statement:
In the town of Glacier View, Alaska, the sky doesn't get dark on the 4th of July, so there are no fireworks. Instead, the town launches old junked cars horizontally off a cliff $$90\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall. (This really happens!)

How fast would a car have to be going at the cliff edge to make it all the way to the water, $$97\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the base of the cliff? Solve in two steps, using the fact that an object falling from rest covers a distance $$d=\dfrac12 gt^2$$ in time $$t,$$ with $$g\approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$:

__(a)__ Use the __vertical__ information to find how long the car is in the air. (A car launched horizontally starts with zero vertical velocity, so its fall is exactly like a fall from rest.)

__(b)__ Use the __horizontal__ information to find the minimum launch speed. Convert your answer roughly to miles per hour using $$1\;\mathrm{m/s}\approx 2.2\;\mathrm{mi/h}.$$

label: MCH03
name: Squirts from a Fountain — A water fountain shoots individual squirts of water along identical paths, one…
desc: A water fountain shoots individual squirts of water along identical paths, one squirt following another. Model each squirt as a point; each point moves along the same __parabola__, $$y = a(x-x_0)^2 + b$$ for some constants $$a, x_0,$$ and $$b.$$ Consider two adjacent squirts…
statement:
A water fountain shoots individual squirts of water along identical paths, one squirt following another. Model each squirt as a point; each point moves along the same __parabola__, $$y = a(x-x_0)^2 + b$$ for some constants $$a, x_0,$$ and $$b.$$

Consider two adjacent squirts that are in the air at the same time. (The distance between two points is given by the Pythagorean theorem: the square of the distance is the square of the horizontal separation plus the square of the vertical separation. Plugging two quadratic trajectories into that formula would get messy — there is an easier way using the fact that horizontal and vertical motions can be analyzed separately.)

__(a)__ What happens to the __horizontal__ distance between the two squirts as time passes?

__(b)__ At what moment are the two squirts closest to each other?

label: MCH03
name: Jumping Half as Many Cars — A daredevil on a motorcycle uses a ramp to jump over $$24$$ parked cars, leaving…
desc: A daredevil on a motorcycle uses a ramp to jump over $$24$$ parked cars, leaving the top of the ramp at speed $$v.$$ I am more modest and only want to jump $$12$$ cars from the same ramp. To simplify, assume takeoff and landing happen at the same height, and ignore air…
statement:
A daredevil on a motorcycle uses a ramp to jump over $$24$$ parked cars, leaving the top of the ramp at speed $$v.$$ I am more modest and only want to jump $$12$$ cars from the same ramp. To simplify, assume takeoff and landing happen at the same height, and ignore air resistance.

Because the ramp fixes the takeoff direction, going slower scales down the horizontal and vertical components of takeoff velocity by the same factor. Two useful facts: a projectile's vertical velocity changes at the steady rate $$g$$ (so the time in the air is proportional to the takeoff vertical velocity), and with no horizontal acceleration, the horizontal distance is $$x = v_x t.$$

__(a)__ Suppose I take the ramp at half the daredevil's speed, $$\dfrac{v}{2}.$$ How long am I in the air, compared to the daredevil?

__(b)__ How many cars do I clear at that speed?

__(c)__ What speed do I actually need in order to jump $$12$$ cars?

label: MCH03
name: Weightless in a Falling Elevator — When you accelerate vertically, it feels as if gravity changed: if your…
desc: When you accelerate vertically, it feels as if gravity changed: if your vertical acceleration is $$a_y,$$ everything feels as if the free fall acceleration $$g$$ were replaced by $$g + a_y.$$ (That is why you feel heavier when an elevator accelerates upward and lighter when it…
statement:
When you accelerate vertically, it feels as if gravity changed: if your vertical acceleration is $$a_y,$$ everything feels as if the free fall acceleration $$g$$ were replaced by $$g + a_y.$$ (That is why you feel heavier when an elevator accelerates upward and lighter when it accelerates downward.) Also recall that what you normally feel as your weight is the floor pushing up on you, preventing you from accelerating downward.

__(a)__ Suppose an elevator accelerates __downward__ at exactly $$g.$$ What would a person inside feel? What would a bathroom scale under their feet read?

__(b)__ For a cheap experiment, you can seal a lit candle inside a box and drop the box off a bridge. The film below shows the result: the flame pulls itself into a small ball. Explain why.

__(c)__ Now imagine a huge elevator containing a basketball hoop. The elevator accelerates downward at $$g$$ while you attempt a free throw. What does the ball's path look like to you inside the elevator, and do you have any chance of making a normal-looking shot?

__(d)__ Suppose a box has a constant __horizontal__ velocity while also accelerating downward at $$g,$$ so it moves through the air along a parabola, like a thrown projectile. Do objects inside it still float weightlessly? Explain by choosing a clever inertial reference frame. (This is the principle behind the "vomit comet," a reduced-gravity airplane that flies in parabolas.)

label: MCH03
name: The Vomit Comet's Flight Path — A reduced-gravity aircraft (nicknamed the "vomit comet") makes its passengers…
desc: A reduced-gravity aircraft (nicknamed the "vomit comet") makes its passengers weightless by flying with a constant downward acceleration of $$g.$$ The idea that being in an accelerating reference frame is exactly the same as changing $$g$$ is called the __equivalence…
statement:
A reduced-gravity aircraft (nicknamed the "vomit comet") makes its passengers weightless by flying with a constant downward acceleration of $$g.$$ The idea that being in an accelerating reference frame is exactly the same as changing $$g$$ is called the __equivalence principle__: with vertical acceleration $$a_y,$$ passengers feel an effective gravity of $$g + a_y.$$

Below is a published graphic of one cycle of the maneuver, showing the plane's altitude versus time. According to the graphic, the weightless portion runs from $$20\;\mathrm{s}$$ to $$45\;\mathrm{s}$$ (so it is $$25\;\mathrm{s}$$ long), the plane is climbing until $$32.5\;\mathrm{s}$$ and descending after that, and the altitude changes by about $$250\;\mathrm{m}$$ during the weightless portion. From $$65\;\mathrm{s}$$ to about $$85\;\mathrm{s},$$ the altitude graph is a parabola opening upward.

__(a)__ Passengers are weightless only while the plane's downward acceleration equals $$g.$$ What shape does the altitude-versus-time graph have during that portion? Why are the passengers weightless even from $$20\;\mathrm{s}$$ to $$32.5\;\mathrm{s},$$ while the plane is still climbing?

__(b)__ What do the passengers feel from $$65\;\mathrm{s}$$ to $$85\;\mathrm{s},$$ where the graph is a parabola opening upward?

__(c)__ Check the graphic for consistency. An object with downward acceleration $$g$$ and no initial vertical velocity drops $$\Delta y = \dfrac12 g\,(\Delta t)^2$$ in time $$\Delta t.$$ Apply this to the second half of the weightless portion (from the peak of the arc to its end) and compare with the $$250\;\mathrm{m}$$ altitude change shown. Are the graphic's numbers consistent? Use $$g\approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(d)__ Could a plane fly a route with weightless portions but __no__ extra-heavy portions to compensate? Use the fact that the signed area under a graph of vertical acceleration $$a_y$$ versus time equals the change in vertical velocity, $$\Delta v_y.$$

statement:
Archer fish hunt by shooting streams of water into the air to knock insects into the water.

An archer fish shoots a squirt of water so that the squirt's initial velocity points __directly at__ a cricket resting on a nearby leaf. At the very moment the water leaves the fish's mouth, the cricket loses its grip and falls from rest. Ignore air drag. Does the water hit the cricket?

__(a)__ Analyze the situation in the falling cricket's reference frame. Useful fact: in the reference frame of one freely falling object, other freely falling objects move in straight lines at constant velocity. What does the water's path look like to the cricket, and does the water hit it?

__(b)__ Now analyze it again in the fish's reference frame. If there were no gravity, where would the water go? Compare how far the water and the cricket are each deflected below their no-gravity positions after a time $$t$$ (an object in free fall falls $$\dfrac12 gt^2$$ below where it would otherwise be). Does the fish's analysis agree?

__(c)__ Why must the two analyses reach the same conclusion? What was the advantage of the cricket's reference frame?

statement:
The world's highest-jumping robot was built by the Hawkes lab at the University of California, Santa Barbara. The robot has a mass of only about $$30\;\mathrm{g}$$; it jumps by straightening its spring-loaded arms over $$9.2\;\mathrm{ms},$$ flinging itself into the air. (Air resistance changes the answers below by only $$20\%$$ or so, so we will ignore it.)

One motivation for a jumping robot is exploring the moon, where rough terrain is hard to drive over. In this problem you will work out how far the robot could jump horizontally on the moon. Below is a figure from the lab's scientific article; part (c) of the figure shows the robot's parabolic trajectory, with a person $$1.83\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall included for scale. Measuring pixels shows the jump peaks about $$17$$ times as high as the person's height.

Use $$g\approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ on Earth and $$g_{\rm moon}\approx 1.6\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ on the moon. Useful facts: an object in free fall starting from rest falls $$\Delta y = \dfrac12 g t^2$$ in time $$t,$$ and on a graph of vertical velocity versus time, the slope is the acceleration $$-g.$$

__(a)__ Estimate the height of the robot's jump on Earth.

__(b)__ How long does the whole jump (up and back down) last on Earth?

__(c)__ How fast is the robot moving just after leaving the ground?

__(d)__ If the robot made the same vertical jump on the moon — same takeoff speed, straight up — how long would it stay off the ground, and how high would it go?

__(e)__ To jump far rather than high, the robot takes off at an angle. Suppose it jumps at $$60^\circ$$ above the horizontal at its full speed from part (c). Find the horizontal and vertical components of its takeoff velocity, $$v_x$$ and $$v_y.$$ (Taking just one dimension of a two-dimensional quantity is called __projection__; the components satisfy the Pythagorean relation $$v_x^2+v_y^2=v^2.$$ Hint: put the velocity triangle together with its mirror image to form an equilateral triangle.)

__(f)__ Find how far the robot would travel horizontally on the moon with that $$60^\circ$$ takeoff. (Two steps: use the vertical component of velocity and $$g_{\rm moon}$$ to find the time off the ground, then use the horizontal component and that time to find the distance.) Show that in general the range is $$\Delta x = \dfrac{2 v_x v_y}{g}.$$

__(g)__ Could the robot do even better at a different angle? Using $$\Delta x = \dfrac{2v_xv_y}{g}$$ and $$v_x^2+v_y^2=v^2,$$ show that the range is maximized when the launch angle is $$45^\circ$$ (hint: substitute $$u = v_x^2$$ to get a quadratic), find the maximum range formula in terms of $$v$$ and $$g,$$ and evaluate it for the robot on the moon.

name: This problem is for practice with two different skills. First, there's a lot of…
desc: This problem is for practice with two different skills. First, there's a lot of interpreting the meaning of different mathematical notation. Second, there's understanding what scientific hypothesis mean, and when two differently stated hypotheses are actually the same thing…
statement:
This problem is for practice with two different skills. First, there's a lot of interpreting the meaning of different mathematical notation. Second, there's understanding what scientific hypothesis mean, and when two differently stated hypotheses are actually the same thing.

--------

In class, we generated the hypothesis that the quantity $$v^2 + 2gy$$ is conserved along an object's trajectory when we use a model that: - the object can be modeled as a single point - there is free fall acceleration - there can be other simple influences, such as sliding or swinging on a string, known as "constraints" - friction, air drag, and similar complications are negligible

Now let's imagine several other physics classes, each of which came up with their own hypothesis for the same type of motion. Each answer choice to this question is one of the hypotheses.

Most of these hypotheses may make the same prediction as ours in every circumstance. In that case, the two hypothesis is equivalent to ours. We could say they are the same hypothesis written in different mathematical notation. Experiments cannot give evidence favoring any one of the various equivalent hypotheses.

Two of hypotheses below are different. They each make different predictions than ours (and than each other). Experiments can favor one hypothesis in particular between those two hypotheses and ours.

__Select the **two** hypotheses that are **not** equivalent to our hypothesis.__

The variables in these hypotheses have the same definitions as our variables, with the addition that $$h$$ is a height (a specific value that $$y$$ could take) that is constant throughout any given experiment, but can be different from experiment to experiment. Also, $$\Delta$$ is used to mean "change in", so $$\Delta (v^2)$$ is how much the quantity $$v^2$$ has changed since the beginning of the experiment.

When there is a hypothesis stated as an equation, the hypothesis is that the equation is true at all times during the experiment.

Our hypothesis: $$v^2 + 2gy$$ is conserved.

$$\dfrac12v^2 + gy$$ is conserved

$$v + \sqrt{2gy}$$ is conserved

$$v^2 + 2g(y-h)$$ is conserved

$$\dfrac12 m v^2 = - mg (y - h)$$

$$v^2 = -2gy$$

$$\Delta (v^2) = - \Delta (2gy)$$

name: When a ball bounces off the ground, it loses some kinetic energy, so if the vertical…
desc: When a ball bounces off the ground, it loses some kinetic energy, so if the vertical component of the ball's velocity is $$v_{y0}$$ just before hitting the ground and $$v_{yb}$$ just after bouncing, then $$v_{yb} < -v_{y0}.$$ $$v_y$$ is positive in the upward direction, so…
statement:
When a ball bounces off the ground, it loses some kinetic energy, so if the vertical component of the ball's velocity is $$v_{y0}$$ just before hitting the ground and $$v_{yb}$$ just after bouncing, then $$v_{yb} < -v_{y0}.$$

$$v_y$$ is positive in the upward direction, so $$v_{y0} < 0,$$ since the ball is moving down just before bouncing. The inequality $$v_{yb} < -v_{y0}$$ is comparing two positive quantities, and is saying the same thing as $$|v_{yb}| < |v_{y0}|\,.$$

One simple model says that when a ball bounces, there is always the same ratio between $$v_{y0}$$ and $$v_{yb}\,.$$

For example, suppose a ball bounces off a floor with $$v_{y0} = -4 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and then bounces with $$v_{yb} = 3 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ This model would say that $$v_{yb} = -\dfrac34 v_{y0}$$ for any bounce. If the ball were instead approaching the floor with $$v_{y0} = -6 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ the model says that $$v_{yb}$$ would be $$v_{yb} = -\dfrac34 \cdot 6 \;\mathrm{m/s} = 4.5 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

The ratio of $$v_{yb}$$ to $$-v_{y0}$$ is called the __coefficient of restitution__, and often given the symbol $$e.$$ We can write this as the equation $$e = \dfrac{-v_{yb}}{v_{y0}}.$$

**Estimate the coefficient of restitution for the basketball bounce shown below. **

You should be within $$0.03$$ of our answer.

statement:
Part A. This week, instead of doing an experiment that seeks to confirm or discover a scientific law, we'll try to put what we've learned in practice to design something.

Here's a gif of a toy car making a jump:

Darek Dewey, Twitter

To get the car going fast enough to make the jump, it could start by rolling down a ramp.

Suppose we want our car to make a jump of a horizontal distance $$d$$ starting at an angle of $$30^\circ.$$

We could use our knowledge of projectile motion to figure out how fast the car needs to be going at takeoff, and we could use our knowledge of energy conservation to figure out how tall the ramp needs to be to get the car to that speed.

However, there are several different heights we could measure, including

$$\begin{aligned} h_1: & \text{ height of back of ramp above the ground} \\ h_2: & \text{ height of back of ramp above end of takeoff ramp} \\ h_3: & \text{ height of car release point above the ground} \\ h_4: & \text{ height of car release point above end of takeoff ramp} \end{aligned}$$

Although the car is drawn with some size in the figure, we'll model it as a point for this problem. This avoids worrying about whether we're measuring from the front or back of the car.

Which height is most important to making calculations that will ensure the car can make the jump?

statement:
You stand on the roof of a building of height $$H$$ holding two identical rocks. You launch rock $$A$$ perfectly horizontally off the building with initial speed $$v_0.$$ You launch rock $$B$$ straight downward (from just past the edge of the building), also with initial speed $$v_0.$$ Once released, each rock is in free fall: it accelerates straight downward at the constant free-fall acceleration $$g.$$ Ignore air resistance. Which rock is going faster when it hits the ground?

__(a)__ First, consider solving this with the projectile-motion tools of kinematics. When rock $$A$$ hits the ground, in what direction is it moving? If you knew its horizontal and vertical velocity components $$v_x$$ and $$v_y$$ at that moment, how would you combine them to get its speed?

__(b)__ The plot below shows rock $$B$$'s vertical velocity $$v_y$$ versus time. It starts at $$-v_0$$ (negative because $$B$$ moves downward) and decreases with slope $$-g$$ until $$B$$ lands at time $$t_B$$ with vertical velocity $$v_{y;B}.$$ Where is the height $$H$$ of the building represented in this plot?

__(c)__ Setting the quantity you identified in (b) equal to $$H$$ gives an equation that is quadratic in $$t_B,$$ and you would still need more work to find the landing speed. Instead, use a shortcut. For motion like this — a point-like object in free fall with negligible air resistance — experiments show that the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ is __conserved__: it keeps the same value $$c$$ at every moment of the motion. (Here $$v$$ is the rock's speed and $$y$$ is its height above the ground.) Using rock $$A$$'s values at the moment it is launched, find the constant $$c$$ in terms of $$v_0,$$ $$g,$$ and $$H.$$

__(d)__ Use the conservation law to find $$v_A,$$ the speed of rock $$A$$ just before it hits the ground.

__(e)__ Repeat the reasoning for rock $$B.$$ Which rock hits the ground faster? With what speed would a rock launched at speed $$v_0$$ at __any__ angle hit the ground?
