statement:
In the PhET "Energy Skate Park" simulation, a skater named Emilie rides back and forth on a frictionless W-shaped track. You can experiment with the simulation at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/energy-skate-park/latest/energy-skate-park_en.html (click "Intro," then choose the W-shaped track). A speedometer reads her speed $$v,$$ and a tape measure gives her height $$y$$ above the ground.

A class repeatedly freezes the simulation at random moments and records Emilie's height and speed. Plotted with $$v$$ on the vertical axis and $$y$$ on the horizontal axis, the data do not fall on a straight line: the lower Emilie is, the faster she moves, and the curve steepens sharply at its right edge. The shape is well fit by the top half of a parabola opening to the left.

__(a)__ To test the parabola hypothesis we __linearize__ the data: we choose new variables to plot so that, if the hypothesis is right, the data should fall on a straight line. A sideways parabola satisfies $$y=av^2+b$$ for constants $$a$$ and $$b.$$ What quantity should we plot against $$y$$ to get a straight line?

__(b)__ The plot below shows $$v^2$$ versus $$y$$ for one careful set of measurements, along with the best-fit line. The line's $$v^2$$-intercept is $$90\;\mathrm{m^2/s^2},$$ and the line reaches $$v^2=0$$ at $$y=4.6\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Find the slope of the line, including its units.

__(c)__ The slope's units are those of an acceleration. Is the slope equal to Emilie's acceleration as she rides the track? How can you tell?

__(d)__ Compare the slope's value with the free-fall acceleration $$g=9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and conjecture a simple formula for the slope. Then write an equation for the best-fit line in the form $$v^2=\ldots$$

__(e)__ To test the conjecture, the experiment is repeated with the simulation's "Gravity" slider set to a new, unknown value $$g_{\rm new},$$ with Emilie released from the same starting point. The new best-fit line has $$v^2$$-intercept $$122\;\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$$ and the same run, again reaching $$v^2=0$$ at $$y=4.6\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Assuming the slope really is $$-2g,$$ find $$g_{\rm new}.$$ A separate measurement — timing Emilie in free fall at the same gravity setting — gave $$g_{\rm new}=13.1\pm0.3\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ What do you conclude?

__(f)__ Writing the $$v^2$$-intercept as $$c,$$ the result of this experiment is $$v^2+2gy=c.$$ Within a single run, which of the four quantities $$v,$$ $$g,$$ $$y,$$ and $$c$$ change as Emilie skates back and forth? What do physicists call a quantity that does not change over time?

label: MCH04
name: When Is the Conservation Law Valid? — Experiments show that in real life the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ — where…
desc: Experiments show that in real life the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ — where $$v$$ is a moving object's speed and $$y$$ is its height — is very nearly conserved (constant over time) as long as: (1) friction, air drag, and similar effects are negligible; (2) there are no collisions; (3)…
statement:
Experiments show that in real life the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ — where $$v$$ is a moving object's speed and $$y$$ is its height — is very nearly conserved (constant over time) as long as: (1) friction, air drag, and similar effects are negligible; (2) there are no collisions; (3) the moving object can be modeled as a point; (4) the free-fall acceleration $$g$$ is constant; and (5) any other influences come from objects whose shape does not change.

For each scenario below, decide whether $$v^2+2gy$$ is (at least very nearly) conserved for the moving object, and if it is not, name the condition from the list that fails.

__(a)__ A pendulum: a weight swings back and forth on the end of a string of fixed length.

__(b)__ A box bounces up and down on the end of a spring.

__(c)__ A planet orbits the Sun on a long, stretched-out orbit, sometimes passing close to the Sun and sometimes swinging far away.

__(d)__ A box is pushed up a hill by a person.

__(e)__ A water tower — a heavy tank on a slender, rigid support — tips over and falls. (Consider the tank's motion before anything hits the ground.)

label: MCH04
name: How Fast Should You Throw? — A ball is released from rest from a height $$H$$ and hits the ground moving at…
desc: A ball is released from rest from a height $$H$$ and hits the ground moving at $$4\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ You want to throw a second, identical ball straight downward from the same height and have it hit the ground at $$5\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ How fast should you throw it? Ignore air…
statement:
A ball is released from rest from a height $$H$$ and hits the ground moving at $$4\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ You want to throw a second, identical ball straight downward from the same height and have it hit the ground at $$5\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ How fast should you throw it? Ignore air resistance. You may use the fact that for an object in free fall, the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ is conserved (constant in time), where $$v$$ is the ball's speed, $$y$$ its height, and $$g$$ the free-fall acceleration.

__(a)__ There is a common, tempting answer: throw the ball at $$1\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ What reasoning leads to that answer, and why is it wrong?

__(b)__ Without calculating anything, should you throw faster or slower than $$1\;\mathrm{m/s}?$$

__(c)__ The flawed answer assumed a falling ball always gains the same amount of __speed__ over a given distance of falling. That is false — but because $$v^2+2gy$$ is conserved, every decrease in height of $$\Delta y$$ increases $$v^2$$ by the fixed amount $$2g\,\Delta y,$$ no matter how fast the ball is already moving. Both balls fall the same height, so they gain the same amount of $$v^2.$$ Use this to find the correct throwing speed.

label: MCH04
name: Measuring g with an Atwood Machine — An __Atwood machine__ is two boxes connected by a string that runs over…
desc: An __Atwood machine__ is two boxes connected by a string that runs over a pulley. Box $$M=560\;\mathrm{g}$$ is slightly heavier than box $$m=550\;\mathrm{g}.$$ When the machine is released, $$M$$ falls and $$m$$ rises, both with the same constant magnitude of acceleration $$a$$…
statement:
An __Atwood machine__ is two boxes connected by a string that runs over a pulley. Box $$M=560\;\mathrm{g}$$ is slightly heavier than box $$m=550\;\mathrm{g}.$$ When the machine is released, $$M$$ falls and $$m$$ rises, both with the same constant magnitude of acceleration $$a$$ and — since the string does not stretch — the same speed $$v$$ at every instant. Assume the pulley and string are massless and frictionless.

In an experiment (you can find video of one by searching for "Low Friction Atwood Machine" by mittechtv on YouTube), the lighter box starts at the ground and rises $$D=1.00\;\mathrm{m}$$ — while $$M$$ falls $$1.00\;\mathrm{m}$$ to the ground — in $$t=4.82\;\mathrm{s}.$$ The goal of this problem is to use that data to measure the free-fall acceleration $$g.$$

__(a)__ For a single freely moving object, the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ is conserved ($$v$$ = speed, $$y$$ = height). A first guess for the Atwood machine is to add this quantity for the two boxes: $$\left(v_m^2+2gy_m\right)+\left(v_M^2+2gy_M\right).$$ Using $$v_m=v_M=v$$ and the fact that $$y_m+y_M$$ never changes (every centimeter $$m$$ rises, $$M$$ falls a centimeter), show that if this sum were conserved, the boxes could never speed up at all. (Experimentally, the sum is __not__ conserved.)

__(b)__ A better hypothesis weights each box's contribution by its mass: $$m\left(v^2+2gy_m\right)+M\left(v^2+2gy_M\right)$$ is conserved. (Imagine cutting each box into many identical $$1$$-gram pieces and adding up $$v^2+2gy$$ for every piece.) Evaluate this quantity at the moment of release, when $$v=0,$$ $$y_m=0,$$ and $$y_M=D.$$

__(c)__ Evaluate the same quantity at the end of the run, just before $$M$$ reaches the ground ($$y_m=D,$$ $$y_M=0,$$ speed $$v$$). Set it equal to your answer from (b) and solve for the final speed $$v.$$

__(d)__ The boxes start from rest and accelerate uniformly, so $$D=\dfrac12 at^2$$ and the final speed is $$v=at.$$ Combine these with your result from (c) to show that $$a=g\,\dfrac{M-m}{M+m}.$$

__(e)__ From the data, the measured acceleration is $$a=\dfrac{2D}{t^2}=\dfrac{2\left(1.00\;\mathrm{m}\right)}{\left(4.82\;\mathrm{s}\right)^2}=0.0861\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Solve your equation from (d) for $$g$$ and plug in the numbers. Then: any real Atwood machine has a little friction and air resistance, and must make its pulley spin. Do these effects make your measured $$g$$ an overestimate or an underestimate?

label: MCH04
name: Kinetic and Potential Energy — For a single point-like object of mass $$m,$$ speed $$v,$$ and height $$y,$$…
desc: For a single point-like object of mass $$m,$$ speed $$v,$$ and height $$y,$$ physicists define the __energy__ $$E=\dfrac12mv^2+mgy.$$ Energy comes in two types: __kinetic energy__ ($$KE$$), the energy due to motion, and __potential energy__ ($$U$$), the energy due to…
statement:
For a single point-like object of mass $$m,$$ speed $$v,$$ and height $$y,$$ physicists define the __energy__ $$E=\dfrac12mv^2+mgy.$$ Energy comes in two types: __kinetic energy__ ($$KE$$), the energy due to motion, and __potential energy__ ($$U$$), the energy due to interactions like gravity and to where objects are located, with $$E=KE+U.$$ When there are several objects, the total energy is the sum of $$\dfrac12mv^2+mgy$$ over all of them.

__(a)__ Which term of $$E=\dfrac12mv^2+mgy$$ is the kinetic energy and which is the potential energy? How can you tell?

__(b)__ In situations where the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ is conserved for an object (a projectile, say, or a skater on a frictionless track), explain why $$E$$ is conserved too.

__(c)__ An Atwood machine has a heavier box $$M$$ and a lighter box $$m$$ joined by a string over a pulley; when released, $$M$$ falls and $$m$$ rises, and both boxes move with the same, steadily growing speed. For the two-box system, state whether each of the kinetic energy, the potential energy, and the total energy increases, decreases, or stays constant during the run.

__(d)__ The system's potential energy is $$U=mgy_m+Mgy_M.$$ As the machine runs, one of these terms increases and the other decreases. Explain how you can be sure the __total__ $$U$$ decreases.

label: MCH04
name: Energy Conservation in a Moving Reference Frame — The __principle of relativity__ says that the laws of…
desc: The __principle of relativity__ says that the laws of physics work the same in every inertial reference frame. This lesson's conservation law — that $$v^2+2gy$$ stays constant for a point-like object when friction, drag, and collisions are negligible, $$g$$ is constant, and any…
statement:
The __principle of relativity__ says that the laws of physics work the same in every inertial reference frame. This lesson's conservation law — that $$v^2+2gy$$ stays constant for a point-like object when friction, drag, and collisions are negligible, $$g$$ is constant, and any other influences come from objects whose shape does not change — is a law of physics. So if it holds in one inertial frame $$S,$$ we should ask whether it still holds in another inertial frame $$S'$$ moving at constant velocity relative to $$S.$$

Let $$S'$$ move with constant velocity components $$v_{x0}$$ (horizontal) and $$v_{y0}$$ (vertical) as measured in $$S.$$ Measured in $$S',$$ an object's velocity components and height are $$v_x'=v_x-v_{x0},$$ $$v_y'=v_y-v_{y0},$$ and $$y'=y-y_0-v_{y0}t,$$ where $$y_0$$ is a constant offset between the frames at $$t=0.$$

__(a)__ A quantity that has the same value in all inertial reference frames is called __invariant__. Which of $$v,$$ $$y,$$ and $$g$$ are invariant?

__(b)__ Is the question "is $$v^2+2gy$$ invariant?" the same as the question "is $$v'^2+2gy'$$ conserved in $$S'$$?" Explain the difference.

__(c)__ Writing $$v^2=v_x^2+v_y^2,$$ suppose $$v_x^2+v_y^2+2gy=c$$ holds at all times in frame $$S.$$ Substitute the primed expressions ($$v_x=v_x'+v_{x0},$$ etc.) and show that $$v_x'^2+v_y'^2+2gy'=c_2-2\left(v_x'v_{x0}+v_{y0}\left(v_y'+gt\right)\right),$$ where $$c_2=c-v_{x0}^2-v_{y0}^2-2gy_0$$ is a constant.

__(d)__ For projectile motion, $$v_x'$$ is constant, and since the vertical acceleration is $$-g$$ in both frames, $$v_y'+gt$$ is constant too. What do you conclude about whether $$v'^2+2gy'$$ is conserved in $$S'$$ for projectiles?

__(e)__ For a skater riding a curved track that is at rest in $$S$$ (like Emilie in the skate-park simulation), $$v_x'$$ and $$v_y'+gt$$ are __not__ constant, so the right-hand side in (c) changes with time and $$v'^2+2gy'$$ is __not__ conserved in $$S'$$ — even though every condition in the list above is still met, since none of those conditions depends on the reference frame. The principle of relativity is not wrong; instead, the list of conditions must be incomplete. What is physically different about the track when viewed from $$S',$$ and what condition is missing?

statement:
This conceptual problem should give you a chance to think about when we can and cannot apply energy conservation to a system.

------------

A famous demonstration in physics involves a bowling ball hung from the ceiling by a long rope. A physicist pulls the bowling ball back a long way, storing gravitational potential energy in it. They let the bowling ball go and it swings away, then turns around and swings back.

Although the bowling ball is quickly approaching the physicist's face, the physicist doesn't flinch; they are confident that, due to conservation of energy, the ball cannot rise higher than it was released from and will turn around before making contact.

This demo is dangerous - the bowling ball sometimes hits the physicist and can injure them!

Which one of the following could **not** be a reason that the bowling ball hits the physicist when this demo goes wrong?

$$g$$ is slightly higher than the normal value where the demo is performed, so the bowling ball will accelerate more, go faster than normal, and therefore rise higher.

The physicist accidentally gives the bowling ball a push forward instead of releasing it from rest.

The physicist moves some after releasing the ball.

statement:
Part A. In this multi-part problem, we explore kinetic energy quantitatively, linking it back to Professor John Dabiri's ideas about wind turbines.

------------

Our kinetic energy formula was $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2$$

When the wind blows at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ each A __cubic meter__, or $$\mathrm{m}^3,$$ is a unit of volume. It is the volume of a cube one meter on each side. This is about the volume of a large refrigerator. of air has a kinetic energy of about $$15 \;\mathrm{J}.$$

How much kinetic energy does one cubic meter of air have when the wind blows at $$10 \;\mathrm{m/s}?$$ (Assume the mass of a cubic meter of air doesn't change as the wind speed changes.)

Use the figure of $$15 \;\mathrm{J}$$ at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and scale it up; don't look up some values and then calculate the answer from scratch.

Part B. Suppose a wind turbine operates right at the The __Betz limit__ is something we discussed in class. Windmills cannot extract all the energy from wind that passes through them. The maximum fraction of energy they can extract is called the Betz limit., so it extracts exactly $$\dfrac{16}{27}$$ of the kinetic energy of air that approaches it.

If the wind speed is $$v_1 = 5 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ the wind turbine generates a The __power__ is the rate of energy extraction, or energy extracted per unit time. It is measured in watts. One watt is one joule per second. of $$P(v_1) = 6 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{W}.$$

This could form a point of comparison for a hypothetical improved wind turbine.

Is your estimate an overestimate, and underestimate, correct, or does it depend on how the wind varies?

statement:
Part A. This multi-part problem explores an important physics technology - a particle collider. It lets you practice with energy conceptually without worrying about the details of calculations. However, it introduces lots of new context, and requires careful interpretation of the graphs and figures.

---------------------------

The main way that physicists study the structure of subatomic particles is with __particle accelerators__. These are giant machines (kilometers long) that accelerate particles to very high speed before crashing them into each other. By studying the debris, physicists can learn more about particles and their interactions.

Below is a diagram illustrating a __linear__ accelerator. (Other accelerators make particles go in a circle.)

By Chetvorno - Own work, CC0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=68477306

The cylinders labelled $$C_1, C_2,$$ etc. are called __klystrons__.

The red dots are particles. The green line shows the potential energy of the particles as a function of distance down the line. (The simulation uses $$V$$ instead of $$U$$ for potential energy.)

The setup has to be timed precisely so that the time it takes a particle to cross a klystron is the same as the time for the green line to flip upside down.

(The potential energy in this case is electrical potential energy, but we don't need to be concerned with where the potential energy comes from for this question.)

Why do the klystrons get longer as we move towards the right?

the potential energy of the particle is increasing, so klystrons have to be longer to contain it

the particle is accelerating, so it travels further in the time it takes the green line to flip upside down

the particle velocity constantly switches from positive to negative, so the klystrons alternate in size

abc

Part B. The fluctuating green line labeled $$V(x)$$ can be thought of as a plot of the potential energy of the particles versus their position along the accelerator. (It is electrical potential energy, but the exact type isn't important for our analysis.)

For example, at this moment, the potential energy of both particles is positive and at its maximum value.

In which part of the accelerator do the particles accelerate?

inside the klystrons

in the gap between klystrons

in all portions

it's the time, not the position, that matters for acceleration

Part C. Particle physicists often measure the energy of particles in __electron-volts,__ $$\mathrm{eV}.$$

Electron-volts are related to joules by

$$1 \;\mathrm{eV} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \;\mathrm{J}$$

The mass of an electron is $$ m_e \approx 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

Old TVs and computer monitors used simple particle accelerators called __cathode ray tubes__, which accelerated electrons from the back of the device to the screen in front. When electrons hit the screen, they made it light up in that particular spot. TVs and computer monitors did this many times per second all over the screen to make images.

A cathode ray tube inside an early Macintosh Computer By © Cody Logan / Wikimedia Commons / "Macintosh Plus interior", CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=71940343

Electrons gained a kinetic energy of around $$KE = 3 \times 10^4 \;\mathrm{eV}$$ while shooting from the back of the TV to the screen.

Using $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2,$$ what is the speed to which these TVs accelerated electrons?

The klystrons in an accelerator are similar to a long line of powerful cathode ray tubes; each adds a few million $$\mathrm{eV}$$ to the energy of an electron as it travels down the accelerator. There are 240 klystrons at the Stanford Linear Accelerator. They're in a long tunnel called the "Klystron Gallery", which is more than two miles long.

The SLAC Klystron Gallery SLAC Virtual Tour, https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/virtual-tour/klystron-gallery

We could again use $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2$$ to calculate the speed of electrons at SLAC.

statement:
Part A. Over this multi-part problem, we'll engage with a real scientific research project that used the physics concepts we've recently been studying.

------------------

The fastest animal in the world is the peregrine falcon. It hunts by flying high in the sky until it sees a small bird below it. Then the peregrine dives at the small bird from above. Peregrines reach up to $$108 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (242 mph) while diving.

National Geograph, "Skydiving Falcon", YouTube

In 2014, a team of German scientists trained peregrine falcons to dive in front of a dam and recorded the dives with high-resolution video.

Ponitz, Benjamin, et al. "Diving-flight aerodynamics of a peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus)." PLoS One 9.2 (2014): e86506.

You can assume the falcons began their dive from the top of the dam. They do not "fly downward"; they are in a tucked position and are pulled down by gravity while diving.

same source

Based on the photos of the dam, did the falcons in the study reach speeds above $$100 \;\mathrm{m/s}?$$

Yes; that's the speed peregrine falcons dive, so that's how fast they went in this study

No; the dam is too short to allow that

No; they could reach that speed, but they wouldn't have time to stop before hitting the ground if they did

There's no way to know given just this information how fast the falcons dove in the study

Part B. We can model the dive of a peregrine as beginning from rest and falling vertically. (In reality, there is horizontal motion, but it isn't very important to understanding the dive speed.)

The peregrine is initially in free fall, but as it falls faster and faster, it encounters more and more air drag. Eventually, the peregrine falls at some maximum speed, given its size, shape, and the air it's falling through. This maximum speed is the falcon's __terminal velocity__.

Match each plot to whether it shows the height, speed, or magnitude of acceleration of a peregrine falling through air, starting from rest, as a function of time. These plots only show the portion of the dive while the peregrin is approaching terminal velocity. They do not show the bird pulling out of the dive, capturing prey, landing on the ground, etc.

Part C. Draw a plot of the kinetic, thermal, gravitational potential, and total energies as a peregrine falcon dives, starting from rest and reaching terminal velocity. Start your plots right when the falcon starts diving. Stop the plots before the falcon pulls out of its dive.

Your drawing should show four curves, one for each energy you're plotting. The curves should all be plotted on the same set of axes. Label the curves according to which type of energy they represent. You should also label the axes, but you don't need a scale for them.

The roiling air behind the falcon technically has kinetic energy, but in a matter of seconds, that kinetic energy will be dissipated to thermal energy, so you can count any energy in the air as thermal energy in this problem. For thermal energy, draw the change in thermal energy from the time that the falcon starts diving, so this curve should begin at zero.

Your plot can be qualitative, but should show the trend in each type of energy.

For this part, you can turn in a labelled plot without detailed written explanation.

Part D. In class, we built a model for air drag. In this model, an object moving through the air leaves a tube of roiling air behind it. The speed of the air is similar to the object's own speed, and the tube's cross-sectional area is similar to the object's own cross-sectional area.

In their research, the German scientists found that the cross-sectional area of a typical diving peregrine was about $$0.012 \;\mathrm{m}^2.$$ The density of air is about $$1.2 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ These quantities are approximations, but they are accurate to within $$10\%$$ or better for real peregrines diving close to $$90 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

The mass of an adult peregrine is between $$0.7 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and $$1.5 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

Use these figures to estimate the terminal velocity of a peregrine, showing your work.

Is your result close to the observed $$90 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ speed of a peregrine? If not, briefly speculate on what you think the most important source of error in the calculation is and why you think it might be a significant source of error. Your answer doesn't have to be perfectly accurate as long as it demonstrates an understanding of the model used here.

Note: all the measurements given in this problem are accurate enough to find a terminal velocity close to the observed terminal velocity of real peregrines, given the right model. If there is a discrepancy between your calculation and the real terminal velocity, look for it in the model, not in the figures you used.

name: Emilie Rolls Down the Ramp — Emilie the skater starts from rest at the top of a ramp and rolls down to its…
desc: Emilie the skater starts from rest at the top of a ramp and rolls down to its bottom edge. There is no friction or air resistance. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Let her mass be $$m,$$ let $$y_1$$ be the height of the top of the ramp above the ground, and let $$y_2$$ be the…
statement:
Emilie the skater starts from rest at the top of a ramp and rolls down to its bottom edge. There is no friction or air resistance. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Let her mass be $$m,$$ let $$y_1$$ be the height of the top of the ramp above the ground, and let $$y_2$$ be the height of the bottom edge, as in the figure below. Her __gravitational potential energy__ at height $$y$$ is $$U = mgy,$$ and her __kinetic energy__ at speed $$v$$ is $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2.$$ (You can experiment with a similar setup in PhET's "Energy Skate Park" simulation.)

__(a)__ What are Emilie's kinetic and potential energies at the top of the ramp, and what are they at the bottom edge? With no friction, what must be true about her total energy at the two places? Write the resulting equation.

__(b)__ Letting $$\Delta y = y_1 - y_2$$ be how far she descends, solve your equation for her speed $$v$$ at the bottom edge. (Cancel everything you can.)

__(c)__ A tape measure in the simulation shows that the bottom edge of the ramp is $$\Delta y = 0.92\;\mathrm{m}$$ below the top. Find Emilie's speed at the bottom edge.

The simulation also displays an energy __bar chart__ with four bars: kinetic energy, potential energy, thermal energy, and total energy. At the moment Emilie is released, all of her energy is potential:

__(d)__ As Emilie rolls down the ramp, state whether each of the four bars grows, shrinks, or stays the same, and why.

__(e)__ After leaving the bottom edge, Emilie flies off and becomes a projectile. While she is in the air, her kinetic energy grows much faster than it did on the ramp. Explain why, by comparing her acceleration in the air with her acceleration on a ramp that drops a height $$h$$ over a slope of length $$L.$$

label: MCH05
name: Stopping at the Very Edge: Speed or Energy? — Emilie the skater (mass $$m = 60\;\mathrm{kg}$$) rolls from…
desc: Emilie the skater (mass $$m = 60\;\mathrm{kg}$$) rolls from rest down a first ramp, flies off its edge, lands on a second ramp across a gap, and rolls along the second ramp. She likes to play with fire: she wants to come to rest __exactly__ at the far edge of the second ramp —…
statement:
Emilie the skater (mass $$m = 60\;\mathrm{kg}$$) rolls from rest down a first ramp, flies off its edge, lands on a second ramp across a gap, and rolls along the second ramp. She likes to play with fire: she wants to come to rest __exactly__ at the far edge of the second ramp — any extra speed and she drifts off the wrong side and falls. The simulation lets us add adjustable friction to slow her down before she launches. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Kinetic energy is $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2,$$ measured in __joules__: $$1\;\mathrm{J} = 1\;\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2/s^2}.$$

With no friction at all, her speed is $$4.3\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ at the end of the first ramp and $$2.2\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ at the far edge of the second ramp. (Between those points she trades some kinetic energy for height, and loses some in the impact when she lands on the second ramp.)

__(a)__ A rival physics class proposes this plan: assume Emilie always loses the same amount of __speed__ between the end of the first ramp and the far edge of the second ramp. Under that assumption, what should her speed be at the end of the first ramp so she arrives at the far edge with zero speed?

__(b)__ When the friction was tuned to give her exactly that launch speed, Emilie turned around well short of the far edge. Explain what is wrong with the constant-speed-loss assumption. (Hint: if Emilie moves faster, how long does she spend decelerating on the second ramp?)

__(c)__ Compute Emilie's kinetic energy at the end of the first ramp and at the far edge of the second ramp in the frictionless run, and the amount of kinetic energy she loses in between. Show that the units of your calculation work out to joules.

__(d)__ Now assume instead that she always loses the same amount of kinetic __energy__ between those two points — the amount you found in part (c). How much kinetic energy should she have at the end of the first ramp so she arrives at the far edge with zero kinetic energy? What launch speed does that correspond to?

label: MCH05
name: A Model for Sliding Friction — A box is given a push and released with initial speed $$v_0$$ on a horizontal…
desc: A box is given a push and released with initial speed $$v_0$$ on a horizontal floor. Friction with the floor slows it until it stops after sliding a total distance $$\Delta x_{\rm tot}.$$ As the box slides, its kinetic energy $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2$$ is converted into __thermal…
statement:
A box is given a push and released with initial speed $$v_0$$ on a horizontal floor. Friction with the floor slows it until it stops after sliding a total distance $$\Delta x_{\rm tot}.$$ As the box slides, its kinetic energy $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2$$ is converted into __thermal energy__; call the amount converted while sliding a distance $$\Delta x$$ by the name $$\Delta E_{\rm th}.$$ In this problem you will build a model (a formula) for $$\Delta E_{\rm th}$$ in terms of the box's mass $$m,$$ the sliding distance $$\Delta x,$$ and the free-fall acceleration $$g.$$

Experiments with sliding boxes show two key facts. First, the stopping distance does not depend on the mass: load the box with books and push it at the same initial speed, and to a good approximation it slides just as far. Second, the stopping distance is proportional to the square of the initial speed: $$\Delta x_{\rm tot} \propto v_0^2.$$ (The speed itself doesn't matter beyond this, once you account for distance.)

__(a)__ Even though adding mass doesn't change the stopping distance, the formula for $$\Delta E_{\rm th}$$ __should__ contain $$m.$$ Explain why, and show that doubling $$m$$ (at the same $$v_0$$) doubles $$\Delta E_{\rm th},$$ so that $$\Delta E_{\rm th} \propto m.$$

__(b)__ If you push the box with three times the initial speed, how many times as far does it slide? Then use the fact that all the kinetic energy ends up as thermal energy to argue that $$\Delta E_{\rm th} \propto \Delta x,$$ the distance slid.

__(c)__ Increasing $$g$$ would press the box harder against the floor, increasing the friction; experiments support $$\Delta E_{\rm th} \propto g.$$ Combine the three proportionalities into a single proportionality for $$\Delta E_{\rm th}.$$

__(d)__ A proportionality is still missing a coefficient. The coefficient here is called the __coefficient of friction__, written $$\mu$$ (the Greek letter "mu"). It has no dimensions or units, and it measures how rough or smooth the interaction between the two surfaces is: car tires on asphalt have $$\mu \approx 0.7,$$ while ice skates on ice have $$\mu \approx 0.005.$$ Write the final model for $$\Delta E_{\rm th},$$ and state the kind of situation it applies to.

__(e)__ Use the model: a $$2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ box is pushed at $$3.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ across a floor with $$\mu = 0.30.$$ Taking $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ how far does the box slide before stopping?

label: MCH05
name: How Steep Is Her Hill? — Professional cyclist Ayesha McGowan coasts down a long hill in a tucked-in posture…
desc: Professional cyclist Ayesha McGowan coasts down a long hill in a tucked-in posture (to minimize wind drag) at a constant speed of $$15\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Estimate how steep the hill is. If nothing resisted her motion she would speed up the whole way down — after descending…
statement:
Professional cyclist Ayesha McGowan coasts down a long hill in a tucked-in posture (to minimize wind drag) at a constant speed of $$15\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Estimate how steep the hill is.

If nothing resisted her motion she would speed up the whole way down — after descending $$100\;\mathrm{m}$$ of elevation she would be moving faster than $$45\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ ($$\approx 100$$ miles per hour). Instead, almost all the mechanical energy she releases goes into the air: as she rides, she smashes into the air ahead of her and leaves behind a tube of swirling air — her __slipstream__ — whose motion quickly becomes thermal energy.

Model the slipstream as a tube whose cross-section equals McGowan's own __cross-sectional area__ $$A$$ (the area you see looking at her head-on), and whose air is set moving at roughly her own speed, $$v_{\rm air} \approx 15\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Use the estimates $$m = 60\;\mathrm{kg}$$ (McGowan plus her bike), $$A \approx 0.25\;\mathrm{m^2},$$ air density $$\rho_{\rm air} \approx 1.2\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$$ (the mass of air per unit volume; $$\rho$$ is the Greek letter "rho"), and $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ McGowan's speed is constant, so her kinetic energy is constant. As she descends, which energies are changing, and how must the magnitude of the change in her gravitational potential energy, $$|\Delta U|,$$ compare with the change in thermal energy, $$|\Delta E_{\rm th}|?$$

__(b)__ Suppose she rides a distance $$\ell$$ along the road while dropping an elevation $$|\Delta y|.$$ Write $$|\Delta U|$$ in terms of $$m,$$ $$g,$$ and $$|\Delta y|.$$ Then write $$|\Delta E_{\rm th}|$$ as the kinetic energy given to the tube of air she rides through (its mass is $$\rho_{\rm air}$$ times its volume). Set the two equal and solve for the steepness $$\dfrac{|\Delta y|}{\ell},$$ which is large for steep hills and small for gentle ones.

__(c)__ Check the dimensions of both sides of your formula. What does the check tell you — and what does it __not__ tell you?

__(d)__ Plug in the numbers. Cyclists usually quote a hill's steepness as its slope, or __grade__; for slopes this small, $$\dfrac{|\Delta y|}{\ell}$$ and the grade are essentially equal. Real cyclists report coasting at about $$30$$–$$35$$ miles per hour ($$\approx 15\;\mathrm{m/s}$$) on a $$6\%$$ grade. How does your estimate compare?

label: MCH05
name: The Betz Limit — Wind turbines generate electricity by extracting __kinetic energy__ from moving air…
desc: Wind turbines generate electricity by extracting __kinetic energy__ from moving air. Below is a wind farm of vertical-axis turbines built by Caltech professor John Dabiri, who arranged his turbines the way fish arrange themselves in schools — nearby turbines spin in opposite…
statement:
Wind turbines generate electricity by extracting __kinetic energy__ from moving air. Below is a wind farm of vertical-axis turbines built by Caltech professor John Dabiri, who arranged his turbines the way fish arrange themselves in schools — nearby turbines spin in opposite directions, like the alternating vortices fish shed as they swim.

__(a)__ Air must keep flowing through a turbine for the turbine to keep operating. Use this to explain why a wind turbine can never extract __all__ of the kinetic energy from the air that passes through it.

__(b)__ In a standard model of the best possible turbine, air that approaches at speed $$v_{\rm in}$$ must leave at speed $$v_{\rm out} = \sqrt{\dfrac{11}{27}}\,v_{\rm in} \approx 0.638\,v_{\rm in}$$ to keep air from building up. Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared: $$KE \propto v^2.$$ What fraction of the incoming kinetic energy is still in the air as it leaves the turbine?

__(c)__ What fraction of the incoming kinetic energy does this best-possible turbine extract? (This famous figure is called the __Betz limit__, after Albert Betz, who published it in 1919. Real turbines extract about half the wind's kinetic energy at best — under the limit, but close to it.)

__(d)__ A real turbine extracts less kinetic energy from the air than the turbine in the model. Is the air leaving a real turbine moving faster or slower than the model's $$v_{\rm out}?$$

__(e)__ Dabiri showed — without finding any error in Betz's derivation — that a turbine can beat the Betz limit on average over time. The Betz model assumes the wind blows at a constant speed, while real wind comes in gusts. Explain how a supposed "limit" can be beaten, in light of the scientists' saying, "All models are wrong, but some are useful."

label: MCH05
name: Powering the World with Wind — Can wind power plausibly provide all of humanity's energy needs? Make an…
desc: Can wind power plausibly provide all of humanity's energy needs? Make an estimate using the following facts. The world's total rate of energy use is about $$P_{\rm world} = 1.2 \times 10^{13}\;\mathrm{W}.$$ An energy per unit time is called a __power__; the SI unit of power is…
statement:
Can wind power plausibly provide all of humanity's energy needs? Make an estimate using the following facts.

The world's total rate of energy use is about $$P_{\rm world} = 1.2 \times 10^{13}\;\mathrm{W}.$$ An energy per unit time is called a __power__; the SI unit of power is the __watt__, defined by $$1\;\mathrm{W} = \dfrac{1\;\mathrm{J}}{1\;\mathrm{s}}.$$ A typical wind farm produces about $$2\;\mathrm{W}$$ of power per square meter of land. The radius of the Earth is about $$R = 6.4 \times 10^6\;\mathrm{m},$$ and the surface area of a sphere is $$4\pi R^2.$$

__(a)__ How much wind-farm area would be needed to supply the world's entire power use?

__(b)__ What percent of the Earth's surface is that?

__(c)__ Does your answer settle the question of whether wind alone could power the world? Name at least one real-world complication that the calculation leaves out.

label: MCH05
name: Why Doesn't the Wind Warm the Air? — Today's wind turbines capture only a tiny fraction of the energy in the…
desc: Today's wind turbines capture only a tiny fraction of the energy in the wind. The rest of the wind eventually slows down anyway, as it runs into mountains, buildings, ocean waves, and other layers of air. Energy is conserved, so the wind's kinetic energy doesn't disappear — it…
statement:
Today's wind turbines capture only a tiny fraction of the energy in the wind. The rest of the wind eventually slows down anyway, as it runs into mountains, buildings, ocean waves, and other layers of air. Energy is conserved, so the wind's kinetic energy doesn't disappear — it is dissipated into __thermal energy__, slightly heating the air. Yet wind famously feels __cold__. Let's check how much heating actually occurs.

At a temperature of $$293\;\mathrm{K}$$ (about room temperature), air molecules zip around randomly at roughly $$500\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Here $$\mathrm{K}$$ is the symbol for the __kelvin__, the SI unit of temperature; $$0\;\mathrm{K}$$ is the coldest possible temperature, which makes kelvin the right unit for this problem. Assume the temperature of air in kelvin is proportional to the kinetic energy of an average molecule, $$T \propto \dfrac12 mv^2.$$

__(a)__ Consider a wind blowing at $$10\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Using $$KE \propto v^2,$$ find the ratio of the air's thermal energy to the wind's mechanical kinetic energy.

__(b)__ Suppose the wind is brought to rest and all of its kinetic energy is thermalized in the same air. By about how many kelvin does the air warm up? Is that a change you would notice when outside?

__(c)__ If wind barely heats the air, why does it feel cold when the wind blows on you?

statement:
A __Roberval balance__ is a device with six pivots as shown.

The bars cannot change length, and the device is rigid except at the pivots. The top and bottom horizontal bars are each single pieces, not two pieces coming together at the pivot.

The Roberval balance has only a single __degree of freedom__, or a single way of moving. After undergoing a displacement, it can look like either of these:

Or it can move larger or smaller amounts in the same way. The Roberval balance is in equilibrium at all these positions when no masses are added to it.

You can see the motion of the Roberval balance in the gif below:

A disc of mass $$m_L$$ is placed at the far left of the left hand bar, and a disc of mass $$m_R$$ is placed on the right hand bar near the vertical crossbar as shown.

Two students are discussing what the relationship should be between $$m_L$$ and $$m_R$$ for the device to be in equilibrium.

Duante says: The law of the lever says that the disc further from the fulcrum should have less mass, so for a lever, $$m_L < m_R.$$ We derived this by thinking about potential energy changes. The Roberval balance can be analyzed using energy, too, so $$m_L < m_R$$ is still correct.

Divya says: But here, there's no single fulcrum, like there is for a lever. We can't analyze this device using energy. We need to use virtual displacements instead. When the Roberval balance moves a little, the left and right discs each have the same virtual displacement, so $$m_L = m_R.$$

From the choices below, select one **incorrect** thing a student said.

Duante's final conclusion, $$m_L < m_R$$

Divya's final conclusion, $$m_L = m_R$$

Duante's claim that we can use potential energy to analyze the device

Divya's claim that we can use virtual displacements to analyze the device

label: MCH06
name: Balancing a Trash Can Against a Fire Extinguisher — A __lever__ is a rigid beam that can rotate about a fixed…
desc: A __lever__ is a rigid beam that can rotate about a fixed axis called the __fulcrum__. On a simple scale, two objects with the same mass balance when they sit at equal distances from the fulcrum. Now we want to balance objects with different masses: a $$5\;\mathrm{kg}$$ fire…
statement:
A __lever__ is a rigid beam that can rotate about a fixed axis called the __fulcrum__. On a simple scale, two objects with the same mass balance when they sit at equal distances from the fulcrum. Now we want to balance objects with different masses: a $$5\;\mathrm{kg}$$ fire extinguisher and a $$10\;\mathrm{kg}$$ trash can.

__(a)__ The fire extinguisher is placed $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ to the right of the fulcrum. Where should the trash can be placed so the lever balances?

__(b)__ Call the two masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ and their distances from the fulcrum $$d_1$$ and $$d_2.$$ Using part (a) as a guide, write an equation relating $$m_1,$$ $$m_2,$$ $$d_1,$$ and $$d_2$$ when the lever balances. (This relation is called the __law of the lever__, and a balanced lever is an example of __equilibrium__.)

Next, two fire extinguishers with identical masses are placed on the lever — the left one, $$L,$$ farther from the fulcrum than the right one, $$R.$$ Supports hold the beam level until they are removed.

__(c)__ When the supports are removed, which side tips down? As the lever tips, state whether each of the following increases, decreases, or stays the same for the whole __system__ (both extinguishers, the lever, and the gravitational interaction with Earth): the kinetic energy, the gravitational potential energy, and the total energy. Assume the thermal energy does not change.

__(d)__ The two extinguishers have equal masses, and as the lever tips, one moves down while the other moves up. Why does the total gravitational potential energy change at all?

__(e)__ Suppose all you can do is slide the extinguishers along the beam, or remove them. How could you make $$L$$ hit the ground moving faster? Explain your answer using energy.

label: MCH06
name: Deriving the Law of the Lever — When a system balances, we can analyze it by imagining a small motion that…
desc: When a system balances, we can analyze it by imagining a small motion that never actually happens, called a __virtual displacement__. We write $$\delta$$ (a lowercase Greek delta, the small version of $$\Delta$$) for changes during a virtual displacement, so $$\delta y$$ is a…
statement:
When a system balances, we can analyze it by imagining a small motion that never actually happens, called a __virtual displacement__. We write $$\delta$$ (a lowercase Greek delta, the small version of $$\Delta$$) for changes during a virtual displacement, so $$\delta y$$ is a small imagined change in height. If a virtual displacement would make the potential energy decrease, the released energy would become kinetic energy, and the system would accelerate. So a system can be in __equilibrium__ only if the potential energy does not decrease under any virtual displacement; for a frictionless lever the condition is $$\delta U = 0.$$

A mass $$m_1$$ sits a distance $$d_1$$ to the left of a lever's fulcrum, and a mass $$m_2$$ sits a distance $$d_2$$ to the right. The figure shows the lever after a small virtual tilt; the dashed line is the original position of the beam. The left mass rises by $$\delta y_1 > 0,$$ and the right mass falls, so its height change $$\delta y_2$$ is negative.

__(a)__ The tilted beam forms a right triangle with the original beam on each side of the fulcrum; the hypotenuses are $$d_1$$ and $$d_2,$$ and the vertical legs are the height changes. Use similar triangles to show that $$\dfrac{\delta y_1}{d_1} = \dfrac{-\delta y_2}{d_2}.$$

__(b)__ The gravitational potential energy of a mass $$m$$ at height $$y$$ is $$U = mgy,$$ so under the virtual tilt the system's potential energy changes by $$\delta U = m_1 g\, \delta y_1 + m_2 g\, \delta y_2.$$ Set $$\delta U = 0$$ and use part (a) to derive the law of the lever, $$m_1 d_1 = m_2 d_2.$$

__(c)__ In terms of energy, explain why you could tip a balanced lever — lifting one side and lowering the other — without putting any energy in or taking any out.

label: MCH06
name: The Doctor's Scale — A __simple machine__ lets a small input mass balance a much larger output mass. Its…
desc: A __simple machine__ lets a small input mass balance a much larger output mass. Its __mechanical advantage__ is $$\text{MA} = \dfrac{m_{\rm output}}{m_{\rm input}},$$ the output mass divided by the input mass that balances it. A doctor's scale uses small sliding weights (called…
statement:
A __simple machine__ lets a small input mass balance a much larger output mass. Its __mechanical advantage__ is $$\text{MA} = \dfrac{m_{\rm output}}{m_{\rm input}},$$ the output mass divided by the input mass that balances it. A doctor's scale uses small sliding weights (called __poise__) to weigh a person roughly $$1000$$ times more massive.

__(a)__ By the law of the lever ($$m_1 d_1 = m_2 d_2$$), balancing a $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ poise against a $$100\;\mathrm{kg}$$ person on a single lever requires $$d_{\rm poise} \approx 1000\, d_{\rm person}.$$ Why is a single lever impractical here?

__(b)__ Instead, several levers can be chained together: the long end of each lever drives the short end of the next, as in the schematic below. Each lever's fulcrum is placed so that the lever by itself has a mechanical advantage of $$10.$$ What is the mechanical advantage of the three-lever chain? Can a $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ box balance a $$100\;\mathrm{kg}$$ box this way?

__(c)__ Mechanical advantage can also be written using the distances the input and output move. Which formula is correct: $$\text{MA} = \dfrac{d_{\rm output}}{d_{\rm input}}$$ or $$\text{MA} = \dfrac{d_{\rm input}}{d_{\rm output}}$$? Explain, using the fact that a light input balancing a heavy output must move a long way while the output barely moves.

__(d)__ When you stand on a doctor's scale and the $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ poise drops $$0.5\;\mathrm{cm},$$ about how far do you rise, if your mass is $$50\;\mathrm{kg}$$ — that is, $$500$$ times the poise's mass? Compare your answer to the thickness of a sheet of notebook paper, about $$10^{-2}\;\mathrm{cm}.$$

__(e)__ A lever balances a $$10\;\mathrm{kg}$$ trash can against a $$5\;\mathrm{kg}$$ fire extinguisher. Taking the trash can as the input and the fire extinguisher as the output, what is the mechanical advantage? What is it with the roles reversed?

label: MCH06
name: Pulleys and the Block and Tackle — In the pulley system below, a single string starts at the ceiling, passes…
desc: In the pulley system below, a single string starts at the ceiling, passes down and around a __movable__ lower pulley, goes up and over an upper pulley fixed to the ceiling, and finally connects to box $$A.$$ Box $$B$$ hangs from the movable pulley. The string segments are…
statement:
In the pulley system below, a single string starts at the ceiling, passes down and around a __movable__ lower pulley, goes up and over an upper pulley fixed to the ceiling, and finally connects to box $$A.$$ Box $$B$$ hangs from the movable pulley. The string segments are labeled: $$s_1$$ runs from the ceiling anchor down to the movable pulley, $$s_2$$ runs from the movable pulley up to the fixed pulley, and $$s_3$$ runs from the fixed pulley down to box $$A.$$

__(a)__ Box $$A$$ is pulled down $$1\;\mathrm{cm},$$ so segment $$s_3$$ gets $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ longer. The total length of the string cannot change. What happens to the lengths of $$s_1$$ and $$s_2,$$ and how far does box $$B$$ rise?

__(b)__ The __mechanical advantage__ of a machine is $$\text{MA} = \dfrac{d_{\rm input}}{d_{\rm output}},$$ the distance the input moves divided by the distance the output moves (defined to be positive). Taking $$A$$ as the input and $$B$$ as the output, what is the mechanical advantage of this system? (For comparison, an __Atwood machine__ — two boxes hanging from opposite sides of one fixed pulley — has $$\text{MA} = 1$$: when one box falls $$1\;\mathrm{cm},$$ the other rises $$1\;\mathrm{cm}.$$)

__(c)__ If box $$A$$ has mass $$m,$$ what must the mass of box $$B$$ be for equilibrium? Justify your answer by showing that the gravitational potential energy does not change under a small virtual displacement.

__(d)__ Below is a system with many pulleys. Nine vertical rope segments connect a horizontal bar to the frame above it. An experimenter pulls down on the leftmost segment through a spring scale that reads $$1\;\mathrm{kg}$$; a second scale connects the bar to the load. When the bar rises $$1\;\mathrm{mm},$$ each of the other eight segments gets $$1\;\mathrm{mm}$$ shorter, and all that rope feeds into the segment being pulled. What is the mechanical advantage of this system, and roughly what does the second scale read?

__(e)__ The same arrangement with its pulleys lined up side by side is called a __block and tackle__ (pictured below). A single student used a block and tackle with mechanical advantage $$8$$ to lift the school principal — a job that took five students pulling on a plain fixed pulley. If the principal rises $$0.5\;\mathrm{m},$$ how much rope does the student pull through the block and tackle? Does the block and tackle reduce the __energy__ needed to lift the principal $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$? Explain.

label: MCH06
name: How Much Friction Holds a Half-Atwood Machine? — A block of mass $$M$$ rests on a horizontal table. A string…
desc: A block of mass $$M$$ rests on a horizontal table. A string runs from the block, over a pulley at the table's edge, down to a hanging block of mass $$m.$$ This setup is called a __half-Atwood machine__. The coefficient of friction between $$M$$ and the table is $$\mu.$$ When…
statement:
A block of mass $$M$$ rests on a horizontal table. A string runs from the block, over a pulley at the table's edge, down to a hanging block of mass $$m.$$ This setup is called a __half-Atwood machine__. The coefficient of friction between $$M$$ and the table is $$\mu.$$ When $$M$$ slides a distance $$\Delta x$$ along the table, friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy according to the model $$\Delta E_{\rm th} = \mu M g\, \Delta x.$$

__(a)__ If there were no friction at all, would this system be in equilibrium for any hanging mass $$m > 0$$? (For reference: without friction the system accelerates at $$a = \dfrac{gm}{M+m}.$$)

__(b)__ To test for equilibrium with friction, imagine a small __virtual displacement__ in which the hanging block moves down: its height changes by $$\delta y < 0,$$ and the block $$M$$ slides a distance $$-\delta y$$ toward the pulley. Write expressions for the change in gravitational potential energy, $$\delta U,$$ and for the thermal energy generated, $$\delta E_{\rm th}.$$

__(c)__ With dissipation, the condition for equilibrium is that a virtual displacement leaves no energy over for kinetic energy: the thermal energy generated must absorb at least all of the potential energy released, $$\delta E_{\rm th} \ge -\delta U.$$ Use your expressions from part (b) to find the minimum coefficient of friction, $$\mu_{\rm min},$$ that keeps the system in equilibrium.

label: MCH06
name: Stable, Neutral, and Unstable Equilibrium — A skater rides a curved track with a little friction, so she…
desc: A skater rides a curved track with a little friction, so she gradually slows down. Whether a resting point is an equilibrium — and what kind — can be tested with __virtual displacements__: imagine moving the system a tiny amount in each direction and ask how the potential energy…
statement:
A skater rides a curved track with a little friction, so she gradually slows down. Whether a resting point is an equilibrium — and what kind — can be tested with __virtual displacements__: imagine moving the system a tiny amount in each direction and ask how the potential energy changes ($$\delta U$$). If $$\delta U > 0$$ for displacements in either direction, the equilibrium is __stable__. If $$\delta U = 0,$$ it is __neutral__. If $$\delta U < 0$$ in both directions, it is __unstable__. And if $$U$$ decreases one way but increases the other, the point is not an equilibrium at all.

__(a)__ The skater rolls back and forth on the track below, slowly losing energy to friction. Where does she eventually come to rest, and what kind of equilibrium is that point?

__(b)__ Once at rest there, she is given a small push to the right. Does she drift away at constant speed, accelerate away, or come back? Explain using energy.

__(c)__ On the track below, where could the skater be placed so that she is in __unstable__ equilibrium? What happens if she is then displaced just a little?

__(d)__ A frictionless lever is built so that it balances at __every__ angle: its potential energy is the same no matter how it is tilted. The level lever is given a small tap, starting it rotating slowly. Does it accelerate to the ground, rotate to the ground at a constant rate, move a little and stop, or return to level? Explain using energy, and name the type of equilibrium.

__(e)__ Mechanical systems settle at minima of potential energy — but only __local__ minima. Explain how the skater can come to rest at the bottom of the small dip shown below, even though it is not the lowest point on her track.

label: MCH06
name: Why a Real Scale Tips Only Part Way — An idealized lever — a beam passing straight through its fulcrum — is…
desc: An idealized lever — a beam passing straight through its fulcrum — is either perfectly balanced or it tips all the way over. A real scale behaves differently: the lever below is loaded slightly unevenly, and when its supports are removed it tips only part way, coming to rest at…
statement:
An idealized lever — a beam passing straight through its fulcrum — is either perfectly balanced or it tips all the way over. A real scale behaves differently: the lever below is loaded slightly unevenly, and when its supports are removed it tips only part way, coming to rest at some angle $$\theta_e.$$

The key difference is __where the beam sits relative to the fulcrum__. In real scales, the beam and its masses hang __below__ the fulcrum, as in the lower diagram. In both diagrams the masses are equal ($$m_1 = m_2$$) and equidistant from the fulcrum ($$d_1 = d_2$$); the dashed lines show the untilted positions.

__(a)__ First consider the idealized lever (beam through the fulcrum) with equal masses at equal distances. When the beam tilts, compare how far the two masses move vertically. What does this say about how the total gravitational potential energy $$U$$ depends on the tilt angle $$\theta$$? What kind of equilibrium is the level position?

__(b)__ Now suppose the beam, with its masses, is rigidly attached a short distance __below__ the fulcrum (lower diagram), again with equal masses at equal distances. When the assembly tilts, which mass moves farther vertically — the one that rises or the one that falls? What happens to $$U$$?

__(c)__ Describe the graph of total gravitational potential energy versus tilt angle $$\theta$$ for the beam-below-the-fulcrum lever with equal loading. What kind of equilibrium is $$\theta = 0$$?

__(d)__ Finally, load the beam-below-the-fulcrum lever slightly unevenly, as in the photo above. How does the $$U(\theta)$$ curve change, and why does the lever come to rest tipped part way at $$\theta_e$$ rather than falling all the way over?

In this demo, a physicist releases a pendulum, which swings back and forth.

The video has been edited to point out that the pendulum rises to the same height it was released from (or really, a tiny bit lower) due to conservation of energy (and due to some small amount of energy being dissipated to thermal energy).

Next, the physicist inserts a peg in the path of the pendulum, so the string will hit the peg when the pendulum is vertical.

Here is the path of the pendulum with the peg inserted:

It doesn't happen in this video, but if the peg is inserted correctly, the pendulum will swing all the way around in a full circle, wrapping completely around the peg without going slack.

Suppose a pendulum has length $$L$$ and assume that the peg will be inserted so that the pendulum string hits the peg when it is vertical.

Where should the peg be located so that the pendulum swings all the way around?

You can ignore the radius of the peg and the size of the weight at the bottom of the pendulum. Assume that there is zero dissipation to thermal energy.

label: MCH07
name: Finding the Circular-Motion Acceleration — An object moving around a circle of radius $$R$$ at a constant…
desc: An object moving around a circle of radius $$R$$ at a constant speed $$v$$ is in __uniform circular motion__. Even though its speed never changes, its velocity is constantly changing direction, so the object is accelerating. In this problem you will find the formula for the…
statement:
An object moving around a circle of radius $$R$$ at a constant speed $$v$$ is in __uniform circular motion__. Even though its speed never changes, its velocity is constantly changing direction, so the object is accelerating. In this problem you will find the formula for the magnitude $$a$$ of that acceleration in two independent ways.

__(a)__ Use __dimensional analysis__: a formula can only be correct if its dimensions match. Writing $$\mathrm{M}$$ for the dimension of mass, $$\mathrm{L}$$ for length, and $$\mathrm{T}$$ for time, the dimensions of the three quantities are $$=\mathrm{L}\cdot\mathrm{T}^{-2},$$ $$=\mathrm{L},$$ and $$=\mathrm{L}\cdot\mathrm{T}^{-1}.$$ Find the combination of $$v$$ and $$R$$ that has the same dimensions as $$a.$$ (Hint: deal with the time dimension first — only $$a$$ and $$v$$ contain any $$\mathrm{T}.$$) Dimensional analysis only gives the formula up to a dimensionless constant; it turns out that constant is $$1.$$

The figure shows the object at two moments: first on the right side of the circle moving straight down with speed $$v,$$ and later, after going halfway around, on the left side moving straight up with speed $$v.$$ Take the $$y$$ axis vertical with up positive, so the initial $$y$$-velocity is $$v_{y;i}=-v$$ and the final one is $$v_{y;f}=+v.$$

__(b)__ Find $$\Delta v_y,$$ the change in the $$y$$-component of velocity between the two moments.

__(c)__ Find $$\Delta t,$$ the time to travel halfway around the circle, and compute the average acceleration $$a_{\rm avg}=\dfrac{\Delta v_y}{\Delta t}$$ as a number times $$\dfrac{v^2}{R}.$$

__(d)__ Now suppose the speed is doubled on the same circle. Using $$a=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t},$$ identify __two__ separate effects that each make the acceleration larger, and find the overall factor by which the average acceleration grows. What feature of the formula from part (a) does this explain? Similarly, what does doubling the radius $$R$$ (at the same speed) do to $$\Delta t,$$ and therefore to the acceleration?

__(e)__ If instead we compare two moments only a __quarter__ circle apart, the velocity turns by $$90^\circ,$$ and the magnitude of the velocity change works out to $$|\Delta v|=\sqrt{2}\,v.$$ Compute the average acceleration over the quarter circle as a number times $$\dfrac{v^2}{R}.$$ Why are the averages in (c) and (e) smaller than $$\dfrac{v^2}{R},$$ and what happens as the two moments are taken closer and closer together?

label: MCH07
name: Artificial Gravity on a Spinning Space Station — In the film __2001: A Space Odyssey__, a wheel-shaped space…
desc: In the film __2001: A Space Odyssey__, a wheel-shaped space station spins to create gravity for the astronauts living on its rim. The station has a diameter of $$300\;\mathrm{m}$$ and a rotational __period__ — the time to spin all the way around once, written $$T$$ — of…
statement:
In the film __2001: A Space Odyssey__, a wheel-shaped space station spins to create gravity for the astronauts living on its rim. The station has a diameter of $$300\;\mathrm{m}$$ and a rotational __period__ — the time to spin all the way around once, written $$T$$ — of $$61\;\mathrm{s}.$$

Background: an object in uniform circular motion with radius $$R$$ and speed $$v$$ has an acceleration of magnitude $$a=\dfrac{v^2}{R}$$ pointing toward the center of the circle (a __centripetal__ acceleration). A person who is accelerating feels an __artificial gravity__ equal in strength to their acceleration but pointing in the __opposite__ direction. (In an elevator accelerating upward, you feel extra gravity downward; passengers in an airplane accelerating downward at $$g$$ feel artificial gravity upward that cancels real gravity, so they feel weightless.)

__(a)__ In terms of $$R$$ and $$T,$$ how fast is a point on the rim of the station moving?

__(b)__ Show that the acceleration of a point on the rim is $$a=\dfrac{4\pi^2R}{T^2},$$ and evaluate it for this station. How does it compare to Earth's free fall acceleration $$g\approx9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}?$$

__(c)__ What would the rotational period of the same station have to be for the artificial gravity to match Earth's free fall acceleration?

__(d)__ What direction does the artificial gravity point for an astronaut standing on the rim? Explain using the direction of the centripetal acceleration.

__(e)__ An astronaut starts at the hub (the center of the station) and slowly climbs down a spoke toward the rim. Describe how the artificial gravity they feel changes along the way, and why.

label: MCH07
name: The Gravitron — A carnival ride called the Gravitron is a large spinning room. Once it spins fast enough…
desc: A carnival ride called the Gravitron is a large spinning room. Once it spins fast enough, riders can hang out on the walls without touching the floor. Here is the view from inside, and from outside: An older version of the ride, the Rotor, had exactly vertical walls; assume…
statement:
A carnival ride called the Gravitron is a large spinning room. Once it spins fast enough, riders can hang out on the walls without touching the floor. Here is the view from inside, and from outside:

An older version of the ride, the Rotor, had exactly vertical walls; assume vertical walls throughout this problem. From the videos, the radius of the ride is about $$R=5\;\mathrm{m}$$ (about three adults lying down). According to Wikipedia, the ride spins at up to $$24\;\mathrm{rpm}$$ (revolutions per minute — it can spin around $$24$$ times in one minute). Use $$g_{\rm Earth}=10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Background: riders moving in a circle of radius $$R$$ with period $$T$$ have a centripetal acceleration $$a=\dfrac{4\pi^2R}{T^2}$$ toward the center, and therefore feel an artificial gravity of that strength pointing __outward__, pressing them into the wall. (At the very center of the ride, $$R$$ is tiny, so the operator standing there feels almost no artificial gravity.)

__(a)__ A rotation rate like $$24\;\mathrm{rpm}$$ is a __frequency__ — the number of times something repeats in a given interval of time, symbol $$f.$$ Frequency and period determine each other: $$T=\dfrac1f.$$ Frequency can be measured in __hertz__, defined by $$1\;\mathrm{Hz}=1\;\mathrm{s}^{-1}.$$ Find the ride's period $$T$$ in seconds and its frequency $$f$$ in hertz.

__(b)__ Find $$g_{\rm rot},$$ the artificial gravity pressing riders into the wall, in $$\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and in gees (multiples of $$g_{\rm Earth}$$).

__(c)__ Real Earth gravity still pulls the riders down; friction with the wall is what holds them up. Recall the class model of friction: when an object of mass $$m$$ slides a distance $$\Delta x$$ along a surface, the thermal energy generated is $$\Delta E_{\rm th}=\mu m g_{\rm press}\Delta x,$$ where $$\mu$$ is the coefficient of friction and $$g_{\rm press}$$ is the effective gravity pressing the object against the surface. Imagine a small virtual displacement $$\delta y$$ of a rider down the wall. For the rider to stay in equilibrium, the thermal energy friction would dissipate must be at least the gravitational potential energy that would be released. Use this to find the minimum coefficient of friction between rider and wall.

__(d)__ For each change below, decide whether it would __decrease__ the coefficient of friction needed: (i) increasing the frequency $$f$$ with $$R$$ fixed; (ii) increasing the period $$T$$ with $$R$$ fixed; (iii) increasing $$R$$ with $$T$$ fixed; (iv) increasing $$R$$ while keeping the riders' __speed__ $$v$$ fixed. Reconcile (iii) and (iv): is the centripetal acceleration proportional to $$R,$$ or to $$\dfrac1R?$$

label: MCH07
name: The Rope Swing — Abdus and Donna find an old rope swing over a river. Abdus tests it by hanging straight…
desc: Abdus and Donna find an old rope swing over a river. Abdus tests it by hanging straight down on the rope without swinging, and it holds him. Donna then wants to swing across the river. Abdus's mass is exactly __twice__ Donna's. What is the greatest angle Donna can pull the rope…
statement:
Abdus and Donna find an old rope swing over a river. Abdus tests it by hanging straight down on the rope without swinging, and it holds him. Donna then wants to swing across the river. Abdus's mass is exactly __twice__ Donna's. What is the greatest angle Donna can pull the rope back to and still be sure the rope won't break when she swings?

Background: a person swinging on a rope of length $$R$$ moves along a circle of radius $$R.$$ Moving at speed $$v,$$ they have a centripetal acceleration $$a=\dfrac{v^2}{R}$$ toward the center (the pivot), and so feel an __artificial gravity__ of strength $$a$$ pointing away from the pivot. At the bottom of the swing that artificial gravity points straight down, adding to real gravity — and the rope must support the total. The kinetic energy formula is $$K=\dfrac12mv^2$$ and the gravitational potential energy formula is $$U=mgy.$$

Let $$\theta$$ be the angle Donna pulls the rope back from vertical, which raises her a height $$h$$ above the lowest point of the swing, as shown.

__(a)__ The rope is known to survive supporting Abdus hanging at rest. In terms of $$g,$$ what is the largest total effective gravity (real plus artificial) Donna can safely feel at the bottom of her swing? What is the largest her centripetal acceleration can safely be?

__(b)__ Using conservation of energy, find Donna's speed at the bottom of the swing in terms of $$g$$ and $$h.$$

__(c)__ Find her centripetal acceleration at the bottom in terms of $$g,$$ $$h,$$ and $$R$$; use part (a) to find the largest safe value of $$\dfrac hR$$; and then use the geometry of the swing to find the greatest safe angle $$\theta.$$

__(d)__ For each of the following, would increasing it raise, lower, or not change the maximum safe angle: the free fall acceleration $$g$$; the rope length $$R$$; the ratio of Abdus's mass to Donna's mass?

__(e)__ While swinging, is Donna in __uniform__ circular motion? An object in non-uniform circular motion has, besides its __centripetal__ acceleration toward the center, a __tangential__ acceleration along its direction of motion. Explain why Donna has a tangential acceleration at most points of the swing, but none at the very bottom.

label: MCH07
name: Loop the Loop — A toy car can run around the inside of a vertical circular loop without falling off —…
desc: A toy car can run around the inside of a vertical circular loop without falling off — even upside down at the top. You can do the same trick swinging a cup of water in a vertical circle without spilling, and people have biked and even driven cars around vertical loops. Suppose a…
statement:
A toy car can run around the inside of a vertical circular loop without falling off — even upside down at the top. You can do the same trick swinging a cup of water in a vertical circle without spilling, and people have biked and even driven cars around vertical loops.

Suppose a frictionless roller coaster is released from rest at a height $$h$$ and runs into a vertical circular loop of radius $$R.$$

Background: an object moving at speed $$v$$ around a circle of radius $$R$$ has centripetal acceleration $$a=\dfrac{v^2}{R}$$ toward the center, and feels an artificial gravity of strength $$a$$ pointing __away__ from the center. Without friction, conservation of energy means the quantity $$v^2+2gy$$ stays constant as the coaster rolls (with $$y$$ measured upward). The number of "gees" passengers feel is their total felt gravity — real gravity plus artificial gravity combined — measured in units of $$g.$$

__(a)__ At the top of the loop the passengers are upside down. Explain why they don't fall out if the coaster is moving fast enough, and find the minimum safe speed $$v_{\rm top}$$ at the top in terms of $$g$$ and $$R.$$

__(b)__ Find the minimum release height $$h$$ so the coaster goes around the loop without anyone falling out. (The top of the loop is at height $$2R.$$) Would including friction make the required height higher or lower?

__(c)__ In this minimum design, how many gees do passengers feel at the very top of the loop?

__(d)__ Suppose instead the coaster moves fast enough that passengers at the top feel $$n$$ gees pressing them into their seats. Show that their centripetal acceleration at the top is $$(n+1)g,$$ and then find how many gees they feel at the __bottom__ of the loop.

__(e)__ Real roller coaster loops are not circles — they look more like the loop below. Based on your answer to (d), explain why circular loops have been phased out.

label: MCH07
name: A Loop with Constant Centripetal Acceleration — Real roller-coaster loops, like the one below, are not…
desc: Real roller-coaster loops, like the one below, are not circular. On a circular loop, the coaster's speed — and with it the centripetal acceleration — varies dramatically between the bottom and the top, giving riders wild swings in g-force. In this problem you will design a loop…
statement:
Real roller-coaster loops, like the one below, are not circular. On a circular loop, the coaster's speed — and with it the centripetal acceleration — varies dramatically between the bottom and the top, giving riders wild swings in g-force. In this problem you will design a loop on which the __centripetal acceleration stays constant__ all the way around.

Background: a curve that isn't a circle can still be matched, at any one point, by a __best-fit circle__ — the circle that touches the curve there and follows it as closely as possible. The radius of that circle is called the __radius of curvature__ $$R$$ of the curve at that point. An object moving along the curve at speed $$v$$ has the same centripetal acceleration as an imaginary object moving at speed $$v$$ around the best-fit circle: $$a=\dfrac{v^2}{R},$$ with $$R$$ the radius of curvature. Without friction, $$v^2+2gy$$ is constant; for a coaster released from rest at height $$h,$$ that means $$v^2+2gy=2gh.$$

__(a)__ On the loop, should the radius of curvature get larger or smaller as the coaster climbs to greater heights $$y$$? Explain.

__(b)__ Find the radius of curvature $$R$$ the loop needs at height $$y,$$ in terms of $$g,$$ $$h,$$ $$y,$$ and the constant centripetal acceleration $$a.$$

__(c)__ The constant $$a$$ is a __parameter__ of the loop: it has one value everywhere on a given loop, but different loops can be built with different values of $$a.$$ (By contrast, $$y$$ and $$R$$ are variables that change around the loop.) What is the minimum value of $$a$$ so that riders don't fall out at the top of the loop?

__(d)__ If riders in the middle of the train feel one gee pressing them into their seats at the top of the loop, find the parameter $$a$$ of this loop, and find how many gees those riders feel at the bottom.

__(e)__ The same physical loop is later run with a release height different from the $$h$$ it was designed for (but still high enough to make it around safely). Is the centripetal acceleration still constant around the loop? Explain using your formula from (b).

__(f)__ Several loops are built with the same overall height but different values of the parameter $$a.$$ As $$a$$ grows, does the loop's shape become more circular or more elongated? (Hint: think about the extreme case where $$a$$ is enormous — millions of gees.)

statement:
You swing a ball around your head on a string of length $$L=1.4\;\mathrm{m}.$$ The ball moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed, with the string sloping $$30^\circ$$ below horizontal, and the ball circling $$H=0.7\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground. If the string suddenly breaks, how far does the ball travel horizontally before it hits the ground? Use $$g=10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Background: a ball moving at speed $$v$$ in a horizontal circle of radius $$R$$ has centripetal acceleration $$a=\dfrac{v^2}{R}$$ pointing horizontally toward the center, so it feels an artificial gravity of strength $$a$$ pointing horizontally __outward__. The string lines up with the total apparent gravity the ball feels — the combination of real gravity $$g$$ (downward) and artificial gravity $$a$$ (outward). Also recall that an object falling from rest drops a distance $$\dfrac12gt^2$$ in time $$t.$$

__(a)__ If you spin the ball faster, does the string's angle below horizontal increase or decrease? Explain by considering extreme cases.

label: MCH08
name: In class, we practiced looking at new situations, finding the energy, and using the…
desc: In class, we practiced looking at new situations, finding the energy, and using the coefficients in the equations of kinetic and potential energies to find oscillation periods. Here, we'll practice that same idea in a completely new context. -----------------------------------…
statement:
In class, we practiced looking at new situations, finding the energy, and using the coefficients in the equations of kinetic and potential energies to find oscillation periods. Here, we'll practice that same idea in a completely new context.

-----------------------------------

Radio stations say things like "This is 101.5 FM." This means that the radio station's signal oscillates at frequency of $$101.5 \;\mathrm{MHz} = 1.015 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ To listen to this station, your radio needs to find any radio waves with that frequency and ignore all other radio waves around it.

The radio does this with a "tuner". A simple model for a tuner has two components: an __inductor__ and a __capacitor__. These are devices used in electric circuits. They both store energy. The inductor stores energy when electric charge runs through it, and the capacitor stores energy when there is electric charge on it.

Charge will oscillate between the inductor and capacitor at a certain frequency, which depends on how strong the inductor and capacitor are.

PhET project, "Circuit Construction Kit: DC", https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/circuit-construction-kit-dc

In this animation, the inductor is the coil of wire at the bottom. The capacitor is the two parallel plates at the top. The blue circles are charge. On the left, there is a white circle which can be ignored; in real life the circuit can work without it.

In radios, turning the tuning dial changes the capacitor, affecting the frequency of charge oscillations.

When the frequency of charge oscillations in the tuner is $$1.015 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{Hz},$$ the radio waves from station 101.5 FM will have the same frequency as the tuner. Then the radio waves will push charge around in the tuner. The radio can detect the precise way that charge is moving and turn it into sound.

Other radio stations with different frequencies will not set a significant amount of charge oscillating in the tuner.

The energy stored by a capacitor can be modeled as $$E_C = \dfrac12 \dfrac{1}{C} Q^2$$ where $$Q$$ is the charge on the capacitor and $$C$$ is the __capacitance__, a measure of how large a capacitor it is. This is a potential energy.

The energy stored by an inductor can be modeled as $$ E_I = \dfrac12 L i^2$$ where $$L$$ is the __inductance__, a measure of how strong the inductor is, and $$i$$ is how fast charge runs through the inductor, so $$i$$ is similar to a speed, but for charge. You can think of $$i$$ as a rate of change of $$Q.$$ You can think of the energy in the inductor as playing a role similar to kinetic energy.

You change the tuner on a radio from 101.5 FM to 98.0 FM.

As you do, the capacitance $$C$$ of the capacitor gets multiplied by some factor. What is that factor?

Give your answer as a decimal to three decimal places.

Try making an analogy between the energy formulas for the circuit and the formulas for a mass on a spring. What quantity in a circuit can replace $$x,$$ the position of a mass on a spring? What circuit quantity can replace $$s,$$ the speed of the mass? (There is a hint to the answer to this question in the problem itself.) Once you know that, you should be able to find analogies for the spring constant and mass as well, then get a formula for the frequency of oscillations of the circuit based on the formula for the mass on a spring.

mathjax: $$ \dfrac{C_{\rm 98.0 FM}}{C_{\rm 101.5 FM}} = \blank$$
