statement:
Part A. You and your friend try to construct two identical pendulums, A and B. You each build one in your own home.

You do a video call with your friend and release your pendulums simultaneously. They appear to be in sync. Congrats!

But after a short while, you notice that despite almost no visible damping, the pendulums are not in sync any more. They are getting a little bit further out of sync with each oscillation. You suspect that the lengths are not truly identical.

You can't precisely measure the lengths, but you can tell that pendulum A is a bit ahead of pendulum B. For example, when pendulum B is just finishing its fifth oscillation, pendulum A has already gotten started a bit on its sixth oscillation.

Assuming this is the cause, which pendulum is shorter?

they're the same length

there's not enough information

Part B. You watch the pendulums until they get back in sync, meaning they are at the same point in their swing, just like when they were released.

At that point, pendulum A has made 78.2 oscillations and pendulum B has made 77.2 oscillations.

You and your friend each measure the pendulums' lengths using a ruler marked to the centimeter, and it does seem that $$\ell_B$$ is slightly longer. You find: $$\begin{aligned} \ell_A = 1.535 \pm 0.005 \;\mathrm{m}\\ \ell_B = 1.539 \pm 0.005 \;\mathrm{m} \end{aligned}$$

The measurement uncertainty is about as large as the difference in measurements, so this isn't a significant result on its own. You wonder whether these measurements agree with your idea that the pendulums don't stay in sync because they are different lengths.

According to your measurements on how many times the pendulums swing before syncing up again and the model of small-amplitude pendulum swings we built in class, what is the length difference between the pendulums?

Answer this question using $$\ell_A$$ and the data on oscillations before syncing up, not by directly computing the difference $$\ell_B - \ell_A$$ from the measurements given above. The goal is to see whether the answer computed using the data on oscillations syncing agrees with the length measurements.

Once you have an answer, decide whether a difference in length explains the different periods of the pendulums, or whether you'll have to look for some other difference between them to explain where it comes from.

Use $$g = 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Part C. In this short video, there are two tuning forks. Each plays a note, and to many people, the notes sound like they have the same pitch. However, when the two tuning forks are hit simultaneously, there is a "wa-wa-wa" sound, called "beats".

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V8W4Djz6jnY

The "wa-wa-wa" sound occurs when two musicians are tuning, trying to play the same note, but actually playing at slightly different frequencies. It's the effect of the total sound from the two instruments getting louder, then softer, over and over. The beats disappear when the musicians are in tune.

The beats are similar to the phenomenon with pendulums of slightly different lengths. When the pendulums are totally out of sync (one to the left while the other is to the right), it's analogous to the soft part of the "wa-wa-wa" cycle. When the pendulums are in sync, it's analogous to the loud part. The pendulums had a period of about $$2.4 \;\mathrm{s},$$ but it took them about $$190 \;\mathrm{s}$$ to cycle from in sync to out of sync and back again.

Because beats are much slower than the frequencies that make them, they're easier to measure. They even apply to radio waves - the signals are much too fast to hear, but you can think of a radio tuner as measuring not just one frequency, but several very nearby ones that make beats in just such a way that it turns into music (or talking, if that's the type of radio you listen to)!

We wanted to include the video of beats so you could hear it before answering the next question. We can't include videos in a question that also has multiple choice buttons, so this "reading problem" holds the video and the next problem has a question about it.

Part D. Musicians can adjust the frequency of the note they're playing either up or down. Depending on what they choose, the beats they hear with another musician can get faster or slower. There are two ways to make the beats go away: make them faster and faster until they can't be heard any more, or make them slower and slower until they can't be heard.

Which way should musicians use if they are trying to tune so that they play the same note?

make the beats faster and faster

make the beats slower and slower

it depends on the note and the type of instrument

label: MCH08
name: Part A. In week 5, we studied energy generated by wind turbines, and in the process we…
desc: Part A. In week 5, we studied energy generated by wind turbines, and in the process we mentioned that fish leave trails of whirling patches of water behind them. The whirling patches of water are called __vortices__, and the phenomenon is called __vortex shedding__. (The entire…
statement:
Part A. In week 5, we studied energy generated by wind turbines, and in the process we mentioned that fish leave trails of whirling patches of water behind them. The whirling patches of water are called __vortices__, and the phenomenon is called __vortex shedding__. (The entire pattern of vortices behind the fish is also called its __von Kármán vortex street__.)

The same phenomenon can happen in many other situations. For example, the vortices form behind this tiger walking through algae-covered water https://www.reddit.com/r/woahdude/comments/7s4dw7/this_tiger_walking_through_algae/

They also form as wind blows around islands, like Guadalupe Island in the Pacific, off the shores of Mexico.

MODIS Rapid Response Project at NASA GSFC

The vortices form at a regular frequency. Here is an animation of the process:

By Cesareo de La Rosa Siqueira - http://www.mcef.ep.usp.br/staff/jmeneg/cesareo/vort2.gif, Attribution, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=87351

The theory of vortex shedding involves concepts from __fluid dynamics__, which would require an entire course to study. However, a model for vortex shedding says that whether we look at small examples like the fish or large examples like the island, $$L \approx 5D$$ where $$L$$ is the distance between two adjacent vortices that spin the same way, for example two purple vortices in the animation. $$D$$ is the diameter of the object that the vortices shed off of.

For Guadalupe Island, $$D \approx 8 \;\mathrm{km}$$ when the wind blows to the southeast, as in the photo. At the time of the photo, the wind was blowing about $$9 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ at the island (and had been blowing at that speed for some time).

**What is the frequency of vortex shedding in the Guadalupe Island picture?**

The frequency is defined as the rate at which __pairs__ of vortices, one in each direction, shed off the island. This means the period is equal to the time between two successive clockwise-rotating vortices being created.

Note that the units are per hour, not hertz.

mathjax: $$ f = \blank \;\mathrm{hr}^{-1}$$

allowed: 1.023456789

Part B. Vortex shedding can be dangerous in objects that have a natural oscillation frequency of their own. If the frequency of vortex shedding matches the frequency of oscillations in the object, vortex shedding can cause very large and potentially-destructive oscillations.

For example, in the handout we saw that the wing of an airplane can oscillate:

If the airplane wing also begins vortex shedding at the same frequency as the wing's oscillations, each vortex can wind up pushing the wing to higher and higher amplitudes, eventually damaging or destroying it. This is extremely unlikely in modern airplanes because engineers are aware of the effect and design wings to avoid it, but it destroyed several airplanes in the past.

In 1940, the Washington Toll Bridge Authority constructed a large suspension bridge across the Tacoma Narrows Strait of Puget Sound, south of Seattle. Whenever the wind blew, the bridge would shake dramatically. Then on November 7, 1940, there were particularly strong winds of about $$18 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ that started violent oscillations of the bridge.

Barney Elliot, Stillman Fires Collection https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge_destruction.ogv

This gif is in real time; it is not sped up or slowed down.

Eventually, the bridge collapsed.

Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=9002953

Engineers thought that perhaps the bridge was vortex-shedding at its own natural oscillation frequency, leading to bigger and bigger oscillations, then the collapse.

For the bridge, $$D$$ is the thickness of the roadway, as seen from the side, which was about $$D \approx 2.5 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

Is the vortex-shedding explanation plausible?

Yes, vortex shedding had about the same frequency as the oscillations that destroyed the bridge.

No, the bridge's oscillations had significantly __higher__ frequency than vortex shedding that day.

No, the bridge's oscillations had significantly __lower__ frequency than vortex shedding that day.

label: MCH08
name: From Spinning to Oscillating: the Scotch Yoke — A circular saw blade spins in a circle. A reciprocating saw…
desc: A circular saw blade spins in a circle. A reciprocating saw blade instead moves back and forth along a straight line — it __oscillates__. Motors work by spinning a shaft, so circular motion is the easy kind of motion for a machine to produce. When a machine part needs to…
statement:
A circular saw blade spins in a circle. A reciprocating saw blade instead moves back and forth along a straight line — it __oscillates__. Motors work by spinning a shaft, so circular motion is the easy kind of motion for a machine to produce. When a machine part needs to oscillate, the machine usually starts with circular motion and converts it. One classic converter is the __Scotch yoke__, shown below: a pin sticks out of a rotating disc, and the pin rides inside a slot (the __yoke__) attached to a horizontal shaft.

__(a)__ Describe how the Scotch yoke turns the disc's circular motion into back-and-forth motion of the shaft. If the pin's position has components $$x$$ (along the shaft) and $$y$$ (along the slot), which component does the yoke follow, and what happens to the other component?

__(b)__ Motion that is one component of uniform circular motion is called __simple harmonic motion__, and an object undergoing it is a __harmonic oscillator__. The animation below shows a green ball moving in a circle at constant speed beside a red cylinder oscillating on a spring. They have the same amplitude and the same period, arranged so the two always have the same horizontal position. Which of the two objects has constant __speed__: both, only the ball, only the cylinder, or neither?

__(c)__ The point where the spring is neither stretched nor compressed, so that it does not accelerate the cylinder, is called the __equilibrium position__. At what point in its motion is the cylinder moving fastest, and where is it momentarily at rest?

__(d)__ Since the ball and the cylinder have the same $$x$$ coordinate at every moment, what can you conclude about their $$x$$ components of velocity and acceleration? Why is this conclusion useful?

label: MCH08
name: The Acceleration and Period of a Mass on a Spring — A cylinder of mass $$m$$ slides on a frictionless…
desc: A cylinder of mass $$m$$ slides on a frictionless surface, attached to a massless spring with __spring constant__ $$k$$ (a measure of the spring's stiffness). At the __equilibrium position__ the spring has its __rest length__: it is neither stretched nor compressed, stores no…
statement:
A cylinder of mass $$m$$ slides on a frictionless surface, attached to a massless spring with __spring constant__ $$k$$ (a measure of the spring's stiffness). At the __equilibrium position__ the spring has its __rest length__: it is neither stretched nor compressed, stores no energy, and does not accelerate the cylinder. When the spring is stretched or compressed by $$\Delta\ell,$$ it stores elastic potential energy $$U_{\rm el}=\dfrac12 k\left(\Delta\ell\right)^2.$$ Under these conditions the cylinder undergoes __simple harmonic motion__: pulled a distance $$A$$ from equilibrium and released, it oscillates with __amplitude__ $$A$$ (the maximum distance from equilibrium), and a plot of its displacement $$x$$ from equilibrium versus time is a sine curve.

To analyze the motion, imagine a green ball moving in uniform circular motion on a circle of radius $$R=A$$ with the same period as the cylinder, arranged so that the ball and the cylinder have the same $$x$$ coordinate at every moment, as in this animation. Then they also share the same $$x$$ component of velocity and of acceleration at every instant. Recall that uniform circular motion at speed $$v_{\rm circle}$$ has acceleration of magnitude $$a_{\rm circle}=\dfrac{v_{\rm circle}^2}{R}$$ pointing toward the center of the circle.

__(a)__ Use conservation of energy to find the cylinder's speed as it passes through the equilibrium position. Explain why the ball's constant speed $$v_{\rm circle}$$ equals that value, and conclude that $$v_{\rm circle}=A\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}.$$

__(b)__ The period of the circular motion is the circumference divided by the speed, $$T=\dfrac{2\pi R}{v_{\rm circle}}.$$ Find $$T$$ in terms of $$m$$ and $$k.$$ Is this the period of the ball, the cylinder, or both?

__(c)__ Find the magnitude of the ball's acceleration in terms of $$A,$$ $$k,$$ and $$m.$$ Is this also the magnitude of the cylinder's acceleration at all times?

__(d)__ The figure below shows the ball at a moment when the cylinder's displacement from equilibrium is $$x.$$ The ball's acceleration points from the ball toward the center of the circle, so the acceleration vector and the dotted radius line make similar triangles with the coordinate axes: $$\dfrac{-a_x}{a_{\rm circle}}=\dfrac{x}{A}.$$ Use this to find $$a_x,$$ the acceleration of the cylinder, in terms of $$k,$$ $$m,$$ and $$x.$$

__(e)__ Your formula says the magnitude of the acceleration is proportional to $$k,$$ proportional to $$\dfrac{1}{m},$$ and proportional to $$x.$$ Interpret each of these three facts physically, and explain what the minus sign in the formula is modeling. (The proportionality between acceleration and stretch is called __Hooke's law__.)

__(f)__ A plot of $$x$$ versus time is a sine curve. Describe what a plot of the cylinder's acceleration versus time looks like. Can you say whether the magnitude of the position or the magnitude of the acceleration is greater? Finally, where in the motion is the cylinder's velocity at a maximum, and where is it zero?

label: MCH08
name: Telling Rocks Apart in Space — On Earth, you can tell the difference between a massive rock and a low-mass…
desc: On Earth, you can tell the difference between a massive rock and a low-mass fake rock by picking them both up: the real one feels heavier. Suppose the fake is utterly convincing except for its low mass, and both rocks are floating with you aboard the International Space Station…
statement:
On Earth, you can tell the difference between a massive rock and a low-mass fake rock by picking them both up: the real one feels heavier. Suppose the fake is utterly convincing except for its low mass, and both rocks are floating with you aboard the International Space Station, where everything is weightless.

__(a)__ Could you still tell the rocks apart on the ISS? Describe a way to do it, and explain what the experiment shows about the difference between __mass__ and __weight__.

__(b)__ On the Moon, the free fall acceleration is smaller than on Earth. For a given rock, which is smaller on the Moon than on Earth: its mass, its weight, both, or neither?

__(c)__ Astronauts can lose muscle and even bone in a zero-g environment, so they measure their body's mass about once a month using the Body Mass Measurement Device (BMMD). In the clip below, astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti grabs a plate connected to a spring and lets herself oscillate. A mass $$m$$ oscillating on a spring of spring constant $$k$$ has period $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ Explain how this device can determine her mass.

__(d)__ Suppose Cristoforetti loses some mass before her next BMMD session. What will be different about her oscillations: will the period go up or down, and what about the frequency (the number of oscillations per second)?

label: MCH08
name: Calibrating the Body Mass Measurement Device — The Body Mass Measurement Device (BMMD) on the International…
desc: The Body Mass Measurement Device (BMMD) on the International Space Station is essentially a spring with a plate to grab: an astronaut holds on, oscillates, and the device computes the astronaut's mass from the period of oscillation using $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ Imagine…
statement:
The Body Mass Measurement Device (BMMD) on the International Space Station is essentially a spring with a plate to grab: an astronaut holds on, oscillates, and the device computes the astronaut's mass from the period of oscillation using $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ Imagine the electronic readout breaks. The spring still works fine, but nobody on board knows the spring constant $$k.$$ Astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti, armed with a stopwatch, measures her own oscillation period to be $$T_C=1.99\;\mathrm{s}.$$ To calibrate the device, she and her crewmates strap objects of known mass to the BMMD and time the oscillations. After very careful data-taking they produce: $$\begin{array}{c|c} m\;(\mathrm{kg}) & T\;(\mathrm{s}) \\ \hline 2.45 & 1.012 \\ 7.17 & 1.120 \\ 15.66 & 1.328 \\ 20.03 & 1.430 \\ 22.93 & 1.478 \\ 27.55 & 1.565 \\ 33.82 & 1.686 \\ 38.11 & 1.742 \\ 102.7 & 2.602 \end{array}$$

__(a)__ Timing a single oscillation with a stopwatch is limited by human reaction time. What measurement technique reduces this source of error?

__(b)__ A first idea is to plot $$T$$ against $$m$$ and fit a straight line. When the astronauts fit a line to the data (leaving out the very massive $$102.7\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object), the points at the two ends of the mass range fall below the line and the points in the middle fall above it. What does a systematic pattern like this — as opposed to points scattered randomly above and below — tell you about the straight-line model? Why does including an object far more massive than the rest make the problem with the line even clearer?

__(c)__ Since the theory predicts $$T\propto\sqrt{m},$$ a better idea is to __linearize__: plot $$T$$ against $$\sqrt{m},$$ which should give a straight line through the origin. But when the astronauts try it, the data still don't fit a line well, and extrapolating toward $$m=0$$ suggests that the empty BMMD, with nothing strapped on at all, would oscillate with a period of about $$T_{\rm free}\approx0.95\;\mathrm{s}$$ rather than zero. The spring really is well modeled by $$U_{\rm el}=\dfrac12 k\left(\Delta\ell\right)^2,$$ so the device really is a harmonic oscillator. What feature of the device's construction explains the nonzero $$T_{\rm free},$$ and how should the equation $$T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$$ be modified to account for it?

__(d)__ The astronauts now want to find both $$k$$ and the new constant from part (c) — two unknowns, which is promising because a straight line has two parameters, a slope and an intercept. Show that plotting $$T^2$$ against $$m$$ should produce a straight line, and find what its slope and intercept are in terms of $$k$$ and $$m_{\rm free}.$$

__(e)__ The plot of $$T^2$$ versus $$m$$ is shown below, and the best-fit line is $$T^2=\left(0.0573\;\mathrm{s^2/kg}\right)m+0.884\;\mathrm{s^2},$$ a good fit all the way through. Find $$k$$ and $$m_{\rm free}.$$ Check that your $$m_{\rm free}$$ reproduces $$T_{\rm free}\approx0.95\;\mathrm{s}.$$

__(f)__ Use the best-fit line and $$T_C=1.99\;\mathrm{s}$$ to find Cristoforetti's mass.

__(g)__ Crewmate Terry Virts had argued the original $$T$$ versus $$m$$ data "look close to a line — go ahead and use the line." His best-fit line through the data (without the $$102.7\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object) is $$T=\left(0.0208\;\mathrm{s/kg}\right)m+0.985\;\mathrm{s}.$$ What mass does Virts's line give for Cristoforetti, and why is it an underestimate?

label: MCH08
name: The Pendulum's Period by Dimensional Analysis — Masses on springs are not the only harmonic oscillators…
desc: Masses on springs are not the only harmonic oscillators: musical instruments, buildings, bridges, and even electric circuits oscillate. A classic example is the __pendulum__ — a mass $$m$$ swinging on a string of length $$\ell$$ under free fall acceleration $$g,$$ with amplitude…
statement:
Masses on springs are not the only harmonic oscillators: musical instruments, buildings, bridges, and even electric circuits oscillate. A classic example is the __pendulum__ — a mass $$m$$ swinging on a string of length $$\ell$$ under free fall acceleration $$g,$$ with amplitude $$A,$$ the maximum __angle__ of the swing.

Deriving the pendulum's period $$T$$ directly takes a lot of computation. Instead, use __dimensional analysis__: every mechanical quantity has dimensions built from mass $$\mathrm{M},$$ length $$\mathrm{L},$$ and time $$\mathrm{T},$$ and a correct formula must have the same dimensions on both sides.

__(a)__ Write the dimensions of each of the five variables $$T,$$ $$m,$$ $$g,$$ $$\ell,$$ and $$A$$ in terms of powers of $$\mathrm{M},$$ $$\mathrm{L},$$ and $$\mathrm{T}.$$ (Careful with the amplitude: it is an angle.)

__(b)__ A formula for $$T$$ must produce one power of time. Which variable must therefore appear in the formula, and to what power must it be raised so the time dimensions come out right?

__(c)__ Your answer to (b) brings along unwanted length dimensions. Which variable cancels them, and to what power? Write the resulting proportionality for $$T.$$

__(d)__ Can the mass $$m$$ appear in the formula for $$T?$$ Can the amplitude $$A?$$ Explain both answers.

__(e)__ Searching online for the period of a pendulum turns up $$T_{\rm look\,up}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}}.$$ Which parts of this formula could dimensional analysis never have determined?

name: The Pendulum as a Mass on a Spring — A mass on a spring with spring constant $$k$$ obeys $$U_{\rm…
desc: A mass on a spring with spring constant $$k$$ obeys $$U_{\rm el}=\dfrac12 k\left(\Delta\ell\right)^2,$$ $$KE=\dfrac12 mv^2,$$ and oscillates with period $$T_{\rm spring}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ This problem builds an analogy between that system and a __pendulum__: a mass…
statement:
A mass on a spring with spring constant $$k$$ obeys $$U_{\rm el}=\dfrac12 k\left(\Delta\ell\right)^2,$$ $$KE=\dfrac12 mv^2,$$ and oscillates with period $$T_{\rm spring}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ This problem builds an analogy between that system and a __pendulum__: a mass $$m$$ on a string of length $$\ell$$ under free fall acceleration $$g.$$ As the pendulum swings, let $$d$$ be the distance it has traveled along its arc from the lowest point, and let $$y$$ be its height above the lowest point, as in the figure. Its gravitational potential energy is $$U_g=mgy.$$

__(a)__ For the mass on a spring, the equilibrium position is where the spring is neither stretched nor compressed and stores no potential energy. What is the analogous point for the pendulum, and where should we set $$y=0$$ and $$U_g=0?$$

__(b)__ The path the pendulum travels is a circular arc (the string keeps a constant length), so $$y$$ is __not__ proportional to $$d^2$$ exactly — the true $$y(d)$$ curve is not a parabola. But for small $$d$$ it is very close to one, and the geometry works out to $$y\approx\dfrac{d^2}{2\ell}.$$ Use this to write the pendulum's potential energy in the form $$U_g\approx\dfrac12(\text{something})\,d^2,$$ and identify what plays the role of the spring constant $$k.$$

__(c)__ The kinetic energy formula $$\dfrac12 mv^2$$ is the same for both systems, so $$m$$ plays its own role in the analogy. Substitute your stand-ins for $$k$$ and $$m$$ into $$T_{\rm spring}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$$ to predict the pendulum's period.

__(d)__ Why is your formula only an approximation, and for what kind of swings does it hold? What does this example suggest about other oscillators whose potential energy curves are not exactly parabolas — for instance, atoms in a molecule, whose "Lennard-Jones" interaction energy is close to a parabola only near its minimum?

statement:
Water can slosh back and forth in a U-shaped tube, the level rising on one side while it falls on the other, as in this video clip:

Describe the water with two variables: $$y,$$ the height of the left-hand column above its equilibrium level, and $$s,$$ the speed of the water (assume all the water moves with the same speed — not perfectly true, but close). Let $$m$$ be the total mass of the water and $$L$$ the total length of the water column measured along the tube. For comparison, a mass on a spring obeys $$U_{\rm el}=\dfrac12 k\left(\Delta\ell\right)^2,$$ $$KE=\dfrac12 mv^2,$$ and $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$

__(a)__ Watching the clip, the water sloshes a little less high each time. What is this effect called, what causes it in general, and why can we ignore it when estimating the period?

__(b)__ The system is in equilibrium when the water stands at the same height on both sides. To displace it, imagine starting at equilibrium and moving a slab of water of height $$y$$ from the top of the right-hand column to the top of the left-hand column, leaving the rest of the water undisturbed; every bit of the moved slab rises a distance $$y.$$ Show that the potential energy of the displaced water is $$U_{\rm tube}=\dfrac{mg}{L}\,y^2.$$

__(c)__ Make the analogy to the mass on a spring: what plays the role of $$k,$$ what plays the role of $$m,$$ and what is the period of the sloshing?

__(d)__ The photo below shows the scale of the apparatus — the tube is a bit shorter than an adult's arm, so $$L\approx60\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is a fair estimate. Predict the period using $$g\approx10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Timing the video gives a period of about $$1.0\;\mathrm{s}$$ — how did the model do?

label: MCH08
name: The Clock That Loses Time in Singapore — A pendulum clock keeps time by counting swings of its pendulum…
desc: A pendulum clock keeps time by counting swings of its pendulum, whose small-amplitude period is $$T\approx2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}}.$$ Your clock was calibrated correctly at its factory in the Black Forest region of Germany, but at your home in Singapore it loses about two…
statement:
A pendulum clock keeps time by counting swings of its pendulum, whose small-amplitude period is $$T\approx2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}}.$$ Your clock was calibrated correctly at its factory in the Black Forest region of Germany, but at your home in Singapore it loses about two minutes each day: set it exactly at noon, and the next day at true noon it reads $$11{:}58.$$

__(a)__ Is the pendulum's period too long or too short in Singapore?

__(b)__ One hypothesis: Singapore, near the equator, is much hotter than Germany, and heat might expand the pendulum. Does a longer pendulum push the period in the right direction to explain the problem? Why do clockmakers' designs nevertheless make this explanation unlikely?

__(c)__ Another hypothesis: free fall acceleration differs between the two places. Near the equator you rotate faster as the Earth spins, and the resulting artificial gravity reduces $$g$$: in Singapore $$g_S\approx9.78\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ while in Germany $$g_G\approx9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Does lower gravity make a pendulum clock gain or lose time?

__(d)__ Checking the hypothesis means comparing two nearly equal periods — awkward by direct calculation. Instead, build an approximation tool. Compute $$\left(1+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2,$$ and explain why, when $$x\ll1$$ (much less than one), this shows $$\sqrt{1+x}\approx1+\dfrac{x}{2}.$$ (Check it on a calculator: $$\sqrt{1.02}=1.00995,$$ very close to $$1.01.$$)

__(e)__ Define $$\Delta g=g_G-g_S$$ and $$\Delta T=T_S-T_G.$$ Starting from $$T\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}},$$ show that $$\dfrac{\Delta T}{T_G}\approx\dfrac{\Delta g}{2g_S}.$$ Then compare the predicted fraction of time lost per day with the observed two minutes per day. Is the variation in $$g$$ a plausible explanation for the clock's behavior?

Part A. A DVD is a disk used to store digital data. They're often used to hold movies or video games.

By Marcin Sochacki (Wanted) - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=3749407

The digital data is stored in a long sequence of bumps on the bottom of the DVD. The bumps are all about the same size, and run in a spiral around the DVD.

http://www.futurekids.com.sg/doyouknow.html

Computers and video game consoles can use a device called a DVD player to read the sequence of bumps on the DVD.

Greg Krumm, "See Through DVD Drive", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8fqr-Fsl9xk

There are roughly $$10^{10}$$ bumps on a DVD. They're too small to see individually with your naked eye, but a DVD player can detect them using a laser.

The DVD player shines a laser onto the DVD from below (red cylinder in the image below). The laser light bounces off the DVD, where it enters the DVD player's detector (blue cylinder). The detector can use the reflected light to read the pattern of bumps on the DVD and send the information to a computer, which can then turn the data into a movie or video game.

The DVD player reads the bumps by following the DVD's spiral pattern. It starts near the center of the DVD and ends at the outside edge.

To follow the spiral, the DVD player has two motions. First, it spins the DVD. This brings new bumps over the laser. You can see the spinning motion in the gif above.

Second, the laser itself moves slowly outward as the DVD spins. This allows it to read tracks further toward the edge of the DVD as it advances along the spiral. The tracks of the spiral are all about the same thickness, so the distance of the laser from the center of the DVD is proportional to the number of rotations the DVD has made.

The DVD player needs to move the bumps past the laser at a constant number of bumps per second.

Define $$t_0$$ to be the time it would take the DVD player to read the part of the DVD that has no bumps, if it were filled with bumps all the way through.

What is the relationship between $$\omega$$ and $$(t+t_0)$$ for the DVD player described in part (A)?

**note** We're finding a relationship between $$\omega$$ and $$(t+t_0)$$ instead of $$\omega$$ and $$t$$ because strict proportionalities like $$a \propto b^\alpha$$ imply that when $$b = 0,$$ $$a$$ is either zero or infinite (depending on the sign of $$\alpha$$). Here, because of the area with no bumps at the center, $$\omega$$ starts at some finite value when $$t = 0.$$ Making $$\omega$$ proportional to a power of $$(t + t_0)$$ corrects for the area with no bumps.

You can solve the problem by imagining the DVD has bumps all the way to the center, finding the proportionality between $$\omega$$ and $$t$$ in that case, and using it as the proportionality between $$\omega$$ and $$(t+t_0).$$

statement:
Part A. We've had several applications so far where we want to find the signed area between a curve and the horizontal axis.

For a graph that's a straight line, a semi-circle, or some other simple shapes, we can find this area with basic geometry. But if the graph plots some complicated real-world data, we won't be able to find a simple formula for the area.

Finding the signed area is a mathematical problem called __integration__.

Today, scientists mostly use computers to estimate this area, for example by cutting the area into many small rectangles and counting how many rectangles there are.

However, people needed to solve this problem before the modern computer age.

An early solution was to use an __analog computer__. You may have heard that computers, at their core, represent everything in terms of a series of 1's and 0's, called bits. This is true of __digital__ computers. Your home desktop, smart phone, calculator, etc. are all digital computers.

Analog computers are able to represent values continuously, not just using $$1$$ and $$0.$$

We will look at an analog computer very similar to the friction drive we studied in class. Analog computers similar to these were used as early as 1886. They solved problems such as predicting the tides and calculating the trajectories of missiles. They were mostly phased out in the 1950s and 1960s, when technological breakthroughs made digital computers hundreds of times faster and more reliable.

A simple analog computer is called a "ball and disk integrator". It begins with a sphere above a rotating disk. The sphere can be moved around so that it's either close to the center or close to the edge of the disk. The gif below shows the ball getting gradually closer to the center.

statement:
Part A. This gif seems to show a helicopter taking off without spinning its blades:

ViralHog, "Helicopter Rises Without Moving Its Rotor", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jWIcVP6GRfw

The blades really are spinning; the video simply looks as if they are not. If you were there in-person, you wouldn't see the effect. The blades would appear to be rotating normally. Also, if someone else recorded the helicopter with a video, the blades might appear to spin in that video, especially if they used a high-speed video camera.

The blades appear stationary in this particular video because videos are a series of photographs taken at a certain frequency, and that frequency can match the frequency of rotation of the blades.

For example, imagine that the blades spin with a frequency of $$20 \;\mathrm{Hz},$$ and that a camera is also taking video at a rate of $$20 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ Then the blades will spin all the way around between frames of the video. The blades will be in the same position each time the camera takes a picture, and in the video, it will look like the blades aren't spinning.

This effect is very common in videos of quickly-rotating or quickly-oscillating objects. It is called __aliasing__.

Aliasing does not necessarily make rotating objects appear to be stationary. It can also make them appear to be rotating, but with a different angular speed or direction than their true rotation. For example, videos of cars driving often look as if the wheels are rotating backwards.

Robbie Gonzalez, https://www.gizmodo.com.au/2016/05/why-do-wheels-sometimes-appear-to-spin-backwards/

(There is an extra complication with some wheels, or with the helicopter. The helicopter in the gif has five blades. If the blades each make just one fifth of a full rotation between frames of the video, then the video will still look as if the blades are not moving because the blades switch places with each other between frames, and the blades all look the same. Likewise, the wheel on a car may only have to rotate through a small angular displacement $$\theta$$ to look as if it has not rotated at all, so aliasing can set in at much lower frequencies. The wheel in the gif above appears to be rotating backward if you look at the spokes, but forward if you look at the cap in the center because the fraction of a rotation needed for the wheel to appear not to have moved is different between the spokes and hub. For this problem, assume we're looking at a wheel where all parts of the wheel have been painted differently, so the wheel only looks the same after one complete rotation.)

Part B. This gif is from a video of a spinning top:

Although the top is spinning normally, it can appear to stop and even change direction in the video. You may have seen similar effects in movies, where the wheels of a car appear to change which direction they're spinning. You may even be able to see the effect in real life if you spin a top or fidget spinner under lights that flicker faster than your eyes can see. Some LEDs and fluorescent lights do this; you can find them in bathrooms more often than other rooms. In this problem, you'll work on understanding why this happens and relate it to rotational kinematics.

Imagine you make a video of a toy top spinning. Originally, the top is spinning with a frequency exactly double the frequency of your video, but friction and air drag slow it down steadily (with constant angular acceleration). You're supporting the top so that it can't fall over or wobble around; it simply spins more and more slowly until it stops. Then the top will spin completely twice around between each picture taken for the video, and the top will be in the same position in each picture. When you look at the video, the top will appear not to be moving.

However, in real life, tops spin more slowly over time. This means the top won't continue to look as if it's frozen. The video will look like the top has begun spinning, even though in real life it was already spinning, and is now just spinning a little slower.

Let's assume your top is painted a pattern that has no symmetry, so that it only appears to be in the same position after making one full rotation.

Make a plot of the apparent angular speed of the top $$\omega_a,$$ as seen in the video, over time $$t.$$ For this plot, assume that the frequency of the video is $$10 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ This means the video shows $$10$$ pictures each second. The original frequency of the top is $$20 \;\mathrm{Hz},$$ meaning it spins all the way around $$20$$ times per second. Let the angular acceleration of the top be $$\alpha = 1.0 \;\mathrm{rad \cdot s}^{-2}$$ in the direction that slows the top's rotation down. $$\omega_a$$ should be measured in $$\mathrm{rad \cdot s^{-1}}\,.$$

Assume that the angular acceleration of the top is constant.

You may need a definition of how to find the angular speed of the top in a video. Assume angular speed is found in the following way: Comparing frames $$n$$ and $$n+1$$ of the video, the top will have rotated through an angular displacement $$\Delta \theta.$$ However, it is not possible to tell apart any two values of $$\Delta \theta$$ separated by an integer multiple of $$2\pi.$$ For example, if the true rotation of the top is $$\Delta \theta = 4.25 \pi$$ between the frames, then the first $$4\pi$$ angular displacement spins the top all the way around twice, which isn't visible, and it will look as if $$\Delta \theta_a = 0.25 \pi.$$

(Here we use $$\Delta \theta_a$$ for the apparent angular displacement of the top, as seen in the video.)

To find what the apparent angular displacement $$\Delta \theta_a$$ is, subtract multiples of $$2\pi$$ from the true angular displacement until the value is less than $$\pi$$ and use this as the angular displacement. This means $$\Delta \theta_a$$ is sometimes negative. For example, a true rotation of $$\Delta \theta = 1.9 \pi$$ will have $$\Delta \theta_v = 1.9 \pi - 2\pi = -0.1 \pi.$$

The apparent angular speed $$\omega_a$$ is equal to the apparent angular displacement between frames divided the time between frames.

We have not discussed the concept of __angular velocity__ yet, so we don't have negative values available to us yet. The angular speed is always positive by definition.

To indicate direction of rotation, label on your plot where the top appears to spin the same direction as the real rotation and where it appears to spin the opposite direction.

Turn in your plot with labeled axis and labels showing the forward and backward directions of rotation. You don't need a written explanation for this problem.

Part C. When a microphone records audio, it captures the pressure in the air over and over at times spaced slightly apart. The rate that the microphone makes readings is called its __sampling rate__, and can be measured in hertz. This is very similar to how a video camera takes a picture over and over at times spaced slightly apart. The rate the camera takes pictures is called its __frame rate__ and can also be measured in hertz.

Microphones record sound, which is an oscillation of the air. Since oscillations are periodic just like rotations, aliasing affects audio recordings just like it affects videos of rotating disks.

If we came up with formulas for the apparent frequency $$f_a$$ of a disk rotating at a true frequency $$f$$ and being recorded in a video taken at a frame rate $$f_v,$$ then those same formulas would accurately describe the frequency of the apparent frequency $$f_a$$ of a sound we hear in an audio recording as a function the true sound frequency $$f$$ and the sample rate $$f_s,$$ as long as we make the substitutions

$$\begin{aligned} \text{video } & \to \text{ audio} \\ f_a & \to f_a \\ f & \to f \\ f_v & \to f_s \end{aligned}$$

Microphones typically have sampling rates of either $$f_s = 44.10 \;\mathrm{KHz}$$ or $$48.00 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$ These sampling rates are set high enough so that there will be no aliasing for any sound within the range audible to humans.

An audio engineer makes a recording with a sample rate of $$f_{s1} = 44.10 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$ When she listens to the recording, she hears a sound playing back with a frequency of $$f_{a1} = 11.33 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$

She suspects there is a very high-pitched buzz in the recording studio making a sound at a frequency higher than humans can hear. She makes a new recording at the sampling rate $$f_{s2} = 48.00 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$ This time, there is still an unexplained sound, but its apparent frequency is $$f_{a2} = 15.23 \;\mathrm{KHz}.$$

Assuming both unexplained sounds are aliasing of the same sound in the recording studio, what is the true frequency $$f$$ of the sound in the recording studio?

You can assume $$f < 1 \;\mathrm{MHz}.$$

label: MCH09
name: What a Speedometer Measures — A car's __speedometer__ tells you how fast the car is going — or does it?…
desc: A car's __speedometer__ tells you how fast the car is going — or does it? Suppose you lift a car off the ground on a service lift, start the engine, and press the accelerator. The wheels spin in the air, but the car itself goes nowhere. __(a)__ What will the speedometer show…
statement:
A car's __speedometer__ tells you how fast the car is going — or does it? Suppose you lift a car off the ground on a service lift, start the engine, and press the accelerator. The wheels spin in the air, but the car itself goes nowhere.

__(a)__ What will the speedometer show: zero (the car isn't moving), or a positive reading that grows the faster the wheels spin? What quantity does a speedometer actually measure?

To talk about spinning, we use two new quantities. The __angular displacement__ $$\theta$$ is the angle through which a wheel has turned. The __angular speed__ $$\omega$$ (the Greek letter "omega") is the rate of change of $$\theta$$ — it measures how fast something spins.

__(b)__ Assuming $$\omega$$ is constant, write an equation relating the angular displacement $$\Delta\theta,$$ the angular speed $$\omega,$$ and the elapsed time $$\Delta t.$$ Using the correspondence between linear and angular quantities ($$d\to\theta,$$ $$v\to\omega,$$ $$t\to t$$), what equation for straight-line motion is your equation the analog of?

__(c)__ The clips below show a figure skater spinning and a giant wind turbine turning. (The still photo shows a person standing on a similar turbine for scale — the blades are enormous, far longer than the skater's arms.) In the same stretch of time, the skater completes about $$7.5$$ rotations while the turbine completes about half a rotation. Which has the higher __angular__ speed, and by roughly what factor? Which has the higher __linear__ speed at its outer edge — the skater's elbows or the turbine's blade tips?

__(d)__ Consider a point moving in a circle of radius $$r$$ at angular speed $$\omega.$$ If you double $$r,$$ what happens to the point's speed $$v?$$ If you double $$\omega?$$ Use your answers to explain why $$v=k\,\omega r$$ for some constant $$k.$$ (Angular speed is defined — using the radian, introduced in a later problem — precisely so that $$k=1,$$ giving $$v=\omega r.$$)

__(e)__ Bert and Ernie have identical cars, but Bert's tires are new while Ernie's are old and worn down, so Ernie's tires have a slightly smaller radius. A speedometer really measures the angular speed $$\omega$$ of the tires and converts it to a speed reading by assuming the tires are full-sized. Both drive so that their speedometers read $$30\;\mathrm{mi/h}.$$ Who is actually going faster? Is Ernie's speedometer reading too high or too low? In general: as a car's tires wear down, what happens to its speedometer readings?

label: MCH09
name: Ernie's Odometer — Ernie's car has old, worn-down tires, so their radius $$r$$ is slightly smaller than when…
desc: Ernie's car has old, worn-down tires, so their radius $$r$$ is slightly smaller than when they were new. The car's instruments measure the angular motion of the tires and convert it to speeds and distances assuming the tires are still full-sized. The __speedometer__ reading is…
statement:
Ernie's car has old, worn-down tires, so their radius $$r$$ is slightly smaller than when they were new. The car's instruments measure the angular motion of the tires and convert it to speeds and distances assuming the tires are still full-sized. The __speedometer__ reading is proportional to the tires' angular speed $$\omega$$ (so it reads a bit high, since the speed of the car is $$v=\omega r$$ and Ernie's $$r$$ is smaller than the car assumes). The __odometer__ — the meter that reports the total distance the car has driven — computes its reading from the speedometer.

__(a)__ Suppose you plotted the speedometer's reading over time during a drive, as below. What feature of that graph determines how much the odometer reading changes during the drive?

__(b)__ Suppose the tires turn at constant angular speed $$\omega$$ starting at $$t=0,$$ so their angular displacement is $$\theta=\omega t.$$ Starting from $$d=vt$$ and $$v=\omega r,$$ show that the distance the car travels is $$d=\theta r.$$ The speedometer reading is proportional to the angular speed $$\omega$$ — what angular quantity is the odometer reading proportional to?

__(c)__ Ernie knows that when his tires were new, he could drive $$300\;\mathrm{mi}$$ before refilling his gas tank, and we'll assume that's still true. If Ernie tries to drive until his odometer says he's gone $$300\;\mathrm{mi},$$ will he run out of gas before getting there?

label: MCH09
name: Radians and a Swinging Door — When a wheel rotates through an angle $$\theta,$$ a point on the wheel a…
desc: When a wheel rotates through an angle $$\theta,$$ a point on the wheel a distance $$r$$ from the center travels a distance $$d$$ along its circular arc. The __radian__ is the unit of angle defined so that these are related by $$d=\theta r$$ — equivalently…
statement:
When a wheel rotates through an angle $$\theta,$$ a point on the wheel a distance $$r$$ from the center travels a distance $$d$$ along its circular arc. The __radian__ is the unit of angle defined so that these are related by $$d=\theta r$$ — equivalently, $$\theta=\dfrac{d}{r}.$$ The symbol for radians is $$\mathrm{rad}.$$

__(a)__ What are the dimensions of an angle measured in radians?

__(b)__ Suppose the point makes one full trip around the circle. What is $$d$$ in that case, and therefore what is $$\theta?$$ Use your answer to express one radian in degrees.

__(c)__ The clip below shows a person opening a door. Estimate the angle, in radians, through which they swing the door. (One approach: estimate the angle in degrees first and convert. Another: compare the distance the outer edge of the door moves to the width of the door, and use $$\theta=d/r$$ directly.)

__(d)__ The door handle is about $$0.7\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the hinges. Roughly how far does the handle move in total — including both opening the door and then closing it again?

label: MCH09
name: The Spinning Baseball Bat — A baseball bat is mounted on a motor that spins it at a steady angular speed…
desc: A baseball bat is mounted on a motor that spins it at a steady angular speed $$\omega=85\;\mathrm{s}^{-1}.$$ (Angular speeds measured in radians per second have dimensions of one over time, since radians are dimensionless.) Recall that a point a distance $$r$$ from the rotation…
statement:
A baseball bat is mounted on a motor that spins it at a steady angular speed $$\omega=85\;\mathrm{s}^{-1}.$$ (Angular speeds measured in radians per second have dimensions of one over time, since radians are dimensionless.) Recall that a point a distance $$r$$ from the rotation axis moves with speed $$v=\omega r,$$ and that one full revolution is $$2\pi$$ radians.

__(a)__ The tip of the bat moves at $$73\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ How long is the bat?

__(b)__ How many complete revolutions does the bat make each second?

label: MCH09
name: Mechanical Advantage of a Friction Drive — In a __friction drive__, two disks are held perpendicular and…
desc: In a __friction drive__, two disks are held perpendicular and touching. The __input disk__ (pink in the animation below) is spun at a constant angular speed by a motor, off-screen to the left, that turns the green shaft. Friction at the contact point pushes the large horizontal…
statement:
In a __friction drive__, two disks are held perpendicular and touching. The __input disk__ (pink in the animation below) is spun at a constant angular speed by a motor, off-screen to the left, that turns the green shaft. Friction at the contact point pushes the large horizontal __output disk__ (brown) and makes it spin too. Winding the yellow handle slides the input disk along its shaft, changing where it touches the output disk. Friction drives were used in early cars (the car's wheels turned with the same angular speed as the output disk); they're still used in snowblowers, conveyor belts, and other equipment.

Let $$r_{\rm in}$$ be the radius of the input disk, and let $$r_{\rm out}$$ be the distance from the center of the output disk to the point where the input disk touches it. The dashed circle below marks all the points on the output disk that pass under the input disk as the output disk turns.

__(a)__ The motor can spin the input shaft in only one direction. How can the operator nevertheless make the output disk reverse direction? (This is how a snowblower is put in reverse.)

__(b)__ To make the output disk spin as fast as possible, should the input disk touch it near the edge or near the center? Explain using the dashed circle.

__(c)__ The __mechanical advantage__ of a machine is the ratio of how far the input moves to how far the output moves. For rotating machinery we define it with angles of rotation: $$\text{MA}=\dfrac{\theta_{\rm in}}{\theta_{\rm out}}.$$ The disks roll on each other without slipping, so in any stretch of time, the rim of the input disk and the dashed circle on the output disk move the same distance through the contact point. Using $$d=\theta r,$$ find the mechanical advantage as a function of $$r_{\rm in}$$ and $$r_{\rm out}.$$

__(d)__ If this friction drive powered a car, where should you position the input disk to climb a steep hill? Where should you position it to drive fast on level ground?

label: MCH09
name: Spinning Up a DVD — A DVD player needs its DVD spinning at an angular speed of at least $$\omega_{\rm…
desc: A DVD player needs its DVD spinning at an angular speed of at least $$\omega_{\rm min}=170\;\mathrm{rad}\cdot\mathrm{s}^{-1}$$ before it can begin reading data. When a DVD is inserted, the player spins it up from rest with constant __angular acceleration__…
statement:
A DVD player needs its DVD spinning at an angular speed of at least $$\omega_{\rm min}=170\;\mathrm{rad}\cdot\mathrm{s}^{-1}$$ before it can begin reading data. When a DVD is inserted, the player spins it up from rest with constant __angular acceleration__ $$\alpha=50\;\mathrm{rad}\cdot\mathrm{s}^{-2}.$$ Angular acceleration ($$\alpha,$$ the Greek letter "alpha") is the rate of change of angular speed: for constant $$\alpha,$$ $$\alpha=\dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}.$$ And just as a linear motion starting from rest with constant acceleration covers $$d=\frac12 at^2,$$ a rotation starting from rest with constant angular acceleration turns through $$\theta=\frac12\alpha t^2.$$

__(a)__ Find $$t_{\rm min},$$ the time the DVD takes to spin up — first as a formula in terms of $$\omega_{\rm min}$$ and $$\alpha,$$ then as a number.

__(b)__ Find $$\theta_{\rm min},$$ the total angle the DVD turns through while spinning up — again, both as a formula and as a number.

__(c)__ How many complete revolutions does the DVD make before the player begins reading it?

__(d)__ Suppose the manufacturer redesigns the player with a larger angular acceleration $$\alpha.$$ Does the number of spin-up revolutions increase or decrease? Which makes this easier to see: the formula from part (c), or the numerical value? What does that suggest about "working with variables" versus "working with values"?

label: MCH09
name: Coins on a Spinning Disk — Two identical coins, A and B, sit on a flat circular disk at distances $$r_A$$ and…
desc: Two identical coins, A and B, sit on a flat circular disk at distances $$r_A$$ and $$r_B=2r_A$$ from the center. Starting from rest, the disk spins faster and faster with a small, constant angular acceleration $$\alpha.$$ Friction holds each coin in place — until the "artificial…
statement:
Two identical coins, A and B, sit on a flat circular disk at distances $$r_A$$ and $$r_B=2r_A$$ from the center. Starting from rest, the disk spins faster and faster with a small, constant angular acceleration $$\alpha.$$ Friction holds each coin in place — until the "artificial gravity" the coin feels from moving in a circle becomes too strong, at which point the coin starts to slide. Treat the coins as points, and because $$\alpha$$ is small, ignore the coins' tangential acceleration: assume each coin slips when its __centripetal acceleration__ reaches a threshold value $$a_{c,\rm slip}$$ that is the same for the two identical coins.

The clip below shows the phenomenon with a single coin: as the turntable spins up, the coin eventually slides off.

__(a)__ Before either coin slips, both ride along with the disk. Compare the two coins' angular displacements $$\theta,$$ their angular speeds $$\omega,$$ and the distances they have traveled along their circular paths.

__(b)__ The centripetal acceleration of an object moving in a circle is $$a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}.$$ Substitute $$v=\omega r$$ to rewrite $$a_c$$ in terms of $$\omega$$ and $$r.$$ Now, Mia argues: "Since $$a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r},$$ we have $$a_c\propto\dfrac{1}{r},$$ so coin A — at smaller $$r$$ — has the larger centripetal acceleration." Logan argues: "Since $$a_c=\omega^2 r,$$ we have $$a_c\propto r,$$ so coin B has the larger centripetal acceleration." Who is right in this problem? Then describe a different situation in which the other one would be right.

__(c)__ Which coin starts sliding first?

__(d)__ Let $$\omega_{A,\rm slip}$$ and $$\omega_{B,\rm slip}$$ be the disk's angular speeds at the moments coins A and B slip. Find the ratio $$\dfrac{\omega_{A,\rm slip}}{\omega_{B,\rm slip}}.$$ The disk spins up from rest at constant $$\alpha,$$ so $$\omega$$ is proportional to time — what is the corresponding ratio of slipping times, $$\dfrac{t_{A,\rm slip}}{t_{B,\rm slip}}?$$

__(e)__ Coin B travels a total distance of $$40\;\mathrm{cm}$$ along its circular path before slipping. How far does coin A travel before it slips? (Useful facts: the distance traveled is $$d=\theta r,$$ and starting from rest with constant angular acceleration, $$\theta=\frac12\alpha t^2.$$)

__(f)__ Now suppose $$r_B=8\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ Through how many radians does each coin turn before slipping, and roughly how many full rotations is that for each?

__(g)__ Show that a point riding the disk at distance $$r$$ from the center (spun up from rest at constant $$\alpha$$) has centripetal acceleration $$a_c=2\alpha d,$$ where $$d$$ is the distance the point has traveled so far. Explain why this formula answers part (e) in one line.

label: MCH09
name: Which Coin Slips First, Really? (Tangential Acceleration) — This problem refines the previous one. Coins A…
desc: This problem refines the previous one. Coins A and B sit at radii $$r_A$$ and $$r_B=2r_A$$ on a disk that spins up from rest with constant angular acceleration $$\alpha.$$ Before, we assumed a coin slips when its centripetal acceleration $$a_c=\omega^2 r$$ reaches a threshold…
statement:
This problem refines the previous one. Coins A and B sit at radii $$r_A$$ and $$r_B=2r_A$$ on a disk that spins up from rest with constant angular acceleration $$\alpha.$$ Before, we assumed a coin slips when its centripetal acceleration $$a_c=\omega^2 r$$ reaches a threshold. But that can't be the whole story: centripetal acceleration points toward the center and only changes the coin's __direction__. The coins are also speeding up, and some acceleration must be responsible for that.

__(a)__ The acceleration that changes a coin's speed is the __tangential acceleration__ $$a_t,$$ pointing along the direction of motion, tangent to the coin's circle. The coin's speed is $$v=\omega r,$$ and the rate of change of $$\omega$$ is $$\alpha.$$ Find a formula for $$a_t.$$ Then: as the disk spins faster and faster (with $$\alpha$$ still constant), does the tangential acceleration of a coin that hasn't slipped increase, decrease, or stay the same?

__(b)__ The centripetal and tangential accelerations are perpendicular, so by the Pythagorean theorem the total acceleration has magnitude $$a=\sqrt{a_c^2+a_t^2}.$$ A coin really slips when this __total__ acceleration reaches the threshold, $$a_{\rm slip}.$$ Assuming $$\alpha$$ is small enough that both coins ride the disk at least briefly before slipping, which coin slips first?

__(c)__ For a coin riding the disk, $$a_c=2\alpha d$$ (where $$d$$ is the distance the coin has traveled so far) and $$a_t=\alpha r.$$ Both coins slip at the same total acceleration $$a_{\rm slip}.$$ Derive a formula for $$d_{A,\rm slip}$$ in terms of $$d_{B,\rm slip},$$ $$r_A,$$ and $$r_B.$$ Do the coins still travel equal distances before slipping?

__(d)__ Check your formula in two limits. First, when $$d_{B,\rm slip}\gg r_B$$ (a very gentle spin-up), what should the formula reduce to, and does it? Second, when $$d_{B,\rm slip}\to 0,$$ what is physically happening, and what does the formula then predict if we also let $$r_A\to r_B?$$

__(e)__ A classmate claims the answer is $$d_{A,\rm slip}=\sqrt{d_{B,\rm slip}^2-r_A^2}.$$ Without redoing any analysis, give a reason this must be wrong. Another classmate claims $$d_{A,\rm slip}=d_{B,\rm slip}\,(r_A+r_B).$$ What's wrong with that one?

Part A. Consider a variety of wheels, each connected to a spring at the top. Each wheel is free to rotate but cannot translate.

In each case, the wheel has radius $$r$$ and total mass $$m.$$ All the springs are identical.

(A): A hoop-like wheel with almost all the mass at the rim; the center and spokes are very light.

label: MCH10
name: The Tic Tac's Higher Second Bounce — A tic tac is a small, hard, rounded candy. Physics educator Dianna…
desc: A tic tac is a small, hard, rounded candy. Physics educator Dianna Cowern filmed one bouncing on a table and was amazed by what she saw: the tic tac bounced __higher__ on its second bounce than on its first. Here is another view of the same phenomenon. Watch the spin closely…
statement:
A tic tac is a small, hard, rounded candy. Physics educator Dianna Cowern filmed one bouncing on a table and was amazed by what she saw: the tic tac bounced __higher__ on its second bounce than on its first.

Here is another view of the same phenomenon. Watch the spin closely: the tic tac spins rapidly after its first bounce and slowly after its second.

A moving, spinning object has two kinds of kinetic energy. __Translational__ kinetic energy is energy due to the motion of the entire object — the motion of its center. __Rotational__ kinetic energy is energy due to its spinning motion.

__(a)__ Suppose the tic tac leaves the table spinning and rising vertically. Which of its kinetic energies — translational, rotational, or both — would you need to know to calculate how high it rises? Explain.

__(b)__ Bounces are not perfectly elastic: in every bounce, some kinetic energy is converted to thermal energy, so the tic tac's __total__ kinetic energy decreases from bounce to bounce. Given that, explain how the second bounce can nevertheless be __higher__ than the first. What must happen to the rotational kinetic energy during the second bounce?

label: MCH10
name: The Frozen Soda Can Race — You have two sodas in identical aluminum cans. You freeze one solid, then release…
desc: You have two sodas in identical aluminum cans. You freeze one solid, then release both cans from rest at the same moment at the top of a ramp $$L = 2\;\mathrm{m}$$ long and $$h = 20\;\mathrm{cm}$$ high, and let them roll down. Which can wins the race, and by how much? To build a…
statement:
You have two sodas in identical aluminum cans. You freeze one solid, then release both cans from rest at the same moment at the top of a ramp $$L = 2\;\mathrm{m}$$ long and $$h = 20\;\mathrm{cm}$$ high, and let them roll down. Which can wins the race, and by how much?

To build a mathematical model of the race, make these simplifications. Ignore the sloshing of the liquid soda (it is a minor effect). Ignore the aluminum can itself — its walls are less than $$0.1\;\mathrm{mm}$$ thick, so essentially all the mass is soda. Assume both cans __roll without slipping__: the bottom of the can is never moving relative to the ramp. Rolling without slipping connects the speed $$v$$ of the can's center to its angular speed $$\omega$$ by $$v = \omega r,$$ where $$r$$ is the can's radius, and it also means no mechanical energy is converted to thermal energy by friction.

You will need these facts: gravitational potential energy is $$U = mgh,$$ translational kinetic energy is $$KE_T = \dfrac12 mv^2,$$ and the rotational kinetic energy of a solid disk (a frozen can counts as a solid disk) spinning at angular speed $$\omega$$ is $$KE_R = \dfrac14 mr^2\omega^2.$$ Use $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ In this model, the liquid inside the unfrozen can does not rotate with the can — it just slides along inside. Explain why the liquid can then behaves exactly like a block sliding down a frictionless ramp, and find its speed $$v_\ell$$ at the bottom of the ramp.

__(b)__ The frozen soda __does__ rotate along with its can. Show that the frozen can's total kinetic energy is $$KE = \dfrac34 mv^2,$$ and find its speed $$v_f$$ at the bottom of the ramp.

__(c)__ Explain why dividing $$L$$ by $$v_f$$ does __not__ give the frozen can's trip time, then find the actual time $$t_f$$ for the frozen can to roll down.

__(d)__ Find the liquid can's time $$t_\ell,$$ and the margin of victory predicted by the model.

__(e)__ In the real race shown in the video, the liquid can won by less than one tenth of the ramp length — only about $$5\%$$ in time — a considerably closer race than the model predicts. What did the model leave out, and does that change which can wins?

label: MCH10
name: A Race of Shapes and the Moment of Inertia — A solid sphere (yellow), a hollow sphere (blue), and a hollow…
desc: A solid sphere (yellow), a hollow sphere (blue), and a hollow can race down a ramp. All three have the same mass $$m,$$ all are released from rest at the same moment, and all roll without slipping (so each one's speed and angular speed are related by $$v = \omega r$$), with no…
statement:
A solid sphere (yellow), a hollow sphere (blue), and a hollow can race down a ramp. All three have the same mass $$m,$$ all are released from rest at the same moment, and all roll without slipping (so each one's speed and angular speed are related by $$v = \omega r$$), with no mechanical energy lost.

The rotational kinetic energy of any rotating object has the form $$KE_R = (\text{coefficient})\cdot mr^2\omega^2,$$ where the coefficient depends only on the object's shape. The coefficients are $$\dfrac14$$ for a solid can or disk, $$\dfrac12$$ for a hollow can, $$\dfrac15$$ for a solid sphere, and $$\dfrac13$$ for a hollow sphere.

__(a)__ For a rolling solid can, energy conservation $$mgh = \dfrac12 mv^2 + \dfrac14 mr^2\omega^2$$ together with $$v = \omega r$$ gives a bottom-of-ramp speed of $$v = \sqrt{\tfrac43 gh}.$$ Based on this formula, does the outcome of the race depend on the objects' radii? On their masses?

__(b)__ Using the coefficients above, predict the order in which the three shapes finish. Then explain the order physically, in terms of where each shape's mass sits relative to its rotation axis.

__(c)__ To handle every shape with a single formula, physicists define the __moment of inertia__ $$I$$ of an object about a rotation axis so that the rotational kinetic energy is $$KE_R = \dfrac12 I\omega^2.$$ (Here "moment" is a word borrowed from statistics — it has nothing to do with moments of time — and "inertia" is another word for mass.) Find the moment of inertia of the solid sphere.

__(d)__ Comparing $$KE_T = \dfrac12 mv^2$$ with $$KE_R = \dfrac12 I\omega^2$$ sets up an analogy between linear and rotational quantities. Which rotational quantity plays the role of the mass $$m,$$ and which plays the role of the velocity $$v?$$

The photo below shows the finish of the race (yellow is solid, blue is hollow), so you can check your prediction from part (b).

name: One Hoop, Two Axes — The moment of inertia $$I,$$ defined so that the rotational kinetic energy is $$KE_R =…
desc: The moment of inertia $$I,$$ defined so that the rotational kinetic energy is $$KE_R = \dfrac12 I\omega^2,$$ is not a property of an object alone — it also depends on the __axis of rotation__. Consider a thin hoop of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r.$$ There are two natural ways to…
statement:
The moment of inertia $$I,$$ defined so that the rotational kinetic energy is $$KE_R = \dfrac12 I\omega^2,$$ is not a property of an object alone — it also depends on the __axis of rotation__. Consider a thin hoop of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r.$$ There are two natural ways to spin it about an axis through its center.

It can spin about one of its own diameters, like a spinning ring:

Or it can spin about the axis perpendicular to its plane, like a wheel:

Here are both motions shown together, with their rotation axes drawn in:

__(a)__ Without calculating anything, decide which way of spinning gives the hoop the larger moment of inertia. Explain by thinking about how much the hoop's mass actually moves in each case.

__(b)__ The moment of inertia is built from the __square of the distance__ from the axis to each bit of mass. Set up coordinates in the plane of the hoop with the origin at its center, so a point $$P$$ on the hoop has coordinates $$(x,y)$$ with $$x^2 + y^2 = r^2,$$ as in the figure below. For the wheel-style spin, the axis points out of the page through the center. What is the square of the distance from the axis to $$P?$$

__(c)__ For the ring-style spin, take the axis to be the $$y$$-axis — a diameter of the hoop, drawn dashed in the figure. Now what is the square of the distance from the axis to $$P?$$

__(d)__ For the wheel-style spin, every bit of mass is exactly a distance $$r$$ from the axis, and the moment of inertia comes out to $$I_{\rm wheel} = mr^2.$$ Averaged over the whole hoop, $$x^2$$ and $$y^2$$ have equal averages. Use this to find $$I_{\rm ring}.$$

label: MCH10
name: How Fast Does a Shape Roll? — An object of mass $$m,$$ radius $$r,$$ and moment of inertia $$I$$ rolls…
desc: An object of mass $$m,$$ radius $$r,$$ and moment of inertia $$I$$ rolls without slipping (so $$v = \omega r$$) from rest down a ramp of length $$L$$ and height $$h,$$ with no mechanical energy lost. Its rotational kinetic energy is $$KE_R = \dfrac12 I\omega^2.$$ It is…
statement:
An object of mass $$m,$$ radius $$r,$$ and moment of inertia $$I$$ rolls without slipping (so $$v = \omega r$$) from rest down a ramp of length $$L$$ and height $$h,$$ with no mechanical energy lost. Its rotational kinetic energy is $$KE_R = \dfrac12 I\omega^2.$$ It is convenient to describe the shape by the dimensionless number $$k = \dfrac{I}{mr^2}.$$ Its values: $$k = 1$$ for a hoop or hollow can, $$k = \dfrac12$$ for a solid disk or can, $$k = \dfrac23$$ for a hollow sphere, $$k = \dfrac25$$ for a solid sphere, and $$k \ll 1$$ for a hub-like object — say, a heavy central rod surrounded by a lightweight wheel on light spokes.

For comparison, a block sliding down the same ramp without friction has acceleration $$a_{\rm slide} = g\dfrac{h}{L}.$$ Your goal is to find the acceleration $$a_R$$ of the rolling object without grinding through the full calculation, by figuring out how the formula must behave.

__(a)__ Show that the rolling object's total kinetic energy can be written $$KE = \dfrac12\left(m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}\right)v^2 = \dfrac12(1+k)\,mv^2.$$

__(b)__ Should $$a_R$$ be larger or smaller than $$a_{\rm slide}?$$ Should increasing $$k$$ increase or decrease $$a_R?$$ And what value should $$a_R$$ approach in the limit $$k \to 0?$$

__(c)__ Exactly one of the following formulas is correct. Use your answers to part (b) to eliminate the other three. (i) $$a_R = \dfrac{ghk}{L}$$ (ii) $$a_R = \dfrac{gh(1+k)}{L}$$ (iii) $$a_R = \dfrac{gh}{Lk}$$ (iv) $$a_R = \dfrac{gh}{L(1+k)}$$

__(d)__ An object that starts from rest with uniform acceleration travels $$d = \dfrac12 at^2,$$ so comparing two objects at the same moment, $$d \propto a \propto \dfrac{1}{1+k}.$$ In a race between a solid sphere ($$k = \tfrac25$$) and a hollow can ($$k = 1$$) rolling down the same ramp, what fraction of the way down the ramp should the can be at the instant the sphere reaches the bottom?

__(e)__ Now test the prediction. A photograph of such a race, frozen at the moment the yellow solid sphere reached the bottom, is set up as a measuring tool at https://glowscript.org/#/user/eichenlaub/folder/Mechanics/program/measurecans — click and drag on the photo to measure distances in pixels. One measurement found the can had rolled $$141$$ pixels in the time the sphere rolled $$185$$ pixels. What fraction is that, and what are some reasons the measurement doesn't exactly match the prediction from part (d)?

label: MCH10
name: A Rolling Race Where k Is Greater Than 1 — For an object rolling without slipping down a ramp of length $$L$$…
desc: For an object rolling without slipping down a ramp of length $$L$$ and height $$h,$$ the acceleration is $$a_R = \dfrac{gh}{L(1+k)},$$ where $$k = \dfrac{I}{mr^2},$$ $$I$$ is the object's moment of inertia, and $$r$$ is the radius of the part of the object that actually touches…
statement:
For an object rolling without slipping down a ramp of length $$L$$ and height $$h,$$ the acceleration is $$a_R = \dfrac{gh}{L(1+k)},$$ where $$k = \dfrac{I}{mr^2},$$ $$I$$ is the object's moment of inertia, and $$r$$ is the radius of the part of the object that actually touches the ramp. For ordinary rolling shapes — hoops, disks, spheres — $$k \le 1.$$

The video below shows two disks racing down a pair of rails. The disks do not roll on their rims: instead, thin pegs stick out from their sides, and the pegs are what contact the rails. The two disks have the same shape and the same total mass; the only difference is that extra mass has been added at the __inside__ edge of the disk on the left and at the __outside__ edge of the disk on the right.

(Both disks are rolling forward and are close to rolling without slipping. The strange stuttering appearance of the video is __aliasing__ — an artifact of the camera's frame rate, not the actual motion.)

__(a)__ Explain why $$k > 1$$ for these disks.

__(b)__ Which disk has the greater acceleration? Explain.

__(c)__ Suppose you could replace the pegs with new pegs of a different thickness. How would you change them so that the right-hand disk beats the left-hand disk in a race? Explain why your change works.

label: MCH10
name: The Stick Pendulum — A pendulum is made from a uniform stick of mass $$m$$ and length $$L,$$ suspended from a…
desc: A pendulum is made from a uniform stick of mass $$m$$ and length $$L,$$ suspended from a pivot at one end and swinging at small amplitude. Find its period by analogy with a mass on a spring, following the steps below. Background facts you will need. A mass on a spring has…
statement:
A pendulum is made from a uniform stick of mass $$m$$ and length $$L,$$ suspended from a pivot at one end and swinging at small amplitude. Find its period by analogy with a mass on a spring, following the steps below.

Background facts you will need. A mass on a spring has kinetic energy $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2$$ and potential energy $$U = \dfrac12 kx^2$$ ($$k$$ is the spring constant), and oscillates with period $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ A __point-mass pendulum__ — all its mass at the end of a massless string of length $$L$$ — has period $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}.$$ When a pendulum of length $$L$$ swings so that its tip has moved a horizontal distance $$d,$$ the tip rises by approximately $$y \approx \dfrac{d^2}{2L}$$ (valid for small swings). The moment of inertia of a uniform stick about an axis through its end is $$I = \dfrac13 mL^2,$$ and rotational kinetic energy is $$KE_R = \dfrac12 I\omega^2.$$

__(a)__ The stick pendulum's gravitational potential energy, measured from the bottom of its swing, is $$U = \dfrac{mgy}{2} \approx \dfrac{mgd^2}{4L}.$$ For a point-mass pendulum it would be $$U = mgy.$$ Where does the division by $$2$$ come from?

__(b)__ Let $$v$$ be the speed of the stick's tip, so the stick's angular speed about the pivot is $$\omega = \dfrac{v}{L}.$$ Show that the stick's kinetic energy is $$KE = \dfrac16 mv^2.$$

__(c)__ Rewrite the energies as $$KE = \dfrac12\left(\dfrac13 m\right)v^2$$ and $$U \approx \dfrac12\left(\dfrac{mg}{2L}\right)d^2,$$ and compare them with the mass on a spring. What replaces the spring system's $$m,$$ and what replaces its $$k?$$ Use the analogy to find the period of the stick pendulum.

__(d)__ How long must a stick pendulum be to have the same period as a point-mass pendulum of length $$L?$$

__(e)__ A real "point-mass" pendulum is a heavy weight on a string of small but nonzero mass. If you ignore the string's mass when calculating the period and then use your pendulum as a clock, will the clock run fast or slow? Is an error of $$0.01\%$$ acceptable for a clock?

Part A. Steam engines needed to control how fast they spun. To do this, they used a __centrifugal governor__.

By Dr. Mirko Junge - Own work, CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=9964214

A centrifugal governor consisted of two balls, called "fly balls" that hung freely from the edge of a narrow shaft.

https://gfycat.com/piercingallasianwaterbuffalo

When the shaft spun, the balls would fly out to the sides. Which of the following is a correct description of the relationship between the angular speed $$\omega$$ of the governor and the angle $$\theta$$ that the balls made from the vertical?

You can ignore the width of the shaft. Model the balls as point masses at the ends of strings, each moving in circles with angular speed $$\omega.$$

$$\theta$$ is constant for all $$\omega$$

$$\theta \propto \omega$$

$$\theta \propto \dfrac{1}{\omega}$$

$$\sin\theta \propto \omega$$

$$\sin\theta \propto \omega^2$$

Part B. In the centrifugal governor model in part (A), imagine increasing the length $$\ell$$ of the massless strings that support the fly balls.

How would this affect $$\theta,$$ assuming $$\omega$$ is unchanged?

$$\theta$$ would increase

$$\theta$$ would decrease

$$\theta$$ would not change

whether $$\theta$$ changes depends on the specific values

Part C. In a centrifugal governor, the balls were mechanically connected to a valve. The further the balls swung out (the greater $$\theta$$), the more the valve would close. This would restrict the fuel supply to the steam engine and cause it to slow down, which would bring the balls back down some. If the balls got too low, the valve would open more, increasing the fuel supply and increasing the speed of the steam engine. In this way, the governor kept the steam engine operating at approximately the same angular speed all the time. A system like this is called "negative feedback".

The study of centrifugal governors led to a field known today as __control theory__, which is important in mathematics, engineering, robotics, electronics, and even economics. Ideas from control theory are important to applications such as self-driving cars.

Suppose that a centrifugal governor is operating so that $$\theta = 60^\circ.$$ The operator wants to double the kinetic energy stored Note that this is __not__ saying that the kinetic energy of the fly balls will double. The fly balls and the flywheel behave differently because the flyballs tilt up to higher $$\theta$$ as we increase $$\omega,$$ but the flywheel stays physically the same, except for spinning faster. of the machine. The flywheel is connected to the governor such that they always have the same angular speed as each other.

What should $$\theta$$ be when the kinetic energy of the flywheel has doubled?

Give your answer to the nearest degree.
