statement:
In this writing problem, we'll examine a half-Atwood machine.

Explain your reasoning using equations, diagrams, and words. You may use complete sentences, but don't need to, as long as the grader is easily able to follow your reasoning.

A series of equations without any explanation of where the equations come from or what they mean is not easy to follow. Instead, give a short annotation explaining where the equations come from when they are first introduced.

Consider a frictionless half-Atwood machine.

The box $$M$$ sitting on the table has a pendulum inside, hanging from the top of the box so that it is vertical when the acceleration of the box is zero. The pendulum is damped so that it quickly reaches its equilibrium position if it is disturbed, or if its equilibrium point changes.

While the half-Atwood machine is accelerating, the pendulum leans backward.

The pendulum will be tilted at some angle $$\theta_a$$ to the vertical.

What is the maximum value $$\theta_a$$ can ever have for any $$m$$ and $$M?$$

label: MCH11
name: Leaning in a Rotating Room — The animation below shows a man leaning absurdly far forward without falling…
desc: The animation below shows a man leaning absurdly far forward without falling over. Try it in your room and you will land on your face. He can only do it because the room he is standing in is rotating. (The clip was filmed at the Artificial Gravity Facility at Brandeis University…
statement:
The animation below shows a man leaning absurdly far forward without falling over. Try it in your room and you will land on your face.

He can only do it because the room he is standing in is rotating. (The clip was filmed at the Artificial Gravity Facility at Brandeis University in Massachusetts.) In the rotating frame of the room, a person standing a distance $$r$$ from the center feels an __artificial gravity__ pointing horizontally outward, toward the wall, with magnitude $$\omega^2 r,$$ where $$\omega$$ is the room's angular speed in radians per second.

A quantity with both a __magnitude__ (how big it is) and a __direction__ (which way it points) is called a __vector__. We draw a vector as an arrow whose length is the magnitude. Positions, displacements, velocities, and accelerations are all vectors. A quantity that is just a number (possibly with units), like mass or speed, is called a __scalar__. To mark a quantity as a vector we draw a small arrow over it, as in $$\vec{a};$$ dropping the arrow, as in $$a,$$ denotes the vector's magnitude. Magnitudes are positive by definition.

__(a)__ Let $$\vec{a}$$ be the artificial gravitational acceleration felt by the person. Which of these four equations are correct, and what exactly is wrong with each incorrect one? $$a = \omega^2 r,$$ $$a = -\omega^2 r,$$ $$\vec{a} = \omega^2 r,$$ $$\vec{a} = -\omega^2 r.$$

__(b)__ Let $$\vec{r}$$ be the person's position vector, measured from an origin at the center of the room, so that $$\vec{r}$$ points outward. Multiplying a vector by a scalar gives a new vector with a rescaled magnitude, pointing the same way (or exactly backward, if the scalar is negative). Write a correct __vector__ equation for $$\vec{a}$$ in terms of $$\omega$$ and $$\vec{r}.$$

__(c)__ Viewed from the non-rotating laboratory surrounding the room, there is no artificial gravity. Instead, the person travels in uniform circular motion, with a centripetal acceleration $$\vec{a}_c$$ pointing toward the center of the room. Write a vector equation for $$\vec{a}_c$$ in terms of $$\omega$$ and $$\vec{r}.$$

__(d)__ To __add__ two vectors, draw the first arrow, then draw a copy of the second arrow starting where the first one ends; the sum is the vector running from the start of the first arrow to the end of the second. The person feels both real gravity $$\vec{g},$$ pointing straight down with magnitude $$g,$$ and the artificial gravity $$\vec{a},$$ pointing horizontally outward, as shown below. What they experience as gravity is the vector sum $$\vec{a} + \vec{g}.$$ Do they feel heavier than normal, lighter than normal, or the same?

__(e)__ Below, the two accelerations are added tip-to-tail, and a dashed circle of radius $$g$$ is drawn around the starting point. Is the magnitude of $$\vec{a}+\vec{g}$$ equal to $$a + g?$$ If not, which is bigger? (Because these can differ, we need a notation for the magnitude of a vector expression: vertical bars, as in $$|\vec{a}+\vec{g}|,$$ denote the magnitude of the vector inside.)

__(f)__ The vectors $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{g}$$ are perpendicular. Find $$|\vec{a}+\vec{g}|$$ in terms of the magnitudes $$a$$ and $$g.$$

__(g)__ The man in the video leans roughly $$45^\circ$$ from the vertical, which happens when $$a = g.$$ In that case, is $$\vec{a} = \vec{g}?$$

label: MCH11
name: The Period of the Rotating Room — In the rotating room at Brandeis University's Artificial Gravity Facility…
desc: In the rotating room at Brandeis University's Artificial Gravity Facility, a person standing at distance $$r$$ from the center feels, in the room's rotating frame, an __artificial gravity__ of magnitude $$a = \omega^2 r$$ pointing horizontally outward ($$\omega$$ is the room's…
statement:
In the rotating room at Brandeis University's Artificial Gravity Facility, a person standing at distance $$r$$ from the center feels, in the room's rotating frame, an __artificial gravity__ of magnitude $$a = \omega^2 r$$ pointing horizontally outward ($$\omega$$ is the room's angular speed in radians per second), in addition to real gravity of magnitude $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ pointing down. A person at rest lines their body up with the total felt gravity $$\vec{a}+\vec{g},$$ so the angle $$\theta$$ they lean from the vertical equals the angle between $$\vec{a}+\vec{g}$$ and the vertical. The two perpendicular accelerations form the right triangle below: legs $$g$$ (vertical) and $$a$$ (horizontal), hypotenuse $$\sqrt{a^2+g^2},$$ with $$\theta$$ between the hypotenuse and the vertical leg.

In this problem you will find the rotational period of the room from the video. Watching the man lean, a reasonable estimate of his lean angle is $$\theta \approx 40^\circ.$$ The facility's website says the room is $$22\;\mathrm{feet}$$ in diameter; remember that $$1\;\mathrm{m} \approx 3.2\;\mathrm{feet}.$$

Recall the __trigonometric functions__ for an angle $$\theta$$ in a right triangle: $$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$ and $$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}},$$ where the "opposite" side is the leg farthest from $$\theta$$ and the "adjacent" side is the leg touching $$\theta.$$

__(a)__ Write $$\sin\theta$$ and $$\cos\theta$$ for the triangle above in terms of $$a,$$ $$g,$$ and $$\sqrt{a^2+g^2}.$$

__(b)__ Either equation could be solved for $$a,$$ but the $$\sqrt{a^2+g^2}$$ in the denominators is a pain. Combine the two equations so that the denominators disappear, and show that $$\tan\theta = \dfrac{a}{g},$$ where the __tangent__ is defined as the quotient $$\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}.$$

__(c)__ Use your calculator's $$\tan$$ button (make sure it is in degree mode, not radians!) to find $$a$$ for $$\theta = 40^\circ.$$

__(d)__ Use $$a = \omega^2 r$$ to find the room's angular speed $$\omega,$$ and then its rotational period $$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}.$$

__(e)__ When you play gentle catch with someone $$20\;\mathrm{feet}$$ away, the ball spends about $$1\;\mathrm{s}$$ in the air per toss. About what fraction of a turn does the room complete while the ball is in the air? The animation below shows the consequence: the ball curves away in mid-air and lands nowhere near the catcher. (This sideways deflection seen in rotating frames is called the __Coriolis__ acceleration; we won't analyze it in detail in this course.)

label: MCH11
name: The Optimal Banking Angle at Talladega — In a 2022 NASCAR race, driver Ross Chastain gained five places on…
desc: In a 2022 NASCAR race, driver Ross Chastain gained five places on the final turn with a wild tactic he said he learned from video games: he drove right up against the outside wall, let go of the steering wheel, and kept his foot on the gas. Every car on the track could go that…
statement:
In a 2022 NASCAR race, driver Ross Chastain gained five places on the final turn with a wild tactic he said he learned from video games: he drove right up against the outside wall, let go of the steering wheel, and kept his foot on the gas.

Every car on the track could go that fast on a straightaway — what they can't do is go that fast __while turning__. A car rounding a turn of radius $$r$$ at speed $$v$$ feels, in its own rotating frame, an artificial gravity pointing horizontally outward (away from the center of the turn) with magnitude $$a = \dfrac{v^2}{r}.$$ (In the ground frame this same quantity is the centripetal acceleration the car needs in order to make the turn.) Ordinarily tire friction must supply that acceleration, so drivers slow down for turns; Chastain instead let the wall push his car sideways, toward the center of the turn.

Some race tracks tilt the road surface on the turns so that drivers barely need friction at all. These are called __banked__ turns.

Call the bank angle $$\theta.$$ Define __optimal banking__ to mean the car needs no friction at all: the total felt gravity — the vector sum of real gravity $$\vec{g}$$ (down, magnitude $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$) and the artificial gravity $$\vec{a}$$ (horizontal, outward) — points exactly perpendicular to the road surface, so the car has no tendency to slide either up or down the bank. The figure shows the setup, viewed from behind a car that is turning to the right; the center of the turn is off to the right, so the artificial gravity points left. (Note that $$\vec{a}$$ is horizontal, __not__ parallel to the tilted road.)

__(a)__ Intuitively, a tighter turn (smaller radius $$r$$) at the same speed needs a steeper bank. But the formula $$a = \omega^2 r$$ seems to say $$a \propto r,$$ so a tighter turn would have __less__ artificial gravity and need a __shallower__ bank. What is wrong with that reasoning, and what is the correct proportionality between $$a$$ and $$r$$ when cars take different turns at the same __speed__ $$v?$$

__(b)__ The vector triangle here is exactly the one for the person leaning in a rotating room: a total felt gravity built from perpendicular $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{g}$$ tilts from the vertical by an angle $$\theta$$ satisfying $$\tan\theta = \dfrac{a}{g}.$$ Show that the optimal bank angle obeys $$\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg},$$ so that $$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v^2}{rg}\right).$$ Here $$\tan^{-1}$$ (the calculator button, also written $$\arctan$$) is the __inverse tangent__: the function that reverses the input and output of $$\tan.$$ The $$-1$$ is not an exponent — $$\tan^{-1}\theta$$ does not mean $$\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}.$$

__(c)__ The Talladega Superspeedway in Alabama is $$2.66\;\mathrm{miles}$$ around, and the lap record is $$46.5\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Using $$8\;\mathrm{km} \approx 5\;\mathrm{mi},$$ find the record-setting car's average speed in meters per second.

__(d)__ Below is an overhead photo of the track. Using the fact that the distance around is about $$4.3\;\mathrm{km},$$ make a rough estimate of the radius of the turn on the right-hand side.

__(e)__ Compute the optimal bank angle from your values in parts (c) and (d). The turn is actually banked at about $$33^\circ.$$ Give at least two reasons our calculated angle comes out too steep.

__(f)__ Is there a maximum speed beyond which no optimally banked track can be built, or is there an optimal angle for every speed? (Hint: $$\sin$$ and $$\cos$$ never exceed $$1.$$ Is the same true of $$\tan,$$ which is the slope of the hypotenuse?)

label: MCH11
name: Madame Upanova and the Rain — Ostriches hate getting wet, because their feathers get soaked. Madame Upanova…
desc: Ostriches hate getting wet, because their feathers get soaked. Madame Upanova the ostrich takes out her rain-speedometer and measures the speed of the raindrops to be $$6.04\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ She begins running due north at $$3.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and the rain speed she measures…
statement:
Ostriches hate getting wet, because their feathers get soaked. Madame Upanova the ostrich takes out her rain-speedometer and measures the speed of the raindrops to be $$6.04\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ She begins running due north at $$3.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and the rain speed she measures increases to $$7.31\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Then, remembering that she left her hat behind, she runs due east at $$3.00\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and now measures a rain speed of $$5.36\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Find the velocity of the rain in the reference frame of the ground. (Rain does not necessarily fall straight down — wind can blow it sideways.)

Background you will need. To work with vectors numerically, we break them into __components__. Choose __unit vectors__ — vectors of magnitude exactly $$1$$ — along three perpendicular directions: here $$\hat{x}$$ points east, $$\hat{y}$$ points up, and $$\hat{z}$$ points south. (The "hat" replaces the usual vector arrow and signals that the length is exactly $$1;$$ $$\hat{x}$$ is read "x hat.")

Any velocity can be written $$\vec{v} = v_x\hat{x} + v_y\hat{y} + v_z\hat{z},$$ where the __components__ $$v_x, v_y, v_z$$ are signed numbers with units, not vectors. The magnitude (the speed) comes from the three-dimensional Pythagorean theorem: $$v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2 + v_z^2.$$ To add or subtract vectors, add or subtract their components. Finally, to see the world from a reference frame moving with velocity $$\vec{v}_1,$$ subtract $$\vec{v}_1$$ from every object's velocity; in particular, the rain's velocity in a runner's own frame is $$\vec{v} - \vec{v}_1$$ (and the runner's own velocity becomes zero in their own frame).

__(a)__ Write Madame Upanova's velocity $$\vec{v}_1$$ while she runs north as a vector, using the unit vectors above. (Careful with signs: $$\hat{z}$$ points __south__.)

__(b)__ Let $$\vec{v} = v_x\hat{x}+v_y\hat{y}+v_z\hat{z}$$ be the rain's velocity in the ground frame. Standing still, she measures speed $$6.04\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ so $$v_x^2+v_y^2+v_z^2 = 36.48\;\mathrm{m^2/s^2}.$$ Write out the components of the rain's velocity in her frame while she runs north, and show that her measurement of $$7.31\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ there gives $$v_x^2 + v_y^2 + (v_z + 3\;\mathrm{m/s})^2 = 53.44\;\mathrm{m^2/s^2}.$$

__(c)__ Subtract the two equations in part (b) to find $$v_z.$$

__(d)__ Repeat the idea for her eastward run, where she measures $$5.36\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ to find $$v_x.$$

__(e)__ Use the standing-still equation to find $$v_y.$$ You will have to choose between two roots — pick the physically sensible one and explain why. Then write out the rain's full velocity $$\vec{v}.$$

label: MCH11
name: The Shape of Spinning Water — The animation below shows water, dyed green, spinning on a turntable. The…
desc: The animation below shows water, dyed green, spinning on a turntable. The surface bends into a curve that gets steeper as the water spins faster. In this problem you will find the exact shape of the surface: its height $$y$$ as a function of the distance $$r$$ from the rotation…
statement:
The animation below shows water, dyed green, spinning on a turntable. The surface bends into a curve that gets steeper as the water spins faster. In this problem you will find the exact shape of the surface: its height $$y$$ as a function of the distance $$r$$ from the rotation axis, when the water rotates steadily with angular speed $$\omega.$$

In the frame rotating along with the water, anything at distance $$r$$ from the axis feels an __artificial gravity__ of magnitude $$a = \omega^2 r$$ pointing horizontally outward, in addition to real gravity of magnitude $$g$$ pointing down. (Useful fact from the rotating-room and banked-track problems: a total felt gravity built from perpendicular $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{g}$$ tilts away from the vertical by an angle $$\theta$$ satisfying $$\tan\theta = a/g.$$)

__(a)__ Imagine placing a tiny surfer on the spinning water's surface, initially at rest relative to the water. One might think gravity slides the surfer downhill toward the center; one might instead think the artificial gravity flings the surfer outward. Argue that, in fact, the surfer stays put — they are in equilibrium in the rotating frame. (Hint: if the surfer would get pushed somewhere, think about the patch of water that was underneath them.)

__(b)__ For the surfer to stay put, the total felt gravity $$\vec{a}+\vec{g}$$ must point perpendicular to the water's surface — that is, perpendicular to the surface's __tangent line__ at the surfer's location, as in the figure below; otherwise the felt gravity would have a piece along the surface and would slide the surfer along it. Show that the __slope__ of the water's surface at radius $$r$$ is $$\tan\theta = \dfrac{\omega^2 r}{g}.$$

__(c)__ We now know the slope of $$y$$ as a function of $$r,$$ and we want $$y$$ itself. Use an analogy to uniform acceleration: for an object starting at rest with constant acceleration $$A,$$ the position is $$x = \frac{1}{2}A t^2,$$ and the slope of a plot of $$x$$ versus $$t$$ is the velocity $$v = At.$$ Our surface's slope, $$\dfrac{\omega^2}{g}\,r,$$ has exactly the form $$A t.$$ Identify what plays the role of $$A$$ and of $$t,$$ make the matching substitutions in $$x = \frac{1}{2}At^2,$$ and write down the resulting formula for $$y(r).$$ What shape is the water's surface?

__(d)__ A mirror with exactly this shape is perfect for a telescope, and making one by spinning a liquid (such as a liquid metal) is far easier than grinding solid glass into a precise curve — several working __liquid mirror telescopes__ exist. (Isaac Newton conceived the idea in the 17th century; Henry Skey of New Zealand built the first working one in 1872.) Such telescopes can be large and nearly flawless. What is their one big disadvantage?

label: MCH11
name: Every Point on a Rolling Hoop — A hoop rolls without slipping along level ground, its center moving to the…
desc: A hoop rolls without slipping along level ground, its center moving to the right — the $$\hat{x}$$ direction — at constant speed $$v.$$ Rolling is translation plus rotation: the velocity of any point on the hoop is the vector sum $$\vec{v}_{\rm pt} = \vec{v}_T + \vec{v}_R,$$…
statement:
A hoop rolls without slipping along level ground, its center moving to the right — the $$\hat{x}$$ direction — at constant speed $$v.$$ Rolling is translation plus rotation: the velocity of any point on the hoop is the vector sum $$\vec{v}_{\rm pt} = \vec{v}_T + \vec{v}_R,$$ where $$\vec{v}_T = v\,\hat{x}$$ is the translational velocity, the same for every point (it carries the whole hoop along), and $$\vec{v}_R$$ is the velocity due to the hoop's rotation about its center. Label a point on the rim by the angle $$\theta$$ that its position vector $$\vec{r}$$ (drawn from the center) makes above the horizontal, as in the figure. Because the hoop spins clockwise, $$\vec{v}_R$$ is perpendicular to $$\vec{r},$$ rotated a quarter turn clockwise from it.

__(a)__ Work in the reference frame moving along with the hoop's center. In that frame the hoop spins in place while the ground slides backward beneath it at speed $$v.$$ Use the fact that the hoop does not slip on the ground to explain why __every__ point on the rim moves at speed $$|\vec{v}_R| = v$$ in this frame.

__(b)__ Now find components, back in the ground frame. The translational part is easy: $$v_{Tx} = v$$ and $$v_{Ty} = 0.$$ For the rotational part, first explain why $$\vec{v}_R$$ makes the same angle $$\theta$$ with the downward __vertical__ that $$\vec{r}$$ makes with the horizontal, and then use $$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$ and $$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$ to show that $$v_{Rx} = v\sin\theta$$ and $$v_{Ry} = -v\cos\theta$$ for the point drawn in the figure.

__(c)__ Vectors add component by component. Find the total components $$v_x$$ and $$v_y$$ for the point at angle $$\theta,$$ then use the Pythagorean theorem $$v_\theta = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$$ together with the identity $$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$$ to show that the point's speed is $$v_\theta = v\sqrt{2(1+\sin\theta)}.$$

__(d)__ Which point of the hoop moves fastest, and how fast? Which point moves slowest, and how slow? Explain why the slowest point's speed is exactly what rolling without slipping demands.

statement:
Part A. In projectile motion, we may want to solve the problem of finding the angle $$\theta$$ that a projectile should be launched at in order to have it travel a horizontal distance $$d$$ before returning to the same height it was launched from. In this problem, we do not assume that the speed $$v_0$$ at launch is fixed.

The angle $$\theta$$ is called the __angle of reach__ given a target distance $$d,$$ launch speed $$v_0,$$ and gravitational acceleration $$g.$$

Which of the following is a plot of the angle of reach $$\theta$$ versus $$v_0$$ for a fixed $$d>0$$ and $$g>0?$$

Ignore air resistance in this problem.

(A)

(B)

(C)

(D)

(E)

Part B. In projectile motion, $$\theta, d,$$ and $$v_0$$ can all realistically vary. It can therefore be useful to understand $$\theta,$$ the angle of reach, as a function of __both__ $$d$$ and $$v_0.$$

One way we could do this is by taking the curve from part (A) as a starting point. This curve shows $$\theta$$ as a function of $$v_0,$$ with a fixed $$d.$$ We could then draw more curves on the same plot, each for a different value of $$d.$$

Alternatively, we could first draw a single curve for $$\theta$$ versus $$d,$$ given a fixed $$v_0.$$ Here is one such curve, using $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and a $$v_0$$ which you can calculate, if you find it helpful.

Then we could choose different values of $$v_0$$ and draw new $$\theta$$ versus $$d$$ curves, one for each value of $$v_0.$$ We can also add a A __legend__ is also called a __key__. It's the box on the side that tells you what each different curve means..

Which choice below shows what such a plot looks like?

All the plots use $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Part C. One more way to represent the dependence of $$\theta$$ on both $$d$$ and $$v_0$$ at the same time is with a __contour plot__.

This is a plot on which __both__ axes represent independent variables. In this case, there will be one $$d$$ axis and one $$v_0$$ axis, since $$\theta$$ is a dependent variable that depends on the independent variables $$d$$ and $$v_0.$$

Each point on this plot represents a choice of both $$d$$ and $$v_0.$$ For example, point 1 below represents $$d = 6 \;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$v_0 = 15 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

There are two possible angles of reach at this point. (Most points on the plot have two angles of reach.) We will take the lower angle for this problem, ignoring the higher angle whenever there are two angles of reach.

To complete the plot, we draw a series of lines or curves, called __contours__. These lines or curves connect points on the plot that have the same value of $$\theta.$$

For example we could calculate the angle of reach $$\theta_1$$ at point 1 shown above. Then we could calculate the angle of reach at a few other places on the plot. Any time we found another point where the angle of reach was $$\theta_1,$$ we would plot that point. This would give us a series of points that form some shape on the plot. We could connect those points to form a curve. That curve is the contour $$\theta = \theta_1.$$

Then we could find contours for other values of $$\theta$$ and plot them as well. Finally, we could add labels or a legend to the plot to help us interpret the contours.

-------------------------

Let's look at two examples of contour plots to understand them better before you find contour plots for projectile motion.

You may have already seen __topographical maps__ or __contour maps__.

source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contour_line

The lower map is a topographical map. A map like this tells you the elevation using contours. Each line connects points with the same elevation.

Thought of as a contour plot, a topographical map treats latitude and longitude as independent variables, so there is one on each axis. It treats elevation as a dependent variable. The curves on the lower plot connect points with the same elevation.

As a second example, consider the formula $$ T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$$ for the period $$T$$ of a mass $$m$$ on a spring $$k.$$

To make a plot of $$T$$ as a function of both $$m$$ and $${}k,$$ we can construct a contour plot using $$m$$ and $${}k$$ as independent variables. (It doesn't matter which is horizontal and which is vertical.) The contours connect points that lead to the same period.

The contour map for $$T$$ looks like this:

$$T$$ increases moving up and to the left on this plot. Moving up corresponds to increasing $$m.$$ A higher mass takes longer to oscillate. Moving left corresponds to decreasing $${}k.$$ The lower the spring constant, the longer the period.

To construct this map, we found $$m = \left(\dfrac{T}{2\pi}\right)^2 \cdot k$$ meaning that for a fixed $$T,$$ $$m$$ versus $${}k$$ is a straight line, and the slope is proportional to $$T^2.$$

-----------------------

You may be wondering about the difference between the contour plots introduced here and the plots from part (B).

In this problem, we are interested in finding and representing the angle of reach, $$\theta.$$ We therefore think of $$\theta$$ as the dependent variable, and think of $$d$$ and $$v_0$$ as independent variables.

In part (B), we constructed plots where each curve represented different values of an __independent__ variable; each curve was a different value of $$v_0.$$

Here in part (C), we are looking at plots where each curve represents a different value of the __dependent__ variable; each curve is a different value of $$\theta.$$

If we instead wanted to solve the problem of the speed $$v_0$$ needed to launch a projectile, given the desired angle and range, the plots in part (B) would be contour plots.

In the topographical map example, the equivalent to part (B)'s plots would be to plot elevation versus longitude, and then to draw different curves representing different latitudes. This plot would be harder to interpret during a hike than the topographical map, although they represent the same information. ---------

statement:
Part A. Commercial airplanes can fly around $$90\%$$ the speed of sound, which is around $$300 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ at $$10 \;\mathrm{km}$$ altitude. Most jets don't fly faster than about $$90\%$$ the speed of sound because the aerodynamics of flight near the speed of sound are fundamentally different than at lower speeds, and are very challenging.

There are airplanes that fly faster than the speed of sound, including military jets and a very small number of commercial airliners. Airplanes designed for supersonic (faster-than-sound) flight need to have very high power output, need to resist heating up due to compressing the air they fly through, and need to minimize their drag. Supersonic airliners need longer runways than normal jets because their liftoff speeds are higher due to their smaller wings. They also continuously produce a __sonic boom__ as they fly, which prevents them from flying over populated areas at low altitude. As a result, although supersonic flight for commercial jets is possible, it is very expensive. For the most part, airlines haven't found the cost of buying and maintaining supersonic airliners worthwhile.

Helicopters, unlike planes, don't fly close to the speed of sound. The fastest helicopters only fly around $$90 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ or about $$30\%$$ the speed of sound.

The main factor limiting helicopters' speed is that their __blades__ will travel near the speed of sound long before the helicopter itself gets near the speed of sound. When some part of a helicopter blade approaches the speed of sound, changes in the aerodynamics usually cause severe vibrations in the blade that engineers have not been able to overcome.

The tips of the blades of a helicopter travel faster than the helicopter itself, so if a helicopter were to fly $$90\%$$ the speed of sound, like a commercial jet, parts of its blades would travel faster than the sound barrier. This is not currently something helicopters can do.

Additionally, what matters is not the speed of the blades relative to the helicopter, but relative to the air. This is different on different sides of the helicopter.

https://aviation.stackexchange.com/questions/33596/how-does-wind-speed-affect-helicopter-rotor-speed

This creates another problem for helicopters. The blades that move faster relative to the air generate more __lift__, meaning they push the helicopter up more. If the right and left hand sides of the helicopter produce significantly different amount of lift, it will tip the helicopter over and make stable flight impossible.

Helicopters can adjust for this problem by changing the __angle of attack__ of the blades. This is the angle that the blades are inclined relative to the horizontal plane they rotate in.

LearnEngineering.org

Up to a certain limit (which real helicopters do not reach), increasing the angle of attack increases the lift.

Helicopters adjust the angle of attack of the blades continuously, going up and down one per revolution of the blades. This strategy is called __blade flapping__.

How should a helicopter engineer design the blade flapping of a helicopter? Use the helicopter pictured above - one going forward with blades rotating counterclockwise.

Part A. In this multi-part problem, we'll explore a new mathematical fact related to the center of mass: Pappus' theorem.

----------------------------

Imagine taking a square with side lengths $$s$$ and rotating it one full rotation about an axis along one of the sides of the square.

As the square rotates, we keep track of all the space it passes through. This space is a cylinder with radius $$s$$ and height $$s.$$

The cylinder is called the __solid of revolution__ of the square about that axis.

Match the following plane figures being revolved around the shown axis (left) with the solid of revolution (right).

Part B. The volume of a solid of revolution is called the __volume of revolution__.

Let's again take the example of a square revolved around one side.

The volume of revolution is the volume of the cylinder, $$\begin{aligned} V & = \text{(base area)} \cdot \text{height} \\ {} & = (\pi s^2) \cdot s \\ {} & = \pi s^3 \end{aligned}$$

----------------------------

Next we'll look at a different shape. This time, we move the square away from the axis of rotation, so the center of the square is a distance $$r$$ from the axis of rotation, as shown below.

Which is the correct equation for the volume of revolution of this square about this axis?

$$V = \pi r^2 \cdot s$$

$$V = \pi s^3$$

$$V = \pi \left(r-\dfrac12 s\right)^2 \cdot s$$

$$V = \pi \left(\left(r + \dfrac12s\right)^2 - \left(r - \dfrac12 s\right)^2\right)\cdot s$$

$$V = \pi \left((r+s)^2 - r^2\right)\cdot s$$

Part C. Simplify the answer you chose for part (B).

Which of the following is an interpretation of the result?

The volume of revolution for the square is equal to...

the area of a cube with side length $$s$$

the volume of a disk with radius $$r + \dfrac12 s$$ and height $$s$$

the area of the square times the outer radius of the solid of revolution

the area of the square times the distance the center of mass of the square moves during the rotation

Part D. The interpretation you chose in part (C) is something we've only shown for the case of a square revolved around an axis parallel to one side of the square.

We'd like to know whether the same interpretation applies to any sort of volume of revolution, for example this circle:

To make an argument that it does, we try breaking the shape down into many small squares of side length $$s.$$

To find the volume of revolution of the entire shape, we can find the volume of revolution of each small square, then add them all up.

The goal of this part of the problem is to write an equation expressing this "add up all the squares" process. We can do that with __summation notation__.

Below is a brief example of summation notation. You can read more about summations at the following AoPS Wiki pages: https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/Sigma_notation https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/Summation

We found in the handout that the center of mass of this shape can be defined by

$$\vec{R} = \lim_{s\to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i = 1}^n m_i \vec{r}_i$$

In this equation, we label the squares with a number:

When $$i = 17,$$ for example, we look at this square:

That square has mass $$m_{17}$$ and position vector $$\vec{r}_{17}.$$ The next square has mass $$m_{18}$$ and position vector $$\vec{r}_{18},$$ etc.

The expression $$\sum_{i = 1}^n m_i \vec{r}_i$$ means that we take $$m \vec{r}$$ for each square and add them all together (using vector addition).

$$M$$ is the total mass of a shape.

The part $$\lim_{s\to 0}$$ means that there is some slight error when we approximate a shape by a bunch of squares, due to the edges having partial squares. If we cut the shape into smaller and smaller squares, the square shape gets closer and closer to the original shape, so the error gets smaller and smaller. A formal definition of limits is notoriously challenging. It was almost 200 years between the foundation of calculus, by Isaac Newton, Gottfried Leibniz, and others, until Karl Weierstrass first used the modern definition of a limit. When we need to discuss a limit, we will stick with an intuitive notion of "what the function goes towards". In this case, the quantity calculated using squares of side length $$s$$ goes toward the true center of mass, and not toward any other number as $$s$$ gets smaller.

If we want to break the center of mass into components, we have $$\begin{aligned} R_x & = \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i = 1}^n m_i r_{xi} \\ R_y & = \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i = 1}^n m_i r_{yi} \end{aligned}$$

Build a summation for the volume of revolution of a shape revolved around an axis, assuming the shape is broken down into squares of side length $$s.$$ The axis of rotation points in the $$\hat{y}$$ direction.

Part E. Wen is a physics student who enjoys working on algebraic derivations. Wen arrives at this equation for a volume of revolution:

$$ V = \lim_{s \to 0} \sum_i 2\pi r_i s^2$$

Wen worked on this formula for some time, trying to understand what it meant and how it related to simple cases of volumes of revolution that he understood without the formula.

After a many false starts and failed attempts, Wen finally found some algebraic steps he was satisfied with, and wrote them down as a summary of his work.

First, Wen assumed that the figure he is revolving has a A __surface density__ is a mass per unit area of a surface. This is like a normal density, but in two dimensions instead of three of $$\lambda,$$ so that the total mass of the entire plane shape (not the solid of revolution) is $$M = \lambda A$$ where $$A$$ is the area of the shape being revolved.

Also, the mass of a square of side length $$s$$ is $$m = \lambda s^2$$

Wen then wrote down the following manipulations to his volume formula, all of which are algebraically valid:

$$\begin{aligned} V & = \lim_{s \to 0} \sum_i 2\pi r_i s^2 \\ {} &= \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \sum_i \lambda r_i s^2 \\ {} &= \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \sum_i m_i r_i \\ {} &= \lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda A} A \sum_i m_i r_i \\ {} &= A \cdot 2\pi \left(\lim_{s \to 0} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i r_i\right) \\ \end{aligned}$$

Wen then wrote down some interpretation of these equations. We'll try to understand what that interpretation was.

There are many possible algebraic manipulations of the formula Wen started with for $$V.$$ **Which one of the following is the most likely and most complete explanation for why Wen used these particular algebraic manipulations to summarize his work?**

As you are choosing your answer, you may want to think about what Wen's next algebraic step would be. For example, think about whether there's another physical quantity which can be substituted into the last line of Wen's work, and would be useful for understanding volumes of revolution.

statement:
Part A. Over this week, we've discussed several methods of finding the center of mass of a shape, assuming that the shape is uniform.

These include:

- Drawing a grid on the shape, measuring the position of each square on the grid, and applying the formula $$\vec{R} = \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i \vec{r}_i$$ - Tossing the shape in the air with some spin. - Hanging the shape, drawing a vertical line from the point that it's hung, and repeating. - Balancing the shape on a finger or pencil tip. - For certain shapes, it may be possible to calculate the center of mass via a formula, such as Pappus' theorem.

Take a flat piece of cardboard. Cut out an irregular shape. Find the center of mass of your shape with at least two different methods.

Which methods did you choose? What did you have to figure out in order to use the method? What decisions did you make? What difficulties did you encounter? How well did your methods agree?

Feel free to take photos to share so other students can see what your shape looked like and where its center of mass is!

statement:
A block is released from rest at the top of a frictionless ramp. The ramp makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal, and the __horizontal__ length of its base is $$L.$$ Gravity gives every object near Earth's surface a downward acceleration of magnitude $$g=9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ and an object that starts from rest with uniform acceleration $$a$$ covers a distance $$d=\tfrac12 at^2$$ in time $$t.$$ The base $$L$$ is fixed, but the angle $$\theta$$ is up to you: choose $$\theta$$ so that the block reaches the bottom of the ramp as quickly as possible. (This problem appeared on the 2021 F=ma exam.)

__(a)__ Before calculating, build some intuition. Explain why the trip time $$t$$ is very large when $$\theta$$ is close to $$0,$$ and also very large when $$\theta$$ is close to $$\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$$ (For the second one, be careful: it is the horizontal base $$L,$$ not the ramp itself, that stays fixed — so a very steep ramp is also a very long, very tall ramp.) Then sketch roughly what a plot of $$t$$ versus $$\theta$$ should look like.

__(b)__ To find the block's acceleration, set up a tilted coordinate system: let $$\hat{x}'$$ point down the slope, along the ramp's surface, and let $$\hat{y}'$$ point perpendicular to the surface. The vector $$\vec{g}$$ has magnitude $$g$$ and points straight down. Find its components in the tilted system — that is, fill in $$\vec{g}=g_{x'}\,\hat{x}'+g_{y'}\,\hat{y}'.$$

__(c)__ The ramp prevents any motion perpendicular to its own surface. What is the block's acceleration vector $$\vec{a}?$$

__(d)__ How long is the ramp's sloped surface, in terms of $$L$$ and $$\theta?$$ Combine your answers to find the trip time $$t$$ as a function of $$\theta.$$

__(e)__ Using the identity $$\sin\theta\cos\theta=\tfrac12\sin(2\theta),$$ find the angle $$\theta$$ that minimizes $$t.$$ Does the answer fit your sketch from part (a)?

desc: A stunt cyclist builds a ramp so they can jump over several parked cars. The cyclist starts from rest, rolls down the ramp without pedaling, launches into the air, and lands at the same height as the launch point. Friction and air resistance are negligible. Define: $$H_0,$$ the…
statement:
A stunt cyclist builds a ramp so they can jump over several parked cars. The cyclist starts from rest, rolls down the ramp without pedaling, launches into the air, and lands at the same height as the launch point. Friction and air resistance are negligible. Define: $$H_0,$$ the vertical distance between the top of the ramp and the launch point; $$\theta_0,$$ the angle of the ramp above the horizontal at the launch point; $$X_0,$$ the horizontal distance traveled while the cyclist and bicycle are in the air; and $$m_0,$$ the combined mass of the cyclist and bicycle. The goal: find $$X_0$$ in terms of $$H_0,$$ $$\theta_0,$$ $$m_0,$$ and physical constants. (Adapted from the 2021 AP Physics 1 exam.)

Two earlier results you may reuse without re-deriving. First, the __range formula__: a projectile launched at speed $$v$$ and angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal travels a horizontal distance $$R=\dfrac{v^2\sin(2\theta)}{g}$$ before returning to its launch height. Second, __energy conservation__: with friction negligible, gravitational potential energy $$mgh$$ converts to kinetic energy $$\tfrac12 mv^2.$$

__(a)__ Diving straight into equations is a good way to get lost in algebra. Instead, start with a plan: name one quantity, not given in the problem, that — if you knew it — would reduce this to a problem you already know how to solve. Which problem?

__(b)__ Use energy conservation to find the launch speed. Why is it more convenient to solve for $$v^2$$ than for $$v?$$

__(c)__ Find $$X_0.$$ Which of the quantities you were handed turn out not to matter?

__(d)__ Some students claim that if $$g$$ were smaller, the cyclist would jump farther, since they would hang in the air longer. Identify the __two__ competing effects of lowering $$g,$$ and say what your formula concludes. Then back it up with dimensional analysis: the dimensions of $$g$$ are $$=\mathrm{L\cdot T^{-2}}.$$ Looking at the dimensions of $$H_0,$$ $$\theta_0,$$ and $$X_0,$$ argue that $$g$$ __cannot__ appear in a formula relating them.

__(e)__ Now consider the time $$t$$ the cyclist spends in the air — a quantity that __does__ need $$g.$$ Use dimensional analysis to find the proportionality $$t\propto g^{\,?}.$$ If the whole setup were moved to the Moon, where $$g_{\rm moon}\approx\dfrac{g}{6},$$ would the cyclist still clear the cars? What would the jump look like?

name: The Oddly-Balanced Wheel — A wheel of radius $$r$$ is mounted on a horizontal frictionless axle through its…
desc: A wheel of radius $$r$$ is mounted on a horizontal frictionless axle through its center, so it can spin freely in a vertical plane. The wheel itself is uniform, so on its own it is balanced at every angle. Three small objects are attached to its rim: a mass $$m$$ at the leftmost…
statement:
A wheel of radius $$r$$ is mounted on a horizontal frictionless axle through its center, so it can spin freely in a vertical plane. The wheel itself is uniform, so on its own it is balanced at every angle. Three small objects are attached to its rim: a mass $$m$$ at the leftmost point, a mass $$2M$$ at the rightmost point, and a mass $$M$$ an angle $$\theta$$ up along the rim from the mass $$m,$$ as shown. The system is in equilibrium. Find $$m$$ in terms of $$M$$ and $$\theta.$$ (Adapted from the AP Physics 1 workbook.)

Background — the __virtual work__ method for equilibrium: a system is in equilibrium when an imagined tiny displacement (a __virtual displacement__) produces no change in potential energy, $$\delta U=0.$$ Raising a mass $$m$$ by a small height $$\delta y$$ changes the gravitational potential energy by $$\delta U=mg\,\delta y.$$ When the wheel turns by a small angle $$\delta\theta,$$ each object on the rim moves a distance $$r\,\delta\theta$$ along the rim (the definition of radian measure), in the direction tangent to the rim.

__(a)__ Imagine rotating the wheel by a small angle $$\delta\theta$$ in the direction that raises $$m.$$ In the limit $$\delta\theta\to0,$$ find the height changes $$\delta y_m,$$ $$\delta y_{2M},$$ and $$\delta y_M$$ of the three masses. For the mass $$M,$$ the height change is $$r\,\delta\theta$$ times either $$\sin\theta$$ or $$\cos\theta$$ — decide which by checking the extreme case $$\theta\to0:$$ in that limit, is $$M$$'s motion nearly vertical or nearly horizontal?

__(b)__ Write the equilibrium condition $$\delta U=\delta U_m+\delta U_M+\delta U_{2M}=0$$ and solve for $$m.$$ Which common factors cancel out of every term?

__(c)__ Check your formula in three special cases by reasoning directly about balance: $$\theta=0$$ (where $$M$$ sits at the same point as $$m$$), $$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$ (where $$M$$ sits at the top of the wheel), and $$\theta=\pi$$ (where $$M$$ sits at the same point as $$2M$$).

label: MCH12
name: Balance and the Center of Mass — A uniform wheel of radius $$r$$ spins on a frictionless horizontal axle…
desc: A uniform wheel of radius $$r$$ spins on a frictionless horizontal axle through its center. Point masses are attached to its rim: $$m$$ at the leftmost point, $$2M$$ at the rightmost point, and $$M$$ an angle $$\theta$$ up the rim from $$m.$$ A virtual-work analysis (see the…
statement:
A uniform wheel of radius $$r$$ spins on a frictionless horizontal axle through its center. Point masses are attached to its rim: $$m$$ at the leftmost point, $$2M$$ at the rightmost point, and $$M$$ an angle $$\theta$$ up the rim from $$m.$$ A virtual-work analysis (see the problem "The Oddly-Balanced Wheel") shows that when the wheel is turned by a small angle $$\delta\theta$$ in the direction that raises $$m,$$ the potential energy changes by $$\delta U\propto m\cdot r-2M\cdot r+M\cdot r\cos\theta,$$ and the system is in equilibrium exactly when this expression is zero. This problem uncovers the geometric meaning of that condition.

The __center of mass__ of a collection of point masses is their mass-weighted average position: $$\vec{R}=\dfrac{1}{M_T}\sum_i m_i\vec{r}_i,$$ where $$M_T=\sum_i m_i$$ is the total mass. Its components are $$R_x=\dfrac{1}{M_T}\sum_i m_ir_{xi}$$ and $$R_y=\dfrac{1}{M_T}\sum_i m_ir_{yi}.$$

__(a)__ Put the origin at the axle, with $$x$$ horizontal and $$y$$ vertical. Write down the position vectors of the three masses, and show that $$\delta U\propto-\left(m\,r_{mx}+2M\,r_{2Mx}+M\,r_{Mx}\right)$$ — that is, the potential energy change under a small rotation is built from the $$x$$ components of the positions, even though gravity acts vertically. Why does that make sense?

__(b)__ Rewrite the sum from part (a) in terms of the center of mass, and state the equilibrium condition geometrically: a pivoted system is balanced exactly when its center of mass is __where__?

__(c)__ For the balanced wheel shown in the picture, locate the center of mass of the three point masses as precisely as you can: is it above, below, or at the axle, and is it near the axle or far from it?

__(d)__ So far we've ignored the wheel's own mass. The wheel is uniform, so its own center of mass is at its center. If the wheel's mass $$M_W$$ is included in the system, what happens to the system's center of mass, and is the wheel still balanced?

name: Letters in Flight — Two useful facts about the center of mass. First, the gravitational potential energy of a…
desc: Two useful facts about the center of mass. First, the gravitational potential energy of a whole system is $$U=M_Tg\,R_y,$$ where $$M_T$$ is the total mass and $$R_y$$ is the height of the center of mass $$\vec{R}=\dfrac{1}{M_T}\sum_i m_i\vec{r}_i$$ — as far as gravity is…
statement:
Two useful facts about the center of mass. First, the gravitational potential energy of a whole system is $$U=M_Tg\,R_y,$$ where $$M_T$$ is the total mass and $$R_y$$ is the height of the center of mass $$\vec{R}=\dfrac{1}{M_T}\sum_i m_i\vec{r}_i$$ — as far as gravity is concerned, the system acts like a single mass sitting at its center of mass (assuming $$\vec{g}$$ is the same everywhere over the system). Second, a rigid object tossed spinning through the air rotates about its center of mass. In class we examined slow-motion clips, from Physics Girl's video "Rotation and Torque" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D3_0vHJVHHo), of glowing letters thrown across a dark room.

__(a)__ The glowing letter P below is tossed with some spin. Just by watching the motion, how can you locate the P's center of mass?

__(b)__ The letter Y below is thrown in the dark with glowing markers only at its three tips, which trace out complicated loops and swirls. If one more glowing marker were attached at the Y's center of mass, what path would it trace, and why?

__(c)__ Derive the first fact: starting from the potential energy $$U=\sum_i m_ig\,y_i$$ of the individual masses, show that $$U=M_Tg\,R_y.$$ What assumption about $$\vec{g}$$ does the derivation need?

label: MCH12
name: The Wheel, Revisited: Stability and Oscillations — A wheel — model it as a thin hoop of radius $$r$$ and mass…
desc: A wheel — model it as a thin hoop of radius $$r$$ and mass $$M_W,$$ so all of its mass lies on the rim — spins on a frictionless horizontal axle through its center. Attached to the rim are point masses $$m,$$ $$M,$$ and $$2M,$$ with $$m=M(2-\cos\theta)$$ chosen so the system is…
statement:
A wheel — model it as a thin hoop of radius $$r$$ and mass $$M_W,$$ so all of its mass lies on the rim — spins on a frictionless horizontal axle through its center. Attached to the rim are point masses $$m,$$ $$M,$$ and $$2M,$$ with $$m=M(2-\cos\theta)$$ chosen so the system is in equilibrium when $$m$$ is at the leftmost point, $$2M$$ at the rightmost point, and $$M$$ an angle $$\theta$$ up the rim from $$m$$ (see the problems "The Oddly-Balanced Wheel" and "Balance and the Center of Mass"). In that position the system's center of mass lies directly __above__ the axle, at some distance $$R$$ from it. The total mass is $$M_T=m+3M+M_W.$$ Potential energy is $$U=M_Tg\,R_y,$$ where $$R_y$$ is the height of the center of mass, and systems disturbed from rest tend to settle where their potential energy is lowest.

__(a)__ Take $$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$$ As the wheel rotates, the center of mass is carried along with it. On what curve can the center of mass move? Is the equilibrium described above __stable__ or __unstable__?

__(b)__ Tiny amounts of friction in the axle and air resistance slowly drain the system's energy. If the wheel is nudged away from the equilibrium above, through what angle will it have turned, in total, when it finally comes to rest?

__(c)__ Now find the period of small oscillations about the resting position from part (b). Background to reuse: a mass on a spring has $$U=\tfrac12 kx^2,$$ kinetic energy $$\tfrac12 mv^2,$$ and period $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}.$$ A system rotated by a small angle $$\phi$$ from a stable equilibrium where its center of mass hangs a distance $$R$$ below the pivot has $$U\approx\tfrac12 M_TgR\,\phi^2$$ (just like a pendulum of length $$R$$), and a rotating object has kinetic energy $$\tfrac12 I\omega^2,$$ where $$\omega$$ is the rate of change of $$\phi$$ and $$I=\sum_i m_id_i^2$$ is the __moment of inertia__ ($$d_i$$ is the distance of mass $$i$$ from the rotation axis). By matching the wheel's quantities to the spring's, write the period $$T$$ in terms of $$I,$$ $$M_T,$$ $$g,$$ and $$R.$$

__(d)__ Find the moment of inertia $$I$$ of this system (hoop plus three point masses) in terms of $$M_T$$ and $$r.$$

__(e)__ Find $$R,$$ the distance from the axle to the center of mass. (Hint: at the resting position, $$m$$ is at the rightmost point, $$2M$$ at the leftmost point, and $$M$$ an angle $$\theta$$ __below__ the horizontal — so only $$M$$ lies off the horizontal diameter, and the hoop's own center of mass is at the axle.)

__(f)__ Combine your results into a formula for $$T$$ in terms of $$M,$$ $$M_W,$$ $$\theta,$$ $$r,$$ and $$g,$$ and check that its dimensions work out.

label: MCH12
name: Speeding Up Around a Curve — A car drives along a semicircular racetrack. Its velocity vector is shown at…
desc: A car drives along a semicircular racetrack. Its velocity vector is shown at five points spaced at equal __distances__ along the track, and the arrows grow steadily longer: the car is speeding up, and (as you could verify by measuring the arrows) its speed increases linearly in…
statement:
A car drives along a semicircular racetrack. Its velocity vector is shown at five points spaced at equal __distances__ along the track, and the arrows grow steadily longer: the car is speeding up, and (as you could verify by measuring the arrows) its speed increases linearly in time. Recall from circular motion: an object moving along a circle of radius $$r$$ at speed $$v$$ has a __centripetal__ acceleration component of magnitude $$a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}$$ pointing toward the center of the circle, and if its speed is changing it also has a __tangential__ component equal to the rate of change of its speed, pointing along the direction of motion (or opposite it, when slowing down). Your goal: without detailed computation, draw and describe the car's total acceleration vector at each marked point.

__(a)__ The five points are separated by equal distances. Are they separated by (approximately) equal __times__? How do you know?

__(b)__ Sketch the tangential acceleration vector at each of the five points. What are their directions, and how do their lengths compare to each other?

__(c)__ Sketch the centripetal acceleration vector at each point. What are their directions, and how do their lengths change as the car goes around?

__(d)__ Now combine: as the car rounds the curve, what happens to the __magnitude__ of the total acceleration vector, and what happens to its __direction__? Sketch the five total acceleration vectors.

__(e)__ Centripetal and tangential components are a way of breaking the acceleration vector into pieces, just like $$x$$ and $$y$$ components. What is the key difference between this decomposition and an ordinary $$x$$-$$y$$ coordinate system?

name: Below are a few different situations. In each, we could imagine trying to use momentum…
desc: Below are a few different situations. In each, we could imagine trying to use momentum conservation to make predictions, but momentum conservation only holds when no momentum enters or leaves the system of study. Each situation defines a system, then "inputs", meaning…
statement:
Below are a few different situations. In each, we could imagine trying to use momentum conservation to make predictions, but momentum conservation only holds when no momentum enters or leaves the system of study.

Each situation defines a system, then "inputs", meaning measurements or data we could use to make calculations with momentum, and then a "prediction", meaning a value that we want to calculate using momentum conservation.

**Select the situation in which assuming the momentum of the system is conserved would help make accurate and useful predictions for the behavior of the system.** (There is only one.)

The predictions do not have to be __perfectly__ accurate, since no predictions ever are. However, there is a large gap here between systems where momentum conservation makes largely-accurate predictions and systems where its predictions are very far off.

**(a)** A highway engineer is trying to design safer roads. They are studying the collision that happens when a car suddenly stops, and a large truck that was following the car hits its brakes, but cannot stop in time and hits the car, then they skid together down the road some distance before stopping. **system**: truck and car **inputs**: masses of truck and car, distance between stopped car and truck, initial velocity of truck **prediction**: velocity of car and truck after sliding $$50 \;\mathrm{m}$$ down the road after the collision

**(b)** An astrophysicist is studying a __galaxy merger__, the collision of two galaxies in deep space. International Gemini Observatory / NOIRLAB / NSF / AURA, retrieved https://www.cbsnews.com/news/galaxies-stunning-photo-cosmic-collision-milky-way/ Usually, stars don't literally slam into each other in a galaxy merger, since there is so much space between the stars, but the galaxies do interact via gravity, and can combine into one larger galaxy this way. The answer to this problem would be the same whether stars collide or not, though! The two galaxies are far away from other galaxies, and not influenced significantly by anything other than each other. **system**: the two galaxies combined **inputs**: the masses and velocities of all the stars (and all the other matter) in the galaxies **prediction**: the velocity of the center of mass of the combined galaxy after the merger

**(c)** A biomechanist is studying the flight of birds. They want to know how birds go from flying full speed ahead to landing safely on a perch.

https://www.quantamagazine.org/geometric-analysis-reveals-how-birds-mastered-flight-20220803/

**system**: bird **inputs**: mass and velocity of bird when $$10 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away from perch **prediction**: mass and velocity of bird when $$1 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ away from perch

desc: Part A. Light has no mass, but it still has momentum. The formula $$p = mv$$ for the momentum of a particle indicates that if the mass of the particle is zero, so is its momentum. However, physicists have found that the concept of momentum is more important than the specific…
statement:
Part A. Light has no mass, but it still has momentum.

The formula $$p = mv$$ for the momentum of a particle indicates that if the mass of the particle is zero, so is its momentum. However, physicists have found that the concept of momentum is more important than the specific formula for it we've used. Light can collide with things and push on them, for example, a phenomenon called __radiation pressure__. Scientists found new equations that accurately modeled radiation pressure, and decided to call the new mathematical construct "momentum", replacing the old construct of $$p = mv.$$

The new models scientists built for the momentum of light belong to the theory of special relativity. The equations of these models are extremely close to the equation $$p = mv$$ for objects traveling slowly compared to the speed of light, but as the speed increases, the equations become more and more different.

There is a simple equation for the momentum $$p$$ of light with energy $$E.$$ This formula gives the same type of momentum as the formula $$p=mv,$$ which it must since momentum from light can be converted into momentum in massive objects during collisions.

The speed of light is $$c.$$

Which of these equations could be the relation between $$p, c,$$ and $$E$$ for light?

$$p = Ec$$

$$p = E^2 c$$

$$p = c/E$$

$$p = Ec^2$$

$$p = E/c$$

Part B. A __solar sail__ is a spaceship powered by light from the sun. Light from the sun hits the ship, and the momentum of the light pushes the ship away from the sun. Solar sails are a real technology - the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched one called IKAROS (Interplanetary Kite-craft Accelerated by Radiation Of the Sun) in 2010.

Below is an artist's depiction of the IKAROS spacecraft:

By Andrzej Mirecki - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=14656159

For this question, model the solar sail as a uniform flat sheet oriented in the plane perpendicular to the light from the sun.

Let's consider a few potential features of a solar sail:

**Reflectivity** High reflectivity means that light bounces off the solar sail, like a mirror. Low reflectivity means that the solar sail absorbs light that hits it.

**Cross-Sectional Area** High cross sectional area means that the solar sail is large, specifically in the directions perpendicular to the direction of motion of light coming from the sun.

**Density Of Satellite Material** This is the mass per unit volume of the material the solar sail is made from.

**Thickness** This is the thickness of the solar sail in the direction parallel to the direction the light from the sun is moving.

Part C. The main purpose of the IKAROS mission was to test the spacecraft's ability to use radiation pressure to accelerate - an engineering mission focused on light sail technology. It also made scientific measurements of gamma ray bursts, solar wind, and cosmic dust as it traveled the solar system.

IKAROS made a flyby of Jupiter, and now orbits the sun between Venus and Earth, although the satellite is now defunct.

The IKAROS solar sail is a square $$14 \;\mathrm{m}$$ on a side. It is made from a specially-designed plastic, and is only about $$7.5 \times 10^{-6} \;\mathrm{m}$$ thick. The density of the plastic is about $$1.1 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$

Near Venus, sunlight delivers a power per unit area of about $$2.5 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{W/m^2}$$ to any object absorbing all the sunlight that hits it. One watt is one joule per second. Sunlight delivers $$2.5 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{J} = 2.5 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{kg\, m^2 \, s^{-2}}$$ every second to something with an area of $$1 \;\mathrm{m}^2,$$ when it's near Venus and its cross-section is facing the sunlight.

The speed of light is $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Using this data and your answer to part (A), find the maximum acceleration of a solar sail like IKAROS when near to Venus.

You can assume that the reflectivity of the satellite is whatever maximizes its acceleration.

statement:
A train rides north along straight, frictionless tracks with no air drag. It is snowing: snowflakes fall straight down and stick to the train. At some instant, the system consisting of the train plus all the snow currently stuck to it has mass $$m$$ and velocity $$v.$$ Snow lands on the train at a steady rate; the __mass flux__ $$j_m$$ is the mass of snow added to the train per unit time. The goal of this problem is the train's instantaneous acceleration.

__(a)__ If it weren't snowing, the train's speed would stay constant. With the snow, does the train speed up, slow down, or keep the same speed? Answer using momentum conservation, with no algebra. (Hint: the still-falling snow carries no horizontal momentum, so it adds __mass__ to the system without adding any horizontal momentum.)

__(b)__ Visualize the momentum $$p = mv$$ as the area of a rectangle of length $$m$$ and height $$v.$$ After a short time $$\Delta t,$$ both $$m$$ and $$v$$ have changed, by $$\Delta m$$ and $$\Delta v.$$ The figure below draws both as increases because that's easiest to see; when a quantity actually decreases, the minus sign in the algebra takes care of it. Use the diagram to explain why $$\Delta p = v\,\Delta m + m\,\Delta v + \Delta m\,\Delta v.$$

__(c)__ The average acceleration over the interval is $$a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t},$$ so $$\Delta v = a\,\Delta t.$$ The snow adds mass at the rate $$j_m,$$ so $$\Delta m = j_m\,\Delta t.$$ The system's momentum is conserved, so $$\Delta p = 0.$$ Combine these with part (b) to solve for $$a$$ in terms of $$v,$$ $$j_m,$$ $$m,$$ and $$\Delta t.$$

__(d)__ Part (c) gives the __average__ acceleration over the time $$\Delta t.$$ What mathematical step turns it into the __instantaneous__ acceleration? Take that step and write down the train's instantaneous acceleration.

__(e)__ Check the formula against intuition: explain in words why $$j_m$$ and $$v$$ belong in the numerator and $$m$$ in the denominator.

__(f)__ Physics works in any inertial reference frame, so re-analyze the problem in the frame in which the train is (momentarily) at rest. In that frame the train, of mass $$m_t,$$ is stationary, the ground slides backward with velocity $$-v,$$ and the snowflakes fall diagonally, with horizontal velocity $$-v.$$ In a short time $$\Delta t,$$ how much horizontal momentum does the landing snow deliver to the train? Use it to find the train's acceleration in this frame, and compare with part (d).

label: MCH13
name: The Leaky Cart — A cart full of water rolls to the right at constant velocity $$v.$$ There is no friction…
desc: A cart full of water rolls to the right at constant velocity $$v.$$ There is no friction or air drag — no dissipation of mechanical energy at all. A hole opens in the bottom of the cart and water runs out. What happens to the velocity of the cart? Four students weigh in. Kiran…
statement:
A cart full of water rolls to the right at constant velocity $$v.$$ There is no friction or air drag — no dissipation of mechanical energy at all. A hole opens in the bottom of the cart and water runs out. What happens to the velocity of the cart?

Four students weigh in. Kiran says: "As water leaves, $$m$$ decreases. Since $$p = mv$$ and momentum is conserved, $$v$$ must increase."

Laura says: "That sounds intuitively wrong to me. In the extreme case that the water is much more massive than the cart, the cart would wind up going extremely fast, just because water drained out!"

Marcel says: "We should think of the cart and water together as a system, and account for the momentum of the water after it leaves the cart."

Noam says: "But after water leaves the cart, its velocity is zero and it has no momentum."

__(a)__ Analyze the situation in the __cart's reference frame__: state the horizontal velocities of the cart, the water still in the cart, the water currently falling, and the ground. Use your answers to find the mistake in Noam's claim.

__(b)__ Back in the ground frame, what does the stream of water under the cart look like as the cart rolls along? Then take Marcel's suggestion — consider the system of the cart plus __all__ the water, including water that has already left — and determine what happens to the cart's velocity.

__(c)__ Kiran's argument has four steps: (1) the momentum of the "cart plus water still aboard" system is $$p = mv;$$ (2) the mass $$m$$ is decreasing; (3) momentum is conserved for this system, i.e. $$p$$ is constant; (4) therefore $$v$$ is increasing. Exactly one step contains an error. Which one, and what is the error?

__(d)__ A second cart is identical, except the hole is on the __left side__ of the cart, near the bottom, so water squirts out horizontally to the left. What happens to this cart's velocity? Explain using momentum, and name the phenomenon.

__(e)__ A student stands on a small boat on calm water, holding a fire extinguisher:

What will happen when he pulls the trigger, shooting foam to the right?

label: MCH13
name: Bouncy Ball versus Clay — A bouncy rubber ball and a ball of clay have equal mass. Each hangs from a string…
desc: A bouncy rubber ball and a ball of clay have equal mass. Each hangs from a string as a pendulum beside a wooden block standing on a table. Each ball is pulled aside to the same height and released; it swings down and strikes the block at the bottom of its swing. The bouncy ball…
statement:
A bouncy rubber ball and a ball of clay have equal mass. Each hangs from a string as a pendulum beside a wooden block standing on a table. Each ball is pulled aside to the same height and released; it swings down and strikes the block at the bottom of its swing. The bouncy ball bounces backward off the block, while the clay hits with a thud and comes to a dead stop. Each ball sends momentum into the block, and the more momentum the block receives, the more likely it tips over.

__(a)__ Which ball has more momentum just before hitting the block? (The momentum of an object is $$p = mv.$$)

__(b)__ The clay stops completely when it hits. What fraction of its momentum does it deliver to the block?

__(c)__ The amount of momentum transferred from one system to another is called the __impulse__. Which ball delivers the larger impulse to the block, and is therefore more likely to knock it over? Explain how a ball can deliver __more__ momentum to the block than the ball ever had. To make it concrete, suppose the bouncy ball rebounds with half its incoming speed, and compare its impulse to the clay's.

label: MCH13
name: The Pile of Books — Winnie lies on her back holding a big pile of books over her stomach. Grogg slams his…
desc: Winnie lies on her back holding a big pile of books over her stomach. Grogg slams his fists down as hard as he can on the pile of books — and Winnie barely feels a thing. Some physics teachers perform an extreme version of this demonstration: a student lies on a bed of nails…
statement:
Winnie lies on her back holding a big pile of books over her stomach. Grogg slams his fists down as hard as he can on the pile of books — and Winnie barely feels a thing. Some physics teachers perform an extreme version of this demonstration: a student lies on a bed of nails with a heavy slab on their chest, and the teacher swings a sledgehammer down onto the slab. The student is fine. (If you try anything like this, use a $$50+$$ pound pile of books and fists — never the sledgehammer version, which does serious damage if it misses.)

Build a simple model. Treat Grogg's fists as disembodied objects of mass $$m$$ flying downward with speed $$v.$$ They hit the books and stop completely. The books then fly downward, hit Winnie, and stop completely. In the model, the books start slightly separated from Winnie so the two collisions can be analyzed one at a time, and gravity is ignored because the impacts are too brief for gravity to change any momentum significantly. The pile of books has $$20$$ times the mass of the fists.

__(a)__ How much momentum goes into the books when the fists hit them? How much momentum then goes into Winnie when the books hit her? And how much momentum would go into Winnie if there were no books at all and the fists hit her directly?

__(b)__ One hypothesis: the books protect Winnie by spreading the momentum over a larger __area__ — in the sledgehammer demo, the slab's area might be $$100$$ times the hammer head's, so the momentum per unit area is far lower. To test the hypothesis, Grogg repeats the slam with a pile of books half as tall: half the mass, but the same area. What does the area hypothesis predict Winnie will feel? In fact, Winnie reports feeling a noticeably bigger impact with the half-size pile. What does that tell us?

__(c)__ Starting from $$KE = \tfrac12 mv^2$$ and $$p = mv,$$ show that kinetic energy can be written as $$KE = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}.$$

__(d)__ The books leave their collision with the same momentum the fists had, but with $$20$$ times the mass. What fraction of the fists' kinetic energy do the moving books carry? Where did the rest of the kinetic energy go?

__(e)__ Complete the sentence and defend it: "The pile of books shields Winnie from the ______ of Grogg's fists." Then list at least two simplifications in our model.

label: MCH13
name: The Bullet and the Block — A rifle is fired straight up at a wooden block from below. The bullet hits the…
desc: A rifle is fired straight up at a wooden block from below. The bullet hits the block, sticks inside it, and the block — bullet embedded — flies up into the air. (The experiment was filmed by an experienced professional crew including a certified range officer. Never fire a rifle…
statement:
A rifle is fired straight up at a wooden block from below. The bullet hits the block, sticks inside it, and the block — bullet embedded — flies up into the air. (The experiment was filmed by an experienced professional crew including a certified range officer. Never fire a rifle upward yourself: the falling bullet is deadly.)

In one trial the bullet hits the exact center of the block. In a second trial everything is the same, but the block is shifted slightly so the bullet hits off-center — and this block visibly __spins__ as it rises.

__(a)__ Asked which block rises higher, physicist Henry predicted: "When you hit the block off-center, some kinetic energy is used to spin the block. By conservation of energy, there's less energy available for translation, so the off-center block goes slower and won't rise as high." Henry's argument has a flaw. The block is about $$150$$ times the bullet's mass, and the bullet buries itself in the wood. What form of energy did Henry forget, and why does forgetting it ruin the argument?

__(b)__ Use conservation of momentum instead. Compare the momentum of each "bullet + block" system just after its collision, and decide which block rises higher. (The height risen depends only on the upward speed of the system's center of mass just after the collision.)

__(c)__ Some viewers predicted the off-center block would also fly off to one side. Use a momentum argument to show that it won't.

__(d)__ This setup can be used to __measure the speed of a bullet__. Let the bullet's mass be $$m$$ and its speed just before impact $$v;$$ the block's mass is $$M,$$ the height the block rises is $$H,$$ and the gravitational acceleration is $$g.$$ The computation has two stages: (1) find the speed $$v_{\rm cm}$$ of the block just after impact; (2) relate that speed to the height risen, using energy conservation in the form $$\tfrac12 (m+M)v_{\rm cm}^2 = (m+M)gH.$$ One stage must use momentum conservation and the other energy conservation. Decide which law goes with which stage — and why you can't swap them — then find $$v$$ in terms of $$m,$$ $$M,$$ $$g,$$ and $$H.$$

__(e)__ With $$g = 9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ $$H = 1.58\;\mathrm{m},$$ $$m = 9.53\;\mathrm{g},$$ and $$M = 1.42\;\mathrm{kg},$$ how fast was the bullet going? (The first measurements of bullet speeds ever made used essentially this method — mathematician Benjamin Robins's __ballistic pendulum__, 1742, with a hanging pendulum in place of the block.)

statement:
Part A. You throw a ball at a cart.

We'll examine three possibilities:

**(a)** The ball sticks to the cart.

**(b)** The ball stops, so its velocity is zero relative to the ground after hitting the cart.

**(c)** The ball bounces elastically off the back of the cart, so its velocity changes direction during the collision with the cart.

Rank these three possibilities in order of how fast the cart moves after the collision.

Assume the ball has the same mass and is thrown with the same initial velocity in each case. The ball's velocity is horizontal at the moment it hits the cart. Assume there are no outside influences in the horizontal direction on the cart / ball system.

Use the $$=$$ sign for any ties.

Part B. You have both a very bouncy ball, which you assume to be elastic, and a completely inelastic ball. You want to do an experiment testing the ideas in part (A). (You will ignore the case where the ball stops after impacting the cart.)

The only measurement device you can find is a ruler, but you know that the ball's mass is less than the cart's mass.

You set up the cart so that, after it is hit by the ball, it rolls off the edge of a table. You measure $$d,$$ how far from the edge of the table the cart hits the floor. You also measure $$h,$$ the height of the table.

You repeat the experiment with each ball.

Assume the balls have the same (unknown) mass and the same (unknown) velocity just before impacting the cart. Also assume that the cart doesn't lose any mechanical energy while rolling or falling, and can be treated as an ideal projectile. Although the cart in the drawing is large, so we can see it, you can treat it as a point.

Recall that if the ball's mass is $$m$$ and the cart's mass is $$M,$$ then we've already found that in the case where the ball sticks to the cart, the cart's speed after the collision will be $$v_{\rm cart, stick} = v_0 \dfrac{m}{m+M}$$ where $$v_0$$ is the speed of the ball before the collision.

If the ball bounces elastically, we've found $$v_{\rm cart, bounce} = v_0 \dfrac{2m}{m+M}.$$

You know the value of $$g$$ where you did the experiment.

**Which one of the following should you be able to infer from your data?**

You don't need to find a formula for how you'd calculate these values based on your data. Here we're just answering whether or not such a formula exists.

the speed of the cart just after the collision

the speed of the ball just before the collision

the mass of the cart

the mass of the ball

the ratio of masses between the cart and ball

If we find a scale and measure the mass of the ball and the mass of the cart, those measurements could be combined with our other measurements to test the theory.

statement:
Part A. Two carts are on an air track. Collisions on an air track can be made extremely close to elastic by putting magnets in the carts and arranging the magnets to create a repulsive force. The carts will trade momentum and kinetic energy back and forth via magnetic interactions, but because they don't physically touch each other, there are very few vibrations, shocks, etc. in the molecules of the carts to dissipate kinetic energy.

Here's an example in which the masses of the two carts are nearly the same:

Physics Demos, "Collisions: Two Carts" https://youtu.be/jRliH0jVilM

Suppose that in some other example, the collision can be modeled as elastic, but the masses of the carts are not necessarily the same.

Cart A is initially moving to the right with velocity $$v_0 > 0.$$ Cart B is stationary. The carts collide at the center of an air track.

After the collision, carts A and B have the same speed, but move in opposite directions.

Find the speed $$|v|$$ of the carts after the collision.

Part C. The carts in part (B) travel to opposite ends of the air track. Because they are going the same speed, they reach the opposite ends simultaneously. There, they undergo elastic collisions and rebound. They meet again in the center of the air track and collide again. What happens just after the collision?

**(a)** The carts bounce off each other, again changing directions, so they both travel at speed $$|v|$$ and in opposite directions.

**(b)** Cart A stops completely and cart B moves to the right. Its velocity is $$v_0.$$

**(c)** Cart B stops completely and cart A moves to the left. Its velocity is $$-v_0.$$

**(d)** Both carts move to the right, but at different speeds.
