name: Part A. There is a famous physics toy called __Newton's cradle__. It was invented by…
desc: Part A. There is a famous physics toy called __Newton's cradle__. It was invented by Isaac Newton's contemporary, French physicist Edme Mariotte. The toy consists of a series of five balls suspended from wires: Amazon.com (The toy is sold with different numbers of balls, but we…
statement:
Part A. There is a famous physics toy called __Newton's cradle__. It was invented by Isaac Newton's contemporary, French physicist Edme Mariotte.

The toy consists of a series of five balls suspended from wires:

Amazon.com

(The toy is sold with different numbers of balls, but we will assume there are five in this question.)

If you pull back one ball on the left and let it go, it will swing down, hit the remaining four balls, and stop. The three middle balls will not move. One ball will bounce up from the right hand side. When that ball comes back, the process will reverse. The rightmost ball will hit the four stationary balls and stop, and the leftmost ball (the one that was dropped originally) will bounce up into the air:

xmphysics, "Newton's Pendulum (Gangnam Style)" https://youtu.be/YB7KUGdP7wI

Our description is not perfect; the three middle balls do not remain completely stationary, for example. However, for this question, we'll idealize the behavior to say that they stay completely stationary and only the leftmost and rightmost balls move.

If you pull back two balls and release them, they'll again stop when they hit the remaining balls, and two balls will come out on the right. The middle ball remains (nearly) stationary:

The same works for more balls, e.g. here are three and four balls pulled back:

One can create more complicated patterns of bounces by pulling multiple balls back different distances before releasing them:

For this question, we'll focus on the case of pulling back one ball and releasing it to collide with four stationary balls. The result, as shown at the top of the question, is that the ball stops and one ball comes out the other side of the cradle with the same velocity as the incoming ball.

Some sources explain this observation by invoking momentum and kinetic energy. They say that if the collisions are modeled as elastic, then combining momentum and energy conservation, the only possibility is for the incoming ball to stop, and for one ball to come out on the other side.

We will examine whether this explanation of Newton's cradle is accurate and complete.

Suppose one ball approaches at speed $$v$$ from the left and that, as a hypothesis, that ball will stop, and two balls will pop out together from the right hand side at speed $$v_r.$$

What does $$v_r$$ need to be according to momentum conservation? What does it need to be according to kinetic energy conservation?

Give your answers as decimals to two decimal places.

mathjax: \begin{align*} \text{ according to momentum conservation,} \,\, v_r & = \blank v\\ \text{ according to kinetic energy conservation,}\,\, v_r & = \blank v \end{align*}

allowed: 1.023456789

Part B. In part (A), you should have found different answers for momentum and kinetic energy conservation.

Consider a few different claims about the meaning of this calculation.

**(a)** Aaron says: If someone throws the ball, they're putting energy into it, so the calculation based on kinetic energy conservation will give good predictions of experiments in that case. However, if the ball is simply moving before coming into the collision, it has momentum because of its mass and velocity, so the calculation based on momentum conservation will give accurate predictions.

**(b)** Bryn says: Momentum is conserved in collisions, but kinetic energy can be converted into thermal energy. The momentum-based calculation is the correct one to use, assuming that one ball stops and two come out. However, I'm not sure whether we can get Newton's cradle to actually do that.

**(c)** Chris says: The calculation shows that it's impossible to conserve both momentum and kinetic energy in this scenario. A good model for Newton's cradle is that both are conserved. If we do the experiment, we will not be able to get the incoming ball to stop and two balls to come out together on the right hand side.

**(d)** Deven says: I agree with Chris. This is a proof that, assuming momentum and energy conservation, when one ball comes in, it stops, and one ball comes out the other side. That's what we have already observed anyway!

**Which claims are correct?**

Select two. The claims do not have to be complete explanations to be correct. They only need to avoid saying things that are incorrect.

To judge whether claims are correct, you can continue assuming that gravity and influences from the strings are negligible during the collisions.

Elastic collisions are a good model for Newton's cradle, but don't count a claim as incorrect just because it speculates about using inelastic collisions as a model.

Bryn's

Chris's

Deven's

Part C. A different possibility for what could happen in Newton's cradle is that when one ball comes in from the left with velocity $$v,$$ it bounces back at velocity $$v_1,$$ while the remaining four balls move to the right together with velocity $$v_4.$$

Assuming momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved in the collision, what are $$v_1$$ and $$v_4$$ in terms of $$v?$$

Give your answers as decimals to two decimal places.

If it is not possible to conserve both momentum and kinetic energy in this type of collision, enter 0 for each.

mathjax: \begin{align*} v_1 & = \blank v \\ v_4 & = \blank v \end{align*}

allowed: -1.023456789

Part D. You have just done the calculation in part (C). There, we used momentum and energy conservation to calculate what happens when one ball approaches four stationary balls, but the result was different from experiment. Experiment shows that (to a good approximation), the incoming ball stops and one ball leaves from the right hand side.

Which of the following are accurate interpretations of the calculation and the experimental result?

Select all the correct interpretations.

**(a)** Because the calculation and experiment don't agree, and the calculation was based on momentum and energy conservation, either momentum is not conserved in the collisions or energy is not conserved in them.

**(b)** While elastic collisions that conserve momentum are a good model for Newton's cradle, they are not enough to determine what will happen. We would need to make additional modeling assumptions to match Newton's cradle experiments to theory.

**(c)** In part (C), we made strong assumptions about how the balls move, then calculated two velocities. If we allow all the balls to have any velocity before and after the collision, the real experimental result will be one possible solution to the momentum and energy conservation equations, but there will be many others.

**(d)** Because there are different ways to conserve both momentum and energy, Newton's cradle cannot be accurately modeled. It is one of the phenomena in science that can only be understood based on experimental evidence, not theory.

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

desc: For a simple home collision demonstration, stack a tennis ball on top a basketball and drop them. The tennis ball can bounce much higher than it was dropped from: In collaboration with your classmates, try to figure out how this demonstration works. Some questions you could…
statement:
For a simple home collision demonstration, stack a tennis ball on top a basketball and drop them. The tennis ball can bounce much higher than it was dropped from:

In collaboration with your classmates, try to figure out how this demonstration works. Some questions you could answer include:

**Experimental**

- How high does your tennis ball bounce, as a function of the height you drop it from, when stacked on the basketball? - How high do your basketball and tennis ball bounce on their own? - What techniques help you maximize the height that the tennis ball bounces to? - What balls besides a basketball and tennis ball work well? - Can you get a stack of three or more balls to bounce like this? - How are you making your measurements?

**Theoretical**

- What is the maximum height that the tennis ball can bounce to, assuming the basketball is much more massive than the tennis ball, and that there is a small gap between the basketball and the tennis ball, allowing you to analyze each collision independently? - Can you modify the previous calculation to account for the finite mass of the tennis ball? - Can you modify it for more than two balls? - What are some limitations of this calculation?

Don't be constrained to these questions. Feel free to come up with your own to discuss with classmates.

label: MCH14
name: DART: Crashing a Spacecraft into an Asteroid — On September 26, 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft…
desc: On September 26, 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid. The mission was called __DART__ — the Double Asteroid Redirection Test — and its goal was to change the asteroid's orbit, a technology that will be useful if we ever detect a large asteroid on a…
statement:
On September 26, 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid. The mission was called __DART__ — the Double Asteroid Redirection Test — and its goal was to change the asteroid's orbit, a technology that will be useful if we ever detect a large asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The spacecraft was $$2.6\;\mathrm{m}$$ tall and had a mass of $$610\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Its target, Dimorphos, is about $$160\;\mathrm{m}$$ across with a mass of about $$5\times10^{9}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ In Dimorphos's own reference frame, the spacecraft was moving at about $$6.3\times10^{3}\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ when it hit.

__(a)__ Find the ratio of the spacecraft's mass to the asteroid's mass. An elephant has a mass close to $$5000\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Hitting Dimorphos with the spacecraft is like hitting an elephant with what — another elephant, a stuffed elephant toy, a raisin, or a speck of dust?

__(b)__ Model the impact as __perfectly inelastic__: the spacecraft buries itself in the asteroid and they move together afterward. Dimorphos starts at rest in its own frame, so momentum conservation says $$m_{\rm spacecraft}\,v_{\rm spacecraft}=\left(m_{\rm Dimorphos}+m_{\rm spacecraft}\right)\Delta v_{\rm Dimorphos}.$$ Explain why the $$m_{\rm spacecraft}$$ on the right-hand side can be ignored, and compute the change $$\Delta v_{\rm Dimorphos}$$ in the asteroid's velocity.

__(c)__ Suppose we wanted to redirect an asteroid like Dimorphos away from a collision course with Earth. For a rough estimate of how far in advance the deflection must happen, divide the radius of the Earth, about $$6.4\times10^{6}\;\mathrm{m},$$ by your $$\Delta v$$ from part (b) — that is roughly how long the tiny velocity change needs to act in order to shift the asteroid's path by an Earth radius. Convert your answer to years using the rule of thumb that a year is about $$\pi\times10^{7}\;\mathrm{s}.$$

__(d)__ Telescope measurements after the impact showed that Dimorphos's actual $$\Delta v$$ was about $$3.6$$ times larger than the answer to part (b). One proposed explanation: maybe the spacecraft bounced off instead of sticking. An __elastic__ bounce — one that conserves kinetic energy — is the best-case scenario for transferring momentum in a bounce. By comparing how much the spacecraft's own velocity changes when it sticks (from $$v$$ to nearly $$0$$) versus when it bounces elastically (from $$v$$ to nearly $$-v$$), decide whether bouncing can explain the factor of $$3.6.$$

__(e)__ The real explanation: the impact was violent and threw about a million kilograms of rock, called __ejecta__, out into space. The animation below, based on data from the Atlas telescope, shows the ejecta spraying away (the spacecraft itself, too small to see, came in from the left moving right). In which direction must the ejecta be thrown to boost Dimorphos's $$\Delta v$$ the most — the same direction as the spacecraft's velocity, the opposite direction, or perpendicular to it? Explain using momentum conservation. (Scientists call the resulting boost factor the __momentum enhancement__; measuring it was one of DART's biggest goals.)

__(f)__ Months after the impact, the ejecta were still visible from telescopes, forming a long tail like a comet's. The tail does not point "out the back" of the asteroid along its path — it points directly away from the Sun. Given that light carries momentum and can transfer it to objects it strikes (__radiation pressure__), and that only the smallest bits of ejecta form the tail, explain why.

label: MCH14
name: Is a Golf Shot an Isolated Collision? — Momentum conservation only makes useful predictions for systems that…
desc: Momentum conservation only makes useful predictions for systems that are __isolated__ from outside influences — and a golf club striking a golf ball is not truly isolated. Gravity pulls on both club and ball, the ball touches the tee, and a golfer is gripping and swinging the…
statement:
Momentum conservation only makes useful predictions for systems that are __isolated__ from outside influences — and a golf club striking a golf ball is not truly isolated. Gravity pulls on both club and ball, the ball touches the tee, and a golfer is gripping and swinging the club. Nevertheless, physicists routinely model the impact as a momentum-conserving collision. This problem shows why that's justified, using estimates. Take the club head's speed to be about $$40\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and note that the ball's speed changes by around $$70\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ during the impact. The ball is about $$4\;\mathrm{cm}$$ across, and high-speed video (below) shows the club moves only about $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ forward between first touching the ball and the ball flying off.

__(a)__ Estimate how long the club is in contact with the ball.

__(b)__ To show that gravity is negligible during the collision, calculate how much gravity changes the velocity of a free-falling object during the contact time from part (a). (Free fall changes an object's velocity by $$g\approx10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ each second.) Compare your answer to the ball's $$70\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ change in speed.

__(c)__ During the impact the ball compresses, storing elastic potential energy that turns back into kinetic energy as the ball springs away. We can model the collision as a rigid ball with a spring attached, struck by a rigid club. If the golfer swings the club __faster__, does the contact time from part (a) increase, decrease, or stay the same? (Useful fact: the period of a harmonic oscillator does not depend on the amplitude of its oscillation.)

__(d)__ After the impact, the club keeps moving forward quickly, so it still has kinetic energy. It would seem more "efficient" for the club to stop dead and send __all__ of its kinetic energy into the ball. For a rigid, non-rotating object, momentum and kinetic energy are related by $$p=\sqrt{2m\cdot KE}.$$ The ball is much less massive than the club head. Explain why no one can design a club that stops dead at impact.

label: MCH14
name: Elastic or Inelastic: How Much Does the Golf Club Slow Down? — An __elastic__ collision is one that conserves…
desc: An __elastic__ collision is one that conserves kinetic energy — a perfectly bouncy collision. A __perfectly inelastic__ collision is one where the objects stick together and move off as one; it dissipates the maximum possible kinetic energy. (Momentum is conserved in both.) No…
statement:
An __elastic__ collision is one that conserves kinetic energy — a perfectly bouncy collision. A __perfectly inelastic__ collision is one where the objects stick together and move off as one; it dissipates the maximum possible kinetic energy. (Momentum is conserved in both.) No real collision is perfectly elastic, but a golf ball bounces well and leaves the club much faster than the club is moving, so an elastic collision is a reasonable model for a golf shot.

A golf club head of mass $$4m$$ moving at speed $$v$$ strikes a stationary golf ball of mass $$m.$$

__(a)__ Warm-up: suppose instead the collision were perfectly inelastic, with club and ball moving together at speed $$v_f$$ afterward. Find $$v_f$$ and the amount by which the club slows down, in terms of $$v.$$

__(b)__ Now take the collision to be elastic, with the club moving at $$v_c$$ and the ball at $$v_b$$ afterward. Write the momentum-conservation equation and the kinetic-energy-conservation equation. Explain how you know these two equations are enough to determine both unknowns.

__(c)__ There is a shortcut that avoids the quadratic energy equation. In any elastic collision, the distance between the two objects grows after the collision at the same rate it shrank before the collision; here that means $$v_b-v_c=v.$$ Justify this rule by analyzing the collision in the __center of mass frame__ — the reference frame in which the system's center of mass is at rest, so the total momentum is zero. What must each object do in that frame for both momentum and kinetic energy to be conserved?

__(d)__ Combine the rule $$v_b-v_c=v$$ with momentum conservation to find $$v_c$$ and $$v_b.$$ How does the club's slowdown compare with the perfectly inelastic case from part (a)?

__(e)__ If the ball travels a horizontal distance $$d$$ before landing in the perfectly inelastic case, how far does it travel in the elastic case? Ignore air resistance, assume the ball lands at the height it was hit from, and recall that a projectile's flight time is proportional to its launch speed (at a fixed launch angle). Ignoring air resistance is only a good model for short shots on Earth — but it's perfect on the Moon, where Apollo 14 commander Alan Shepard hit a golf ball in 1971:

__(f)__ A golfer wants a longer shot. They can either increase the mass of their club by $$10\%$$ while keeping its speed fixed, or keep the same club and swing it $$10\%$$ faster. For an elastic collision, the ball's speed is $$v_b=v\,\dfrac{2\mu}{1+\mu},$$ where $$\mu=\dfrac{m_c}{m_b}$$ is the ratio of club mass to ball mass (here $$\mu=4$$). By what percentage does each option increase the ball's speed? The plot below shows the factor $$\dfrac{2\mu}{1+\mu}$$ — use it to explain why making the club heavier stops paying off.

The total momentum of any system can be written $$\vec{p}_{\rm total}=M\vec{v}_{\rm cm},$$ where $$M$$ is the system's total mass and $$\vec{v}_{\rm cm}$$ is the velocity of its center of mass. Here is a ceiling fan, spinning steadily:

The wobbling fan is __unbalanced__: its center of mass is not exactly on its rotation axis. Model it as a uniform rotating disk with a small extra mass attached near one edge, as below. Where is the center of mass of disk-plus-extra-mass? If the disk spins about its own center, what path does the center of mass follow?

__(c)__ A free object — like a spinning projectile in the air — rotates about its own center of mass, which moves smoothly. Use parts (a) and (b) to explain why an unbalanced fan wobbles.

name: Collision at an Intersection — A car with a mass of $$1000\;\mathrm{kg}$$ is heading north at…
desc: A car with a mass of $$1000\;\mathrm{kg}$$ is heading north at $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ It runs a red light and collides __perfectly inelastically__ with a truck of mass $$2000\;\mathrm{kg}$$ heading east at $$16\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ — the two vehicles lock together and slide off as…
statement:
A car with a mass of $$1000\;\mathrm{kg}$$ is heading north at $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ It runs a red light and collides __perfectly inelastically__ with a truck of mass $$2000\;\mathrm{kg}$$ heading east at $$16\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ — the two vehicles lock together and slide off as one. In two dimensions, momentum is a vector, and momentum conservation reads $$\vec{p}_c+\vec{p}_t=\vec{p}_f,$$ where the subscripts $$c$$ and $$t$$ label the car and truck before the collision and $$f$$ labels the wreck just afterward. Each component of momentum is conserved separately.

__(a)__ What outside influence makes momentum conservation questionable for car crashes? Why is it nevertheless a reasonable model, especially for high-speed collisions?

__(b)__ Take east as the $$\hat{x}$$ direction and north as the $$\hat{y}$$ direction, and let $$v_{fx}$$ and $$v_{fy}$$ be the components of the wreck's velocity just after the collision. Write momentum conservation separately for the $$x$$ and $$y$$ directions, and solve for $$v_{fx}$$ and $$v_{fy}.$$

__(c)__ Find the angle $$\theta$$ north of east in which the wreck travels, using $$\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_{fy}}{v_{fx}}.$$ The momentum-addition picture below shows the same relationship: the final momentum is the vector sum of the car's and truck's momenta.

__(d)__ Find the wreck's speed just after the collision.

label: MCH14
name: A Lonely Electron Never Absorbs a Photon — In the __photoelectric effect__, an electron absorbs a "photon" —…
desc: In the __photoelectric effect__, an electron absorbs a "photon" — a small particle of light. Modeling this effect helped win Einstein his Nobel Prize, and it powers several modern technologies. Photons have no mass, but a photon with energy $$E$$ carries momentum…
statement:
In the __photoelectric effect__, an electron absorbs a "photon" — a small particle of light. Modeling this effect helped win Einstein his Nobel Prize, and it powers several modern technologies. Photons have no mass, but a photon with energy $$E$$ carries momentum $$p=\dfrac{E}{c},$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light. An electron has mass $$m_e,$$ and a slowly-moving (non-relativistic) particle's kinetic energy is related to its momentum by $$KE=\dfrac{p^2}{2m_e}.$$ Curiously, although electrons inside atoms absorb photons all the time, a __lone__ electron — one with nothing else around — never absorbs a photon. This problem explains why, using only conservation of momentum and energy.

__(a)__ Suppose a lone, stationary electron absorbed a photon of momentum $$p$$ coming in from the left. After the absorption, only the electron remains. With nothing else around, there is nowhere for energy to become thermal energy, so the collision would have to conserve kinetic energy as well as momentum. Use momentum conservation to find the electron's momentum afterward, set the electron's kinetic energy equal to the photon's energy $$E=pc,$$ and solve for $$p.$$ Then compute the electron's speed $$v=\dfrac{p}{m_e}$$ and explain what's impossible about the result.

__(b)__ Part (a) leaned on the formula $$KE=\dfrac{p^2}{2m_e},$$ which the theory of relativity modifies at high speeds, so here is an argument that avoids formulas. Analyze the absorption in the __center of mass frame__ — the frame where the total momentum is zero: the photon moves right with momentum $$p'$$ and the electron moves left with momentum $$-p'.$$ After the photon is absorbed, what must the electron be doing in this frame, by momentum conservation? What has happened to the energy?

__(c)__ Electrons that are part of an atom __can__ absorb photons. What changes?

__(d)__ The __positron__ is the antimatter partner of the electron: same mass, opposite charge. When an electron and a positron collide, they can annihilate, converting into photons. By analyzing the collision in the center of mass frame — where the electron and positron approach each other with equal speeds and the total momentum is zero — explain why they can never annihilate into a __single__ photon, but can annihilate into __two__ photons. If a moving electron annihilates with a __stationary__ positron, do the two photons fly off in exactly opposite directions?

Part A. Here's a small steel ball bouncing off a hard surface:

Steve Mould, "Weird metal that's also glass is insanely bouncy", https://youtu.be/QpuCtzdvix4

Because the ball is small and light, and because both surfaces are hard, there is very little deformation of either the ball or surface during the bounce.

The ball always feels a gravitational force $$\vec{F}_{g; E \to B} = m \vec{g} = -mg \, \hat{y}$$ downward.

If the ball were to sit on the surface, it would feel a force $$mg\, \hat{y}$$ upward. This force would cancel the downward force from gravity so that the ball would not accelerate. This force is called the The word "normal" here means "perpendicular to". The force is perpendicular to the plane of the surface the ball is bouncing off. We write the normal force as $$\vec{F}_{N, S \to B}.$$ The $${}_N$$ indicates that it's a normal force. The $${}_{S \to B}$$ means it's a force from the surface to the ball.

Thus, if the ball sits on the surface without moving, we have

$$\begin{aligned} \vec{F}_{N; S \to B} & = - \vec{F}_{g; E \to B} \\ {} & = mg \, \hat{y} \end{aligned}$$

However, we only know this equation to model the ball sitting stationary on the surface.

When bouncing, the ball is accelerating because it changes from moving downward before the bounce to moving upward after the bounce. It makes this change over a short time.

The force that accelerates the ball during a bounce is the normal force from the surface.

How large is the magnitude $$F_{N; S \to B}$$ of the normal force during a bounce?

$$F_{N; S \to B} = 0$$

$$F_{N; S \to B} = mg$$

$$mg < F_{N; S \to B} \le 2 mg$$

$$2mg < F_{N; S \to B} \le 10 mg$$

$$10mg < F_{N; S \to B}$$

Once the anemometer is rotating, the forces on the cups may change because the speed of wind, relative to the cup, changes due to the cup's motion.

Let's suppose that the air is still and the anemometer is stationary. Then a steady wind picks up, blowing from left to right at speed $$v_w,$$ and hits the anemometer. The anemometer begins rotating.

The anemometer rotates faster and faster until the cups move at some speed $$v_c$$ relative to ground. At this point, the anemometer rotates at a steady angular speed until the wind changes or dies away.

Let's suppose that the speed $$v_c$$ is such that the forwardmost cup and rearmost cup experience forces from the wind of the same magnitude.

Under this assumption, what is $$v_c$$ as a fraction of $$v_w?$$

Give your answer as a decimal to two decimal places.

This device has some similarity to the cup anemometer, but it is used to measure the intensity of light, not wind.

We will assume that the Crookes radiometer is under a partial vacuum, but there is still some air in the radiometer.

The radiometer consists of four vanes. Each vane is black on one side and white or reflective on the other. The black side absorbs most light that hits it. The white side reflects most light that hits it.

When light shines on the radiometer, it begins to spin.

Andrejdam, Wikimedia Commons

As can be seen in the above gif, the white side of the vane moves toward the light source and the black side moves away from the light source.

Some people believed that the Crookes radiometer was driven by radiation pressure, a phenomenon we studied with the IKAROS solar sail. Radiation pressure is a force from light hitting an object.

Which of the following are accurate descriptions of the Crookes radiometer? Choose one.

The radiometer behaves as we would expect if driven by radiation pressure.

The radiometer rotates in the opposite direction we would expect based on radiation pressure.

Radiation pressure should not put any force on the radiometer because it rotates about its axis, so its center of mass doesn't move.

If we shone light from the other side, the radiometer would change its direction of rotation.

name: Consider an Atwood machine in which each mass is attached to a spring.
desc: Consider an Atwood machine in which each mass is attached to a spring. We will assume that $$m_B > m_A.$$ The springs are identical. The more force a spring has to exert on a box it's attached to, the more it will have to stretch to do it. __Hooke's law__ states that $$\Delta…
statement:
Consider an Atwood machine in which each mass is attached to a spring.

We will assume that $$m_B > m_A.$$

The springs are identical. The more force a spring has to exert on a box it's attached to, the more it will have to stretch to do it. __Hooke's law__ states that $$\Delta \ell,$$ the amount that the spring has been stretched, is proportional to the force the spring exerts.

The springs are significantly damped, so that the masses will quickly stop oscillating after the masses are released.

Model the rope, springs, and pulley as massless, and ignore any friction or air drag in the pulley or on the boxes.

Once the springs stop oscillating, but while the Atwood machine is still accelerating, which spring will be longer?

Explain your reasoning.

By analyzing the potential and kinetic energy, we have previously found that the acceleration of an Atwood machine has magnitude $$a = \dfrac{(m_B - m_A)g}{m_B + m_A}$$

You can use this fact without proving it in your response.

Each box experiences a force from gravity and a force from the spring. You will have to account for both these forces. Newton's second law for the system of one box applies to the vector sum of the two forces on that box. I.E. $$\vec{F}_{g; E \to A} + \vec{F}_{s\to A} = m_A \vec{a}_A,$$ and likewise for box $$B.$$ Here $$\vec{F}_{s\to A}$$ is the force from the spring on box $$A.$$

label: MCH15
name: Why Eggs Break: Defining Force — You throw an egg as hard as you can at a brick wall. Predictably, it…
desc: You throw an egg as hard as you can at a brick wall. Predictably, it smashes. But in a classic demonstration, an egg thrown just as hard at a hanging bedsheet survives: the sheet billows backward, catches the egg gently, and the egg doesn't break. (If the sheet were nailed flat…
statement:
You throw an egg as hard as you can at a brick wall. Predictably, it smashes. But in a classic demonstration, an egg thrown just as hard at a hanging bedsheet survives: the sheet billows backward, catches the egg gently, and the egg doesn't break. (If the sheet were nailed flat against a wall, the egg would break again — the cloth would still be soft, but it couldn't move out of the way, so the egg would stop suddenly.)

__(a)__ In both throws the egg has the same mass $$m,$$ arrives at the same speed $$v,$$ and ends up at rest. Compare the egg's change in __momentum__, change in __kinetic energy__, and change in __velocity__ for the wall throw versus the sheet throw. Do any of these quantities explain why one egg breaks and the other doesn't?

__(b)__ Physicists capture the difference with a new quantity, the __force__, defined as the rate of change of momentum: $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t}.$$ The momentum change $$\Delta \vec{p}$$ itself is called the __impulse__. In terms of this definition, why is the force on the egg smaller when it's thrown against the sheet?

__(c)__ The impulse can also be written $$\Delta \vec{p} = m\,\Delta \vec{v}.$$ Substitute this into the definition of force. What familiar physical quantity appears, and what is the resulting famous equation called?

__(d)__ When we compute $$\vec{a} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$$ over some time interval, do we get the instantaneous acceleration or an average? How would you modify the definition $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t}$$ so that it defines the force at a single instant?

__(e)__ Armando, a professional baseball pitcher, hurls his egg at the sheet at $$100\;\mathrm{mph}.$$ Benigno, a gentle soul, gives his a soft $$10\;\mathrm{mph}$$ toss. Who exerts the greater force on his egg __while throwing it__? Once the eggs are in the air, traveling toward the sheet, whose egg most likely has the greater force on it, and what force is that? (Consider air resistance.)

__(f)__ Now ignore air resistance. While the eggs are in the air, the only force on each is gravity, $$\vec{F}_g = m\vec{g}.$$ If Benigno's egg happens to be a little heavier than Armando's, whose egg has the larger force on it in flight? What does this tell you about the relationship between force and motion?

label: MCH15
name: Snowballs, Walls, and Stings — In the Japanese sport of __yukigassen__ ("snow battle"), teams pelt each other…
desc: In the Japanese sport of __yukigassen__ ("snow battle"), teams pelt each other with snowballs. A player throws a snowball, which flies across the court and hits an opposing player — the "target." The snowball's momentum changes by roughly the same amount at each end of the trip…
statement:
In the Japanese sport of __yukigassen__ ("snow battle"), teams pelt each other with snowballs. A player throws a snowball, which flies across the court and hits an opposing player — the "target." The snowball's momentum changes by roughly the same amount at each end of the trip: the thrower takes it from rest to velocity $$\vec{v},$$ and the target takes it from approximately $$\vec{v}$$ back to rest. Recall that force is the rate of change of momentum, $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t}.$$

__(a)__ The thrower's arm sweeps through about a meter while accelerating the snowball, while the target's body hardly moves as the snowball stops against it. Who takes a longer time to change the snowball's momentum? Who therefore exerts the greater force on the snowball — and who is more likely to feel a sting?

__(b)__ Baseball players throw with a bare hand but catch with a padded glove. Explain why this makes sense, using $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t}.$$

__(c)__ Now you throw a tennis ball with velocity $$\vec{v}$$ against a brick wall, and it bounces back. The __coefficient of restitution__ $$c$$ measures the quality of the bounce: the ball leaves the wall with velocity $$-c\vec{v}.$$ For a tennis ball on brick, $$c$$ is around $$0.5$$ to $$0.6.$$ Which causes the larger momentum change in the ball — your hand during the throw, or the wall during the bounce — and by roughly what factor? Combining this with the contact times, which one exerts the larger force on the ball?

__(d)__ While the tennis ball is in contact with the wall, is the ball exerting a force on the wall, is the wall exerting a force on the ball, both, or neither? A brick wall seems perfectly rigid — by what mechanism does it manage to push on the ball?

__(e)__ Getting hit by a snowball hurts less than getting hit by a rubber ball of the same mass and speed, even if the rubber ball doesn't bounce. Give two reasons, both based on $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t}.$$ (Hint: a snowball explodes on impact, and its back keeps moving forward about a snowball-diameter after its front has stopped.)

__(f)__ When one billiard ball strikes another, the balls are so hard that they compress only an invisibly small amount, and the struck ball seems to leap away almost instantaneously. Is the momentum transferred in a short time or a long time? What does that imply about the size of the forces between the balls?

label: MCH15
name: A Finger, Two Boxes, and a Balloon — A balloon $$B$$ is sandwiched between a heavy box $$H$$ and a light box…
desc: A balloon $$B$$ is sandwiched between a heavy box $$H$$ and a light box $$L,$$ with a loose band holding the stack together. You press your finger $$f$$ against the outside of box $$H$$ and push the whole system to the right across a table. Ignore friction. (We'll push gently…
statement:
A balloon $$B$$ is sandwiched between a heavy box $$H$$ and a light box $$L,$$ with a loose band holding the stack together. You press your finger $$f$$ against the outside of box $$H$$ and push the whole system to the right across a table. Ignore friction. (We'll push gently enough that the balloon doesn't pop.)

__(a)__ What happens to the center of mass of the system of two boxes plus balloon? Using Newton's second law $$\vec{F} = m\vec{a},$$ write the system's acceleration in terms of your push $$\vec{F}$$ and the masses $$m_H,$$ $$m_B,$$ and $$m_L.$$ (Careful: which mass belongs in the formula?) Besides accelerating, what visibly happens to the balloon?

__(b)__ We label forces by the interaction and the objects involved: $$\vec{F}_{c;\,f \to H}$$ is the force from the finger $$f$$ on box $$H.$$ The subscript $$c$$ marks it as a __contact force__ — a force that occurs where two objects touch. (Most forces we'll meet are contact forces; the main exception is gravity, which acts between objects that aren't touching.) In this notation, what is the symbol for the force from box $$H$$ on the balloon? Why would it be wrong to say that box $$H$$ "transmits" your finger's force to the balloon?

__(c)__ When you push on box $$H,$$ momentum flows from your finger into the box. Use conservation of momentum to explain why there must also be a force $$\vec{F}_{c;\,H \to f}$$ from the box back on your finger, and write an equation relating it to $$\vec{F}_{c;\,f \to H}.$$ This relationship is called __Newton's third law__.

__(d)__ The magnitude $$F_{c;\,f \to H}$$ is the rate that rightward momentum flows __into__ box $$H,$$ and $$F_{c;\,H \to B}$$ is the rate that rightward momentum flows __out__ of box $$H$$ into the balloon. Given that box $$H$$ is accelerating to the right, is more rightward momentum flowing in or out? Which of these two forces is larger in magnitude?

__(e)__ Rank the six magnitudes $$F_{c;\,f \to H},$$ $$F_{c;\,H \to B},$$ $$F_{c;\,B \to L},$$ $$F_{c;\,L \to B},$$ $$F_{c;\,B \to H},$$ and $$F_{c;\,H \to f}$$ from largest to smallest, using equals signs for any ties. Explain where the equalities come from.

__(f)__ The forces $$F_{c;\,H \to B}$$ and $$F_{c;\,B \to L}$$ are not exactly equal, but they are very nearly so. What feature of the balloon makes them so close?

name: Which Balloon Gets Squished? — Two boxes slide on a table with a balloon sandwiched between them: $$H$$ is…
desc: Two boxes slide on a table with a balloon sandwiched between them: $$H$$ is heavy and $$L$$ is light. A rope tied to the rear box (the one farther from the pulley) runs over a pulley at the table's edge to a hanging weight, which drags the whole train along. In version A, the…
statement:
Two boxes slide on a table with a balloon sandwiched between them: $$H$$ is heavy and $$L$$ is light. A rope tied to the rear box (the one farther from the pulley) runs over a pulley at the table's edge to a hanging weight, which drags the whole train along. In version A, the light box $$L$$ is in front (nearest the pulley); in version B, the heavy box $$H$$ is in front. The balloons differ only in color — they are physically identical — and everything else is the same between the two setups. Ignore friction.

A balloon compresses when squeezed, and the more force on it, the more it compresses. The main question: __in which version is the balloon compressed more?__ Work up to it through the parts below.

__(a)__ In which version is the acceleration of the boxes-and-balloon train larger?

__(b)__ A student asks, "In which version is there more force?" Why is this question, as posed, too vague to answer?

__(c)__ In which version is the force from the balloon on the __front__ box larger? Explain what job that force is doing.

__(d)__ Now answer the main question: in which version is the balloon compressed more?

__(e)__ A balloon makes force visible: more compression means more force. Engineers refine this idea into steel "proving rings" — stiff rings with a precision micrometer inside that measures how much the ring compresses when forces push on its bosses (the nubs at each end). Proving rings can measure forces with relative uncertainty down to about $$0.01\;\%.$$ What single idea do the balloon and the proving ring share?

name: Forces on a Firehose — Firefighters brace themselves and often handle firehoses as a team, because moving…
desc: Firefighters brace themselves and often handle firehoses as a team, because moving water can put large forces on a hose. Recall that force is the rate of change of momentum, $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t},$$ and that by Newton's third law, whenever the hose puts a…
statement:
Firefighters brace themselves and often handle firehoses as a team, because moving water can put large forces on a hose. Recall that force is the rate of change of momentum, $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t},$$ and that by Newton's third law, whenever the hose puts a force on the water, the water puts an equal and opposite force on the hose.

__(a)__ Consider four situations: (i) the hose is off; (ii) the hose is first being turned on; (iii) water flows at a steady rate through a straight section of hose; (iv) water flows at a steady rate around a bend in the hose. In which situations does the water exert a significant force on the hose? Explain, paying attention to the difference between __having__ momentum and __changing__ momentum.

__(b)__ In one section, the water flows due north, rounds a bend, and then flows due east at the same speed, as shown below. Toward which compass direction does the water push the hose at the bend? (Track which components of momentum the water gains and loses, and use conservation of momentum.)

__(c)__ Near the open end of a hose, the nozzle narrows, so the water speeds up — gaining momentum along the direction the tip points — just before it leaves. Suppose the tip points to the right, as below. Which way does the water push the tip? Use your answer to explain why a strongly flowing, unattended hose can whip violently back and forth instead of settling down.

label: MCH15
name: A Firehose Jetpack — A water jetpack lifts a rider on a plume of water pumped up a hose from a lake below…
desc: A water jetpack lifts a rider on a plume of water pumped up a hose from a lake below. The water arrives at the pack on the rider's back moving __upward__, and the pack redirects it to shoot straight back __down__. Could an ordinary fire hose power a jetpack? According to an…
statement:
A water jetpack lifts a rider on a plume of water pumped up a hose from a lake below. The water arrives at the pack on the rider's back moving __upward__, and the pack redirects it to shoot straight back __down__.

Could an ordinary fire hose power a jetpack? According to an internet search, a typical fire hose has diameter $$D = 2.5\;\mathrm{in}$$ and delivers $$f = 300$$ gallons of water per minute. Converted to SI units, $$D = 0.0635\;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$f = 0.019\;\mathrm{m^3/s}.$$ The density of water is $$d = 1000\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ You'll need the definition of force, $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t},$$ and Newton's third law, $$\vec{F}_{A \to B} = -\vec{F}_{B \to A}.$$

__(a)__ Explain qualitatively, in terms of momentum, why redirecting the water produces an upward force on the jetpack.

__(b)__ First find the speed $$v$$ of the water. In a time $$\Delta t,$$ the water leaving the hose forms a cylinder with cross-sectional area $$A = \dfrac{\pi D^2}{4}$$ and length $$\ell = v\,\Delta t$$ (see figure), so its volume is $$V = A\ell.$$ The same volume can also be written using the flow rate: $$V = f\,\Delta t.$$ Solve for $$v$$ in terms of $$f$$ and $$D,$$ and evaluate it. (Sanity check: if $$D$$ decreased with $$f$$ fixed, should $$v$$ increase or decrease?)

__(c)__ At the jetpack, the water's velocity reverses: it changes from $$v$$ upward to $$v$$ downward, so $$\Delta \vec{v} = -2v\,\hat{y},$$ where $$\hat{y}$$ points up. The mass of water passing through the pack in a time $$\Delta t$$ is $$m = d\,V = d\,f\,\Delta t.$$ Find the force of the water on the jetpack, $$\vec{F}_{W \to J}$$ — first symbolically in terms of $$d,$$ $$f,$$ and $$D,$$ then numerically. The SI unit of force, $$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},$$ is called the __newton__, with symbol $$\mathrm{N}.$$

__(d)__ To lift the rider, the upward force must exceed the force of gravity, $$\vec{F}_{g;\,E \to J} = -m_J\,g\,\hat{y},$$ with $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ Estimating the rider plus pack at about $$100\;\mathrm{kg},$$ can the fire hose work as a jetpack? What is the heaviest rider-plus-pack it could lift?

label: MCH15
name: The Thrust of a Small Rocket — A rocket accelerating upward must have an upward force __on__ it. But every…
desc: A rocket accelerating upward must have an upward force __on__ it. But every force has the form $$\vec{F}_{A \to B}$$ — some object $$A$$ exerts it. This problem explores what pushes rockets, using real data from "Amelia 2," a small Polish sounding rocket (a rocket built to…
statement:
A rocket accelerating upward must have an upward force __on__ it. But every force has the form $$\vec{F}_{A \to B}$$ — some object $$A$$ exerts it. This problem explores what pushes rockets, using real data from "Amelia 2," a small Polish sounding rocket (a rocket built to measure atmospheric conditions, not to reach space). Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ and recall Newton's second law $$\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$$ and the force definition $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t}.$$

__(a)__ For a rocket in flight, what object exerts the upward force on the rocket? (In this context the force is called the __thrust__.) For contrast: what object exerts the forward force on an accelerating car? Explain why, in both cases, the answer cannot be "the engine," using conservation of momentum. (Hint for the car: driving on slippery ice is difficult and dangerous.)

__(b)__ Below is Amelia 2's measured __thrust curve__ — a plot of thrust versus time. The motor produces a roughly constant thrust of about $$700\;\mathrm{N}$$ for about one second, followed by a long, low tail. The rocket's altitude data show that, starting from rest, it climbs about $$\Delta y = 20\;\mathrm{m}$$ during its first $$\Delta t = 0.8\;\mathrm{s}$$ of flight. The thrust is nearly constant over that interval, so the acceleration is too. Use $$\Delta y = \tfrac12 a\,(\Delta t)^2$$ to estimate the rocket's acceleration.

__(c)__ If you simply set $$700\;\mathrm{N} = ma,$$ you'll get the mass slightly wrong, because there are __two__ forces on the rocket. Newton's second law applies to the __sum__ of the forces: $$\vec{F}_{th;\,f \to r} + \vec{F}_{g;\,E \to r} = m\vec{a},$$ where $$th$$ stands for thrust, $$f$$ for fuel, $$E$$ for Earth, and $$r$$ for rocket, and the gravitational force is $$\vec{F}_{g;\,E \to r} = -mg\,\hat{y}.$$ Find the mass of the rocket.

__(d)__ The thrust curve isn't constant — after the main burn it has a long, low tail. The average force satisfies $$\Delta \vec{p} = \vec{F}_{\rm av}\,\Delta t,$$ just as $$\Delta v = a_{\rm av}\,\Delta t$$ for acceleration. When acceleration varied with time, we found $$\Delta v$$ as the signed area between the acceleration curve and the time axis. What is the physical interpretation of the signed area under a thrust curve?

desc: Part A. In the handout, we discussed lifting a book of mass $$m$$ a distance $$\Delta y.$$ There, we imagined a portion of the lift during which the force we applied to the book was constant and we lifted the book at constant velocity $$v.$$ We'll call this "gentle" lifting, and…
statement:
Part A. In the handout, we discussed lifting a book of mass $$m$$ a distance $$\Delta y.$$

There, we imagined a portion of the lift during which the force we applied to the book was constant and we lifted the book at constant velocity $$v.$$ We'll call this "gentle" lifting, and give it the subscript $$G.$$ In gentle lifting, the force was $$\vec{F}_{H \to B; G} = - m \vec{g}$$ where $$H \to B$$ means "from the hand, to the book."

The work done by the hand on the system of the book and its gravitational interaction with Earth was $$W_{H \to B; G} = mg \Delta y$$

The book gained gravitational potential energy $$\begin{aligned} \Delta U_G & = W_{H \to B; G}\\ {} & = mg \Delta y \end{aligned}$$

It is also possible to lift the book with a larger force. We'll call this "violent" lifting, and give it the subscript $$V.$$ Suppose you lift the book a distance $$\Delta y$$ using violent lifting with constant force $$\vec{F}_{H \to B;V} = -1.5 m \vec{g} $$

Your hand does some work $$W_{H \to B; V}$$ in this case, and the gravitational potential energy of the book increases by some amount $$\Delta U_V.$$

Select the **two** of the following statements, equations, or inequalities about work, energy, acceleration, and velocity are correct descriptions of violent lifting.

Although the book might continue moving after reaching the height change $$\Delta y,$$ ignore any further motion, and answer just for the period during which the book undergoes a height change $$\Delta y.$$

$$W_{H \to B;V} > W_{H \to B;G}$$

$$\Delta U_{V} > \Delta U_G$$

The book continuously gains kinetic energy in violent lifting, but not in gentle lifting.

The book has kinetic energy in violent lifting, but not in gentle lifting.

name: Part A. Below is Olympic champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen running.
desc: Part A. Below is Olympic champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen running. https://www.facebook.com/ingebrigtsenjakob/photos/a.975757819230692/1380573998749070/?type=3 Ingebrigtsen also frequently runs on treadmills. https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=218821882501882 Some people have an…
statement:
Part A. Below is Olympic champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen running.

https://www.facebook.com/ingebrigtsenjakob/photos/a.975757819230692/1380573998749070/?type=3

Ingebrigtsen also frequently runs on treadmills.

https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=218821882501882

Some people have an intuition that a treadmill belt "pulls" your feet along, making it easier to run at a given pace. Others believe running on treadmills and running outside are largely the same. In this problem, we'll examine running both outside and on a treadmill from the point of view of work and energy.

We can assume that Ingebrigtsen's foot does not slip relative to whatever surface he is running on. This means that, when running outside, the velocity of the bottom of his shoe is zero while it touches the ground. (Ingebrigtsen's center of mass continues moving forward even though his shoe's velocity is zero. His shoe, foot, and leg fall behind for a while, and then he swings them forward to catch up while in the air and while the other leg is touching the ground. Running consists of doing this over and over, alternating legs.)

Likewise, when Ingebrigtsen runs on a treadmill, his shoe has the same velocity as the surface of the treadmill while he runs. (In real life, there is probably some small amount of slipping, but it is usually very small, and we will ignore it.)

The motion of running is quite complicated - many different body parts are moving simultaneously. We will assume that Ingebrigtsen is running a very even pace. If running outside, he takes essentially the same amount of time to run each hundred meters he travels. If running on a treadmill, he keeps the treadmill belt moving at constant speed. This means his time-averaged acceleration is close to zero. However, the horizontal component of force between his shoe and the belt is sometimes forward and sometimes backward.

Below is a sample plot of measurements of both the vertical force component $$F_V$$ and horizontal force component $$F_H$$ from a runner on the surface they are running on. The plot shows three strides.

Chang, Young-Hui, and Rodger Kram. "Metabolic cost of generating horizontal forces during human running." Journal of Applied Physiology 86.5 (1999): 1657-1662.

You can assume a plot of Ingebrigtsen's forces would be similar.

Consider Ingebrigtsen (along with his clothing and shoes) and his gravitational interactions with Earth as one system, the treadmill as another, and the air as a third.

For this part of the problem, assume that both the ground and the treadmill are flat.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

Answer each from the reference frame of the ground / floor.

Outside, Ingebrigtsen does positive work on the ground throughout his stride.

Outside, the ground does positive work on Ingebrigtsen throughout his stride.

Outside, Ingebrigtsen alternately does positive, then negative work on the ground at different parts of his stride.

On the treadmill, Ingebrigtsen does positive work on the ground throughout his stride.

On the treadmill, the ground does positive work on Ingebrigtsen throughout his stride.

Then according to the principle of relativity, we can analyze the treadmill from any reference frame.

Use this fact to help you choose all the correct statements below.

Running on the treadmill when it is flat is physically the same as running on a similar surface outside.

Part C. A significant difference between a treadmill and running outside is that there is very little wind resistance on a treadmill; we can model the wind resistance as zero on a treadmill.

Even if the air is still, there is still wind resistance when running outside because your body moves forward relative to the air, i.e, if Ingebrigtsen runs at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ outside, he experiences a headwind of $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ even when the air is still. When he runs at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ on a treadmill, he experiences effectively no wind resistance.

We have previously modeled the effect of wind resistance. Our model is equivalent to a force $$F_D = \dfrac12 C_D \rho A v^2$$ where $$F_D$$ is the magnitude of wind drag force an object feels, $$C_D$$ is its drag coefficient, $$\rho$$ is the density of air, $$A$$ is the object's cross-sectional area, and $$v$$ is the speed of the wind relative to the object.

To compensate for the lack of wind resistance on a treadmill, Ingebrigtsen could set the treadmill to an incline, making running more difficult in a way similar to how wind resistance makes running more difficult.

Treadmills measure inclines using "percentages." For example, a treadmill incline of $$1\%$$ means that if the treadmill belt is $$2 \;\mathrm{m}$$ long, it rises $$2 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ from back to front.

Suppose Ingebrigtsen wants to set the incline of the treadmill so that he exerts the same power to run at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ on the treadmill as he does running at $$5 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ outside. Assume that all factors aside from the wind resistance and incline of the treadmill are identical between outside and the treadmill.

What should the incline of the treadmill be?

Give your answer to the nearest percent.

statement:
Particle physicists use large colliders to smash particles into each other, creating new particles. Large detectors are able to follow the paths that the newly-created particles take for a short time.

Below is the ATLAS detector at CERN.

By Maximilien Brice - http://cds.cern.ch/record/910381, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=47143612

Each of the eight large tubes around the detector is a powerful magnet. There are people in the photo; they can serve as a scale.

Particle detectors have strong magnetic fields in the region where the new particles are created. Particles with no electric charge (e.g. neutrons) are unaffected by magnetic fields, but particles with electric charge (e.g. electrons and protons) Note that we're saying __magnetic__ fields put force on __electric__ charges. The connection between electricity and magnetism may not seem very strong when we think about light bulbs or static discharge as representatives of electricity and refrigerator magnets or compasses as representatives of magnetism, but electric and magnetic fields are closely linked, and described together in a single mathematical theory. Electric fields also put forces on electric charges. This issue of "magnetic charges" is more complicated, and best left for a class dedicated to electricity and magnetism. from the magnetic field.

We can model force from the magnetic field on a particle with electric charge as always being perpendicular to the direction of motion of the charge, and to the magnetic field itself.

This situation is similar to that of gravitational force and circular orbits. There, the gravitational force is always perpendicular to the motion of the orbiting object.

Using this model of magnetic forces, what is the work done by the magnetic field on an electron when the electron makes one full circular orbit in the magnetic field?

label: MCH16
name: The Moving Sidewalk Does No Work — At the 1900 Paris Exposition, visitors rode a __moving sidewalk__ — a…
desc: At the 1900 Paris Exposition, visitors rode a __moving sidewalk__ — a horizontal belt that carried standing passengers along at a constant velocity $$v.$$ Florence stands on the moving sidewalk. Her mass is $$m,$$ and the coefficient of friction between her shoes and the belt is…
statement:
At the 1900 Paris Exposition, visitors rode a __moving sidewalk__ — a horizontal belt that carried standing passengers along at a constant velocity $$v.$$ Florence stands on the moving sidewalk. Her mass is $$m,$$ and the coefficient of friction between her shoes and the belt is $$\mu.$$ Ignore air resistance and any friction inside the sidewalk's machinery.

__(a)__ Florence is already on the sidewalk, moving along with the belt. How much energy must the sidewalk supply to carry her an additional distance $$\Delta x$$? Three candidate answers: almost none, $$\tfrac12 mv^2,$$ or $$mg\,\Delta x.$$

__(b)__ Use Newton's second law to find the horizontal component and the vertical component of the force the sidewalk exerts on Florence. (Careful: $$\mu mg$$ is a tempting candidate for the horizontal component.)

__(c)__ In the vertical direction, Newton's second law gives $$F_{y;\mathrm{net}} = m\,a_y = 0.$$ Why doesn't this mean the sidewalk exerts zero vertical force on Florence?

__(d)__ The contact force from the sidewalk on Florence is called the __normal force__. "Normal" means "perpendicular" — the force is perpendicular to the sidewalk's surface. What is the relationship between the direction of the normal force and the direction of Florence's motion, and what does that relationship tell you about the energy the sidewalk transfers to her?

label: MCH16
name: Powering the World's Longest Escalator — The longest escalator in the world is in a metro station in St…
desc: The longest escalator in the world is in a metro station in St. Petersburg, Russia. It is $$L = 137\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, rises at an angle of $$30^\circ,$$ and a ride to the top takes $$160\;\mathrm{s}.$$ In this problem you will estimate the minimum power needed to run it…
statement:
The longest escalator in the world is in a metro station in St. Petersburg, Russia. It is $$L = 137\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, rises at an angle of $$30^\circ,$$ and a ride to the top takes $$160\;\mathrm{s}.$$ In this problem you will estimate the minimum power needed to run it. __Power__ is the rate at which energy is delivered: $$P = \dfrac{E}{\Delta t}.$$ The dimensions of energy are $$ = \mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}},$$ and gravitational potential energy changes by $$\Delta U = mg\,\Delta y$$ when a mass $$m$$ rises a height $$\Delta y.$$ Use $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ What are the dimensions of power? The SI unit of power is the __watt__: $$1\;\mathrm{W} = 1\;\mathrm{J/s}.$$

__(b)__ The escalator increases its riders' energy. Two candidates for the energy that matters: the riders' kinetic energy and their gravitational potential energy. Which one should we estimate, and why is the other negligible?

__(c)__ The photos below show escalator stairs. Estimate the depth of a single stair, and use it to estimate the number of stairs on the $$137\;\mathrm{m}$$ escalator. (Careful: the stairs are horizontal, so they add up to the __horizontal__ extent of the escalator, not its full length.)

__(d)__ In the photo of the long escalator, the "up" side mostly has a single person, then a gap of a few steps, then another person. Estimate the number of people riding up at a given moment, and then the total mass $$m$$ the escalator is lifting. Take a typical adult mass to be $$70\;\mathrm{kg}.$$

__(e)__ Find the height $$\Delta y$$ that the escalator lifts its riders, and combine your estimates into the minimum power, $$P_{\rm min} = \dfrac{mg\,\Delta y}{\Delta t}.$$ Express your answer as a power of ten times a small number.

label: MCH16
name: Work and Power on an Escalator Rider — When a force transfers energy from one system to another, we say the…
desc: When a force transfers energy from one system to another, we say the force __does work__. The work done by a force of magnitude $$F$$ is $$W = F\,d_{\parallel},$$ where $$d_{\parallel}$$ is the component of the object's displacement parallel to the force. Equivalently, $$W =…
statement:
When a force transfers energy from one system to another, we say the force __does work__. The work done by a force of magnitude $$F$$ is $$W = F\,d_{\parallel},$$ where $$d_{\parallel}$$ is the component of the object's displacement parallel to the force. Equivalently, $$W = F_{\parallel}\,d$$: you may either take the component of the displacement along the force, or the component of the force along the displacement — they give the same answer. To track which systems exchange energy, we write $$W_{A \to B}$$ for the work done by system $$A$$ on system $$B.$$

A rider of mass $$m_1 = 70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ stands on the long St. Petersburg escalator: $$137\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, inclined at $$30^\circ,$$ raising its riders a height $$\Delta y \approx 70\;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$160\;\mathrm{s}$$ at constant velocity. Two forces act on the rider: gravity, downward, and the contact force — the __normal force__ — upward from the horizontal escalator step. Define the rider plus their gravitational interaction with the Earth as one system, and the escalator as a second system. Use $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ Which of the two forces does work on the rider–Earth system? (A force acting between two parts of the __same__ system is called an __internal force__.)

__(b)__ What is the magnitude of the normal force on the rider?

__(c)__ Find the work done by the escalator on the rider–Earth system during the full ride.

__(d)__ Now consider a rider coming __down__ the matching escalator on the other side. Is the work done by the escalator on that rider positive, negative, or zero? What could an idealized, frictionless escalator do with this fact if people rode down as often as they rode up?

__(e)__ Starting from $$P = \dfrac{W}{\Delta t},$$ show that the power delivered by a force can be written $$P = F\,v_{\parallel},$$ where $$v_{\parallel}$$ is the component of the object's velocity parallel to the force. Then compute the power the escalator delivers to the $$70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ rider.

label: MCH16
name: Six Graphs for a Fan Cart — A small cart carries a battery-powered fan that blows air backward; the air…
desc: A small cart carries a battery-powered fan that blows air backward; the air pushes back on the cart, driving it forward. Model the situation simply: the cart, of mass $$m,$$ feels a constant horizontal force of magnitude $$F$$ and rolls without friction, starting from rest. Two…
statement:
A small cart carries a battery-powered fan that blows air backward; the air pushes back on the cart, driving it forward. Model the situation simply: the cart, of mass $$m,$$ feels a constant horizontal force of magnitude $$F$$ and rolls without friction, starting from rest. Two energy facts will help. First, a constant force $$F$$ pushing an object through a distance $$d$$ along its motion does work $$W = Fd,$$ and that work equals the kinetic energy the object gains. Second, the power delivered by a force is $$P = F\,v_{\parallel}.$$

Sketch (or describe) the shape of each of the following graphs for the cart. In particular, say whether each is a straight line, a curve bending upward, or a curve bending downward.

__(a)__ velocity versus time; __(b)__ momentum $$p = mv$$ versus time; __(c)__ kinetic energy $$KE = \tfrac12 mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$$ versus time;

__(d)__ power delivered to the cart versus time; __(e)__ kinetic energy versus __distance traveled__; __(f)__ momentum versus distance traveled.

label: MCH16
name: A Fan-Cart Race: Same Force, Same Distance — Two fan carts are identical, except that some extra mass has…
desc: Two fan carts are identical, except that some extra mass has been added to cart $$B,$$ so $$m_B > m_A.$$ Each cart's fan pushes it with the same constant horizontal force $$F.$$ Both carts start from rest at one edge of a table of width $$L$$ and accelerate, friction-free…
statement:
Two fan carts are identical, except that some extra mass has been added to cart $$B,$$ so $$m_B > m_A.$$ Each cart's fan pushes it with the same constant horizontal force $$F.$$ Both carts start from rest at one edge of a table of width $$L$$ and accelerate, friction-free, across it. Recall two facts: a constant force $$F$$ acting through a distance $$d$$ along the motion does work $$W = Fd,$$ which equals the kinetic energy gained, and a constant force acting for a time $$\Delta t$$ delivers momentum $$p = F\,\Delta t$$ to an object starting from rest.

Two students discuss which cart is moving faster when it flies off the far edge. Deyemi says: "Cart $$A$$ has less mass, so its acceleration is greater, and it will be going faster when it reaches the edge." Uche replies: "You're right that $$A$$ has more acceleration. However, cart $$B$$ accelerates for a longer time, and it winds up reaching the same speed cart $$A$$ had when it left the table."

__(a)__ Who is right? Try to decide without a detailed calculation.

__(b)__ One quantity __is__ exactly the same for the two carts at the moment they leave the table: their mass, their velocity, their momentum, or their kinetic energy. Which one, and why?

__(c)__ Suppose $$m_B = 4\,m_A.$$ Find $$v_A,$$ the speed with which cart $$A$$ leaves the table, in terms of $$v_B.$$

__(d)__ Letting the carts travel the same __distance__ gave them the same kinetic energy. How could you arrange for the two carts to end up with the same __momentum__ instead?

label: MCH16
name: Stopping a Box with a Spring — A box of mass $$m$$ slides to the right at speed $$v$$ on a frictionless…
desc: A box of mass $$m$$ slides to the right at speed $$v$$ on a frictionless surface and runs into a spring whose far end is attached to an immovable wall. The spring obeys __Hooke's law__: compressed by a distance $$\Delta\ell,$$ it pushes back with a force of magnitude $$F =…
statement:
A box of mass $$m$$ slides to the right at speed $$v$$ on a frictionless surface and runs into a spring whose far end is attached to an immovable wall. The spring obeys __Hooke's law__: compressed by a distance $$\Delta\ell,$$ it pushes back with a force of magnitude $$F = k\,\Delta\ell,$$ where $$k$$ is the __spring constant__, and it stores elastic potential energy $$U = \tfrac12 k\,(\Delta\ell)^2.$$

__(a)__ Treating the box plus the spring and wall as a single system whose energy is conserved, find the maximum compression $$\Delta\ell_{\rm max}$$ of the spring.

__(b)__ Now treat the box as one system (system $$m$$) and the spring plus wall as a second system (system $$S$$). As the spring compresses, which system does positive work on the other?

__(c)__ Setting the work done by the box on the spring equal to the energy the spring stores, $$W_{m \to S} = \tfrac12 k\,(\Delta\ell_{\rm max})^2,$$ and writing the work as $$W_{m \to S} = F_{m \to S}\,\Delta\ell_{\rm max},$$ we get $$F_{m \to S} = \tfrac12 k\,\Delta\ell_{\rm max}.$$ But by Hooke's law the actual force grows from $$0$$ to $$k\,\Delta\ell_{\rm max}$$ as the spring compresses. What exactly is the quantity $$\tfrac12 k\,\Delta\ell_{\rm max}$$ — the maximum force, an average force over time, or an average force over distance? Why does that kind of average belong in the work formula?

__(d)__ Averages over time and over distance are genuinely different. Consider a fan cart accelerating from rest with constant acceleration, reaching maximum speed $$v_{x;\rm max}$$ at the end of a run. Averaged over __time__, its velocity is $$\tfrac12 v_{x;\rm max}.$$ Is its velocity averaged over __distance__ greater than, less than, or equal to that? (Hint: a graph of $$v_x$$ versus distance $$d$$ has the shape $$v_x \propto \sqrt{d}.$$ You can also think about which half of the run the cart spends more time in.)

__(e)__ Plot the Hooke's-law force $$F_{m \to S} = k\,\Delta\ell$$ against the compression $$\Delta\ell.$$ Where on this plot is the total work done by the box on the spring? Verify that it equals $$\tfrac12 k\,(\Delta\ell_{\rm max})^2.$$

label: MCH16
name: A Cart with Two Angled Fans — Cart 1 is a fan cart: its single fan pushes it with a constant horizontal force…
desc: Cart 1 is a fan cart: its single fan pushes it with a constant horizontal force of magnitude $$F,$$ and it accelerates from rest, friction-free, across a table of width $$L,$$ leaving the table at speed $$v_1.$$ Cart 2 is built from an identical cart, but it carries __two__…
statement:
Cart 1 is a fan cart: its single fan pushes it with a constant horizontal force of magnitude $$F,$$ and it accelerates from rest, friction-free, across a table of width $$L,$$ leaving the table at speed $$v_1.$$ Cart 2 is built from an identical cart, but it carries __two__ fans. Two fans don't quite fit side by side pointing straight back, so each is angled $$20^\circ$$ toward its own side of the cart, as in the top view below; each fan still produces a force of magnitude $$F$$ on the cart (red arrows show the forces from the air on the carts). Ignore the mass of the extra fan. Recall that only the component of a force parallel to the displacement does work, $$W = F_{\parallel}\,d,$$ and that the work done on a cart starting from rest equals its kinetic energy.

__(a)__ In which direction does Cart 2 move, and why?

__(b)__ With two fans, you might guess Cart 2 receives twice the work: $$W_2 = 2\,W_1.$$ Find the actual relationship between $$W_2$$ and $$W_1$$ for crossing the table.

__(c)__ Find the speed $$v_2$$ with which Cart 2 leaves the table, as a numerical multiple of $$v_1.$$

__(d)__ For what fan angle $$\theta$$ would Cart 2 leave the table at exactly $$v_1$$?

label: MCH16
name: Anti-Lock Brakes and the Work Done by the Road — If the driver of an old car hits the brakes hard, the wheels…
desc: If the driver of an old car hits the brakes hard, the wheels lock and the tires skid along the road. A modern car's anti-lock braking system (ABS) instead keeps the wheels rolling without slipping while the car stops. This problem compares the two cases using work and energy…
statement:
If the driver of an old car hits the brakes hard, the wheels lock and the tires skid along the road. A modern car's anti-lock braking system (ABS) instead keeps the wheels rolling without slipping while the car stops. This problem compares the two cases using work and energy. One refinement of the power formula is essential here: the power a force delivers is $$P = F_{\parallel}\,v_{\rm touch},$$ where $$v_{\rm touch}$$ is the velocity of the __point where the force is applied__ — not necessarily the velocity of the object as a whole.

__(a)__ What force speeds a car up when the driver hits the gas, and slows it down during braking? Explain why it cannot be a force from the engine. (The clip below, of a car spinning its wheels uselessly on ice, is a hint.)

__(b)__ The animation below shows a tire rolling without slipping while the car brakes, as ABS arranges. At any given moment, what is the velocity of the part of the tire touching the road? How much power does the road deliver to the car, and how much work does the road do as the car stops?

__(c)__ Suppose you (incorrectly) used $$v_{\rm car},$$ the velocity of the car's center of mass, in the power formula instead of $$v_{\rm touch}.$$ Show that this leads to an absurd conclusion about a car __accelerating__ from rest up to driving speed.

__(d)__ If the road does no work on the car, the kinetic energy a braking car loses must go somewhere, and the kinetic energy an accelerating car gains must come from somewhere. Where, in each case?

__(e)__ The quantity $$F_{\rm net}\,d_{\rm cm,\parallel},$$ built from the net force on a system and the displacement of its __center of mass__, is called the __pseudowork__; it equals the change in the translational kinetic energy $$\tfrac12 m v_{\rm cm}^2.$$ When we analyzed fan carts with $$KE = Fd,$$ we were really computing pseudowork — the actual force acts between the fan blades and the air, both of which move in complicated ways. Why was the fan-cart analysis still legitimate?

__(f)__ Now the skidding car, shown below: with the wheels locked, the tire surface slides along the road, and friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy — energy of the random motions of molecules — at the rate $$\Delta E_{\rm th} = \mu m g\,\Delta x$$ over a sliding distance $$\Delta x,$$ where $$\mu$$ is the friction coefficient. Treating the car and road together as one system (so that friction is an internal force), find how far a car of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v$$ skids before stopping.

desc: Part A. A box sits stationary and undisturbed on a table. generated by StableDiffusion Svetlana is a student taking her first physics class. Although a box sitting on a table is a mundane scenario, she wants to study it anyway. Her goal is to improve the connection between her…
statement:
Part A. A box sits stationary and undisturbed on a table.

generated by StableDiffusion

Svetlana is a student taking her first physics class. Although a box sitting on a table is a mundane scenario, she wants to study it anyway. Her goal is to improve the connection between her everyday intuition and the models, terminology, and equations she's been using in her class.

First, Svetlana thinks about the situation as if she had not taken physics at all. From this perspective, it doesn't seem to Svetlana that the table is doing anything to the box. The table doesn't get tired, or seem visibly affected by the box. At most, she intuitively thinks of the table as "getting in the box's way", or perhaps "supporting" the box, so it doesn't fall.

Svetlana then thinks about the box in terms of physics concepts. She considers

1. forces 2. energy 3. kinematics (e.g. velocity and acceleration)

She writes a summary of the box-table situation from each of these three perspectives.

Svetlana works in the reference frame of the table. She assumes the table is flat and horizontal.

Let's figure out Svetlana's conclusions for ourselves.

**According to the models of physics we've studied over this course, which one of the following is an accurate description of the box-table situation?**

Only select an option if the value discussed is non-zero. For example, choice (a) is "The table is exerting a normal force on the box." If you think of the table as exerting a normal force, but with magnitude zero, then do not select this option.

Do select an option if the value is negative. For example, choice (c) is "The table is doing work on the box." Select this even if you find that the table is doing negative work on the box.

Svetlana is mostly focused on the table's effect on the box, so we don't have choices related to force exerted by the box on the table, etc. That doesn't mean that force doesn't exist. It only means we aren't focused on that force in this problem.

The table is exerting a normal force on the box.

The table is exerting a friction force on the box.

The table is doing work on the box.

The box has velocity.

The box has acceleration.

Part B. Svetlana realizes that, according to her pre-physics intuition, the table doesn't react to the box. It's an inanimate object, and it is "doing nothing."

Nonetheless, Svetlana's analysis says that the table is "exerting force" on the box. She is confused; the table cannot be both "exerting a force" and "doing nothing."

Early in her physics class, Svetlana didn't worry about counterintuitive ideas. As a beginner, she realized she couldn't build a deep understanding all at once. She is good at algebra and focused on the mathematical calculations.

When she can blend her visualizations of the world with physics equations, vocabulary, and graphs, Svetlana thinks of it as having "physics intuition." She's now focusing on building this intuition up by taking counterintuitive ideas and breaking them down.

Svetlana finds a video by YouTuber Derek Muller The video is 2:24 long. It's linked to the left. You can watch the video, or skip the video and use the summary below. in intuitive terms.

In the video, Muller stands on the ground. An arrow pointing downward shows up above him, representing a gravitational force downward on his body, from the entire Earth. Then two upward arrows show up, one at each foot. These represent the a normal force upward on Muller from the ground beneath his feet.

Veritasium, "What Forces Are Acting on You?", YouTube

To explain how the inanimate ground exerts a force, Muller then steps on the spring-supported horse toy.

ibid.

As Muller stands on the horse, its spring compresses under his weight. The compressed spring pushes back up on Muller, and this push upward is the normal force.

Muller then explains:

The ground is very similar to this spring. The ground is just a very stiff spring. But every time you step, you compress the ground a little bit, and that is enough to make the ground create a force on you, pushing you back upwards. And the force of the ground upwards must be equal to the gravitational force downwards so that you stay at rest.

Svetlana wants to adapt Muller's explanation to the situation with a box on a table.

Which one of the following statements **__disagrees__** with Muller's explanation of normal force?

There is a normal force from the table on the box.

Although the table appears unaffected by the box, the box really does have an effect on the table.

The table is slightly compressed by the weight of the box.

The table is like a very stiff spring.

The magnitude of the normal force from the table on the box is larger than the magnitude of the gravitational force on the box.

If you were to pick the box up off the table, the shape of the table's surface would change (a tiny bit).
