Part C. Svetlana thinks Muller's explanation makes some sense, but when she puts a box on a table, there's no visible deflection of the table.

Svetlana at first thinks of the idea that the ground or a table is "like a spring" as only an analogy, but not a meaningful real-world idea. She wonders whether the table really compresses a microscopic amount, or whether we're just supposed to think of it that way.

Svetlana takes a few meter sticks and uses them to make a bridge between two stacks of books. This forms a simple "table." She places a marshmallow on top the meter sticks. According to Muller's explanation, the meter sticks should be deflected downward by the marshmallow, but Svetlana doesn't see anything.

Next, Svetlana places a cell phone on the meter sticks, but still doesn't see a deflection. Then she puts a book on them, and thinks that maybe she sees a little bit of deflection. Eventually, she puts a bowling ball on the meter sticks, causing a large, obvious deflection.

Marc Reif, https://fysicsfool.wordpress.com/2017/07/09/a-physics-teachers-strongman-trick/

One interpretation is that even a marshmallow caused some deflection of the meter sticks, but it was too small to see. Another is that large, heavy objects cause a lot of deflection, medium objects cause a smaller deflection, but light objects like a marshmallow don't cause any real deflection of a meter stick, much less a sturdy table.

Similarly, Svetlana imagines pushing on a wall. She can imagine that when she presses against a flimsy wall, she deforms it, but finds it hard to imagine she can deform or compress a sturdy large wall or a heavy steel beam just by pressing lightly against them.

Svetlana finds a description of a demo to visualize the deflection of heavy walls, steel beams, tables, etc. The setup is shown below.

ibid.

A rod is connected to a heavy steel beam (called a "girder" in the photo). This way, if the steel beam deflects a tiny amount, it will push the rod.

A second rod, called a dowel, lies underneath the first rod at a right angle to it. If the beam deflects a small amount, it will push the rod connected to it. That will rotate the dowel through a small angle.

A mirror is attached to the dowel. The mirror will rotate a tiny bit along with the dowel.

Finally, a laser reflects a beam of light off the mirror, creating a spot of laser light on another wall on the opposite side of the room (not shown in picture).

To summarize, the idea is: - Svetlana will push on the steel beam with her hands - this will cause a microscopic deflection of the beam - the beam will push the first rod a little bit - the first rod will rotate the dowel a little bit - the dowel will rotate the mirror a little bit - rotating the mirror will change the reflection of the laser light - the dot of laser light on the far wall will move

The point of this system is that the laser light moves a much greater distance than any deflection of the beam. In fact, the dot of laser light can move tens of thousands of times further than the deflection of the beam, since even a small change in the angle of the mirror can result in a significant motion of the laser light after it travels across the entire room.

After acquiring some materials and building her own version of this setup, Svetlana pushes on the steel beam. As she pushes, she can see the laser light move.

ibid.

Svetlana interprets this as showing that even when we can't see the deflection of tables, the ground, steel beams, etc, they really do deflect each time they exert a force.

Which one of the following is an **__inaccurate__** description of what Svetlana should see as she pushes on the steel beam?

If Svetlana pushes on the beam three times (relaxing between pushes), the laser dot deflects three times.

If Svetlana leans against the beam, the laser dot deflects for a brief period while the wall is reacting, but once she is leaning steadily at equilibrium, the laser dot is back at its original location.

If Svetlana leans against the beam, as long as she continues leaning, the laser dot remains deflected from its original position, only going back when she stops leaning.

The harder Svetlana pushes against the beam, the more the laser dot deflects.

If Svetlana pulls outward on the beam, the laser dot deflects the opposite direction as it did when she pushed.

Part D. To explain why objects like tables and steel beams compress, Svetlana's teacher has a kit of red plastic spheres and springs.

Pasco Scientific, https://www.pasco.com/products/lab-apparatus/mechanics/centripetal-force-and-rotation/me-9825

The red spheres represent atoms, and the springs represent bonds between the atoms. They can be assembled into a three-dimensional grid, representing the structure of atoms in a solid material. The type of grid these spheres can be assembled into is called a "primitive cubical grid."

ibid.

When Svetlana presses on the assembled We have mostly discussed __conceptual models__ in this class. These are made of equations, graphs, drawings, etc. that represent something real. A __physical model__ is a made of real stuff itself, but represents a different real thing. Here, plastic spheres and springs represent atoms and bonds., it compresses under her hand.

ibid.

Svetlana's teacher explains that the atoms in a steel beam get closer together when the beam is compressed. The bonds between the atoms are so strong that the compression is slight, and we don't usually notice it unless we build the laser apparatus from part (C). She also says that different materials have bonds of different strength.

The model is intended to give a good approximation of how atoms and bonds work in materials, without necessarily being a perfect representation of every solid in every detail.

After thinking about this model, which one of the following is **__not__** a reasonable conclusion for Svetlana to draw about atoms, bonds, and solid materials?

In a solid, individual atoms can all jiggle around, and this explains where the solid stores thermal energy. If we heat the solid up, the jiggling will increase.

If we compress a solid from all sides, shrinking it, the atoms in the solid get closer to each other.

Different materials can be harder or easier to compress, based at least partially on the types of bonds between the atoms in the material.

Atoms in a solid maintain roughly the same neighbors over time. If atom A is right next to and bonded to atom B right now, they will likely still be right next to each other a short time later. They are not moving around at random all the time.

Every solid material has all its atoms in a perfect primitive cubical grid. Ignoring atoms on the surface, each atom makes exactly six bonds, one to a neighbor above, below, left, right, forward, and behind.

statement:
You are pushing a couch across the floor. Since the couch is fairly low, you're leaning into it and pushing downward in addition to forward.

Getty Images

We can model your push as the contact force $$\vec{F}_{c; Y \to C}$$ from you to the couch, which is at some angle $$\theta$$ below the horizontal.

As you increase the angle $$\theta$$ between the horizontal and the direction of your push, i.e. as your push gets closer to vertical, you have to push harder to move the couch.

You find that if $$\theta > 1.13 \,\mathrm{rad},$$ the couch won't move, no matter how hard you push. Even if you recruit friends to help you push at that angle, or build a machine that can push at that angle with a very large force, the couch won't slide. (Eventually it will get crushed by the huge force, or the floorboards will break, etc.)

When $$\theta < 1.13,$$ you can push the couch as long as you use enough force.

Given this result, what is the static friction coefficient between the couch and the floor?

Give your result to two decimal places.

desc: Part A. In our experiment this week, we'll examine static and kinetic friction. We have already done some work examining an object on an inclined plane. One of our conclusions was that the maximum angle the inclined plane can be tilted to before the object begins to slide obeys…
statement:
Part A. In our experiment this week, we'll examine static and kinetic friction.

We have already done some work examining an object on an inclined plane.

One of our conclusions was that the maximum angle the inclined plane can be tilted to before the object begins to slide obeys $$\tan \theta_c = \mu_s$$ with $$\mu_s$$ the static friction coefficient between the inclined plane and the object sitting on it.

Wangari is a physics student who comes up with an experiment based on this result. She plans to put different objects on a ramp, one by one. For each object, she'll incline the ramp steeper and steeper until the object begins slipping. Then she will use the equation above to calculate the coefficient of static friction between the ramp and the object.

Which **two** of the following are accurate statements about this experiment?

To collect good data, Wangari should build the ramp with a way to increase the angle slowly and smoothly.

The experiment, on its own, provides a meaningful test that the model of static friction we're using in this class makes accurate predictions.

If Wangari's uncertainty in her measurements of $$\theta_c$$ (measured in radians) is $$\pm 0.01,$$ then her uncertainty in $$\mu_S$$ will also be $$\pm 0.01.$$

If an object falls or tumbles over due to the incline before it slides, Wangari should not use the angle at which the object fell/tumbled to calculate the friction coefficient.

Part B. Wangari's daughter Wanjira suggests adding a second phase to the experiment. In this phase, the ramp will be laid horizontal, $$\theta = 0.$$ The object will be placed back on the ramp and connected to a string that goes over a pulley to a box, making a half-Atwood machine.

This phase of the experiment uses the same ramp and object as the phase from part (A), so the static friction coefficient $$\mu_s$$ should be the same. Only the object experiences a friction force. The box does not.

The mass of the box is adjustable, since one can put items in or take them out. Wanjira proposes increasing the mass of the box until the object begins sliding horizontally across the ramp.

Wanjira points out that Wangari can use the result of her first measurement (with the ramp tilted) to predict the weight at which the object will first slide.

Part C. The two phases of Wangari's experiment are:

Phase 1: Tilt an inclined plane until an object begins to slide.

Phase 2: Add mass to a half-Atwood machine until an object begins to slide across the horizontal ramp.

In both phases, the object eventually slides across the ramp. When it slides, the friction between the object and the ramp it's on switches from static friction to kinetic friction. Because kinetic friction is lower than static friction, the forces on the object are unbalanced, and it accelerates. Even if Wangari increases the angle of the ramp very slowly or adds only a very small amount of mass to the box at a time, there will be some minimum acceleration of the object once sliding begins.

Call the minimum acceleration of an object in phase 1 $$a_1$$ and the minimum acceleration of an object in phase 2 $$a_2.$$

According to Amontons's model of friction, should these accelerations be equal? Which one should be larger, or will it vary from object to object?

label: MCH17
name: The Monkey and the Bananas — A rope hangs over a pulley. On one side of the rope hangs a monkey of mass…
desc: A rope hangs over a pulley. On one side of the rope hangs a monkey of mass $$m,$$ and on the other side hangs a bunch of bananas, also of mass $$m.$$ The rope is massless and the pulley is frictionless. A force exerted by a rope is called a __tension force__, and the magnitude…
statement:
A rope hangs over a pulley. On one side of the rope hangs a monkey of mass $$m,$$ and on the other side hangs a bunch of bananas, also of mass $$m.$$ The rope is massless and the pulley is frictionless.

A force exerted by a rope is called a __tension force__, and the magnitude of the force a rope exerts is the __tension__ in the rope. In this course we use a "standard rope model": (1) there is a tension in the rope; (2) the rope exerts tension forces that point along the direction of the rope; (3) the tension is constant along the rope; (4) the rope is inextensible, meaning its length cannot change; (5) the rope is massless.

__(a)__ To justify point (3), consider a small segment in the middle of a stationary rope. The rest of the rope pulls on this segment from both sides. Explain why the two pulls must have equal magnitudes, and why this means the tension is constant all along the rope. (For the rope over the pulley, the frictionless pulley exerts no force along the rope's direction, so the tension is constant over the pulley too.)

__(b)__ While the monkey simply hangs from the rope without climbing, what is the tension in the rope? Draw (or describe) a __free body diagram__ — a picture showing all the forces — for the bananas. The monkey and the bananas each pull down on the rope with force $$mg$$ — explain why the tension is nevertheless not $$2mg.$$

__(c)__ The monkey and bananas together pull down on the rope with a total force $$2mg,$$ and the rope isn't accelerating, so something must supply a balancing upward force on the rope. What supplies it? Suppose the pulley itself is massless and hangs from a second rope attached to the ceiling. What is the tension in that second rope?

__(d)__ Now the monkey pulls down on the rope, exerting a force on the rope greater than $$mg.$$ What happens to the tension in the rope? Draw a free body diagram for the monkey and one for the bananas — being careful to include only forces exerted __on__ each system — and determine what each one does: accelerate up, accelerate down, or stay still.

label: MCH17
name: Which Rope Breaks? — A box of mass $$m$$ hangs from the ceiling by a rope, and an identical rope hangs down…
desc: A box of mass $$m$$ hangs from the ceiling by a rope, and an identical rope hangs down from the bottom of the box. You grab the lower rope and pull straight down on it with a force $$F.$$ Each rope breaks when the tension in it exceeds the same breaking tension. __(a)__ You…
statement:
A box of mass $$m$$ hangs from the ceiling by a rope, and an identical rope hangs down from the bottom of the box. You grab the lower rope and pull straight down on it with a force $$F.$$ Each rope breaks when the tension in it exceeds the same breaking tension.

__(a)__ You start with a weak pull and increase $$F$$ gradually, so that the box stays in equilibrium, until one rope breaks. Find the tension in each rope while you pull with force $$F,$$ and determine which rope breaks first.

The animation below shows this demonstration: the experimenter pulls down on the lower string, increasing the force gradually.

The top string broke, as your analysis should predict. But in a second trial, shown below, the experimenter chops downward suddenly on a stick threaded through a loop in the bottom string — and this time the __bottom__ string breaks.

__(b)__ During a sudden yank, the box may accelerate. Let $$T_U$$ and $$T_L$$ be the magnitudes of the tensions in the upper and lower ropes, and let $$a$$ be the box's vertical acceleration, treated as signed so that $$a$$ is negative for downward acceleration. Apply Newton's second law, $$\vec{F}_{\rm net}=m\vec{a},$$ to the box to find an equation relating $$ma$$ to $$T_U,$$ $$T_L,$$ and $$mg.$$

__(c)__ The lower rope breaks first when its tension is the larger one, $$T_L>T_U.$$ Use your equation from part (b) to show that this happens exactly when $$a<-g.$$

__(d)__ Our standard rope model says ropes are inextensible — their lengths cannot change. Explain why that assumption cannot be exactly right if the box is to accelerate downward. Then, using the fact that real ropes stretch slightly before breaking, explain in words why a sudden yank breaks the bottom rope while a gradual pull breaks the top one.

label: MCH17
name: The Jar Gripper and Anti-Lock Brakes — A rubber gripper pad like the one below helps open a stuck jar.
desc: A rubber gripper pad like the one below helps open a stuck jar. Any force perpendicular to a surface is called a __normal force__ $$N.$$ A force parallel to a surface is a __friction force__ $$F_f.$$ We model friction with __Amontons's model__: (1) there are two different…
statement:
A rubber gripper pad like the one below helps open a stuck jar.

Any force perpendicular to a surface is called a __normal force__ $$N.$$ A force parallel to a surface is a __friction force__ $$F_f.$$ We model friction with __Amontons's model__: (1) there are two different friction coefficients; (2) the first, $$\mu_s,$$ is the static friction coefficient, used when the surfaces are not slipping; (3) the second, $$\mu_k,$$ is the kinetic friction coefficient, used when the surfaces __are__ slipping; (4) $$\mu_s>\mu_k$$; (5) when not slipping, $$F_f\le\mu_s N,$$ and static friction opposes any potential slipping; (6) when slipping, $$F_f=\mu_k N,$$ and kinetic friction opposes the slipping.

__(a)__ When you grip a stuck jar lid tightly with your bare fingers, you exert a large normal force on the rim of the lid. The normal force itself does nothing to open the jar — opening it requires twisting. According to Amontons's model, why does squeezing harder still help you open the jar?

__(b)__ The gripper pad doesn't let you squeeze any harder than your bare hand does. What quantity in Amontons's model does it increase?

__(c)__ The animation below shows a braking car whose wheels have locked: the tires are not rotating, and the car slides forward.

Is the friction between the tires and the road static or kinetic? Be careful: the tire isn't rotating, which might make it appear "static."

__(d)__ For a car tire on a dry asphalt road, typical coefficients are $$\mu_s=0.9$$ and $$\mu_k=0.7.$$ To stop as quickly as possible, should a car use static or kinetic friction? The animation below shows a car stopping with anti-lock brakes (ABS): the wheels keep rotating, rolling without sliding, all the way to a stop.

Even though this tire is rotating, the friction between it and the road is static. Explain why. Then explain how ABS — which automatically lightens up on the brakes just before the wheels lock — makes a car stop faster by braking __less__ hard.

label: MCH17
name: The Tilted Scale — Three rubber bears sit on a kitchen scale, which reads $$63\;\mathrm{g}.$$
desc: Three rubber bears sit on a kitchen scale, which reads $$63\;\mathrm{g}.$$ You then slowly tilt the whole scale, bears and all, to an angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, as in the clip below. The bears are rubbery enough that they don't slide. What happens to the reading?…
statement:
Three rubber bears sit on a kitchen scale, which reads $$63\;\mathrm{g}.$$

You then slowly tilt the whole scale, bears and all, to an angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, as in the clip below. The bears are rubbery enough that they don't slide. What happens to the reading?

__(a)__ As the scale tilts, does the mass of the bears change? Does their weight $$mg$$ change? If a scale always displayed the mass or the weight of its load, what would happen to the reading as the scale tilts?

__(b)__ Analyze the forces on the bears when the scale is tilted at angle $$\theta.$$ There are three: gravity $$mg$$ straight down, the __normal force__ $$N$$ from the scale's surface (perpendicular to the surface), and the friction force $$F_f$$ (parallel to the surface, pointing up the slope, keeping the bears from sliding). A useful trick is to tilt the coordinate system so the $$x$$ axis points along the incline; then the weight has component $$mg\sin\theta$$ along the slope and $$mg\cos\theta$$ perpendicular to it. The bears aren't accelerating. Find the magnitudes $$N$$ and $$F_f.$$

__(c)__ A scale measures forces pressing on its surface, so we should check whether it responds to forces __parallel__ to its surface (like the friction force) as well as perpendicular ones. Here is a test: the bears are clipped to a piece of twine, which runs over a pulley and is taped to the scale's top surface, so the twine can pull on the scale parallel to its surface.

With the clip and twine attached and the bears resting on top of the scale, it reads $$72\;\mathrm{g}.$$ When the bears instead hang from the twine as in the photo — so that they pull on the scale only parallel to its surface — it reads $$-2\;\mathrm{g}.$$ What does this test suggest about how the scale responds to forces parallel to its surface?

__(d)__ Putting it together: the scale's reading is proportional to the __normal__ force on its surface. Predict the reading as a function of the tilt angle $$\theta,$$ and state whether the reading rises, falls, or stays the same as the scale tilts.

label: MCH17
name: The Vibratory Feeder Bowl — The bowl below has a ramp spiraling up its inside wall, with a line of small…
desc: The bowl below has a ramp spiraling up its inside wall, with a line of small yellow parts on the ramp. Watch closely: the parts are marching __uphill__. These __vibratory feeder bowls__ are common in factories: pour in a bag of parts, and they sort themselves into a line and…
statement:
The bowl below has a ramp spiraling up its inside wall, with a line of small yellow parts on the ramp. Watch closely: the parts are marching __uphill__.

These __vibratory feeder bowls__ are common in factories: pour in a bag of parts, and they sort themselves into a line and climb the ramp, ready to be fed into a machine. Nothing visibly touches the parts — the only clue is that the bowl "hums," vibrating too fast to see. Model one part as a block resting on a ramp inclined at angle $$\theta,$$ as in the figure below, and suppose the static friction coefficient $$\mu_s$$ is large enough that the block stays put when the bowl is turned off.

You will need these facts. Static friction obeys $$F_f\le\mu_s N,$$ where $$N$$ is the normal force, and it opposes any potential slipping. The steepest incline on which a block can rest obeys $$\tan\theta=\mu_s.$$ By the __equivalence principle__, when the ramp accelerates with magnitude $$a,$$ everything on it behaves as if there were extra "artificial gravity" of strength $$a$$ pointing __opposite__ the acceleration. Finally, for a mass oscillating up and down on a spring, the upward acceleration is greatest at the bottom of the oscillation and the downward acceleration is greatest at the top.

__(a)__ What forces act on a part sitting on the ramp, and which of them could be pushing the parts up the ramp?

__(b)__ Suppose first that the ramp vibrates straight up and down in simple harmonic motion, like a mass on a spring. At what point in the oscillation is the normal force on the block greatest, and at what point is it smallest?

__(c)__ Use the formula $$\tan\theta=\mu_s$$ together with the equivalence principle to explain why purely vertical vibration never makes the block slip at all — no matter how large the amplitude — as long as the ramp's acceleration stays below $$g$$ (so the block never leaves the ramp).

__(d)__ Suppose instead the ramp vibrates horizontally. Explain why this, if anything, tends to move the block __down__ the ramp rather than up. (Consider the two halves of the cycle: artificial gravity pointing horizontally toward the downhill side, then toward the uphill side.)

__(e)__ Finally, suppose the ramp (which rises to the left in the figure) vibrates back and forth along a tilted axis: either axis A (up-and-to-the-right, then down-and-to-the-left) or axis B (up-and-to-the-left, then down-and-to-the-right). One of these makes the block climb the ramp in a series of tiny steps. Which one, and why?

label: MCH17
name: Two Horses or One? — The original Levi's logo shows two horses pulling on a pair of jeans in opposite…
desc: The original Levi's logo shows two horses pulling on a pair of jeans in opposite directions, one hitched to each leg, to advertise that the jeans are so strong they won't tear. A competitor advertises that its jeans hold up when just __one__ horse pulls on them, with the other…
statement:
The original Levi's logo shows two horses pulling on a pair of jeans in opposite directions, one hitched to each leg, to advertise that the jeans are so strong they won't tear.

A competitor advertises that its jeans hold up when just __one__ horse pulls on them, with the other leg tied to an immovable post. Assume every horse pulls equally hard, with force $$F,$$ and treat the jeans like a rope: they carry a tension equal to the magnitude of the force they exert on whatever pulls on them.

__(a)__ What is the tension in the Levi's jeans, with two horses each pulling with force $$F$$ in opposite directions? (Hint: apply Newton's third law to one horse at a time.)

__(b)__ What is the tension in the competitor's jeans, with one horse pulling with force $$F$$ against the post? Which feat is more impressive?

statement:
A string is tied to a post, runs horizontally a length $$L$$ to a pulley, passes over the pulley, and hangs straight down to a $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight, as in the photo below. Then a $$50\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight is hung from the midpoint of the horizontal stretch. The stretch sags into a shallow "V," string slides over the pulley, and everything settles into equilibrium. Use the standard rope model — in particular, the tension is constant along the whole string and the string's total length is fixed — and take $$g=10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ When the $$50\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight is hung on, will the $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight rise? Could even a $$1\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight lift the $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight this way?

__(b)__ Once the system reaches equilibrium, what is the tension $$T$$ in the string?

__(c)__ In equilibrium, each half of the sagging stretch makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal, as in the figure below. Both halves pull on the $$50\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight, and each pull has vertical component $$T\sin\theta.$$ Find $$\sin\theta.$$

__(d)__ The post and the pulley don't move, so the sagging stretch still spans the same horizontal distance $$L$$: if its new total length is $$\ell,$$ then $$\ell\cos\theta=L.$$ The extra length $$\ell-L$$ was fed over the pulley from the vertical side. How far does the $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight rise, in terms of $$L?$$ (You will need $$\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}.)$$

__(e)__ The midpoint of the stretch drops by $$\dfrac{L}{2}\tan\theta,$$ which is how far the $$50\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight falls. Let $$Y=\dfrac{-\Delta y_{50}}{\Delta y_{100}}$$ be the ratio of the $$50\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight's drop to the $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight's rise. Before calculating, explain why energy conservation requires $$Y\ge2.$$ Then compute $$Y,$$ and estimate what fraction of the potential energy released by the falling $$50\;\mathrm{g}$$ weight became thermal energy as the system shook its way to equilibrium.

statement:
Our phrasing of Newton's three laws was:

**First Law:** If there are no external forces on a system, then the velocity of its center of mass will not change.

**Second Law:** The acceleration of the center of mass of a system and the net force on a system are related by $$\vec{F}_{\rm net} = m \vec{a}_{\rm cm}$$ where $$m$$ is the total mass of the system.

**Third Law:** When systems $$A$$ and $$B$$ interact, there will be a force from system $$A$$ on system $$B$$ and a force from system $$B$$ on system $$A.$$ These forces are related by $$\vec{F}_{A \to B} = - \vec{F}_{B \to A}$$

Below is Isaac Newton's original phrasing of the three laws of motion (translated from Latin). They are presented in a random order.

**Description A** To every action, there is always opposed an equal reaction; or, the mutual actions of the two bodies upon each other are always equal, and directed to contrary parts.

**Description B** The change of motion of an object is proportional to the force impressed; and is made in the direction of the straight line in which force is impressed.

**Description C** Every body continues in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a straight line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impressed upon it.

Match Newton's descriptions to the law of motion. There is a one-to-one match up for this question.

Make two selections: - either (a) or (b) for what will happen - either (c), (d), or (e) for a reasonable explanation in terms of Newton's laws of motion

The potato will fall off the end of the knife.

After several strikes, the knife will poke through the bottom of the potato. The potato will be stuck on the knife.

Newton's first law says the potato doesn't accelerate unless there's force on it. The force from the knife on the potato is relatively small, so the potato doesn't move much and the knife moves downward through the potato.

Newton's second law says the downward force on the potato accelerates it downward, meaning it moves past the end of the knife and falls.

Newton's third law says that the potato exerts an upward force on the knife, so the knife accelerates upward away from the potato, making the potato fall.

Arbor Scientific

The car is very simple. It has a battery and an electric motor. There's an on/off switch. Once the car is turned on, it runs at nearly a constant velocity, as long as it's on a flat surface and is unobstructed.

Leymah and Tawakkul each have a constant velocity car. They line their cars up facing each other.

They turn the cars on so they push against each other.

Although the cars are all ostensibly the same, there will always be slight differences between cars during the manufacturing process, or two cars' batteries may supply slightly different voltages, etc. This means that when Leymah and Tawakkul's cars push on each other, they won't necessarily be deadlocked. **Leymah** says, "I will add some mass to my car. Then it will be harder to push out of the way and it will win if we do this again."

A few more voices chime in:

**Kailash** says, "Increasing the mass on Leymah's car will increase the friction force on it. That makes it harder for the car to go forward, so putting mass on Leymah's car makes it more likely to lose."

statement:
Part A. This week, we'll work on the setup of an experiment to test Newton's second law. We'll conduct the experiment and analyze the results in next week's homework.

----------------

Below is a child's toy schoolbus. To use it, a child can pull it backward while keeping the wheels on the ground. When released, the schoolbus rolls forward.

This toy does not have batteries, an electric motor, etc.

The further back the child (or physicist) pulls the bus backwards, the further it travels forward across the floor when released.

Over this multi-part problem, we will work through an experiment to investigate the motion of the bus, and review some ideas about force and energy.

To begin, let's think about what the models of motion we've studied so far tell us about the operation of the bus.

Which one of the following statements about the bus agrees with our models of motion?

By conservation of energy, the bus cannot go forward further than it is pulled backward.

By Newton's third law, when a child pulls backward on the bus, the bus exerts a forward force on the child.

While a child is exerting a backward force and pulling the bus backward, friction from the floor is exerting a forward force on the bus. Because the bus is going backwards, we know that the child's force is greater than the friction force.

By conservation of momentum, the bus cannot go forward without something else going backward at the same speed.

The child exerts a backward force to pull the bus backward, and by Newton's third law, when the child releases the bus an equal and opposite forward force takes over to push the bus forward.

left align

Part B. Inside the bus isThe actual spring inside the toy looks a little different than the springs we're used to, but model it as the type of spring we're used to for the purpose of this problem which does not necessarily obey Hooke's law. As the child pulls the bus backward, the spring gets compressed, storing elastic potential energy.

Inside the bus, gears and other mechanisms link the rotation of the wheels to the compression of the spring. The amount the spring is compressed is proportional to how far the bus is pulled back.

We pull the bus backward at constant velocity with a pulling force $$\vec{F}_{\rm pull}$$ that is parallel to the ground. The wheels do not slip.

At the same time that we exert force $$\vec{F}_{\rm pull},$$ the spring exerts a force $$\vec{F}_{\rm spring}$$ on the mechanism it's connected to.

What is the relationship between the magnitudes $$F_{\rm pull}$$ and $$F_{\rm spring}?$$

Ignore any friction forces and assume that no mechanical energy is lost.

You may want to briefly review the gif in part (A) while answering this question.

$$F_{\rm pull} > F_{\rm spring}$$

$$F_{\rm pull} = F_{\rm spring}$$

$$F_{\rm pull} < F_{\rm spring}$$

abc

new lines

Part C. We would like to use the bus to test Newton's second law of motion, $$\vec{F}_{\rm net} = m\vec{a}$$

We can add mass to the bus by placing items inside it. Then we can run the bus with varying amount of mass and observe the motion.

Friction from the ground will push the bus forward, but we don't know what the magnitude $$F_{\rm push}$$ of that friction force will be as the bus moves forward.

We decide to measure $$F_{\rm push}$$ before designing an experiment on Newton's second law.

Which one of these procedures would **not** let us determine the general shape of the force extension curve for the spring in the bus?

Assume each step is feasible. Judge only whether the procedure measures $$F_{\rm push}$$ or not.

**(a)** Take the spring out of the bus. Put it on the scale and If the weight of the spring is $$0.05 \;\mathrm{N},$$ the scale will read $$0.05 \;\mathrm{N}$$ when we put the spring on it. When we press down on the spring with $$0.10 \;\mathrm{N}$$ more force, the scale will read $$0.15 \;\mathrm{N},$$ so its reading is higher than the force we exert. Instead, we can put the spring on the scale, then press the "tare" button. The scale will read zero, and when we press down on the spring with $$10 \;\mathrm{N}$$ of force, the scale will read $$10 \;\mathrm{N}.$$with the spring uncompressed. Then press down on the top of the spring with varying forces.

For each force, record how much the spring is compressed and the reading on the scale. Take the scale readings as measurements of $$F_{\rm push}.$$

**(b)** Start the bus stationary on the floor. Push it backward a fixed distance using just our hands. Put the scale on the front of the bus, allowing the bus to push forward against the scale. Gradually pull the scale backwards. The bus will roll forward to continue pressing against the scale.

Stop periodically to read the scale and record how far the bus has rolled forward. Continue until the bus no longer pushes up against the scale. Use the scale readings at $$F_{\rm push}.$$

**(c)** Start the bus stationary on a table. Pull the bus backward a fixed distance. Set up a pulley at the edge of the table, and a box on a string of negligible mass hanging off the pulley. Tie the other end of the string to the back of the bus, resembling a half Atwood machine.

Allow the bus to move forward small amounts. Each time, stop the bus and adjust the mass in the box until it remains stationary, held by the tension in the string. After each measurement, record how far the bus has moved and use the scale to find the weight of the box. Take the weight of the box as $$F_{\rm push}.$$

(a)

(b)

(c)

Part D. To measure $$F_{\rm push},$$ we placed a kitchen scale in front of the bus. To secure the scale at a fixed angle, we tied it to a stack of books. The entire assembly is in a cardboard box to allow us to slide it back and forth. (We had to try several iterations before finding a setup that gave reasonably consistent results.)

We pulled the bus back $$33 \;\mathrm{in}$$ (inches), then allowed it to roll forward until it no longer pressed against the scale. We recorded the scale reading after $$11\;\mathrm{in}.$$ (The readings are in multiples of $$11\;\mathrm{in}$$ because we used $$11\;\mathrm{in}$$ sheets of notebook paper as a distance measurement, rather than a tape measure or meter stick.)

The scale reading was in grams, which we converted to newtons assuming $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ We also converted $${}d$$ to meters.

We repeated the measurement four times and averaged the results. A plot of $$F_{\rm push}$$ is below.

--------------

In this problem, you'll use knowledge of $$F_{\rm push}$$ to design an experiment to test Newton's second law.

We can assume that the mass of the bus doesn't affect $$F_{\rm push}.$$ This is because $$F_{\rm push}$$ is proportional to $$F_{\rm spring},$$ which should depend only on the state of the spring, not the motion of the bus or other features of the bus. (This also assumes the wheels don't slip relative to the floor.)

However, as the data in the reading problem above shows, we cannot assume that $$F_{\rm push}$$ is constant, or that it obeys Hooke's law.

We want to test the idea $$ F_{\rm net} = ma $$

We won't measure force directly in the second phase of the experiment; that is impractical when the bus is moving. Instead, we'll test whether $$ a \propto \dfrac{1}{m} $$ which is a consequence of Newton's second law.

All of the following procedures would work to test this proportionality if $$F_{\rm push}$$ were constant, but instead, let's make the following assumptions:

- $$F_{\rm push}$$ is not constant. - $$F_{\rm push}$$ depends only on $$d.$$ - The plot of $$F_{\rm push}$$ versus $${}d$$ is the same in every trial. - Newton's second law of motion is correct. - For this analysis, we ignore the error in our measurements of $$a$$ and $$m.$$

**Given these assumptions, which __one__ of the proposed procedures will give $$a \propto \dfrac{1}{m}?$$**

We are not asking whether $$a$$ described in the procedures below is the true acceleration of the bus, or whether it is truly the average acceleration of the bus over time, etc. Instead, we are asking whether the quantity we will record as $$a,$$ as described in the procedures below, will be related to mass via $$a \propto \dfrac{1}{m}.$$

**(a)** Pull the bus back $$1 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in every trial. Release the bus from rest and let it run for $$2.0 \;\mathrm{s}.$$ Record $$d,$$ the distance the bus travels in $$2.0 \;\mathrm{s}.$$

The formula $$d = \dfrac12 at^2$$ is equivalent to $$a = \dfrac{2d}{t^2}$$ so plug in $${}d$$ and $$t = 2.0 \;\mathrm{s}$$ to find $$a.$$ Use the scale to find the mass $$m$$ of the bus and record that as well.

Repeat several times to get a sense of the uncertainty in the distance measurements.

Then put various items inside the bus to change its mass. Repeat the procedure, collecting new data. In each trial, we fix the time at $$t = 2.0 \;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$d$$ varies due to the changing mass. Each trial ultimately results in one value of $${}a$$ and one value of $${}m,$$ along with their uncertainties, for each mass of the bus we test.

Although the acceleration of the bus may vary over a single trial, we treat the $$a$$ value calculated in this procedure as an average acceleration over the trial, and then test whether $$a \propto \dfrac{1}{m}.$$

**(b)** Everything in this procedure is the same as in (a), with one difference. In (a), we let the bus run for a fixed time (always $$2.0 \;\mathrm{s})$$ and measured how far it traveled. Here we always let the bus travel $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ forward, and we measure the time this takes using a stopwatch. The $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ distance is chosen because this is about how far the bus can travel forward and still have $$F_{\rm push} > 0.$$

Aside from this change, do everything the same way as in (a).

**(c)**

This procedure is similar to (a) and (b), but we do not fix $${}d$$ or $${}t.$$ Every trial, we pull the bus back $$1 \;\mathrm{m}$$ and release it, but we let the bus travel as far as we like and time how long it takes. We let the bus go a wide variety of distances to get more different data points.

Aside from this change, everything else is the same as procedures (a) and (b). We use different masses, we use our distance and time measurements to calculate $$a$$ for each trial with the same formula, etc.

(a)

(b)

(c)

statement:
A car is driving to the right along a straight, level road when the driver hits the brakes, and the car begins to slow down.

__(a)__ While the car is braking, what direction does the net force on the car point, and what kind of force is it? Do objects always move in the same direction as the net force on them?

__(b)__ What kinematic quantity __does__ always point in the same direction as the net force on an object? Write the equation that relates the two. (This relationship is called __Newton's second law__.)

__(c)__ In each diagram below, an object moves with velocity $$\vec{v}$$ while a net force $$\vec{F}$$ acts on it. Classify each diagram according to what is happening to the __speed__ of the object: increasing, decreasing, or not changing. If an angle looks like a right angle, assume it is a right angle. Do the magnitudes of $$\vec{v}$$ and $$\vec{F}$$ matter for this classification, or only the angle between them?

__(d)__ Below, a car brakes hard — and its hood flies forward off the car. A puzzled bystander asks, "What force threw the hood forward?" Answer the bystander's question. The principle involved — velocity does not change unless there is a force — is called __Newton's first law__.

__(e)__ While the car brakes, the road exerts a backward friction force on the car. What force does the braking car exert on the road? The general rule, $$\vec{F}_{A \to B} = -\vec{F}_{B \to A},$$ is called __Newton's third law__.

label: MCH18

desc: __Neutrinos__ are light subatomic particles created in nuclear reactions. They travel near the speed of light, and they have almost no interaction with other matter — a neutrino can zip straight through the entire Earth without noticing it at all. __(a)__ Newton's first law says…
statement:
__Neutrinos__ are light subatomic particles created in nuclear reactions. They travel near the speed of light, and they have almost no interaction with other matter — a neutrino can zip straight through the entire Earth without noticing it at all.

__(a)__ Newton's first law says that an object's velocity does not change unless a force acts on it. What does the trajectory of a neutrino look like — a spiral, a circle, a parabola, or a straight line? Explain.

__(b)__ Physicists detect neutrinos with enormous detectors like Super-Kamiokande, a giant tank of purified water buried about $$1\;\mathrm{km}$$ underground near Hida, Japan. A very small percentage of the neutrinos passing through the tank collide with a water molecule, and detectors lining the walls record the light given off when that happens.

Given that such collisions occur, are neutrinos a __perfect__ example of Newton's first law? Can you think of anything that is?

desc: In the movie "How the Grinch Stole Christmas," the Grinch grabs a tablecloth set with dishes and candles and yanks it downward and toward himself — and the stuff stays on the table, barely moving. To analyze the trick, model the tablecloth as being pulled horizontally to the…
statement:
In the movie "How the Grinch Stole Christmas," the Grinch grabs a tablecloth set with dishes and candles and yanks it downward and toward himself — and the stuff stays on the table, barely moving.

To analyze the trick, model the tablecloth as being pulled horizontally to the left from under the "stuff" on the table, as shown below.

__(a)__ Newton's third law says that when systems $$A$$ and $$B$$ interact, $$\vec{F}_{A \to B} = -\vec{F}_{B \to A}.$$ We call such a pair of forces a __third-law pair__. Someone might guess the stuff should fly away from the Grinch "because of Newton's third law." What force actually forms a third-law pair with the force the Grinch exerts on the tablecloth? Which of Newton's laws actually explains why the stuff barely moves?

__(b)__ Watching closely, the stuff does slide a little bit as the cloth is pulled out. What kind of force from the tablecloth makes the stuff slide: normal, static friction, kinetic friction, gravitational, or elastic? How do you know?

__(c)__ A student says, "Kinetic friction opposes the motion. The tablecloth is moving left, so the kinetic friction is to the right." This is vague: there are __two__ kinetic friction forces at the tablecloth–stuff surface, and they form a third-law pair. Identify both forces. Which one points to the right? Which direction is the kinetic friction force __on the stuff__?

__(d)__ The student objects: "But the stuff moves to the left. To oppose the motion, the friction on the stuff should point right. What's going on?" Resolve the confusion: exactly what motion does kinetic friction oppose?

__(e)__ If the Grinch had pulled the tablecloth slowly rather than quickly, what would have happened to the stuff, and why?

desc: A tennis racket is coated with loose powder, which simply sits on the strings (it is not sticky). Someone throws a tennis ball at the racket, and we watch in slow motion as the ball strikes and the racket suddenly deflects downward. __(a)__ When the racket suddenly moves…
statement:
A tennis racket is coated with loose powder, which simply sits on the strings (it is not sticky). Someone throws a tennis ball at the racket, and we watch in slow motion as the ball strikes and the racket suddenly deflects downward.

__(a)__ When the racket suddenly moves downward, what does the powder do? Which of Newton's laws explains this? (Newton's first law: an object's velocity does not change unless a force acts on it.)

__(b)__ After the racket drops away, the powder appears to hang motionless in the air for a split second before falling. Does the powder really have zero acceleration for a while before it begins to fall, or is it accelerating the whole time? Explain how your answer is consistent with what the video looks like.

__(c)__ The powder that was directly underneath the ball moves much more suddenly than the rest, roiling and swirling right after the impact — even powder the ball never touched. That roiling must be caused by forces. Forces from what?

__(d)__ Here is a kid jumping onto a trampoline that is covered with fallen leaves. Using the same reasoning as above, predict what happens.

name: The Skateboarder on the Truck — A skateboarder stands on his board in the bed of a stationary flatbed truck.
desc: A skateboarder stands on his board in the bed of a stationary flatbed truck. The truck suddenly starts driving forward (to the left in the clip below) — and the skateboarder falls off the back. __(a)__ The driver asks, "The skateboarder fell off the back. What force pushed him…
statement:
A skateboarder stands on his board in the bed of a stationary flatbed truck.

The truck suddenly starts driving forward (to the left in the clip below) — and the skateboarder falls off the back.

__(a)__ The driver asks, "The skateboarder fell off the back. What force pushed him backward?" Is there any backward force on the skateboarder? Describe the skateboarder's horizontal motion as seen from the ground, and name the law of motion that accounts for it. The skateboarder does drift forward slightly — what force causes that? (Ignore the details of the rolling skateboard wheels.)

__(b)__ Now imagine the skateboarder lying down flat in the truck bed instead. Call the original clip scenario $$A$$ and the lying-down version scenario $$B.$$ In $$B,$$ friction holds the skateboarder, and he accelerates along with the truck. Assume the truck accelerates the same way in both scenarios. The force that accelerates the truck is friction from the road on the truck. In which scenario is that road-friction force greater? Explain by considering the forces on just the truck itself, using Newton's second and third laws.

__(c)__ In the driver's reference frame, the skateboarder in scenario $$A$$ accelerates backward — yet the only horizontal force on him, the small friction from the truck, points forward. This seems to violate Newton's second law, $$\vec{F}_{\rm net}=m\vec{a}.$$ Resolve the paradox. In what kind of reference frames do Newton's laws apply? What are the made-up forces called that one must invent to patch up Newton's second law in the driver's frame?

__(d)__ Later, the truck is moving at __constant__ velocity, and the skateboarder wants to do a kickflip on the truck bed. Is the trick any harder than on the ground? Justify your answer two ways: using the principle of relativity, and by considering how adding a constant velocity $$\vec{v}_{\rm truck}$$ to the skater and board affects $$\vec{a}=\dfrac{\Delta\vec{v}}{\Delta t}$$ and hence the forces required.

statement:
A boxer can hit hard when striking a heavy punching bag hung from chains.

Now imagine the boxer punches a single sheet of toilet paper hanging in midair instead. The boxer is no weaker or slower when punching the paper.

__(a)__ Which can the boxer hit with more force — the punching bag or the paper?

__(b)__ A friend explains: "Newton's second law says $$\vec{F}_{\rm net}=m\vec{a}.$$ The paper has very little mass, so the forces on it must be small." When punched, which undergoes the greater acceleration — the bag or the paper? Use your answer to explain why the friend's argument, as stated, is incomplete.

__(c)__ Instead of analyzing the force from the hand on the paper directly, consider a different force that must have the same magnitude. Use that force, together with the observed motion of the boxer's hand, to give a complete argument that the boxer cannot exert much force on the paper.

label: MCH18
name: The Ball Race — Two tracks sit side by side. One is flat in the middle; the other has a dip in the…
desc: Two tracks sit side by side. One is flat in the middle; the other has a dip in the middle. A ball is placed at the top left of each track, and the two balls are released simultaneously, racing to the far end. Call the ball on the flat-middle track $$F$$ and the ball on the…
statement:
Two tracks sit side by side. One is flat in the middle; the other has a dip in the middle. A ball is placed at the top left of each track, and the two balls are released simultaneously, racing to the far end. Call the ball on the flat-middle track $$F$$ and the ball on the dipped track $$D.$$ Model the tracks as frictionless and ignore the rolling of the balls (this simplifies the forces without changing anything important). Which ball wins the race?

__(a)__ The balls begin at the same height and end at the same height. Use conservation of energy to compare their speeds at the end of the track. Does your answer mean the race is a tie?

__(b)__ Is the momentum of either ball conserved during the race?

__(c)__ The figure below shows a ball on a flat section of track with the two forces acting on it: a gravitational force of magnitude $$mg$$ downward and a normal force $$\vec{N}$$ from the track. What is the magnitude of the normal force? Are the normal force and the gravitational force on the ball a __third-law pair__ — that is, a pair of forces obeying $$\vec{F}_{A\to B}=-\vec{F}_{B\to A}?$$ If not, what is the actual third-law pair of each force?

__(d)__ Now ball $$D$$ rolls down the slope into the dip, as shown below, moving with velocity $$\vec{v}$$ along the track. Which of the two forces on the ball is different than on the flat section? The ball speeds up as it descends — which force is responsible for the increase in speed, and what does the other force do? (Recall from the slope angle $$\theta$$ that gravity has a component $$mg\sin\theta$$ parallel to the track.)

__(e)__ Write the velocity of ball $$D$$ as $$\vec{v}_D = v_{Dx}\,\hat{x} + v_{Dy}\,\hat{y},$$ where $$x$$ is horizontal (the direction of the race) and $$y$$ is vertical. Which quantity — the speed $$v_D,$$ the component $$v_{Dx},$$ or the component $$v_{Dy}$$ — is the most important one for deciding who is ahead in the race? (Hint: imagine watching the race from directly overhead.)

__(f)__ As ball $$D$$ enters the dip, which force changes $$v_{Dx}?$$ Does $$v_{Dx}$$ increase or decrease? Use your answers to determine which ball wins the race. (Assume the dip is gentle enough that the balls never fly off the track.)

statement:
Part A. A ball of mass $$m$$ sits on a frictionless table. The ball is connected to a string of length $$\ell.$$ The other side of the string is connected to the table and cannot move. The string is initially stretched tight with no slack.

An external constant force $$\vec{F}$$ is applied to the ball. This force is not initially aligned with the direction of the string. However, the angle $$\theta$$ between $$\vec{F}$$ and the string obeys $$\theta \ll 1.$$

These pictures are both top views, looking down on the table from above.

Due to the force $$\vec{F},$$ the ball will accelerate. As the ball accelerates, the same constant force $$\vec{F}$$ is applied to the ball, regardless of its position. There will also be a tension force $$\vec{T}$$ from the string on the ball. The magnitude $$T$$ of the tension may vary.

We will use our standard model for a string - it is massless and can't change length, and the tension it exerts always points in the direction of the string.

Gravity and a normal force from the table will cancel out and don't need to be modeled here.

name: Part A. Last week, we looked at a toy bus powered by a spring inside.
desc: Part A. Last week, we looked at a toy bus powered by a spring inside. To test Newton's second law of motion, we repeated the following procedure: 1. Begin with the bus at a marked spot on the floor with the spring completely uncompressed. 2. Pull the bus backward $$0.83…
statement:
Part A. Last week, we looked at a toy bus powered by a spring inside.

To test Newton's second law of motion, we repeated the following procedure:

1. Begin with the bus at a marked spot on the floor with the spring completely uncompressed. 2. Pull the bus backward $$0.83 \;\mathrm{m},$$ pushing down while pulling back to ensure the wheels do not slip. This winds the spring inside the bus. 3. Release the bus. It accelerates forward, pushed by friction from the floor. 4. Allow the bus to accelerate forward until it hits a rolled-up carpet. The carpet was placed $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from the point where the bus was released. Time how long it takes the bus to reach the carpet. 5. Repeat four more time (five times total) to get a sense of the spread in the data.

We conducted this entire procedure, then added some household items to the bus to increase its mass, then repeated the procedure. (We model the bus and the items inside as a single system.)

We did this for six different masses, using a kitchen scale to record the mass.

We measured distances using pieces of notebook paper laid end-to-end on the floor.

The data we collected is below $$ \begin{array}{c | c | c | c} \text{ m (g)} & \bar{t} \,\,(\mathrm{s}) & \sigma_t \,\,(\mathrm{s})\\ \hline 467 & 1.56 & 0.06 \\ 615 & 1.83 & 0.03 \\ 712 & 2.01 & 0.05 \\ 994 & 2.56 & 0.07 \\ 1261 & 3.17 & 0.05 \\ 1386 & 3.55 & 0.04 \end{array} $$

$$m$$ is the total mass of the bus plus any items inside it. The mass of the bus alone was $$467 \;\mathrm{g}.$$

$$\bar{t}$$ is the average time it took the bus to travel $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from rest.

$$\sigma_t$$ is the standard deviation of the times we collected.

The uncertainty in the mass is approximately $$1 \;\mathrm{g},$$ which is small enough to ignore.

Make a plot of this data, including error bars. You may want to attempt a best-fit line as well.

Use the plot you draw to select the best description from below.

There are only six data points, so if you notice a slight or subtle curvature, it could be due to random error added on top of a linear model. Only select option (c) or (d) if the curvature is large and obvious at a quick glance, so that random error could not reasonably explain it.

The data appears roughly linear, and a best fit line goes through most or all error bars.

The data appears nearly linear, but no line can go through most of the error bars.

The data has a large and obvious curve downward.

The data has a large and obvious curve upward.

This means we can find the relationship between variables like $$a,$$ the acceleration of the bus, $$t,$$ the time for the bus to complete a given distance, and $$m,$$ the mass of the bus, assuming the force on the bus is constant.

We would like to make a plot with $$m$$ on the horizontal axis, and the vertical axis chosen so that the plot should be linear, assuming our model accurately describes the data.

Recall that we are assuming Newton's second law is true, the distance $${}d$$ of each trial is the same, and that the force on the bus is constant over the experiment.

Because the bus starts at rest, we can then describe its motion in any given trial using $$d = \dfrac12 a t^2$$

Part D. The data in part (A) does not match the predicted shape from part (B). Also, the plot in the solution to part (C) is clearly not linear. In this question, you'll select explanations that could theoretically explain why the data don't match the theory in this experiment.

Here, we aren't judging whether the explanations are likely. Instead, we're judging whether, if they were correct, logically they would explain why our data didn't match our predictions.

For example, another explanation, not included below, is that all the distance measurements are wrong. We assumed each piece of paper was $$11 \;\mathrm{in}$$ long, some paper is $$11.7 \;\mathrm{in}$$ long. If we had the wrong type of paper, all our distance measurements would be too long by about $$6\%.$$ If that explanation were included on the list, you should not select it. The reason is that adjusting all the distance measurements would adjust all the accelerations we calculate, but it would adjust them all by the same factor. It wouldn't affect the overall shape of the graph. Therefore, while this error in the experiment is possible, it can't explain the data in part (C) not being linear.

On the other hand, another explanation could be that the distance measurements were wrong in random ways because the paper we used to make measurements slid around on the floor without us noticing. In that case, the explanation is very broad, and there exists some type of sliding of the papers at various points in the experiment that would affect our distance measurements in the right way to make the data in part (C) look like it does, instead of a straight line. This explanation isn't very likely, since we would probably have noticed the paper sliding around that much, but logically it's a conceivable explanation. If that explanation were included in the list below, it would be counted as a possible explanation.

Which one of the following could theoretically explain why the data don't match theoretical predictions in this experiment?

The question isn't asking which of (a) through (d) is likely. Instead, it's asking which, if it were true (however implausible), could potentially explain why the data and theory don't match.

**(a)** The bus is driven forward by friction on its back wheels. On the front wheels, there was a constant backward force from friction, but we neglected that. If we had included a constant backward force in our model, the theoretical prediction in part (B) would change to a good match for the data in part (A), assuming we chose the magnitude of the backward force correctly.

**(b)** We assumed $$F_{\rm push}$$ was constant, but we know it actually varied over the course of a run. We could build a new model where $$F_{\rm push}$$ varies, but the plot of $$F_{\rm push}$$ versus $$d$$ is the same for every trial. If we did that, it would change the prediction to be a good match to the data.

**(c)** The framework of Newtonian mechanics is not a good model for the acceleration of the bus.

**(d)** When the bus's mass is low, static friction with the floor is not always high enough to keep the wheels from slipping. The wheels slip a bit at low mass, relaxing the spring and lowering the force pushing the bus forward. The wheels do not slip when the bus has high mass. We don't know the exact extent of the slipping, but it means we would need to model the force as a decreasing function of the mass of the bus, rather than a constant. With this modification to the model, it would be possible to get predictions that closely match the data.

name: An example of slip-stick motion you may be able to reproduce at home is a __glass harp__.
desc: An example of slip-stick motion you may be able to reproduce at home is a __glass harp__. Take a clean wine glass, and make sure your hands are clean as well. Wet your index finger and rub in a steady circle around the rim of a wine glass. With some practice, you should be able…
statement:
An example of slip-stick motion you may be able to reproduce at home is a __glass harp__.

Take a clean wine glass, and make sure your hands are clean as well. Wet your index finger and rub in a steady circle around the rim of a wine glass.

With some practice, you should be able to hear the glass play a note. You can pour water in the glass to change the note it plays.

To find the frequency your cup is playing, you could use a smartphone app such as PhyPhox or PhysicsToolbox. You may also have an electric tuner at home, or if you have a piano or other instrument, you could play notes on that instrument until you match the frequency of your wineglass, then look up the frequency. You could also use your computer or tablet and any digital instrument tuner webpage, either to detect the pitch using your computer's microphone, or to generate pitches of different frequencies until you match your wine glass.

**(a)** Can you find a relationship between the total mass of the cup and the frequency played? There should be a clean quantitative relationship here, and you should be able to relate it back to our understanding of harmonic oscillators. What data did you collect to answer this question, and how did you analyze the data?

**(b)** Is there a relationship between how fast you have to move your finger and the frequency? If the finger is undergoing slip-stick motion, we expect faster motion of the finger to lead to higher frequency. Our class calculation estimating the frequency of slip-stick motion in a violin is an example. (Your class may or may not have done this calculation, depending on time. If not, feel free to ask on the message boards for the relevant bit of bonus material on this topic.) Do you still get a clean quantitative relationship between finger speed and frequency, and is it the relationship you expect? Again, tell your classmates how you investigated this question and share your data.

statement:
Part A. This gif shows a parachutist opening their parachute.

The camera operator was a second parachutist falling alongside the one in the clip. The camera operator opened their parachute after the clip ends. Model the camera operator as having constant velocity the entire time.

Below, "parachutist" refers to the parachutist visible in the clip, not to the camera operator.

The parachutist was at terminal velocity before opening their parachute. Model the parachutist and their parachute together as a single system.

**Charles** says: "The net force on the parachutist was close to zero just before the parachute opened, but upward just after it opened."

**Haruta** says: "By Newton's second law, the parachutist had an upward acceleration just after opening their parachute."

**Una** says: "Acceleration is a change in velocity. That's why the parachutist went from falling downward to having an upward velocity in the reference frame of the ground during the clip."

**Talia** says: "No, the parachutist seems to gain a velocity upward in the clip, but that's from the reference frame of the camera operator. In the reference frame of the ground, the parachutist's velocity was downward the entire time, even when the net force on them was upward."

**Esme** says: "And we shouldn't try to apply Newton's laws in the reference frame of the camera operator. Since they're moving, it's an accelerated frame and Newton's laws don't apply without special modifications."

For each statement, explain whether it agrees with our models of Newtonian mechanics. If you decide it disagrees, explain where. If you decide it agrees, explain how you made that decision. You should write between one and three sentences for each statement.

label: MCH19
name: Steady Currents, Sudden Earthquakes — During a large earthquake, the ground shakes violently for seconds to…
desc: During a large earthquake, the ground shakes violently for seconds to minutes. Earthquakes happen at __faults__ — places where two huge pieces of Earth's crust slide past each other. The animation below shows a __strike-slip fault__, where the two pieces slide past each other…
statement:
During a large earthquake, the ground shakes violently for seconds to minutes. Earthquakes happen at __faults__ — places where two huge pieces of Earth's crust slide past each other. The animation below shows a __strike-slip fault__, where the two pieces slide past each other horizontally. The motion comes in sudden, irregular bursts; each burst is an earthquake.

What drives this motion? The crust (together with the very top of the mantle) forms the __lithosphere__. Beneath it lies the rest of the __mantle__, where rocks are so hot they are molten. Heated rock expands, and this drives giant __convection currents__ — a slow circulation of molten rock, shown below. Convection is gradual and steady: the speeds are a few centimeters per year, and the masses involved are so great that any acceleration is minuscule.

__(a)__ The convection currents are the ultimate cause of the crust's motion. State the puzzle: comparing how the currents move with how the crust moves during earthquakes, what needs explaining?

__(b)__ A great deal of energy is released in an earthquake, but convection delivers energy to the crust only slowly and steadily. In what form, and where, is that energy stored during the years just before an earthquake? (A clue: rock is slightly elastic. The clip below shows an earthquake scientist squeezing two sides of a rock and letting them rebound. The motion is subtle, but built up over kilometers of rock, it amounts to a lot of deformation.)

__(c)__ Build a simple tabletop model of a fault out of a wooden block, a sheet of sandpaper underneath it, and a spring connecting the block to a wall. The sandpaper is pulled out from under the block at a slow, steady speed. Describe the motion of the block over time, and say which part of the model plays the role of (i) the steady convection currents, (ii) the friction between the pieces of crust, and (iii) the crust's stored energy. (The clip below shows such a model, with the sandpaper mounted on a motorized belt so it can run continuously.)

__(d)__ Consider four features of real earthquakes: their sudden release of energy, their gradual buildup, the fact that they recur in the same places over and over, and the fact that they are highly irregular and unpredictable. Which of these does the simple one-block model capture, and which does it miss?

label: MCH19
name: When Does the Block Slip? — Here is a quantitative version of the slip-stick model of an earthquake fault. A…
desc: Here is a quantitative version of the slip-stick model of an earthquake fault. A block of mass $$m$$ rests on a sheet of sandpaper. A spring with spring constant $$k$$ connects the block to a wall. The sandpaper is pulled to the right at a slow, steady speed $$v.$$ The…
statement:
Here is a quantitative version of the slip-stick model of an earthquake fault. A block of mass $$m$$ rests on a sheet of sandpaper. A spring with spring constant $$k$$ connects the block to a wall. The sandpaper is pulled to the right at a slow, steady speed $$v.$$ The coefficient of static friction between the block and the sandpaper is $$\mu_s.$$ Let $$x$$ be the position of the center of the block, with $$x=0$$ at the block's initial position, where the spring is unstretched.

Two facts about the forces: a static friction force can have any magnitude up to $$\mu_s N,$$ where $$N$$ is the normal force pressing the surfaces together ($$N = mg$$ here, since the surface is horizontal and nothing else pushes down on the block); and a spring stretched by $$\Delta x$$ pulls with a force of magnitude $$k\,\Delta x.$$ (As a vector the spring force is $$\vec{f} = -k\,\Delta\vec{x},$$ but only magnitudes are needed in this problem.)

__(a)__ The spring starts unstretched. Describe the block's motion during the first stretch of time after the sandpaper starts moving.

__(b)__ At the moment the block is just about to slip, which two forces on the block are equal in magnitude? Use this to find $$\Delta x_{\rm max},$$ the stretch of the spring at the moment the block begins to slip.

__(c)__ In this model, every "earthquake" begins with the spring at the same stretch $$\Delta x_{\rm max},$$ so all the slips are about the same size — unlike real earthquakes, which vary enormously in size. Explain why the slips are always the same size in this model.

__(d)__ One way to get earthquakes of varying sizes is to use __two__ blocks, each pulled through its own spring, with different friction coefficients, as in the clip below. The masses and spring constants are the same for both blocks. In the clip, the red block slips frequently, before the springs stretch very much, while the blue block slips only once in a while. Which block has the higher coefficient of static friction?

label: MCH19
name: The Gutenberg–Richter Law and the Limits of Prediction — Real earthquakes come in a huge range of sizes…
desc: Real earthquakes come in a huge range of sizes: small tremors are common, while massive quakes are rare. The plot below shows data on earthquakes in one region. The horizontal axis is earthquake magnitude, and the vertical axis is the number of earthquakes of at least that…
statement:
Real earthquakes come in a huge range of sizes: small tremors are common, while massive quakes are rare. The plot below shows data on earthquakes in one region. The horizontal axis is earthquake magnitude, and the vertical axis is the number of earthquakes of at least that magnitude. The red curve is the __Gutenberg–Richter law__, a mathematical equation Gutenberg and Richter published in 1944 to fit data like this — at the time, with no physical model behind it.

__(a)__ Reading from the plot, there were about $$350$$ earthquakes of magnitude at least $$3.0,$$ about $$50$$ of magnitude at least $$4.0,$$ and about $$7$$ of magnitude at least $$5.0.$$ What happens to the count each time the magnitude increases by $$1.0?$$ State the general pattern that the Gutenberg–Richter law describes.

__(b)__ In 1989, Per Bak and Chao Tang built a model of earthquakes (a similar model dates back to 1967). It is a slip-stick model with many blocks: an array of little blocks rests on a floor, with friction between each block and the floor. Each block is connected by springs to its neighboring blocks, and by another spring to a top sheet that moves steadily sideways. One piece of the model is sketched below. When one block slips, why might its neighbors slip too?

__(c)__ In Bak and Tang's model, sometimes a single block slips (a tiny tremor), sometimes a few nearby blocks slip together, and once in a while a huge chunk of blocks slips at once (a massive earthquake). The model reproduces the Gutenberg–Richter law. Moreover, if you run the model twice with nearly identical — but not exactly identical — initial positions of the blocks, the first few earthquakes look very similar, but before long the two runs look completely different. Does this model help scientists predict earthquakes? What does it suggest about earthquake prediction in the real world?

name: The Slip-Stick Frequency of a Violin — __Slip-stick motion__ is a repeating cycle in which friction holds two…
desc: __Slip-stick motion__ is a repeating cycle in which friction holds two surfaces together while elastic potential energy builds up gradually, until the surfaces suddenly slip and release the energy. It powers earthquakes — and also bowed string instruments. When a violinist draws…
statement:
__Slip-stick motion__ is a repeating cycle in which friction holds two surfaces together while elastic potential energy builds up gradually, until the surfaces suddenly slip and release the energy. It powers earthquakes — and also bowed string instruments. When a violinist draws a bow across a string, friction between the bow hair and the string (violinists rub the sticky substance __rosin__ on their bows to increase this friction) drags the string sideways. The string itself plays the role of the spring: it is elastic, so being dragged sideways stretches it slightly and stores potential energy until it slips back. The steadily moving bow plays the same role as the steady convection currents that drive earthquakes.

__(a)__ The clip above shows a violinist playing in real time. A violin bow is about $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, and the violinist takes about $$2\;\mathrm{s}$$ to draw the full length of the bow across the string. Estimate the speed of the bow.

__(b)__ The clip above is a slow-motion close-up of a bow crossing a string: the string is repeatedly dragged along with the bow and snaps back. Because the clip is slowed down, you cannot simply time the cycles with a stopwatch and take the reciprocal. Instead, use a sense of scale: a violin string is roughly $$0.5\;\mathrm{mm}$$ thick, and in the clip the bow advances about one string-width per slip-stick cycle. Assuming the bow moves at roughly the speed you estimated in part (a), estimate the time one slip-stick cycle takes, and from it the frequency of the slip-stick motion.

__(c)__ Violins play notes with frequencies from about $$200\;\mathrm{Hz}$$ to $$2500\;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ Comparing with your answer to part (b), what do you conclude about the relationship between the slip-stick motion and the note you hear?

Block $$A$$ (mass $$m_A$$) is pressed against the flat, vertical left face of block $$B$$ (mass $$m_B$$). Block $$B$$ rests on a __frictionless__ floor. The coefficient of static friction between blocks $$A$$ and $$B$$ is $$\mu_s.$$ You push horizontally on block $$A$$ with a force $$F.$$ Block $$A$$ touches only your hand and block $$B$$ — nothing else holds it up. Recall that a static friction force can have any magnitude up to $$\mu_s N,$$ where $$N$$ is the normal force pressing the two surfaces together. Find the minimum push $$F_{\rm min}$$ that keeps block $$A$$ from sliding down.

__(a)__ Your push on $$A$$ is horizontal, so it cannot directly balance the downward gravitational force on $$A.$$ What force holds $$A$$ up? And if that force — not your push — is what holds $$A$$ up, why does the size of $$F$$ matter at all?

__(b)__ Before calculating, predict: would increasing $$m_A$$ increase, decrease, or not affect $$F_{\rm min}?$$ What about increasing $$m_B?$$ (For the second question, it may help to imagine the extreme case $$m_B \to 0.$$)

__(c)__ When you push with exactly $$F_{\rm min},$$ block $$A$$ is just on the verge of slipping, and the two blocks accelerate together to the right (the floor is frictionless, so nothing prevents that). Work out $$F_{\rm min}$$ step by step: first find the friction force $$F_f$$ between $$A$$ and $$B,$$ then the normal force $$N$$ between them, then the acceleration $$a$$ of the blocks, and finally $$F_{\rm min}$$ itself.

__(d)__ Check your answer. Does it have the right dimensions? Does it change in the directions you predicted in part (b) as $$m_A$$ and $$m_B$$ increase? Finally, rewrite it as a sum of two terms and interpret the term that survives as $$m_B \to \infty$$: what simpler problem does that term solve?

name: Part A. We began this problem set imagining Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on another planet.
desc: Part A. We began this problem set imagining Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on another planet. Asteroids have mass, and there's gravitational acceleration near their surface. However, asteroids are small enough that the gravity there is weak, meaning Imatorbhebhe could jump very high…
statement:
Part A. We began this problem set imagining Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on another planet.

Asteroids have mass, and there's gravitational acceleration near their surface. However, asteroids are small enough that the gravity there is weak, meaning Imatorbhebhe could jump very high.

If an asteroid is small enough, Imatorbhebhe could even jump completely off it, so the asteroid's gravity would never pull him back down.

We'd like to know the size of an asteroid Imatorbhebhe could jump off, but to answer that question, we need to understand the role of __energy__ in Newton's gravitational model. That's what we'll do in this multi-part problem.

-----------------------

When objects $$A$$ and $$B$$ interact, there are gravitational forces between them.

Another perspective is that the $$AB$$ system has __gravitational potential energy__. (We'll define "the $$AB$$ system" to be the two objects, together with their gravitational interaction.)

We've already seen the the relationship between gravitational forces and gravitational potential energy in the special case of objects near the surface of Earth, where we model $$\vec{g}$$ as constant. Then we have $$\begin{aligned} \vec{F}_{g; E \to O} & = m_O \vec{g} \\ U_{g; EO} & = mgh \end{aligned}$$ where the $$O$$ subscript stands for an object and $$h$$ is the height of the object above whatever height we decide to be zero. (We might choose $$h = 0$$ at sea level, but for an experiment done in a physics classroom, we might choose $$h = 0$$ to be at the floor of the room, or the table we're working on, or even the ceiling of the room, if we want.)

Those equations only apply in the simplified model where gravitational interactions don't change with distance and always point in the same direction. This model is fine for studying everyday things like a roller coaster or an Atwood machine. To study __Celestial mechanics__ is the study of the motion of planets, stars, asteroids, galaxies, etc. we need a new model.

We want to study energy again, but this time using Newton's universal law of gravitation as a model for the force: $$ \vec{F}_{A \to B} = -\dfrac{G m_A m_B}{r_{AB}^2} \hat{r}_{A \to B}$$ (We'll assume spherical symmetry of $$A$$ and $$B,$$ which simplifies the model.)

Our goal will be to find, understand, and apply a formula for the gravitational potential energy of the $$AB$$ system. We'll call that energy $$U_{g; AB}.$$

Let's begin with dimensional analysis.

The relevant quantities are $$G, m_A, m_B,$$ and $$r_{AB}.$$

Find the proportionality between $$U_{g, AB}$$ and those quantities.

It may help to first find and list the dimensions of $$U_{g; AB}$$ and everything it depends on. You can assume $$m_A$$ and $$m_B$$ have the same exponent in the formula for $$U_{g; AB}.$$

mathjax: $$U_{g;AB} \propto G^\blank m_A^\blank m_B^\blank r_{AB}^\blank$$
