Part B. The dimensional analysis in part (A) takes us most of the way to a formula for $$U_{g;AB},$$ but to understand the meaning of this dimensional result, and to finish turning it into a complete formula, let's make an analogy with a situation where we already know equations for both force and potential energy: the ideal spring.

------------------------

Imagine a spring with one end attached to a wall. We could push on the opposite end with a force $$\vec{F}_s$$ to compress the spring.

We modeled the force required with Hooke's law, $$\vec{F}_s = k \Delta \vec{x}$$ Here, $$\Delta \vec{x}$$ is the displacement of the left hand side of the spring.

As we push the spring, its displacement and the force we exert on it are in the same direction, so we do work on the spring. That means energy enters the spring, and it stores that energy as potential energy, $$U_s = \dfrac12 k (\Delta x)^2$$

We would like to find $$U_{g; AB},$$ a potential energy formula for gravitational interactions between spheres $$A$$ and $$B.$$ The process is similar to finding the formula $$U_s$$ for springs.

We can begin by setting $$A$$ and $$B$$ on opposite ends of a flat frictionless table on Earth. The spheres will attract each other with gravitational forces.

To mimic the spring system, we will anchor sphere $$B$$ to the table. Then sphere $$A$$ will move to the right across the table, pulled by the gravitational force from $$B.$$ In real life, we wouldn't be able to measure this because the gravitational force is weak, and we can't get a table that's flat enough, frictionless enough, etc. $$A$$ moves across the table as a thought experiment.

The gravitational force from $$A$$ to $$B$$ still exists, even though we didn't draw it above. That force is cancelled by a normal force from the pin in $$B,$$ so $$B$$ doesn't move.

We could attach sphere $$A$$ to a half-Atwood machine. If the load were light enough, sphere $$A$$ could lift the load while continuing to move toward sphere $$B.$$

As sphere $$A$$ approaches sphere $$B,$$ what happens to their gravitational potential energy, $$U_{g;AB}?$$

Here, we are asking for the gravitational potential energy of the interaction __between the two spheres__, so ignore any gravitational potential energy related to interactions with the Earth.

$$U_{g; AB}$$ increases as the spheres get closer

$$U_{g; AB}$$ decreases as the spheres get closer

$$U_{g; AB}$$ stays the same as the spheres get closer

---------------------------

As we compress the spring system described in part (B), we could make a plot of the force $$\vec{F}_s$$ we need to exert on the spring versus how far we have compressed the spring. The work we do on the spring to compress it some amount $$\Delta x_1$$ is the signed area between the force and the horizontal axis:

Now we would like to repeat the procedure, but using spheres with a gravitational interaction instead of a spring.

Let the original distance between the center of the spheres be $$L.$$

The half-Atwood machine applies a tension force $$\vec{T}$$ to sphere $$A.$$ We adjust $$\vec{T}$$ This means that, as the gravitational force $$\vec{F}_{B \to A}$$ gets continuously stronger, we continuously add mass to the load so that $$\vec{T}$$ exactly cancels $$\vec{F}_{g; B \to A}.$$ so that $$A$$ moves with some constant velocity $$\vec{v}_A.$$

Part D. Here, we use the graphs for force versus displacement from part (C) to think about work and energy in both the spring and gravitational systems.

------------

As we compress the spring, it moves to the right, and the force $$\vec{F}_s$$ we apply to it is to the right. That means the force does positive work on the spring. We can call that work $$W_{F \to s}.$$

The work done in compressing the spring a distance $$\Delta x_1$$ is the signed area between the plot of $$F_{s;x}$$ and the horizontal axis. The area begins at $$\Delta x = 0,$$ where we begin pushing. It ends at $$\Delta x_1,$$ where we finish pushing.

The work $$W_{F \to s}$$ done by the external force $$\vec{F}_s$$ on the spring is stored by the spring as potential energy $$U_s,$$ so we find $$\begin{aligned} U_s & = W_{F \to s}\\ {} & = \dfrac12 \,(\text{width of shaded region}) \cdot (\text{height of shaded region}) \\ {} & = \dfrac12 (\Delta x_1)(F_s) \\ {} & = \dfrac12 (\Delta x_1)(k \Delta x_1) \\ {} & = \dfrac12 k (\Delta x_1)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Part E. At last, we're ready to return to the problem of Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping off an asteroid.

--------------------------

Having plotted $$U_{g; AB}$$ and found most of a formula for it by dimensional analysis, our knowledge is nearly equivalent to knowing the entire formula, which is below (click to reveal).

$$ U_{g; AB} = - \dfrac{Gm_A m_B}{r_{AB}}$$

Recall that we can set $$U = 0$$ wherever we want when using potential energy. The standard in physics is to set $$U_{g; AB} \to 0$$ and $$r_{AB} \to \infty.$$ In other words, spheres never have potential energy of zero, but as they get further and further apart, their potential energy gets closer and closer to zero.

The gravitational potential energy is negative, meaning that it increases (moves toward zero) as $$A$$ and $$B$$ get further apart. These features of the formula replicate your findings in parts (A) through (D).

Now we imagine Josh Imatorbhebhe jumping on an asteroid. Model the asteroid as a sphere of radius $$R$$ and uniform density. Model Imatorbhebhe's jump as straight up - directly away from the center of the asteroid.

We will refer to Imatorbhebhe and the asteroid together as simply "the system."

When Imatorbhebhe is on the surface of the asteroid, he's a distance $$R$$ from its center. (We ignore Imatorbhebhe's own height.) According to the formula for $$U_g,$$ the system's potential energy is negative.

When Imatorbhebhe jumps, he gains kinetic energy. The total mechanical energy of the system becomes $$E = U_g + KE$$

(We ignore kinetic energy in the asteroid since it is far more massive than Imatorbhebhe and is negligibly pushed away when he jumps. We also work in the inertial reference frame of the asteroid.)

After Imatorbhebhe jumps, he goes higher and higher, but slows down as he rises. The system's potential energy increases and its kinetic energy decreases. The total mechanical energy of the system is conserved.

If the asteroid is large enough, Imatorbhebhe will eventually come back down. Otherwise, he'll continue rising forever, never turning around.

Which of the following describes the condition that needs to be met for Imatorbhebhe to rise forever and never fall back down, according to Newton's model of gravity?

$$E, KE,$$ and $$U_g$$ are total mechanical energy, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy of the system respectively.

That can't happen; Imatorbhebhe will always come back down because the gravitational force on him never goes to zero.

$$E \ge 0$$

$$KE > U_g$$

$$KE < U_g$$

$$KE > 0$$

$$U_g > 0$$

Part A. Kepler 452b is an exoplanet renowned for its similarity to Earth. It is about $$1{,}800$$ light-years from Earth, in the constellation Cygnus. Its star is similar to the Sun, and it's distance from its star is similar to Earth's distance from the Sun.

name: Orbits and the Discovery of Neptune — A planet orbits a star, with nothing else nearby. The planet's path is…
desc: A planet orbits a star, with nothing else nearby. The planet's path is an __ellipse__ — a sort of stretched-out circle — with the star inside it. German astronomer Johannes Kepler discovered this pattern in 1609 by studying the planets of our own solar system; it is now called…
statement:
A planet orbits a star, with nothing else nearby. The planet's path is an __ellipse__ — a sort of stretched-out circle — with the star inside it. German astronomer Johannes Kepler discovered this pattern in 1609 by studying the planets of our own solar system; it is now called __Kepler's first law__. The animation below shows such a system, with the gravitational force on each body drawn as an arrow and the __center of mass__ of the system marked with an ×. You can run simulations like this one yourself at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/my-solar-system/latest/my-solar-system_en.html.

__(a)__ The planet is clearly accelerating as it loops around. Does the __star__ accelerate too? What does your answer tell you about the forces in the system?

__(b)__ Call the gravitational force the star exerts on the planet $$\vec{F}_{g;S\to P}$$ and the force the planet exerts on the star $$\vec{F}_{g;P\to S}.$$ The star is far more massive than the planet. Which force has the greater magnitude — or are they the same? Explain how you know.

__(c)__ In the animation, the lengths of the force arrows change during each orbit. At what point in the orbit is the gravitational force strongest, and what does that tell you about how gravitational force depends on distance?

__(d)__ Now give the planet a moon. Is the moon's path through space a perfect ellipse? Is the planet's path still a perfect ellipse? Explain.

Kepler knew only the six planets visible to the naked eye (Mercury through Saturn). Uranus was recognized as a planet, using telescopes, in the early 1780s, and in 1821 French astronomer Alexis Bouvard used Newton's model of gravity to predict Uranus's orbit into the future. As the years passed, Uranus sometimes ran ahead of Bouvard's predictions and sometimes lagged behind. Bouvard suspected the cause was an unknown planet beyond Uranus. The diagram below shows Uranus on the inner orbit and a hypothetical mystery planet on the outer (purple) orbit; both orbit clockwise.

__(e)__ In configuration (a) of the diagram, is the mystery planet's gravity speeding Uranus's orbit up or slowing it down? What about in configuration (b)?

__(f)__ Uranus and the mystery planet exert gravitational forces on each other at every moment, all the way around their orbits. Why are the perturbations to Uranus's orbit only significant when the two planets are in roughly the same part of their orbits?

name: Saturn or Carrie? — In the movie __Star Wars__ (which was filmed on Earth), Carrie holds onto Mark while the…
desc: In the movie __Star Wars__ (which was filmed on Earth), Carrie holds onto Mark while the two of them swing across a gap. Which exerted more gravitational force on Mark during the swing — Carrie, or the planet Saturn? In __Newton's law of universal gravitation__, __any__ two…
statement:
In the movie __Star Wars__ (which was filmed on Earth), Carrie holds onto Mark while the two of them swing across a gap. Which exerted more gravitational force on Mark during the swing — Carrie, or the planet Saturn?

In __Newton's law of universal gravitation__, __any__ two systems with mass exert gravitational forces on each other — Mark and Carrie included, whether they're touching or light-years apart. Two proportionalities set the strength. First, the force between objects $$A$$ and $$B$$ is proportional to both masses: $$F_{g;A\to B}\propto m_Am_B.$$ Second, the force obeys an __inverse square law__ in the distance: $$F_{g;A\to B}\propto \dfrac{1}{r_{AB}^2},$$ so putting something twice as far away cuts the force to one quarter.

Here is the data you need. Saturn's mass is $$m_S=5.6834\times10^{26}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Take Carrie's mass to be $$m_C=56.834\;\mathrm{kg}$$ (about $$125\;\mathrm{lbs}$$ — chosen so that $$\dfrac{m_S}{m_C}=10^{25}$$ exactly). The distance from Earth to Saturn varies; take $$r_{MS}=1.6\times10^{12}\;\mathrm{m}.$$ For the Mark-to-Carrie distance, averaged over their bodies, estimate $$r_{MC}=0.5\;\mathrm{m}.$$

__(a)__ Both forces we're comparing are forces __on Mark__. Why don't we need to estimate Mark's mass?

__(b)__ Nobody has ever put Saturn on a scale, or sampled its deep interior to measure its density. What observations let astronomers determine Saturn's mass to five significant figures?

__(c)__ Why isn't the distance from Earth to Saturn a single fixed number?

__(d)__ Estimate the ratio of the two gravitational forces on Mark and answer the question: which force is bigger, and by roughly what factor? (Since you only want a __ratio__ of forces, the proportionalities above are enough — you never need the full force equation.)

label: MCH20
name: Weighing the Earth — Find the mass of the Earth, using measurements made at its surface. People knew the…
desc: Find the mass of the Earth, using measurements made at its surface. People knew the radius of Earth long before they knew its mass — finding the mass is hard because we only have access to the crust and the upper mantle, and we've never been to the deep interior to measure its…
statement:
Find the mass of the Earth, using measurements made at its surface. People knew the radius of Earth long before they knew its mass — finding the mass is hard because we only have access to the crust and the upper mantle, and we've never been to the deep interior to measure its density. (Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann first showed Earth has a solid inner core in 1936, using earthquake waves that reflect off it.) Plots of Earth's density versus radius, like the one below, are built from indirect evidence — earthquakes, the magnetic field, and so on — and are uncertain by at least $$1\%.$$

Yet Earth's __total mass__ is known to about $$0.01\%$$ — a hundred times better. The key is the __shell theorem__: when an object is spherically symmetric, the gravitational force it exerts on anything __outside__ it is exactly the same as if all its mass were located at its center. For spherically symmetric bodies, Newton's law of universal gravitation reads $$F_{g;A\to B}=\dfrac{Gm_Am_B}{r_{AB}^2},$$ where $$r_{AB}$$ is the center-to-center distance and $$G$$ is the __gravitational constant__. The best current measurement is $$G=6.674\,30(15)\times10^{-11}\;\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$$ (the parentheses give the uncertainty in the last two digits).

__(a)__ Use the shell theorem to explain why our large uncertainty about __where__ Earth's mass is (denser core versus denser mantle) doesn't prevent an accurate measurement of __how much__ mass there is.

__(b)__ Earth isn't a perfect sphere: it bulges at the equator by about $$20\;\mathrm{km},$$ so the poles are closer to Earth's center than the equator is. A pendulum clock ticks at angular frequency $$\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{\ell}},$$ where $$\ell$$ is the pendulum's length and $$g$$ is the local free fall acceleration. Considering only this distance effect, where does an identical pendulum clock run faster — at the poles or at the equator? Why?

__(c)__ Consider a stone of mass $$m_s$$ in free fall just above the equator, where the measured free fall acceleration is $$g_e\approx9.78\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and the sea-level distance to Earth's center is $$R_{\oplus;e}=6.378\,137\times10^6\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Write Newton's gravitational law for the force on the stone and set it equal to the force given by Newton's second law. Show that the stone's mass cancels, and solve for the mass of Earth $$m_{\oplus}$$ in terms of $$g_e,$$ $$R_{\oplus;e},$$ and $$G.$$

__(d)__ Evaluate your formula numerically. The accepted value is $$m_{\oplus}=5.972\,17\times10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$

__(e)__ Your answer to (d) is off from the accepted value by a few tenths of a percent. What's the biggest limitation of this method?

label: MCH20
name: The Orbit of the International Space Station — The International Space Station (ISS) orbits about…
desc: The International Space Station (ISS) orbits about $$400\;\mathrm{km}$$ above the surface of the Earth. Find its orbital period $$T$$ — the time for one full trip around the Earth. Assume a circular orbit. Useful facts: the radius of Earth is…
statement:
The International Space Station (ISS) orbits about $$400\;\mathrm{km}$$ above the surface of the Earth. Find its orbital period $$T$$ — the time for one full trip around the Earth. Assume a circular orbit. Useful facts: the radius of Earth is $$R_{\oplus}\approx6.4\times10^6\;\mathrm{m}$$ and its mass is $$m_{\oplus}=5.97\times10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg};$$ the gravitational constant is $$G=6.674\times10^{-11}\;\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}};$$ the magnitude of the gravitational force between spherically symmetric bodies is $$F_{g;A\to B}=\dfrac{Gm_Am_B}{r_{AB}^2};$$ in uniform circular motion at angular speed $$\omega,$$ the acceleration points toward the center with magnitude $$a=\omega^2r;$$ and $$\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}.$$

__(a)__ Find $$r_{\oplus I},$$ the distance from the center of the Earth to the ISS. (Careful: it's not $$400\;\mathrm{km}.$$)

__(b)__ The force-magnitude equation above carries no direction information. The full vector form is $$\vec{F}_{g;\oplus\to I}=-\dfrac{Gm_{\oplus}m_I}{r_{\oplus I}^2}\hat{r}_{\oplus\to I},$$ where $$\hat{r}_{\oplus\to I}$$ is a unit vector pointing from the center of Earth to the ISS, as in the figure. Why does the equation need a minus sign?

__(c)__ Gravity is the only force on the ISS, so Newton's second law says $$\vec{F}_{g;\oplus\to I}=m_I\vec{a}_I.$$ Show that the ISS's mass cancels out of this equation. Then use the circular-motion acceleration $$a_I=\omega^2r_{\oplus I}$$ (pointing toward Earth) and $$\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$$ to derive a formula for the period $$T$$ in terms of $$G,$$ $$m_{\oplus},$$ and $$r_{\oplus I}.$$

__(d)__ Your formula contains the proportionality $$T\propto r_{\oplus I}^{3/2}.$$ This is __Kepler's third law__ — Kepler found it empirically from the orbits of the planets around the Sun, decades before Newton explained it. If Kepler had written your full formula for a planet's orbit, whose mass would have appeared in it?

__(e)__ Evaluate $$T$$ numerically. Roughly how many sunrises does an ISS astronaut see per day?

label: MCH20
name: A Bigger Earth — Imagine we doubled the radius of the Earth while keeping its average density the same…
desc: Imagine we doubled the radius of the Earth while keeping its average density the same. What would be the orbital period of a space station circling $$800\;\mathrm{km}$$ above the new planet's surface? You may use these results from the ISS calculation: the period of a circular…
statement:
Imagine we doubled the radius of the Earth while keeping its average density the same. What would be the orbital period of a space station circling $$800\;\mathrm{km}$$ above the new planet's surface? You may use these results from the ISS calculation: the period of a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a body of mass $$m$$ is $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{Gm}},$$ and the real ISS — orbiting $$400\;\mathrm{km}$$ above the real Earth, a distance $$r=6.8\times10^6\;\mathrm{m}$$ from its center — has a period of about $$93$$ minutes.

__(a)__ It's convenient that the problem puts the new station $$800\;\mathrm{km}$$ up rather than $$400\;\mathrm{km}.$$ Why?

__(b)__ Kepler's third law says $$T\propto r^{3/2},$$ so doubling $$r$$ multiplies the period by $$2^{3/2}=2\sqrt{2}\approx2.83.$$ It's tempting to conclude that the new station's period is $$2\sqrt{2}\times93\;\mathrm{min}\approx263\;\mathrm{min}.$$ What does that argument overlook?

__(c)__ Since we only need the new period __compared with__ the ISS's, proportionalities are enough — no need for $$G$$ or the factor of $$2\pi.$$ From the formula, $$T\propto r^{3/2}m^{-1/2}.$$ For planets that share the same density, how does the mass $$m$$ scale with the planet's radius? Combine the two proportionalities to find how $$T$$ depends on $$r$$ in this problem, and state the new station's orbital period.

__(d)__ Which has a longer orbital period: a satellite in a low orbit around a gas giant (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), or a satellite in a low orbit around a rocky planet (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars)? Gas giants are considerably less dense than rocky planets.

label: MCH20
name: A Tunnel Through the Earth — The __shell theorem__ has a second part: anywhere __inside__ a uniform spherical…
desc: The __shell theorem__ has a second part: anywhere __inside__ a uniform spherical shell of mass, the gravitational force from that shell is exactly zero — the pulls from all directions cancel. So for a person at radius $$r$$ inside the Earth, all the mass farther from the center…
statement:
The __shell theorem__ has a second part: anywhere __inside__ a uniform spherical shell of mass, the gravitational force from that shell is exactly zero — the pulls from all directions cancel. So for a person at radius $$r$$ inside the Earth, all the mass farther from the center than $$r$$ (a stack of spherical shells) exerts no net force, while the mass closer to the center than $$r$$ — call it $$m_r$$ — pulls as if it were a point at the center: $$F_g=\dfrac{Gm_rm_{\rm person}}{r^2}.$$

Now imagine drilling a straight tunnel from the north pole to the south pole, right through the center of the Earth, and removing all the air from it. Pretend the Earth has uniform density. Three facts from earlier lessons will help: an orbit skimming just above Earth's surface takes about $$90$$ minutes (and we showed that for planets of uniform density, the period of such an orbit doesn't depend on the planet's radius at all); a mass on a Hooke's-law spring — restoring force proportional to displacement — oscillates with a period that is __independent of the amplitude__; and simple harmonic motion is exactly the projection of uniform circular motion onto one axis.

__(a)__ You step up to the tunnel at the north pole and jump in. Describe your motion. Then use conservation of energy to explain how you know you'd come momentarily to rest exactly at the far end of the tunnel, at the south pole.

__(b)__ When you are a distance $$r$$ from the center, which part of Earth's mass determines the force on you? Using the uniform-density assumption, show that the gravitational force on you obeys $$F_g\propto r.$$ What famous force law has this same form?

__(c)__ Use the result of (b) and the facts listed above to find the period of your oscillations from pole to pole and back. (Hint, illustrated below: simple harmonic motion is the projection of uniform circular motion. Imagine projecting an orbit through a circular tunnel inside the Earth onto the pole-to-pole tunnel.)

__(d)__ In reality, Earth's core is much denser than its crust and mantle. With the real density profile instead of a uniform one, would the period of oscillations in the tunnel increase or decrease? And would the orbital period of the ISS (about $$400\;\mathrm{km}$$ __above__ the surface) change? Explain both answers.

label: MCH20
name: The Pull of a Ring — A circular ring has radius $$R,$$ mass $$m_R,$$ and negligible thickness. A point…
desc: A circular ring has radius $$R,$$ mass $$m_R,$$ and negligible thickness. A point particle of mass $$m_p$$ sits on the ring's symmetry axis, a distance $$y$$ from the ring's center, as shown below. How does the magnitude of the gravitational force on the particle depend on…
statement:
A circular ring has radius $$R,$$ mass $$m_R,$$ and negligible thickness. A point particle of mass $$m_p$$ sits on the ring's symmetry axis, a distance $$y$$ from the ring's center, as shown below. How does the magnitude of the gravitational force on the particle depend on $$y?$$ Recall that Newton's law $$F_{g;A\to B}=\dfrac{Gm_Am_B}{r_{AB}^2}$$ (with $$r_{AB}$$ the center-to-center distance) holds exactly only for __spherically symmetric__ bodies — and a ring is not a sphere.

__(a)__ Some students reasoned: "Every point of the ring is the same distance $$d=\sqrt{y^2+R^2}$$ from the particle, and gravity is an inverse square law, so the force is $$F=\dfrac{Gm_Rm_p}{y^2+R^2}.$$" Their distance is correct, but their conclusion is flawed. What's wrong with applying the inverse square law this way? For what values of $$y$$ is their answer approximately right anyway?

__(b)__ What is the net gravitational force on the particle when $$y=0,$$ at the center of the ring? Explain.

__(c)__ Using your answers to (a) and (b), describe qualitatively what a plot of the force magnitude versus $$y$$ must look like.

__(d)__ Exactly one of the following expressions is the actual magnitude of the gravitational force on the particle. Use dimensional analysis and your special cases from (a)-(c) to eliminate the impostors and identify it. (Note that $$\dfrac{Gm_Rm_p}{r^2}$$ has the dimensions of force whenever $$r$$ is a length.)

(i) $$\dfrac{Gm_Rm_p}{y^2}$$

(ii) $$\dfrac{Gm_Rm_p\,y}{R^2+y^2}$$

(iii) $$\dfrac{Gm_Rm_p\,y}{R^3}$$

(iv) $$\dfrac{Gm_Rm_p\,y^{3/2}}{\left(R^2+y^2\right)^{3/2}}$$

(v) $$\dfrac{Gm_Rm_p\,y}{\left(R^2+y^2\right)^{3/2}}$$

statement:
In a previous homework set, we studied the Ikaros light sail, which can control what direction it is facing by changing its reflectivity.

As a simple model, imagine a square sheet with side length $$s$$ and mass $$m.$$ The left half of the sheet is black and absorbs all light that hits it. The right half of the sheet is reflective. All light that hits it bounces back.

Sunlight approaches the sheet directly perpendicular to the sheet.

The intensity of the sunlight is $$I_0.$$ This means that the sunlight carries power $$I_0$$ per unit area.

Recall that the momentum of light with energy $$E$$ is $$p = \dfrac{E}{c}.$$

Find a proportionality for the angular acceleration $${}\alpha$$ of the sheet about its center of mass in terms of $$I_0, m, s,$$ and $$c.$$

Also indicate whether the angular acceleration is clockwise or counterclockwise.

If you want to find the exact value of $$\alpha,$$ you'll need to know that the moment of inertia of the sheet about its center of mass is $$I = \dfrac{1}{12} ms^2.$$

Alternatively, the question doesn't require you to find the coefficient in the equation for $$\alpha,$$ so you could answer more intuitively by thinking about how each quantity should affect $$\alpha,$$ and also by thinking about the dimensions of all the quantities.

statement:
This week's lab requires a yoyo. An inexpensive one sold in toy stores should be sufficient. If you can't find a yoyo, you could use a toilet paper roll, making this experiment similar to the one from our rotational dynamics lesson, but with a different analysis and final goal.

If you hold the end of a yoyo string and drop the yoyo, it will unwind and begin spinning as it falls.

As the yoyo is unwinding, there is a tension force from the string on the yoyo.

This tension force causes the acceleration of the yoyo to be less than $$g$$ as it unwinds.

We can choose the center of the yoyo as a reference point. The tension force from the string exerts a torque about this point, causing the yoyo to have angular acceleration.

Drop a yoyo while holding the end of the string and let the yoyo unwind. Measure the distance the yoyo falls and the time it takes. Calculate the acceleration of the yoyo. Calculate the angular acceleration as well.

Measure the distance of the string from the center of the yoyo and compute the torque on the yoyo per unit mass.

The moment of inertia of the yoyo is $$I = k \cdot mR^2$$ with $$R$$ the radius of the yoyo.

Measure $$R$$ and compute $$k.$$

We have previously found that when rolling down a ramp inclined from the horizontal at angle $$\theta,$$ the acceleration of the yoyo should be $$a = \dfrac{1}{1+k} g\sin\theta $$

Build a ramp and predict the time it will take the yoyo to roll down. Let the yoyo roll down and measure the time.

How close was your prediction?

label: MCH21
name: Doors, Cantilevers, and the Moment Arm — When a force $$\vec{F}$$ is applied to an object at a point a…
desc: When a force $$\vec{F}$$ is applied to an object at a point a displacement $$\vec{r}$$ away from a chosen pivot, the force exerts a __torque__ about the pivot of magnitude $$\tau = rF\sin\theta,$$ where $$r$$ is the distance from the pivot to the point where the force is applied…
statement:
When a force $$\vec{F}$$ is applied to an object at a point a displacement $$\vec{r}$$ away from a chosen pivot, the force exerts a __torque__ about the pivot of magnitude $$\tau = rF\sin\theta,$$ where $$r$$ is the distance from the pivot to the point where the force is applied and $$\theta$$ is the angle between $$\vec{r}$$ and $$\vec{F}.$$ Torque measures how effective the force is at making the object rotate about the pivot. This problem applies the formula to two everyday structures.

__(a)__ A child wants to push open a heavy door that swings on hinges, shown below. Should the child push near the hinges, in the middle of the door, or at the edge far from the hinges? Use $$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$ to explain why your choice requires the least force.

__(b)__ A __cantilever__ is a part of a structure that hangs out without support from below, like the long overhanging section of the house shown below.

Model the cantilever as a heavy horizontal beam attached to the wall by a pivot at its left end. To hold the beam up, a single vertical rope runs from an overhead support down to the beam. Three possible designs attach the rope at point (A), close to the wall, at point (B), halfway out, or at point (C), near the far end, as shown below. In which design is the rope under the most tension? Explain your reasoning using torque.

__(c)__ In a different set of three designs, the rope is always attached to the far end of the beam, a fixed distance $$r$$ from the pivot, but it is anchored to the wall at three different heights, so the rope makes angles $$\theta_A > \theta_B > \theta_C$$ with the beam, as shown below. Now which rope is under the most tension? Also, using the equivalent formula $$\tau = rT_\perp,$$ where $$T_\perp$$ is the component of the tension perpendicular to the beam, compare the values of $$T_\perp$$ in the three designs.

__(d)__ The torque formula can also be grouped as $$\tau = (r\sin\theta)F.$$ The quantity $$r_\perp = r\sin\theta,$$ the component of $$\vec{r}$$ perpendicular to the force, is called the __moment arm__ of the force. For the three designs in part (c), which rope has the longest moment arm, and how does the moment arm explain your tension ranking?

label: MCH21

desc: You push horizontally on a tall box resting on the floor. Your push $$\vec{F}_P$$ points to the right and is applied to the left side of the box, near the top. Four forces act on the box: your push $$\vec{F}_P;$$ gravity $$m\vec{g},$$ which can be treated as acting at the center…
statement:
You push horizontally on a tall box resting on the floor. Your push $$\vec{F}_P$$ points to the right and is applied to the left side of the box, near the top. Four forces act on the box: your push $$\vec{F}_P;$$ gravity $$m\vec{g},$$ which can be treated as acting at the center of mass, at the center of the box; the normal force $$\vec{N}$$ from the floor, pointing up; and friction $$\vec{F}_f$$ from the floor, pointing left to oppose your push. If the box tips, it will rotate about its bottom right edge, so take that corner, marked $$P$$ in the figure, as the reference point for computing all torques. Recall that $$\tau = rF\sin\theta,$$ which can also be written using the moment arm as $$\tau = r_\perp F.$$

__(a)__ If you try this at home, you'll find that pushing near the top of the box tips it over much more easily than pushing near the bottom with the same force. Explain why, using the moment arm.

__(b)__ Even though your push exerts a torque about $$P$$ no matter how gently you push, the box does not start tipping the moment you touch it. That is because the box only tips if there is a __net__ torque about the pivot. Classify each of the four torques about $$P$$ — $$\tau_P$$ from the push, $$\tau_g$$ from gravity, $$\tau_N$$ from the normal force, and $$\tau_f$$ from friction — as clockwise, counterclockwise, or zero. For any torque that is zero, explain why it vanishes.

__(c)__ To add torques together we need signs. Define counterclockwise torques to be positive and clockwise torques negative. In $$\tau = rF\sin\theta,$$ the magnitudes $$F$$ and $$r$$ are never negative, so the sign must be carried by $$\sin\theta.$$ The rule for finding $$\theta$$: re-draw $$\vec{r}$$ and $$\vec{F}$$ starting at the same point; $$\theta$$ is the angle you rotate $$\vec{r}$$ through to lay it on top of $$\vec{F},$$ always choosing the shorter direction of rotation, with counterclockwise rotations counted as positive. Apply this rule to your push: is $$\theta$$ positive or negative, and does the resulting sign of $$\tau_P$$ agree with your answer to part (b)?

__(d)__ When you push gently, the box neither slides nor tips, so both the net force and the net torque on it are zero. Write the torque balance about $$P$$ and explain how several nonzero torques can add up to zero.

label: MCH21
name: The Wandering Normal Force — A box rests on two identical scales, one under its left edge and one under its…
desc: A box rests on two identical scales, one under its left edge and one under its right edge. Each scale reads the normal force it exerts on the box. A horizontal string is attached to the top of the box, and you pull it gently to the left — not hard enough to make the box slide or…
statement:
A box rests on two identical scales, one under its left edge and one under its right edge. Each scale reads the normal force it exerts on the box. A horizontal string is attached to the top of the box, and you pull it gently to the left — not hard enough to make the box slide or tip, so the box stays in equilibrium: zero net force and zero net torque about any reference point. Treat gravity as acting at the box's center of mass. The scales also exert friction on the bottom of the box.

__(a)__ As you pull on the string, the __sum__ of the two scale readings does not change. Why not?

__(b)__ Choose the reference point for torques at the bottom of the box, directly below the center of mass (the blue dot in the figure). Explain why this is a convenient choice: which forces' torques does it make zero, and why?

__(c)__ While you pull, which scale reading increases and which decreases? Explain using the torque balance about the reference point from part (b). In the demonstration shown below, the scales were tared (zeroed) before the horizontal force was applied; afterward, the left scale read $$+2.86\;\mathrm{g}$$ and the right scale read $$-2.89\;\mathrm{g}.$$ Do these readings match your prediction?

__(d)__ Now set the same box on an ordinary solid floor and pull the string steadily harder (still without sliding or tipping). The floor exerts a single net normal force $$\vec{N}$$ that points straight up, and its magnitude is fixed — it must still balance gravity. Yet the floor's torque must grow to keep the net torque zero. In $$\tau_N = r_N N\sin\theta,$$ which factor changes as you pull harder, and what does that mean physically about __where__ the normal force acts? How far can this go, and what happens if torque balance would require it to go further?

__(e)__ There must be some __mechanism__ for the normal force to move — something about the box and floor must physically change. In an earlier lesson we modeled the matter in a solid as a grid of balls connected by springs, as in the image below; compressing the springs is what creates the normal force. Use this model to explain how the normal force shifts when you pull the top of the box to the left. (Hint: imagine standing barefoot and leaning forward — what do you feel in your feet?)

label: MCH21
name: The Hardest Push That Won't Tip the Box — A box of mass $$m,$$ width $$w,$$ and height $$h$$ stands on a…
desc: A box of mass $$m,$$ width $$w,$$ and height $$h$$ stands on a floor. Friction is strong enough that the box cannot slide. You push horizontally at the very top of the box with force $$\vec{F}_P,$$ pointing right. The floor's normal force can act anywhere under the base of the…
statement:
A box of mass $$m,$$ width $$w,$$ and height $$h$$ stands on a floor. Friction is strong enough that the box cannot slide. You push horizontally at the very top of the box with force $$\vec{F}_P,$$ pointing right. The floor's normal force can act anywhere under the base of the box, and as you push harder it shifts toward the front (right) bottom edge so that the net torque on the box stays zero. The farthest it can shift is the front bottom edge itself — if torque balance would require it to act beyond there, the box tips. Compute torques about the front bottom edge (the pivot $$P$$ in the figure), counting counterclockwise as positive, and treat gravity $$mg$$ as acting at the center of mass, at the center of the box.

__(a)__ When the box is right on the verge of tipping forward, where does the normal force act, and what is its torque about $$P?$$ What is the friction force's torque about $$P?$$

__(b)__ With the normal force and friction contributing nothing, the balance on the verge of tipping reduces to $$\tau_{P;\mathrm{max}} + \tau_g = 0.$$ Find the moment arms $$r_{P;\perp}$$ of the push and $$r_{g;\perp}$$ of gravity about $$P,$$ and solve for the maximum push $$F_{P;\mathrm{max}}$$ that does not tip the box.

__(c)__ The toy blocks shown below are approximately twice as tall as they are wide ($$h = 2w$$). First find $$F_{P;\mathrm{max}}$$ for one such block of mass $$m$$ standing upright. Then consider this demonstration: four blocks are tied together into a stack two blocks wide and two blocks high, a string is attached to the top edge of the stack and run horizontally over a pulley, and a single block of mass $$m$$ hangs from the other end, so the string pulls horizontally on the top of the stack with force $$mg.$$ Show that the stack is right on the verge of tipping. (In the photos, the stack just barely holds — and tips as soon as a little extra mass is added to the hanging block.)

__(d)__ It is nonetheless possible to push on a single upright block with a force much greater __in magnitude__ than $$F_{P;\mathrm{max}}$$ without tipping it over. Give two different ways.

__(e)__ We assumed friction was strong enough that the box tips before it slides. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction $$\mu_{s;\mathrm{min}}$$ for which the top-of-the-box push tips the box rather than sliding it, and evaluate it for the $$h = 2w$$ block.

desc: Torque is defined by $$\tau = rF\sin\theta.$$ In dimensional notation, mass is $$\mathrm{M},$$ length is $$\mathrm{L},$$ and time is $$\mathrm{T};$$ force has dimensions $$\left = \mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}.$$ __(a)__ Find the dimensions of torque, $$\left[\tau\right].$$ __(b)__ What…
statement:
Torque is defined by $$\tau = rF\sin\theta.$$ In dimensional notation, mass is $$\mathrm{M},$$ length is $$\mathrm{L},$$ and time is $$\mathrm{T};$$ force has dimensions $$\left = \mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}.$$

__(a)__ Find the dimensions of torque, $$\left[\tau\right].$$

__(b)__ What other familiar physical quantity has exactly these dimensions?

__(c)__ When a torque $$\tau$$ acts on an object as it rotates through an angle $$\Delta\theta,$$ the work done is $$W = \tau\,\Delta\theta.$$ Explain how this formula is consistent with your answers to (a) and (b).

__(d)__ Energy is measured in joules. Should we report torques in joules too? Explain why or why not, considering what would happen to the numerical values of torques and of energies if we switched our angle unit from radians to degrees.

name: Opening the World's Heaviest Door — Just as a net force causes acceleration ($$\vec{F}_{\rm net} =…
desc: Just as a net force causes acceleration ($$\vec{F}_{\rm net} = m\vec{a}$$), a net torque causes __angular acceleration__: $$\tau_{\rm net} = I\alpha,$$ where the __moment of inertia__ $$I$$ plays the role of mass — it measures an object's resistance to changing its rotation. The…
statement:
Just as a net force causes acceleration ($$\vec{F}_{\rm net} = m\vec{a}$$), a net torque causes __angular acceleration__: $$\tau_{\rm net} = I\alpha,$$ where the __moment of inertia__ $$I$$ plays the role of mass — it measures an object's resistance to changing its rotation. The heaviest door in the world, built to stop high-energy neutrons at the National Ignition Facility, has mass $$m = 4.4\times10^{4}\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and width $$w = 2.4\;\mathrm{m},$$ and is hinged along one vertical edge. Model it as a solid rectangle rotating about one end, which (ignoring its thickness) has moment of inertia $$I = \dfrac13 mw^2.$$ A physicist pushes on the outer edge of the door with a constant force of $$300\;\mathrm{N},$$ always directed perpendicular to the door. The door starts at rest; she pushes one way until the door has rotated one eighth of a full rotation, then pushes the other way with the same force until the door comes to rest after one quarter rotation in total. Ignore friction. For rotation from rest at constant angular acceleration, $$\theta = \dfrac12\alpha t^2.$$

__(a)__ What torque does the physicist exert on the door about the hinge?

__(b)__ What is the door's angular acceleration while she pushes?

__(c)__ Through what angle does she push before reversing direction? What unit must you express it in for the kinematics formula to work, and why? Then find how long the entire door-opening process takes.

__(d)__ Suppose we had worked in symbols to the end, for a door of mass $$m$$ and width $$w,$$ push $$F,$$ and angle $$\theta$$ for each of the two phases. Show that the total time is $$t = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{2\theta mw}{3F}},$$ and explain — by thinking about the effect of each variable — why $$\theta,$$ $$m,$$ and $$w$$ belong in the numerator and $$F$$ in the denominator.

statement:
The rotational analog of Newton's second law is $$\tau_{\rm net} = I\alpha.$$ But the equation comes with fine print, which this problem explores. Two facts to keep in mind: a single force whose line of action passes through an object's center of mass makes the object accelerate __without__ rotating, and the center of mass always obeys $$\vec{F}_{\rm net} = m\vec{a}_{\rm cm},$$ no matter where on the object the forces are applied.

__(a)__ The animation below shows paint being stirred. Why would it make no sense to apply $$\tau_{\rm net} = I\alpha$$ to the paint as a whole?

Now consider three identical uniform rectangular plates, (A), (B), and (C), resting on frictionless ice, viewed from above. The red dot marks each plate's center of mass; the black dot marks its lower-left corner. An identical force $$\vec{F}$$ (pointing right) is applied to each plate: in (A) at the lower-left corner, in (B) at the upper-left corner, and in (C) at the midpoint of the left edge, so that its line of action passes through the center of mass.

__(b)__ The plates are free (not pinned down). Which plate's center of mass undergoes the largest acceleration?

__(c)__ Which plates begin to rotate, and in which direction?

__(d)__ After the force acts on each plate for the same short time, which plate has the __least__ kinetic energy? Explain. (Hint: the work done by the force equals the force times the distance moved by the point where it is applied.)

__(e)__ Plate (C) does not rotate. Yet about the black corner dot, the applied force has a nonzero moment arm and exerts a nonzero (clockwise) torque. Is this a contradiction of $$\tau_{\rm net} = I\alpha?$$ State the fine print that resolves it.

__(f)__ Now each plate is pinned to the ice at its black dot, free to rotate about the pin but not to slide away. Which way does each plate rotate when the force is applied?

__(g)__ The pin in each case exerts whatever force is needed to keep the pinned point in place. Just after the force is applied, which pin exerts the __least__ force on its plate?

name: Simple Pendulum versus Physical Pendulum — A rigid uniform rod of mass $$m$$ and length $$L$$ is attached to…
desc: A rigid uniform rod of mass $$m$$ and length $$L$$ is attached to a frictionless pivot at its left end, free to swing in a vertical plane. It is held horizontal and released from rest. For comparison, a __simple pendulum__ — a point mass $$m$$ on a massless string of length…
statement:
A rigid uniform rod of mass $$m$$ and length $$L$$ is attached to a frictionless pivot at its left end, free to swing in a vertical plane. It is held horizontal and released from rest. For comparison, a __simple pendulum__ — a point mass $$m$$ on a massless string of length $$L$$ — is released from horizontal at the same moment. Useful facts: the rotational second law is $$\tau_{\rm net} = I\alpha;$$ the moment of inertia of a point mass at distance $$L$$ from the pivot is $$I_{\rm simple} = mL^2,$$ while a uniform rod rotating about its end has $$I_{\rm physical} = \dfrac13 mL^2;$$ a uniform rod's center of mass is at its midpoint; and the gravitational torque can be computed as if gravity acted entirely at the center of mass.

__(a)__ Describe the rod's motion after it is released — not just the first instant, but the whole subsequent motion. What is a swinging system like this called?

__(b)__ Which force(s) exert torque on each pendulum about its pivot? When the two pendulums pass through the same angle, which one experiences the greater torque from gravity, and by what factor?

__(c)__ Find the ratio of angular accelerations $$\dfrac{\alpha_{\rm simple}}{\alpha_{\rm physical}}$$ when the two pendulums are at the same angle.

__(d)__ The familiar period formula $$T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$$ for a simple pendulum cannot be used here — why not? Instead, note that the two pendulums are identical in every respect except that their angular accelerations stand in the fixed ratio found in part (c) at every angle. The dimensions of angular acceleration are $$\left[\alpha\right] = \mathrm{T^{-2}},$$ so dimensional analysis gives $$T \propto \alpha^{-1/2}.$$ Use this to express the rod's period $$T_{\rm physical}$$ in terms of the simple pendulum's period $$T_{\rm simple}.$$ If $$T_{\rm simple} = 1.0\;\mathrm{s},$$ what is $$T_{\rm physical}?$$

name: If a cyclist is cycling along a flat section of ground and suddenly hits a rock, their…
desc: If a cyclist is cycling along a flat section of ground and suddenly hits a rock, their bike can flip up off the ground and send the cyclist topping over the handlebars. We'll imagine that the front wheel hits the rock and stops. We'll model the rock as a point at the bottom of…
statement:
If a cyclist is cycling along a flat section of ground and suddenly hits a rock, their bike can flip up off the ground and send the cyclist topping over the handlebars.

We'll imagine that the front wheel hits the rock and stops. We'll model the rock as a point at the bottom of the front wheel, and use it as the reference point about which we calculate any torque or angular momentum.

A moment before hitting the rock, the bike was not rotating, but after hitting the rock, it starts rotating. Several students write explanations for how to account for the phenomenon in terms of torque and/or angular momentum. Choose the single best explanation.

**Azra**: The bike has linear momentum $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$ before hitting the rock. When it hits the rock, the rock acts as a pivot point, converting the linear momentum into angular momentum $$L = I\omega,$$ where $${}I$$ is the moment of inertia of the bike and rider about the rock. Assuming the rider was going fast enough when they hit the rock, they will create enough angular momentum to cause them to flip all the way up and over the handlebars.

**Barrett**: When the front wheel of a bike hits a rock and is prevented from moving, the momentum of the bike and rider is still moving forward. Since the front wheel is no longer able to rotate and absorb this momentum, the force is transferred to the frame of the bike, where it becomes a torque and causes the bike to lift off the ground and rotate forward. This is due to the principle of conservation of angular momentum, which states that the total angular momentum of an isolated system remains constant unless acted upon by an external torque.

**Carina**: The wheels of a bike spin, meaning they have angular momentum. If we stop the rotation of the front wheel suddenly, all that angular momentum it had due to spinning will go into the rest of the bike. That's why the bike rotates clockwise - the front wheel was rotating clockwise as well. There doesn't need to be an external torque because the front wheel's angular momentum accounts for the rotation of the bike.

**Damini**: The bike already had angular momentum about the rock before the collision. This is because the bike had linear momentum, and its center of mass was off the ground. The height of the center of mass off the ground was the moment arm of the linear momentum. Any force from the rock on the bike creates zero torque about the rock because the moment arm of that force is zero. This means that aside from any torque from gravity or normal forces on the bike, angular momentum of the bike is conserved after hitting the rock. The angular momentum of the bike and rider as they start rotating around the rock is approximately the same as the angular momentum they had before the collision.

desc: Part A. In 1967, scientists turned on the Interplanetary Scintillation Array, a radio telescope spanning about four acres of land…
statement:
Part A. In 1967, scientists turned on the Interplanetary Scintillation Array, a radio telescope spanning about four acres of land.

https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co8105496/parts-from-the-cambridge-interplanetary-scintillation-array-radio-telescope-instrument-component

The telescope picked up a signal that the lead astronomer Antony Hewish believed was simply noise. Graduate student Jocelyn Bell was working on the project under Hewish's supervision, and believed the data could be important. Bell and Hewish took new data and found that the signal was pulsing every $$1.337 \;\mathrm{s}.$$ Bell then discovered another pulsing radio source with a different frequency.

Astronomers at the time didn't know of any natural phenomenon that could produce extremely regular pulsing, and Bell and Hewish nicknamed the signals "LGM" for "little green men," a joke that the signal must be generated by aliens.

The radio sources eventually became known as __pulsars__. Hewish was awarded a Nobel Prize for the discovery, but the Nobel comittee neglected to include Bell in the prize.

Today, pulsars are known to be __neutron stars__ - giant balls of neutrons jammed up next to each other. (Matter is made mostly of protons, neutrons, and electrons, but in neutron stars the protons and electrons combine and turn into neutrons.) Neutron stars aren't burning balls of plasma. Instead, they're the remnants of __former__ burning balls of plasma.

Neutron stars are formed from stars called __supergiants__. When supergiants burn through all their fuel, they collapse under their own gravity, forming neutron stars, some of which appear to us as pulsars.

Pulsars emit radiation continuously, but only in the directions of their magnetic poles. They appear to pulse because they are spinning rapidly.

By Michael Kramer - http://www.jb.man.ac.uk/~mkramer/Animations.html, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2848650

The supergiant stars pulsars are formed from don't spin nearly this rapidly. They spin faster and faster as they collapse. The effect is similar to that seen in the toy "Hoberman sphere":

https://imgur.com/gallery/7h5GvdK

Part B. The red supergiant Betelgeuse is likely to collapse into a neutron star.

Some approximate data on Betelgeuse is

$$\begin{aligned} T_0 & \approx 40 \;\mathrm{y} \\ R_0 & \approx 5 \times 10^{11} \;\mathrm{m} \\ M & \approx 4 \times 10^{31} \;\mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}$$

When stars collapse into neutron stars, the neutron stars all have about the same density - the density of neutrons shoved up next to each other with no space in between. (In ordinary materials, the neutrons and protons are at the nucleus of each atom, and are far apart from each other compared to the size of the nucleus.) This density is $$ \rho_f \approx 4 \times 10^{17} \;\mathrm{kg/m^3} $$

Under the model of formation of neutron stars used in part (A), what will the rotational period of Betelgeuse be when it collapses?

Give your answer in normalized scientific notation. Give only one significant figure.

mathjax: $$ T_f \approx \blank \times 10^{\blank} \;\mathrm{s} $$

width: 1,4

allowed: -1.023456789

Part C. There is a significant discrepancy between the value you calculated in part (B) and the observed rates of pulsars. The fastest known pulsars have periods of around $$10^{-3} \;\mathrm{s},$$ and you should have found a period significantly less than that for the expected period of Betelgeuse after it collapses.

Which **two** of the following could account or partially account for this discrepancy, if it were correct?

Note that you are not judging whether these explanations are accurate. You're only judging whether, if what they say is true, they account for the real rotation period of pulsars being longer than the calculation in part (B).

Our mass and radius measurements of Betelgeuse were okay, but its density decreases considerably with distance from its center, unlike our model.

Our density estimate for the neutron star was okay for an average density, but the density of a neutron star decreases considerably with distance from the center.

We assumed the mass was constant during the collapse, but supergiants shed most of their mass in a supernove explosion before collapsing. The mass shed in the supernove can carry angular momentum away as well.

The rotation rate we used for Betelgeuse was for the surface, but the core of the star is rotating with an angular frequency considerably higher.

label: MCH22
name: Earlier in this problem set, we estimated how the Earth's angular speed would change if…
desc: Earlier in this problem set, we estimated how the Earth's angular speed would change if people started moving in the same direction around the equator. The effect was minuscule. Earth's rotational period does change, though. For example, earthquakes can move the mass of Earth…
statement:
Earlier in this problem set, we estimated how the Earth's angular speed would change if people started moving in the same direction around the equator. The effect was minuscule.

Earth's rotational period does change, though. For example, earthquakes can move the mass of Earth around, changing the moment of inertia and thereby changing the rotational period. The length of a day changes by up to a few microseconds after some large earthquakes.

Seasonal processes, such as changes to the jet streams, also move mass around on Earth, affecting the moment of inertia and length of the day.

Over billions of years, the largest influence on the rotational period of Earth comes from the Moon.

The Moon is responsible for tides. Tides slosh water back and forth, and this dissipates kinetic energy. As it loses kinetic energy, Earth's angular velocity decreases.

**Over time, does the tidal interaction between the Earth and the Moon push the Moon further away from Earth, pull the Moon in closer to Earth, or neither?**

Explain your reasoning. Be quantitative. Your reasoning can include: - the idea that tides dissipate mechanical energy, and Earth's angular velocity is decreasing. - ideas about angular momentum. - ideas about orbits, such as Kepler's third law.

You can assume that the Moon's orbit is circular, and that it is "tidally locked," meaning that the same side of it always faces Earth. You can also ignore the center-of-mass motion of the Earth. You can also ignore any outside influences on the Earth-Moon system, such as gravitational forces from the Sun or other planets. Finally, you can assume that the moment of inertia of Earth is constant.

It may be helpful to find the angular momentum of the Moon's orbit as a function of $$r,$$ the Earth-Moon distance. It might also be helpful to focus on proportionalities, rather than complete equations. You should not need to look up the mass of the Moon, the radius of Earth, etc. Those values aren't necessary to answer this question.

label: MCH22
name: Inventing Angular Momentum — Astronaut Dorothy Metcalf-Lindenburger floats inside the International Space…
desc: Astronaut Dorothy Metcalf-Lindenburger floats inside the International Space Station, spinning in place in a tucked position. To start her spinning, another astronaut grabbed her and pushed the two sides of her body in opposite directions. Her center of mass never accelerated…
statement:
Astronaut Dorothy Metcalf-Lindenburger floats inside the International Space Station, spinning in place in a tucked position. To start her spinning, another astronaut grabbed her and pushed the two sides of her body in opposite directions. Her center of mass never accelerated noticeably, so the net __force__ on her was essentially zero. What the other astronaut exerted was a __torque__.

In this problem you will invent the rotational analog of momentum, called __angular momentum__, with the symbol $$L.$$ Like torque, angular momentum depends on the reference point about which it is calculated; unless stated otherwise, use the system's center of mass. We count counterclockwise rotation as positive and clockwise as negative.

__(a)__ For linear motion, the net force on a system is the rate of change of the system's momentum: $$\vec{F}_{\rm net}=\dfrac{\Delta\vec{p}}{\Delta t}.$$ Using the analogies force $$\to$$ torque and momentum $$\to$$ angular momentum, write the rotational version of this law.

__(b)__ The law in part (a) only specifies how $$L$$ __changes__, so we complete the definition with one more condition: $$L=0$$ whenever $$\omega=0,$$ that is, whenever the body is not spinning. ($$\omega$$ is the angular velocity.) A student now claims, "Once the other astronaut stops exerting torque, Metcalf-Lindenburger's angular momentum becomes zero." Correct the student's claim.

__(c)__ The rotational analog of Newton's second law $$F_{\rm net}=ma$$ is $$\tau_{\rm net}=I\alpha,$$ where $$I$$ is the moment of inertia and $$\alpha=\dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$$ is the angular acceleration. Combine this with your law from part (a) and the condition $$L=0$$ when $$\omega=0$$ to find a formula for $$L$$ itself in terms of $$I$$ and $$\omega.$$

__(d)__ What linear-motion equation is your formula from part (c) analogous to, and what plays the role of each quantity? For what kinds of motion does the formula apply?

label: MCH22
name: Skaters, Astronauts, and a Flipped Bicycle Wheel — Two facts govern every demonstration in this problem…
desc: Two facts govern every demonstration in this problem. First, when there is no external torque on a system, the system's angular momentum is constant, because $$\Delta L=\tau_{\rm net}\,\Delta t=0.$$ Second, a body rotating rigidly about its center of mass has angular momentum…
statement:
Two facts govern every demonstration in this problem. First, when there is no external torque on a system, the system's angular momentum is constant, because $$\Delta L=\tau_{\rm net}\,\Delta t=0.$$ Second, a body rotating rigidly about its center of mass has angular momentum $$L=I\omega,$$ and the moment of inertia $$I$$ grows when the body's mass moves farther from the rotation axis. (We count counterclockwise as positive, clockwise as negative.)

__(a)__ A figure skater goes into a spin with her arms and one leg stretched outward, then pulls her limbs in tight against her body, as below. Friction from the skate on the ice is very small. What happens to her angular velocity, and why?

__(b)__ Astronaut Dorothy Metcalf-Lindenburger spins in a tucked position aboard the International Space Station, touching nothing. What will you see if she straightens her body out? What happens when she goes back into a tuck?

__(c)__ A physics teacher stands __stationary__ on a swivel platform that turns with very little friction, holding a heavy weight in each outstretched hand, as below. What happens if he pulls the weights in close to his body? What would happen instead if he were already spinning when he pulled them in?

__(d)__ Quantum computing engineer Ryan Robinson stands stationary on a similar swivel platform, holding a bicycle wheel that is spinning __clockwise__ as seen from above. He then flips the wheel upside down. What happens to Robinson, and what happens when he flips the wheel back the way it was? Explain using the angular momentum of the Robinson-plus-wheel system.

label: MCH22
name: Turning Around in Mid-Air — An astronaut floats in the middle of the International Space Station, touching…
desc: An astronaut floats in the middle of the International Space Station, touching nothing and not rotating. There are no external torques on him, so his angular momentum is zero and must remain zero. Recall that a __rigidly rotating__ body has angular momentum $$L=I\omega,$$ where…
statement:
An astronaut floats in the middle of the International Space Station, touching nothing and not rotating. There are no external torques on him, so his angular momentum is zero and must remain zero. Recall that a __rigidly rotating__ body has angular momentum $$L=I\omega,$$ where $$I$$ is the moment of inertia and $$\omega$$ the angular velocity.

__(a)__ A classmate argues: "Since $$L=I\omega$$ and $$L$$ must stay zero, $$\omega$$ must stay zero. The astronaut can never turn around to face the other direction." And yet astronauts do exactly that, as in the clip below. What is wrong with the classmate's argument?

__(b)__ A cat held upside down and dropped (from a safe height, well within what cats comfortably do) will twist around in the air and land on its feet, even though it cannot create angular momentum while falling. Below, science educator Destin Sandlin demonstrates with a slow-motion camera. Once the cat finishes contorting and braces for landing, does it need to do something to stop its rotation, or does the rotation stop automatically? Explain. (The first video of a cat ever made, by French scientist Étienne-Jules Marey in 1894, was made to study this exact problem.)

__(c)__ A diver leaves the platform somersaulting rapidly, spinning rigidly through most of the fall, and appears to stop rotating just before entering the water, as below. Is it actually possible to stop rotating in mid-air? What is really happening?

label: MCH22
name: A Spinning Disk Dropped onto a Plate — A disk of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ is spinning counterclockwise at…
desc: A disk of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ is spinning counterclockwise at angular velocity $$\omega_0.$$ It is placed, still spinning, onto the exact middle of a stationary circular plate of radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ The plate sits on a frictionless table, but there __is__…
statement:
A disk of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ is spinning counterclockwise at angular velocity $$\omega_0.$$ It is placed, still spinning, onto the exact middle of a stationary circular plate of radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ The plate sits on a frictionless table, but there __is__ friction between the disk and the plate. The moment of inertia of a uniform disk about its center is $$I=\dfrac12\,(\text{mass})(\text{radius})^2,$$ and a rigidly rotating body has angular momentum $$L=I\omega.$$

__(a)__ Describe qualitatively what happens. What does friction do to the disk, and what does it do to the plate? When do the angular accelerations stop?

__(b)__ Let $$I_d$$ and $$I_p$$ be the moments of inertia of the disk and plate. Write the initial and final angular momenta of the disk-plus-plate system, and use conservation of angular momentum to find the final angular velocity $$\omega_f.$$

__(c)__ If $$M=2m$$ and $$R=2r,$$ what is the ratio $$\dfrac{\omega_f}{\omega_0}?$$

__(d)__ Check your formula in the extreme cases $$M\to 0$$ and $$m\to 0.$$ What does it predict in each case, and why does each prediction make sense?

label: MCH22
name: Spin Energy and the Mysterious Baby Bottle — For linear motion, kinetic energy can be written in terms of…
desc: For linear motion, kinetic energy can be written in terms of momentum: $$KE=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}.$$ For a body spinning about an axis, the kinetic energy is $$KE_{\rm spin}=\dfrac12 I\omega^2,$$ and the angular momentum is $$L=I\omega.$$ __(a)__ Using the analogies $$\vec{p}\to L$$…
statement:
For linear motion, kinetic energy can be written in terms of momentum: $$KE=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}.$$ For a body spinning about an axis, the kinetic energy is $$KE_{\rm spin}=\dfrac12 I\omega^2,$$ and the angular momentum is $$L=I\omega.$$

__(a)__ Using the analogies $$\vec{p}\to L$$ and $$m\to I,$$ guess the formula for the kinetic energy of a spinning body in terms of $$L$$ and $$I.$$ Then confirm your guess by eliminating $$\omega$$ from $$KE_{\rm spin}=\dfrac12 I\omega^2.$$

__(b)__ Aboard the International Space Station, an astronaut sets a nearly full baby bottle spinning about its long axis and lets it float, as below. The liquid inside cannot redistribute much, but it does slosh in a complicated way, and friction within the sloshing liquid converts kinetic energy into thermal energy. After a while, the bottle is rotating about a completely different axis, all on its own — tumbling end over end instead of spinning about its long axis. Use your formula from part (a) to explain why. (Hint: while the bottle floats freely, what happens to its angular momentum? About which kind of axis is the kinetic energy smallest?)

__(c)__ Would a solid metal cylinder, set spinning about its long axis the same way, also switch its spin axis? Why or why not?

__(d)__ Two eggs are set spinning, one raw and one hard-boiled. One egg keeps spinning steadily about its original axis; the other shifts to rotating about a new axis, as in the clip below (the second egg shown is the one that shifts its axis). Which egg is the raw one, and how do you know?

desc: Estimate the angular momentum of Earth due to its daily rotation, using the data $$R_\oplus=6.4\times10^6\;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$M_\oplus=6.0\times10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg},$$ the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere, $$I_{\rm sphere}=\dfrac25 MR^2,$$ and the formula…
statement:
Estimate the angular momentum of Earth due to its daily rotation, using the data $$R_\oplus=6.4\times10^6\;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$M_\oplus=6.0\times10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg},$$ the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere, $$I_{\rm sphere}=\dfrac25 MR^2,$$ and the formula $$L=I\omega$$ for a rigidly rotating body.

__(a)__ Earth spins all the way around about once every $$24$$ hours. Use $$\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$$ to find Earth's angular velocity $$\omega_\oplus$$ in $$\mathrm{s^{-1}}.$$

__(b)__ Estimate Earth's angular momentum about its own axis.

__(c)__ The density of the real Earth decreases with distance from its center — the iron core is much denser than the rocky mantle. Does this make your estimate an overestimate or an underestimate of Earth's true rotational angular momentum? Explain.

__(d)__ An online calculator reports an angular momentum for Earth roughly a million times larger than your estimate, as shown below. The calculator is not wrong. What is it computing?

label: MCH22
name: Orbital Angular Momentum and a Gliding Skater — The formula $$L=I\omega$$ applies to rigid rotation about a…
desc: The formula $$L=I\omega$$ applies to rigid rotation about a fixed axis. In this problem we extend angular momentum to objects that are simply moving, not spinning. Recall that the moment of inertia of a point particle a distance $$r$$ from the axis is $$I=mr^2,$$ and that for…
statement:
The formula $$L=I\omega$$ applies to rigid rotation about a fixed axis. In this problem we extend angular momentum to objects that are simply moving, not spinning. Recall that the moment of inertia of a point particle a distance $$r$$ from the axis is $$I=mr^2,$$ and that for motion in a circle of radius $$r$$ at speed $$v,$$ the angular velocity is $$\omega=\dfrac{v}{r}.$$

__(a)__ A point particle of mass $$m$$ travels in a circle of radius $$r$$ about the origin $$O$$ at speed $$v,$$ as below. Explain why $$L=I\omega$$ is valid here even though no rigid body is rotating. (Hint: imagine a massless pole connecting the particle to the origin.) Then find the particle's angular momentum in terms of $$m,$$ $$v,$$ and $$r,$$ and rewrite it using the magnitude $$p$$ of the particle's linear momentum.

__(b)__ The total angular momentum of a system about any point splits into two parts: $$L=L_{\rm rotational}+L_{\rm orbital},$$ where $$L_{\rm rotational}$$ is the angular momentum about the system's own center of mass and $$L_{\rm orbital}$$ comes from the motion of the center of mass itself. (This works because a __couple__ — a pair of forces summing to zero, like the pair that spins a planet up without moving its center — exerts the same torque about every axis.) Using this decomposition, how would you compute Earth's total angular momentum about the Sun, given Earth's moment of inertia $$I_\oplus,$$ spin angular velocity $$\omega_\oplus,$$ mass $$m_\oplus,$$ orbital speed $$v_{\rm orbit},$$ and orbital radius $$r_{\rm orbit}?$$

__(c)__ The ice skaters below glide across the ice in straight lines at constant velocity, without turning (ignore any slight turning in the trick). Do they have rotational angular momentum? Can they have orbital angular momentum? About what kind of reference point?

__(d)__ Pick the reference point $$O$$ to be a spot on the ice directly beneath a skater at one instant, and try the formula from part (a), $$L=pr,$$ where $$r$$ is the distance from $$O$$ to the skater's center of mass. There is no net torque on the skater about $$O$$ (or about any point), so their angular momentum must stay constant as they glide. Show that the formula $$L=pr$$ contradicts this.

__(e)__ Torque obeys $$\tau=r_\perp F,$$ where the moment arm $$r_\perp$$ is the perpendicular distance from the reference point to the line of the force. Modify $$L=pr$$ in the same spirit so that the gliding skater's angular momentum is conserved, and then write the general formula for the total angular momentum of a rigid body about any point.

desc: A uniform solid sphere of mass $$m$$ and radius $$R$$ is set spinning about a horizontal axis at angular velocity $$\omega_0,$$ then gently lowered onto a table. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the sphere and the table is $$\mu_k.$$ As drawn below, the sphere spins…
statement:
A uniform solid sphere of mass $$m$$ and radius $$R$$ is set spinning about a horizontal axis at angular velocity $$\omega_0,$$ then gently lowered onto a table. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the sphere and the table is $$\mu_k.$$ As drawn below, the sphere spins counterclockwise, so its bottom surface initially slides to the right across the table. Assume the sphere is rigid and use the standard model of friction. You will need: the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about its center, $$I=\dfrac25 mR^2,$$ and the total angular momentum of a rigid body about any reference point, $$L=I\omega+r_\perp p,$$ where $$I\omega$$ is the rotational part (about the center of mass) and $$r_\perp p$$ is the orbital part, built from the linear momentum $$p$$ of the center of mass and its moment arm $$r_\perp.$$

__(a)__ Which way does the sphere start to move, and what is its motion in the long run?

__(b)__ Mechanical energy is not conserved here (kinetic friction dissipates it), the sphere's linear momentum is not conserved (friction is a net external force), and the sphere's angular momentum about its own center is not conserved (friction exerts a torque about the center). Explain why the sphere's angular momentum __is__ conserved about a point $$P$$ on the table.

__(c)__ Find the sphere's initial angular momentum about $$P,$$ just as it touches down.

__(d)__ Eventually the sphere rolls without slipping at some speed $$v,$$ with angular velocity related by $$v=\omega R.$$ Find its total angular momentum about $$P$$ in terms of $$m,$$ $$R,$$ and $$v,$$ and use conservation to find $$v$$ in terms of $$\omega_0$$ and $$R.$$

__(e)__ How would increasing the coefficient of kinetic friction $$\mu_k$$ change the final speed? What __would__ it change about the motion?

__(f)__ Suppose instead a thin hoop of mass $$m$$ and radius $$R$$ (moment of inertia $$I=mR^2$$ about its center) is set spinning at $$\omega_0$$ and placed on the table. Will its final speed be faster or slower than the solid sphere's? Find it.

(Sky lanterns are illegal in many areas because they can cause fires. Please don't build one unless you are at an event with approval from local fire safety officials.)

Part D. To estimate the mass of materials we should use in a sky lantern, we need to know how the density of hot air is different than that of cold air.

Air can be modeled closely by an equation called __Charles's law__ after French scientist Jacques Charles. It is an empirical law based on experimental data.

We can state the law as $$\rho \propto \dfrac{1}{T}$$ where $$\rho$$ is the density of air and $$T$$ is the temperature.

However, to use this law, we must measure $$T$$ using an __absolute__ temperature scale, such as the Kelvin scale. In this scale, temperature is measured in units called __kelvin__, $$\mathrm{K}.$$

A change in temperature of $$1 \;\mathrm{K}$$ is equivalent to a change of temperature of $$1 \;\mathrm{C}.$$ However, Kelvin temperatures are 273.15 degrees higher than Celsius temperatures.

For example, if the temperature in a room rises from $$20^\circ \;\mathrm{C}$$ to $$23^\circ \;\mathrm{C},$$ then in the Kelvin scale we'd say the temperature rises from $$293.15 \;\mathrm{K}$$ to $$296.15 \;\mathrm{K}.$$

Suppose we want to build a sky lantern with a radius $$r = 30 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ and a height $$h = 90 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$ From tests with a candle, we find that the candle can heat the air from $$10^\circ \;\mathrm{C}$$ to $$50^\circ \;\mathrm{C},$$ and we expect the outdoor temperature to be about $$10^\circ \;\mathrm{C}$$ at the launch event. The density of our atmosphere at this temperature is approximately $$(1.2 \times 10^{-3} )\;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$.

What is the maximum mass $$m_{\rm max}$$ we can use for the materials that go into building the sky lantern, including the candle (but not the air inside it)?

Since this is an estimation problem, give your answer to only one significant figure. Round __down__ to make sure the mass is below the limit.

statement:
This is the final writing problem in the course. It's a short lab writeup. Although this problem is about Archimedes's principle, the goal is to give you practice __designing__ experiments, not to confirm a specific physics model.

--------------

Archimedes's principle says that if a floating boat of mass $$m$$ has a displacement $$V_d$$ of water then $$ \rho_w V_d = m$$ with $$\rho_w$$ the density of the water.

By now, we've had a number of lab assignments in this course, and you've worked on questions on designing and interpreting experiments in homework and in class.

For this week, design your own experiment to test Archimedes's principle quantitatively.

You should be able to make measurements with relative uncertainty of $$10\%$$ or less, but you don't need to explicitly quantify your uncertainty. Just briefly explain how you minimized uncertainty and what effect it has on your results.

Submit: - A brief description of your setup - What you measured and what your measurements showed - A brief analysis of how well your measurements agreed with Archimedes's principle

Your writeup should take no more than one side of one page, plus potentially one more for figures / graphs.

Feel free to include pictures or diagrams to help describe your experiment. You do not need to include background on the experiment or a quantitative analysis of error. A good format would be to include three sections:

**Methods**

This section describes how you set up your experiment and what measurements you took.

**Results**

This section reports the results of your measurements. A table or graph could be sufficient as long as it is easy to interpret given what you wrote in the methods section.

**Conclusion**

This section discusses the meaning of your results and how well they agree with Archimedes's principle.
