name: Ice Water in an Accelerating Elevator — You step into an elevator holding a cup of ice water, and the…
desc: You step into an elevator holding a cup of ice water, and the elevator begins accelerating upward with magnitude $$a.$$ Useful background: in an accelerating frame there is __artificial gravity__ of strength $$a$$ pointing opposite the acceleration, which adds to true gravity…
statement:
You step into an elevator holding a cup of ice water, and the elevator begins accelerating upward with magnitude $$a.$$ Useful background: in an accelerating frame there is __artificial gravity__ of strength $$a$$ pointing opposite the acceleration, which adds to true gravity. Also recall __Archimedes's principle__: a floating object of mass $$m$$ satisfies $$m=\rho_w V_d,$$ where $$\rho_w$$ is the density of the water and $$V_d$$ — the object's __displacement__ — is the volume of the object below the waterline.

__(a)__ While the elevator accelerates upward, do you feel heavier, lighter, or the same as usual? Explain using artificial gravity.

__(b)__ Relative to the water, do the ice cubes now float higher, float lower, or stay at the same level? Hint: write the condition for floating — weight balancing the buoyant force — using the effective gravity, and see whether the strength of gravity matters.

label: MCH23
name: Melting Ice and the Water Level — A glass holds liquid water of density $$\rho_w$$ with an ice cube of mass…
desc: A glass holds liquid water of density $$\rho_w$$ with an ice cube of mass $$m_{\rm ice}$$ floating in it. As the ice melts, what happens to the water level in the glass? One person argues the level should rise ("the ice is melting, so there's more liquid water than before")…
statement:
A glass holds liquid water of density $$\rho_w$$ with an ice cube of mass $$m_{\rm ice}$$ floating in it. As the ice melts, what happens to the water level in the glass? One person argues the level should rise ("the ice is melting, so there's more liquid water than before"); another argues it should fall ("if you remove an ice cube from water, the level goes down"). Recall __Archimedes's principle__: the floating cube's __displacement__ $$V_d$$ — the volume of ice below the waterline — satisfies $$\rho_w V_d=m_{\rm ice}.$$ When ice melts, it turns into liquid water of density $$\rho_w$$ (the melted water has the same mass as the ice did).

__(a)__ Let $$V_{\rm surface}$$ be the total volume of everything in the glass below the surface of the water. Suppose you lift the ice cube out of the glass. By how much does $$V_{\rm surface}$$ decrease, and what happens to the water level?

__(b)__ Now hold the cube above the glass until it melts, letting all of the meltwater drip back into the glass. What volume of liquid water does this add to the glass? Express your answer in terms of $$V_d.$$

__(c)__ Use parts (a) and (b) to decide what happens to the water level when the ice simply melts while floating in the glass. The time-lapse below shows the experiment — does it agree?

label: MCH23
name: A Stone Frozen in the Ice — An ice cube has a small stone frozen inside it, but the cube still floats in a…
desc: An ice cube has a small stone frozen inside it, but the cube still floats in a cup of water. After the ice melts, the stone sinks to the bottom of the cup. What happens to the water level? To analyze this, simplify: start with an ordinary ice cube floating in water of density…
statement:
An ice cube has a small stone frozen inside it, but the cube still floats in a cup of water. After the ice melts, the stone sinks to the bottom of the cup. What happens to the water level? To analyze this, simplify: start with an ordinary ice cube floating in water of density $$\rho_w,$$ then place a small stone of mass $$m_{\rm stone}$$ and density $$\rho_{\rm stone}>\rho_w$$ on top of the cube; the cube still floats. Recall __Archimedes's principle__: a floating object (or assembly) of total mass $$m$$ has displacement $$V_d$$ — the volume below the waterline — satisfying $$\rho_w V_d=m.$$ Also recall (from the previous problem) that an ordinary ice cube melting on its own leaves the water level unchanged.

__(a)__ When the stone is added, what happens to the ice cube, and what happens to the water level? By how much does the displacement of the floating assembly increase? Call this increase $$\Delta V_d.$$

__(b)__ After the ice melts, the stone rests on the bottom, fully submerged. What is the stone's displacement now? Which is larger — the extra displacement $$\Delta V_d$$ the stone caused while riding on the ice, or its displacement after sinking?

__(c)__ So what happens to the water level as the ice melts and the stone sinks: does it rise, fall, or stay the same?

__(d)__ Suppose the whole cup sits on a scale during the melting. How does the reading on the scale change over time? (Ignore the tiny buoyancy from the atmosphere.)

label: MCH23
name: Floating a 200-Gram Cup in 100 Grams of Water — Is it possible to float a cup with a total mass of…
desc: Is it possible to float a cup with a total mass of $$200\;\mathrm{g}$$ (the cup plus the water inside it) in just $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ of water? By __Archimedes's principle__, a floating object of mass $$m$$ has displacement $$V_d$$ — the volume of the object below the waterline…
statement:
Is it possible to float a cup with a total mass of $$200\;\mathrm{g}$$ (the cup plus the water inside it) in just $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ of water? By __Archimedes's principle__, a floating object of mass $$m$$ has displacement $$V_d$$ — the volume of the object below the waterline — satisfying $$\rho_w V_d=m.$$ Since water's density is $$1\;\mathrm{g/cm^3},$$ the floating cup needs a displacement of $$200\;\mathrm{cm^3},$$ but only $$100\;\mathrm{cm^3}$$ of water is available. The photo below shows the experiment: the $$200\;\mathrm{g}$$ cup floats inside a slightly larger cup, with the $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ of water filling the thin gap between them.

__(a)__ Explain how the floating cup can have a displacement of $$200\;\mathrm{cm^3}$$ even though there is only $$100\;\mathrm{cm^3}$$ of water in the lower cup. What exactly does "displacement" mean?

__(b)__ The water in the gap rises until it is at the same height as the surface of the water inside the floating cup. Explain why.

label: MCH23
name: The Buoyant Force and a Finger in the Water — A cup of water sits on a kitchen scale. You dip a finger into…
desc: A cup of water sits on a kitchen scale. You dip a finger into the water without touching the cup. What happens to the reading on the scale? To answer, think about floating from the viewpoint of __force__. A floating ice cube is pulled down by gravity; the upward force from the…
statement:
A cup of water sits on a kitchen scale. You dip a finger into the water without touching the cup. What happens to the reading on the scale? To answer, think about floating from the viewpoint of __force__. A floating ice cube is pulled down by gravity; the upward force from the water that balances it is called the __buoyant force__ $$F_b.$$

__(a)__ For a floating object of mass $$m,$$ Archimedes's principle says $$m=\rho_w V_d,$$ where $$\rho_w$$ is the water's density and $$V_d$$ is the displacement (the volume of the object below the waterline). Both sides of this equation have dimensions of mass. Multiply both sides by $$g$$ to turn it into a balance of forces, and read off a formula for the buoyant force $$F_b$$ in terms of $$\rho_w,$$ $$V_d,$$ and $$g.$$

__(b)__ The formula from part (a) is a good model even for objects that are not floating — for a stone resting on the bottom, $$V_d$$ is just the stone's full volume — as long as the water is at rest. When you stick your finger in the water, is there a buoyant force on your finger?

__(c)__ By Newton's third law, forces come in pairs. The buoyant force on your finger from the water has a third-law partner. What object does that partner force act on, and which direction does it point?

__(d)__ So what happens to the reading on the scale when you dip your finger in — does it go up, go down, or stay the same? The video below shows the experiment.

desc: Buoyant forces are vertical, but fluids can push in other directions too. The photo below shows an above-ground swimming pool whose walls are bulging worryingly. __(a)__ What direction is the force from the water on the pool walls: inward, outward, up, or down? (As evidence…
statement:
Buoyant forces are vertical, but fluids can push in other directions too. The photo below shows an above-ground swimming pool whose walls are bulging worryingly.

__(a)__ What direction is the force from the water on the pool walls: inward, outward, up, or down? (As evidence, here is what happens when a pool wall fails.)

__(b)__ A small cube of side length $$s$$ is held in the middle of a tank of water, with water touching all six faces. Which way do the forces from the water on the cube's faces point?

__(c)__ Now a larger cube, of side length $$2s,$$ is held at the same place in the same water. The water pushes the same way __per unit area__. If the force on the left face of the small cube is $$F,$$ what is the force on the left face of the larger cube?

__(d)__ In general, if an object has a flat side with area $$A,$$ the inward force from the fluid on that side is $$F=P\cdot A$$ for some coefficient $$P,$$ called the __pressure__ in the fluid. Find the dimensions of pressure: $$=\mathrm{M}^{a}\,\mathrm{L}^{b}\,\mathrm{T}^{c}$$ for what exponents? (Force has dimensions $$\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}.$$)

__(e)__ The SI unit of pressure is the __pascal__ $$(\mathrm{Pa}).$$ Show that $$1\;\mathrm{Pa}=1\;\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m^2}}=1\;\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}.$$

label: MCH23
name: Crushed by the Atmosphere — The pressure of our atmosphere at sea level is about $$P_{\rm…
desc: The pressure of our atmosphere at sea level is about $$P_{\rm atm}\approx10^{5}\;\mathrm{Pa},$$ varying a percent or so from day to day and place to place. The force from pressure on a flat area $$A$$ is $$F=P\cdot A.$$ Use $$g=10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ throughout. __(a)__ A person's…
statement:
The pressure of our atmosphere at sea level is about $$P_{\rm atm}\approx10^{5}\;\mathrm{Pa},$$ varying a percent or so from day to day and place to place. The force from pressure on a flat area $$A$$ is $$F=P\cdot A.$$ Use $$g=10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ throughout.

__(a)__ A person's body surface area is roughly $$2\;\mathrm{m^2}.$$ Estimate the total force the atmosphere exerts on a person's body. (It's more than $$40{,}000$$ pounds!) Why aren't we constantly accelerated by such an enormous force — and why don't we feel crushed by it?

__(b)__ A classic demonstration: pour a little water into an empty soda can and heat it until the water boils, so steam pushes most of the air out of the can. Then quickly flip the can upside-down into a bath of cold water, which makes the water vapor condense back into liquid. What happens to the pressure inside the can, and what happens to the can? (The same trick works on a 55-gallon steel drum, and even a railroad tank car.)

__(c)__ A suction cup pressed against polished glass is hard to pull away, but it won't stick to something rough like cardboard, so it isn't sticky. Explain what actually holds a suction cup against a smooth surface.

__(d)__ A person of mass $$m=70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ wants to hang from the ceiling on a suction cup. Estimate the minimum area the suction cup needs. Is that closer to the area of a bedroom, an office desk, a human palm, or a postage stamp?

__(e)__ In the 17th century, German scientist Otto von Guericke took two copper hemispheres of radius $$10\;\mathrm{cm},$$ put them together, and pumped the air out of the inside with the newly invented vacuum pump. Teams of horses commanded to pull the hemispheres apart usually failed — yet von Guericke could separate them with the flip of a switch. What did the switch do? And why would the horses have a better chance if the experiment were repeated on top of a tall mountain?

label: MCH23
name: Torricelli's Barometer and the Longest Straw — A __barometer__ measures the pressure of the atmosphere. In…
desc: A __barometer__ measures the pressure of the atmosphere. In 1644, Italian scientist Evangelista Torricelli built one using mercury, a liquid metal $$13.5$$ times denser than water $$(\rho=13.5\times10^{3}\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}).$$ He filled a tube about one meter long with mercury…
statement:
A __barometer__ measures the pressure of the atmosphere. In 1644, Italian scientist Evangelista Torricelli built one using mercury, a liquid metal $$13.5$$ times denser than water $$(\rho=13.5\times10^{3}\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}).$$ He filled a tube about one meter long with mercury, then turned it upside-down into an open pool of mercury. The column of mercury fell about $$0.25\;\mathrm{m},$$ leaving a gap at the top of the sealed tube. The surface of the mercury pool was open to the atmosphere.

__(a)__ What is in the gap at the top of the tube: air, water, mercury, or nothing?

__(b)__ Let the tube have radius $$r,$$ and let $$h$$ be the height of the mercury column above the pool's surface; the mercury's density is $$\rho.$$ The forces on the mercury in the tube are an upward pressure force $$P_{\rm atm}(\pi r^2)$$ from below and gravity $$(\pi r^2)h\rho g$$ downward — there is no downward pressure force, because of your answer to part (a). The mercury is in equilibrium. Solve for $$P_{\rm atm}$$ in terms of the other variables.

__(c)__ The standard column height is $$h=760\;\mathrm{mm}$$ (in practice $$750\;\mathrm{mm}<h<775\;\mathrm{mm}$$ except in extreme weather). Use your formula with $$g=9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ to compute $$P_{\rm atm}$$ and check that it is close to $$10^{5}\;\mathrm{Pa}.$$

__(d)__ Before a storm, atmospheric pressure usually decreases. What happens to the mercury level in the tube, and how could a meteorologist use this?

__(e)__ Water is $$\dfrac{1}{13.5}$$ as dense as mercury. How tall a column of water can atmospheric pressure support? Explain why this sets an upper limit on the length of a straw you could possibly drink through, and on how high a vacuum pump can lift water. (The video below shows an attempt on the world's longest straw.)

__(f)__ Your result generalizes: in a fluid of density $$\rho$$ at rest, the pressure at depth $$h$$ beneath a surface where the pressure is $$P_0$$ is $$P=P_0+\rho gh,$$ or $$\Delta P=\rho g\,\Delta h$$ — the equation of __hydrostatic equilibrium__. Use it to explain why you feel the pressure in your ears after diving just a few meters underwater, but notice no pressure change after climbing a hill a few meters tall.

label: MCH23

desc: A cube of side length $$s$$ is held fully submerged in a fluid of density $$\rho$$ at rest. The fluid pushes inward on each face with force $$P\cdot A,$$ where $$A=s^2$$ is the face's area, and the pressure grows with depth according to hydrostatic equilibrium: $$\Delta P=\rho…
statement:
A cube of side length $$s$$ is held fully submerged in a fluid of density $$\rho$$ at rest. The fluid pushes inward on each face with force $$P\cdot A,$$ where $$A=s^2$$ is the face's area, and the pressure grows with depth according to hydrostatic equilibrium: $$\Delta P=\rho g\,\Delta h,$$ where $$\Delta h$$ is the change in depth.

__(a)__ Which face of the cube feels the largest pressure force, and which the smallest? What happens to the forces on the left and right faces?

__(b)__ The cube's bottom face is deeper than its top face by exactly $$s.$$ Find $$P_{\rm bottom}-P_{\rm top}.$$

__(c)__ Find the net force from pressure on the cube — magnitude and direction — in terms of $$\rho,$$ $$g,$$ and $$s.$$

__(d)__ Notice that $$s^3$$ is the cube's volume $$V.$$ What is another name for the net pressure force you just computed? What does this calculation tell you about where buoyancy comes from?

label: MCH24
name: Part A. Physicists have been interested in the circulatory system for a few reasons. One…
desc: Part A. Physicists have been interested in the circulatory system for a few reasons. One is for medical applications - measurements of the speed and volume of blood flow through the circulatory system are important data for doctors treating or diagnosing issues such as…
statement:
Part A. Physicists have been interested in the circulatory system for a few reasons. One is for medical applications - measurements of the speed and volume of blood flow through the circulatory system are important data for doctors treating or diagnosing issues such as cardiovascular diseases, heart valve problems, and thrombosis.

Scientists have also built models of the circulatory system to try to understand the differences between animals of different sizes. For example, physicist Geoffrey West collaborated with biologists James Brown and Brian Enquist to build a model to explain surprising facts, such as that as mammals get larger, their heart rates slow down and their lifetimes get longer, so that (roughly speaking) mammals of all sizes have about the same number of heartbeats in their lives.

In this problem we will get a very brief introduction to the application of fluid dynamics to the circulatory system.

----------------------------

Blood is carried out from the heart via the aorta, the largest of the arteries. The aorta branches many times into smaller arteries. The smaller arteries eventually lead into veins, which return the blood to the heart.

By OpenStax College - Anatomy & Physiology, Connexions Web site. http://cnx.org/content/col11496/1.6/, Jun 19, 2013., CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=30148241

Suppose an artery has radius $$r$$ and blood moves through it at speed $$v.$$

The artery branches into two arteries, each of radius $$r/2.$$

The speed of blood is $$v_2$$ in each of the two smaller arteries. Assume the blood moves parallel to the artery wall and has the same speed all across the artery cross section in each case.

What is $$v_2?$$

Part B. To transition from arteries to veins, blood flows through __capillaries__.

By Community Emergency Response Team - http://www.citizencorps.gov/cert/IS317/medops/medops/ic_04_02_0091.htm, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=29582984

Capillaries are very narrow so that oxygen can diffuse from them into the body. There are capillaries all over your body, delivering oxygen to your cells. You can assume that all the blood that leaves the aorta eventually goes through one capillary before returning to the heart.

Some data on the circulatory system is $$\begin{aligned} v_a & = 100 \;\mathrm{cm/s} \\ r_a & = 1.2 \;\mathrm{cm} \\ v_c & = 0.1 \;\mathrm{cm/s} \\ r_c & = 5 \times 10^{-4} \;\mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}$$ where the $$a$$ subscript stands for the aorta and the $$c$$ subscript stands for a typical capillary.

Given this data, how many capillaries are there in a human body?

Give your answer to one significant figure.

mathjax: $$ N \approx \blank \times 10^{\blank}$$

width: 1,2

allowed: 1023456789

Part C. Bernoulli's equation fails miserably to describe the circulatory system. That equation assumes conservation of mechanical energy, meaning it assumes there is no friction. On the scale of capillaries, flow is dominated by friction.

In high-friction situations like a capillary, a better model for the flow uses the Hagen–Poiseuille equation,

$$ \Delta P = \dfrac{8 \mu L v}{r^2} $$ where $$\Delta P$$ is the pressure change from one side of a blood vessel to another.

$$\mu$$ is a property of fluids called the __viscosity__. You can assume it is constant.

$${L}$$ is the length of the blood vessel. $$v$$ is the speed of blood through the blood vessel. $$r$$ is the radius of the blood vessel.

For example, in a capillary, $$\Delta P$$ would be the pressure at the artery side of the capillary minus the pressure at the vein side of the capillary. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation would let us calculate $$\Delta P$$ reasonably well.

Imagine doubling the radii of all capillaries in the body while keeping the __total volume__ of blood flowing through them per unit time the same. The number of capillaries is also kept the same.

If the initial pressure across each capillary was $$\Delta P_0,$$ what would the pressure difference $$\Delta P_2$$ be after doubling the capillary radii?

Give your answer as a decimal.

statement:
A scientist has a closed tank of water. A floating ball $$F$$ sits on the surface of the water, and a sinking ball $${}S$$ sits at the bottom of the tank.

The tank is equipped with a board that shakes up and down to make waves. The scientist sets the board oscillating, making waves that travel from left to right along the tank.

There is a common model that explains how waves move in deep water. This model predicts that $${}F$$ will go in circles as the waves pass by, but will not drift in any particular direction over the long term, so that its average velocity over a long time is zero. Below is an animation of this model.

Alexander C, "Waves on the surface of water HD", YouTube

The tank is not In physics, we always compare the size of a system to some other size when saying how big the system is. For water to be "deep," there is no fixed depth, such as $$1 \;\mathrm{m}$$ or $$10 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Instead, the water needs to be deep compared to the wavelength of the waves. For example, if the wave peaks are $$20 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ apart, the tank would be "deep" if it were more than about $$2 \;\mathrm{m}$$ deep, since $$2 \;\mathrm{m} \gg 20 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$, though, and $${}F$$ drifts gradually to the right in addition to moving in circles.

Below is the scientist's data, with the path of $${}F$$ tracked by some computer vision software.

Justin Pringle, Twitter

**What is the most likely motion of $${}S$$ while $${}F$$ is drifting to the right?**

You can assume that the balls get pushed along with the water, so their motion is the same as the motion of the water they are next to, i.e., the balls are a convenient way of visualizing the motion of the water.

You can also assume that the average drift velocity in the $${}x$$ direction, as a function of height above the bottom of the tank, either increases, decreases, or remains steady as the height increases, but doesn't do a combination of those, i.e., that function is monotonic.

Use continuity and volume conservation to help you. If water is drifting to the right along the top of the tank, what must it be doing along the bottom?

label: MCH24
name: Water Circulating in a Ring-Shaped Pipe — Water flows around the inside of a pipe bent into a vertical circle…
desc: Water flows around the inside of a pipe bent into a vertical circle — an __annular cylinder__, a cylinder with a hole cut out, standing upright like a wheel. The water circulates around the ring, acted on by gravity and by pressure. The centerline of the ring is a circle of…
statement:
Water flows around the inside of a pipe bent into a vertical circle — an __annular cylinder__, a cylinder with a hole cut out, standing upright like a wheel. The water circulates around the ring, acted on by gravity and by pressure. The centerline of the ring is a circle of radius $$R,$$ so the top of the ring is a height $$2R$$ above the bottom. The water has density $$\rho.$$

__(a)__ Suppose first that the pipe's cross-sectional area $$A$$ is the same everywhere, and that the water's speed is uniform across any one cross section. Flows like this conserve volume, which we express with the __continuity equation__: the volume flow rate $$Q=Av$$ is the same through every cross section of the pipe. Where does the water move fastest — at the top of the ring, at the bottom, or the same speed everywhere?

__(b)__ Water descending the left side of the ring has gravity pulling it along, yet by part (a) it does not speed up. The balancing force comes from pressure. __Bernoulli's equation__ says that along a streamline, $$P+\dfrac12\rho v^2+\rho g y$$ is constant, where $$y$$ is height. Use it to find the pressure difference $$P_{\rm bottom}-P_{\rm top}$$ between the bottom and the top of the ring. How does your answer compare to the pressure difference in __still__ water (hydrostatic equilibrium)?

__(c)__ Now we redesign the pipe so that the pressure is the same everywhere. Then pressure does no net work on the circulating water, and the water speeds up as it descends, like a falling rock, and slows as it climbs. To make this consistent with continuity, should the pipe's cross-sectional area be largest at the top of the ring or at the bottom?

__(d)__ Return to the uniform pipe, and watch one small parcel of water (the dot in the figure below) as it travels around the circle at constant speed. What direction is the net force on the parcel? Across a cross section of the pipe, is the pressure highest at the __outside__ edge of the ring, in the __middle__, or at the __inside__ edge?

__(e)__ Suppose all the water circulates with the same angular velocity $$\omega,$$ so a parcel a distance $$r$$ from the ring's center moves at speed $$v=\omega r$$ — fastest at the outside edge. Bernoulli's principle says that higher speed goes with lower pressure, which seems to contradict your answer to part (d). Resolve the apparent contradiction. (Hint: moving parcels of fluid trace out paths called __streamlines__. Between which points does Bernoulli's equation let us compare $$P+\dfrac12\rho v^2+\rho g y?$$)

__(f)__ In many real flows, the quantity $$P+\dfrac12\rho v^2+\rho g y$$ has the same value on __every__ streamline, so Bernoulli comparisons are allowed between any two points. If that is true of our circulating water, where does the water move fastest — at the inside edge, in the middle, or at the outside edge?

label: MCH24
name: Blowing Between Soda Cans — Flowing air tends to follow along curved surfaces. This is called the __Coandă…
desc: Flowing air tends to follow along curved surfaces. This is called the __Coandă effect__, after Romanian inventor Henri Coandă. For example, if you blow at a round bottle with a lit candle hidden behind it, the airstream bends around the bottle and blows the candle out on the far…
statement:
Flowing air tends to follow along curved surfaces. This is called the __Coandă effect__, after Romanian inventor Henri Coandă. For example, if you blow at a round bottle with a lit candle hidden behind it, the airstream bends around the bottle and blows the candle out on the far side. The trick fails with a boxy bottle: air does not bend well around sharp corners.

Now a demonstrator stands two empty soda cans upright, a couple of centimeters apart, and blows a stream of air through the gap between them.

Seen from above, the blown air curves around the far sides of the cans as it leaves the gap, as in the figure below. Three points are marked in the region where air bends around the upper can: $$C$$ is closest to the can's surface, $$B$$ is farther from the can, and $$A$$ is farther still.

__(a)__ A parcel of air bending around the can moves along a curved path, so it has a centripetal acceleration, and the only force available to supply it is pressure. Use this to decide: at which of the points $$A,$$ $$B,$$ $$C$$ is the pressure lowest?

__(b)__ Bernoulli's equation says $$P+\dfrac12\rho v^2$$ is constant along a streamline (height changes are negligible here). In this demo all the nearby streamlines begin in essentially the same conditions, so they share the same value of that constant, and we may compare points on neighboring streamlines. What happens to the air's speed as it curves around the cans?

__(c)__ What happens to the cans when the demonstrator blows between them? Explain using your answers to parts (a) and (b).

__(d)__ A common explanation of this demo claims that the air coming out of the demonstrator's mouth has low pressure simply because it is moving fast — "Bernoulli says fast air is low pressure." If that were the whole story, the demo should work just as well with small cubes in place of the cans. In fact, with cubes there is little or no effect, as the video below shows. What is wrong with the common explanation, and where does the low pressure actually come from?

__(e)__ Here is an explanation that never mentions pressure: think about momentum. As air curves around the upper can in the figure, what direction of momentum does that air pick up? What does momentum conservation then say the can must do? What does the Bernoulli analysis tell us that this momentum argument does not?

label: MCH24
name: Held Up by Moving Air — Recall two facts about air flows. First, the __Coandă effect__: flowing air tends to…
desc: Recall two facts about air flows. First, the __Coandă effect__: flowing air tends to follow along curved surfaces. Second, when a flow bends, the pressure is high on the outside of the curve and low on the inside, and (when neighboring streamlines share the same value of the…
statement:
Recall two facts about air flows. First, the __Coandă effect__: flowing air tends to follow along curved surfaces. Second, when a flow bends, the pressure is high on the outside of the curve and low on the inside, and (when neighboring streamlines share the same value of the Bernoulli quantity $$P+\dfrac12\rho v^2$$) the bending air speeds up as its pressure drops.

__(a)__ A demonstrator holds a strip of paper by its near edge, so the far end droops downward, and blows a stream of air horizontally over the __top__ of the paper, as shown below. What happens to the paper? Explain using the two facts above and the atmospheric pressure underneath the paper.

A leaf blower pointed straight up can hold a light ball aloft in its airstream. Perhaps it isn't surprising that air blowing upward can balance gravity — the surprising part is what happens when the ball is nudged sideways.

__(b)__ When the ball sits centered in the airstream, streamlines curve around it on either side, as shown below. Is there a net horizontal force on the ball?

__(c)__ Now the ball is given a gentle push to the right, so it is partly out of the airstream, as in the streamline picture below. Which side of the ball — left or right — now has more air curving around it?

__(d)__ Does the displaced ball get pushed farther out of the airstream and fall, or get pulled back toward the center? Explain why.

label: MCH24
name: Water from an Opening — You punch a small opening in the bottom of an open-topped bottle of water, and water…
desc: You punch a small opening in the bottom of an open-topped bottle of water, and water streams straight down out of the hole. The water surface is a height $$h$$ above the opening. The surface of the water in the bottle has area $$A_{\rm top},$$ the opening has area $$A_{\rm…
statement:
You punch a small opening in the bottom of an open-topped bottle of water, and water streams straight down out of the hole. The water surface is a height $$h$$ above the opening. The surface of the water in the bottle has area $$A_{\rm top},$$ the opening has area $$A_{\rm opening},$$ and $$A_{\rm top}\gg A_{\rm opening}.$$ The water has density $$\rho,$$ and atmospheric pressure is $$P_{\rm atm}.$$ How fast does the water leave the opening? We'll work it out in stages, using __Bernoulli's equation__: along a streamline, $$P+\dfrac12\rho v^2+\rho g y$$ is constant. By symmetry, a convenient streamline runs straight down the middle of the bottle and out the hole, as shown.

__(a)__ The top surface of the water moves downward at some speed $$v_{\rm top}$$ as the bottle drains. Use the continuity equation, $$A_{\rm top}v_{\rm top}=A_{\rm opening}v_{\rm opening},$$ to argue that we may take $$v_{\rm top}\approx 0$$ in a simple model.

__(b)__ What is the pressure at the top end of the streamline (at the water's surface)? What is the pressure at the bottom end, just as the water leaves the opening? (Hint for the bottom: once the water leaves the hole it falls straight down — it does not get pushed out sideways into the surrounding air.)

__(c)__ Apply Bernoulli's equation between the top and bottom of the streamline to find $$v_{\rm opening}.$$

__(d)__ Compare your answer to $$v_{\rm drop},$$ the speed an object reaches when dropped from rest through a height $$h.$$ Now suppose we attached a spigot to the opening that redirects the outflow straight upward, as in the picture below. If we had found $$v_{\rm opening}>v_{\rm drop},$$ what absurd machine could we build? What if $$v_{\rm opening}<v_{\rm drop}?$$ What do you conclude?

label: MCH24
name: The Fastest Wind Pressure Can Make — How fast can atmospheric pressure accelerate air? Imagine calm air…
desc: How fast can atmospheric pressure accelerate air? Imagine calm air, initially at rest at atmospheric pressure, rushing toward a region of very low pressure. Ignore gravity, so Bernoulli's equation along a streamline reads $$P_1+\dfrac12\rho v_1^2=P_2+\dfrac12\rho v_2^2.$$ Let…
statement:
How fast can atmospheric pressure accelerate air? Imagine calm air, initially at rest at atmospheric pressure, rushing toward a region of very low pressure. Ignore gravity, so Bernoulli's equation along a streamline reads $$P_1+\dfrac12\rho v_1^2=P_2+\dfrac12\rho v_2^2.$$ Let point $$1$$ be in the calm atmosphere, with $$P_1=P_{\rm atm}\approx 10^5\;\mathrm{Pa}=10^5\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$$ and $$v_1=0.$$ The density of air is $$\rho\approx 1.2\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$

__(a)__ To make the final speed $$v_2$$ as large as possible, what value should the pressure $$P_2$$ at the destination have?

__(b)__ Compute the resulting maximum speed $$v_2,$$ and compare it to highway and airliner speeds. (For reference, $$400\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ is about $$900\;\mathrm{mph}.$$)

__(c)__ The speed of sound in air is around $$330\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (depending on temperature). When a gas flow approaches the speed of sound, the gas's density starts to change significantly throughout the flow. Which assumption behind Bernoulli's equation does this break, and how should we interpret the number from part (b)?

__(d)__ Besides the flow approaching the speed of sound, list some other situations in which an analysis based on Bernoulli's equation has limited or very bad predictive power.

label: MCH24
name: Why Airplane Wings Lift — The figure below shows the side view of an airplane wing. A shape like this is…
desc: The figure below shows the side view of an airplane wing. A shape like this is called an __airfoil__; it is designed to bend the path of the air flowing around it. The top surface is strongly curved, and air bends to follow it (the Coandă effect); the bottom is much flatter, so…
statement:
The figure below shows the side view of an airplane wing. A shape like this is called an __airfoil__; it is designed to bend the path of the air flowing around it. The top surface is strongly curved, and air bends to follow it (the Coandă effect); the bottom is much flatter, so the air below bends only a little.

Recall that when neighboring streamlines share the same value of $$P+\dfrac12\rho v^2,$$ air that bends around a curve speeds up as its pressure drops.

__(a)__ Compare the air just above the wing to the air just below it: which is moving faster, and why?

__(b)__ The air above the wing and the air below the wing are technically on different streamlines. Why is it nevertheless legitimate to use Bernoulli's equation to compare points above and below the wing?

__(c)__ What direction is the net pressure force on the wing? This force has a name — what is it? (There is also a backward force on the wing, called __drag__, but it comes from friction effects in the air that we won't model.)

__(d)__ People sometimes argue about whether "Bernoulli's principle explains why airplanes fly." Does Bernoulli's equation, by itself, tell us how much the air accelerates as it bends over the top of the wing? In what sense is Bernoulli's equation a good model of lift, and in what sense is it incomplete?
